Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions have become a vital arena for investigating quantum electrodynamics (QED) under extreme conditions. Although the production of electron-positron pairs from two-photon fusion is well-established, mechanisms involving harder photons offer the promise of higher statistics and a broader kinematic range. This study examines the electromagnetic interaction between a photon from one nucleus and an electron or positron from the other in ultra-peripheral collisions. We demonstrate that this process is significant, particularly for low transverse momentum particles originating from high-energy collisions. Our analysis covers various particle species, including electrons, positrons, muons, and tau leptons, across a range of collision systems featuring the heaviest nuclei available at current accelerators. Furthermore, we explore the potential of these reactions to generate high-energy leptons in the future. Our findings indicate that, given appropriate luminosity, this channel could be observed at the Large Hadron Collider and potentially at the Energy Frontier. We provide predictions for the resulting spectra and compare them with those from standard two-photon pair production. Additionally, we discuss the associated photon spectra and propose a method for extracting the photon flux at the nucleon level. These results can be utilized to investigate QED in extreme environments, test the Standard Model, and search for new physics. We have also included a C++ implementation of the relevant cross-sections. Finally, we note that the processes discussed here are distinct from electron-nucleus scattering, which is relevant to the LHeC and other future electron-proton collider facilities. Cycling is a popular mode of transport, particularly in urban environments, yet it carries a significant injury and fatality rate. To better understand and mitigate these outcomes, researchers have developed advanced risk models. However, the data underlying these models is often imperfect, and the models themselves frequently overlook critical contextual factors such as time and location. This study introduces a novel, context-sensitive risk descriptor for cyclists that utilizes video footage. The descriptor integrates temporal and spatial context, capturing the temporal dynamics of risk events. By processing video streams, the system automatically identifies the temporal dynamics of interactions between cyclists and other road users, as well as between cyclists and the surrounding environment. This work represents the first integration of video-driven data into context-sensitive risk models. The proposed descriptor was validated using video evidence from a real-world cycling collision dataset. Furthermore, the efficacy of the video-driven approach was benchmarked against methods relying on traditional cyclist interaction data. The findings indicate that the video-driven descriptor is both effective and complementary to conventional techniques. These results highlight the potential for video-driven, context-sensitive risk models to inform policy decisions aimed at enhancing cyclist safety. The video-driven identification of risk contexts and the associated analytical methods can be applied to various video sources, including those from dashcams, bodycams, and surveillance cameras. This research paves the way for future developments in video-driven risk models, which will facilitate more precise and timely policy interventions. The resilient and secure navigation of robots within changing, unpredictable environments is a vital yet difficult challenge in robotics. This study introduces a path planner utilizing Control Barrier Functions (CBF) designed to ensure resilient and secure trajectory tracking for constrained robotic systems. This approach is particularly relevant for robotics in safety-critical domains like autonomous driving and medical surgery. The CBF-based trajectory generator ensures that CBF constraints are met, allowing the robot to evade obstacles and withstand cyberattacks. Security is achieved by incorporating a CBF constraint that maintains a lower bound on the distance between the robot and cyber-attacked vehicles. Furthermore, the resiliency property is demonstrated by proving that the time derivative of the CBF constraint along the vehicle dynamics remains negative definite, thereby guaranteeing a decreasing distance to the constrained vehicle. The framework's effectiveness is validated through extensive numerical simulations. These simulations demonstrate that the robot successfully avoids obstacles, maintains a safe distance from attacked vehicles, and recovers from attack-induced trajectory deviations. Additionally, the study confirms that the recovery time after an attack is directly influenced by the CBF parameters. Finally, the framework is applied to a case study involving two vehicles traveling in the same direction, where one vehicle is subjected to an attack. In this scenario, the other vehicle adjusts its trajectory to maintain a safe separation distance from the attacked vehicle. The proposed framework is implemented in MATLAB. Its application code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmed-abbas-1/CBF-Motion-Planner. The framework is written in Python and is fully open-source. Future work will focus on developing a CBF-based path planner for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to enable secure and resilient navigation in uncertain environments. This will entail adapting the CBF framework to handle 3D dynamics and conducting numerical simulations involving multiple vehicles with one UAV serving as the planner. The UAV path planner will be implemented using MATLAB's CBF Toolbox. This research was conducted during a Visiting Assistant Professorship at the University of Notre Dame. Roughly, a ring $R$ is $\omega$-bounding if the inclusion of the maximal ideal space $\text{Max}(R)$ into $\text{Spec}(R)$ can be extended to the spectrum $\text{Spec}(R^+)$ of the integral closure $R^+$ within the total quotient ring of $R$. This concept is closely tied to the spectrum-preserving properties of $R$. We introduce a broader definition of bounding rings applicable to any commutative ring $R$, termed the "$\lambda$-boundingness" of $R$ for an arbitrary ordinal $\lambda$. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the bounding nature of a ring and its cardinal invariants, specifically the spectrum and co-spectrum. The latter is defined as the supremum of the cofinalities of prime ideal sets that share a fixed contraction within $\text{Spec}(R^+)$. We demonstrate that every commutative ring $R$ possesses an extension $R_1$ satisfying $\text{Spec}(R_1) = \text{Spec}(R)$ and $\text{Max}(R_1) \subseteq \text{Spec}(R^+)$. Additionally, we construct a family of $\omega$-bounding rings featuring a fixed spectrum and a specified co-spectrum value. Finally, we outline the $\lambda$-bounding properties of specific rings, including Dedekind rings, dimension-one rings, and those with a finite basis spectrum. Throughout the study, we provide numerous examples and counterexamples to illustrate the complexity of bounding rings. Given the broad scope of this theory, many fundamental questions remain open. In this paper, we address only a small fraction of these issues, with the intention of returning to explore other significant aspects in future work. For instance, determining the existence of a prime ideal $P$ such that $\text{ht}(P) = \alpha$ and $\text{cf}_1(P) = \beta$ for given ordinal values $\alpha$ and $\beta$ remains an unresolved problem. We also examine the $\alpha$- and $\beta$-boundingness of rings, which concerns the extendability of the inclusion $\text{Spec}(R_\beta) \subseteq \text{Spec}(R)$ to $\text{Spec}(R^+)$. Finally, we analyze the $\alpha$- and $\beta$-semiboundingness of rings, defined as the extendability of the same inclusion to $\text{Spec}(R^{\alpha,\beta})

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous domains, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains a significant barrier to real-world deployment. This vulnerability stems from the presence of anomalous data points, known as adversarial instances, which are often rooted in the DNN's learned feature space. While the Adversarial Training (AT) framework has demonstrated effectiveness, it suffers from a trade-off between robustness and accuracy. In contrast, the Defense Against Adversarial Examples (DAE) framework offers a complementary approach by modifying input data to neutralize adversarial threats. We propose an input transformation framework grounded in the DAE concept to enhance the DNN's resilience against adversarial instances. Our approach employs a meta-learning strategy to determine an optimal transformation for each specific attack, thereby reducing the model's confusion regarding adversarial inputs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric called the Divergence Metric (DM) to assess the efficacy of the transformation. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing AT and DAE approaches in terms of robust accuracy. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenWang1993/DM}. Finally, we release a new benchmark dataset termed CIFAR-100-ADI, which adheres to the adversarial instance generation principle. The paper accompanying this dataset is also accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenWang1993/CIFAR-100-ADI/tree/master/Paper}. We anticipate that this dataset will contribute to the research community's pursuit of organic adversarial robustness. Additionally, our work aims to inspire scholars to explore the underlying causes of adversarial attacks, thereby mitigating their impact. This study examines the singular limit of a kinetic equation featuring nonlocal interactions, specifically a fractional interaction that generates a Drift-Diffusion equation in the macroscopic limit. We demonstrate that for a broad class of functions defining the source and diffusion terms in the Drift-Diffusion equation, a convergence rate of order ${\varepsilon}$ is achieved in the $L^2$ norm. The entropy admissibility of the limit equation is subsequently explored. This work extends the research by Carrillo, Jin, and Zhang (Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal., 2017), which established a ${\varepsilon}$ convergence rate for a local kinetic equation with variable interaction potentials. Furthermore, we investigate the entropy admissibility criteria for general functions describing nonlocal interactions. Finally, we derive20 results for specific models of interest, including the Porous Medium equation. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. Keywords: Boltzmann equation, nonlocal transport, singular limit, entropy admissibility, convergence rate. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 82C40, 82C70, 35L65, 35Q83, 82C26.

Horizon saddle links, introduced by Masur and Phillips, represent a novel class of surfaces arising from critical values of the Masovitch phase function linked to Teichmüller pieces. This work investigates the topology and homology of these links, demonstrating that they are invariably toroidal. We establish a characterization of Morse-Smale dilation surfaces utilizing horizon saddle links and propose the conjecture that every non-exact Masovicot phase function dilation surface conforms to this description. Additionally, we propose a conjecture asserting that horizon saddle links possess the structure of ribbon surfaces. Furthermore, we present an algorithm for calculating horizon saddle links from a given Masovitch phase function and examine specific instances, including those associated with Teichmüller curves and billiards. Finally, one instance is realized as a torus with a single cone point possessing a cone angle of 120 degrees, and the topology of this realization is determined. The methodology employed to construct this realization is extended to yield a new class of dilation surfaces featuring cone points. We conjecture that the horizon saddle links for these surfaces align with the prediction derived from Masur and Phillips' original formulation. Additionally, we outline an algorithm for computing horizon saddle links and their real homology groups directly from a phase function, and we provide a conjecture regarding the invariance of these properties under handle slides. This study introduces a novel brain network analysis framework termed "Mind with Total Association" (MTA). By integrating functional connectivity data from resting-state fMRI and structural connectivity derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) white matter tracts, MTA identifies brain networks that exhibit strong associations with specific cognitive tasks. We demonstrate that MTA uncovers networks more closely linked to task performance than either functional or structural connectivity alone. Furthermore, the method's robustness is validated by its ability to successfully identify networks associated with various mental processes, including attention, working memory, and language. The results indicate that MTA highlights brain networks with a distinct cognitive profile, characterized by unique functional and structural characteristics that differ from those identified using functional connectivity alone. Finally, the findings suggest that MTA offers a complementary approach for investigating the neural mechanisms underlying specific cognitive tasks. This tool is expected to advance our understanding of the complex relationship between brain structure and function. Both methods extend the conventional Segal-Bargmann model, which employs complex-valued L² functions. This paper introduces a new wireless topology designed for ground-based, sky-oriented sensor networks. The system is anticipated to enhance observation capabilities in fields such as astronomy, meteorology, and remote sensing by linking individual sensors to a central processing unit. Each sensor captures data across a specific spatial or spectral range and transmits it via radio waves to the unit, which then localizes the source and generates a complete spatial map of the observed phenomenon. We propose a novel algorithm that enables ground units to rapidly and accurately reconstruct a two-dimensional map of the phenomenon from a limited set of signals. This method is expected to significantly improve the quality of observations and expand the applicable fields. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through examples involving acoustic, optical, and concentration fields. Additionally, the paper outlines potential applications in medicine, meteorology, and astronomy. A key advantage of the proposed method is its robustness against signal loss, allowing the unit to reconstruct the image even if a subset of sensors fails to transmit their data. We also address the challenge of sensor placement and provide a general model for the cost function used to optimize this arrangement. Finally, we show that the algorithm can achieve rapid convergence to an optimal sensor distribution using simulated annealing. The paper concludes by presenting simulation results that illustrate both the algorithm's effectiveness and the characteristics of the resulting optimal sensor distributions. Our approach is distinguished from existing literature because it does not require prior knowledge of the phenomenon's form or any specific features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm can be extended to high-dimensional spaces. The general methodology is expected to have broad applications across various scientific disciplines. Consequently, this connection establishes a bridge between the coset construction in supersymmetric $\sigma$-models and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. Finally, the paper concludes with a brief discussion on the application of these results to the five-dimensional supersymmetric $\sigma$-model. This study investigates the fracture resilience of crystalline materials through molecular dynamics simulations of bulk aluminum and copper subjected to shear. The process resilience is quantified by the energy dissipated during shear localization, which we correlate with a fracture toughness parameter defined as the energy per unit area consumed by the creation of new localized surfaces. Our findings reveal that this fracture toughness remains nearly constant across various initial densities and varies minimally with material type. We demonstrate that these mechanisms align with a model treating the material as an elastic medium with nonlocal dissipation, where the localization zone size is determined by the balance between nonlocal dissipation and elastic nonlinearity. The resulting predictions for the zone size and energy dissipation match our simulation results, thereby validating the proposed model. Furthermore, we examine the influence of material nonlinearity, boundary conditions, and geometry on resilience, concluding that resilience is governed by the material's intrinsic properties and is largely unaffected by these extrinsic factors. Finally, we address the applicability of molecular dynamics simulations to molecular materials. In the molecular case, we observe that intermolecular forces are more nonlocal than in atomic systems, leading to broader localization bands and reduced energy dissipation. Consequently, the localization zone size is dictated by the range of nonlocality in intermolecular forces, while energy dissipation is controlled by the degree of nonlinearity in these forces. These insights deepen our understanding of the resilience inherent to crystalline materials. Our analysis also identifies potential applications for crystalline materials in protective systems, such as armor and shields, where the ability to absorb energy is crucial. Finally, we outline future research directions concerning material design aimed at enhancing resilience. Traditional verification of classical computation typically involves re-running the algorithm to check for errors. This paper introduces an alternative approach where a classical algorithm is executed alongside a quantum algorithm designed to compute the same function. We demonstrate that this method enables traditional verification within linear time using minimal quantum resources. The study examines the quantum resources necessary for the algorithms and compares the overall cost of both computation and verification against re-running only the quantum algorithm. The proposed methods rely on simple error-correcting codes, such as repetition codes, and rely on the assumption that the computer is functioning correctly with high probability. The paper provides explicit constructions for these algorithms and analyzes their resource requirements. Results indicate that for computing classical functions in quantum superposition, the methods are optimal in terms of qubit count and computational complexity. For cocomputing classical functions, the method is computationally optimal and requires an asymptotically smaller number of qubits compared to a naive approach. Although less efficient than the quantum-only approach for cocomputing quantum functions, it still outperforms it in quantum computational complexity. Furthermore, the paper addresses the feasibility of the method by presenting a feasible construction for verifying quantum sorting and discussing how to verify other important classical and quantum functions. Finally, the feasibility of cocomputing quantum functions is demonstrated.

Blockchain technology has gained significant traction in recent years, offering enhanced transparency and traceability in supply chains. This paper introduces a framework for a new application: integrating smart contracts with a private blockchain utilizing off-chain oracles. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through a specific use case: a smart contract for an energy-efficient refrigerator deployed at the end-user level within a food distribution chain. This technique is applied to two distinct classes of cells: mammalian cells with cytoskeletons and bacteria. We show that the method is versatile and capable of modeling diverse cell forms. Furthermore, we have developed a suite of shape priors grounded in the geometries of cells under various biological conditions. These priors facilitate the creation of realistic and biologically plausible synthetic cells for use in machine learning research. Additionally, we have made our implementation public to support research into biological shape analysis and to encourage the development of new shape priors. Finally, we outline future research directions for utilizing implicit neural representations in this field. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepBioIm/ICNRep. Accessing text is essential for individuals with visual impairments, and this capability relies heavily on the accessibility of their text documents. This paper investigates access necessity for the blind by analyzing a large corpus of web pages and news articles. We first examine word usage to characterize the content, distinguishing between terms necessary for access and those merely desirable. Subsequently, we develop a topic modeling approach to identify semantic topics and construct a vocabulary dictionary for each, demonstrating that this dictionary effectively reveals the articles' core content. Leveraging these topic dictionaries, we create a language model that filters out unnecessary words to assess access necessity. Our findings indicate that news access necessity is high at the sentence and paragraph levels but drops significantly at the word level. Additionally, we demonstrate that our topic dictionaries can successfully extract the primary content of the articles. Finally, we evaluate the blind user experience before and after applying the access necessity filter, showing that such filtering enhances the reading experience. Our research underscores the importance of access necessity for users with visual impairments and provides a practical method to optimize their textual content. This paper presents XLNet, a generalized pre-training strategy designed to address the autoregressive constraints of BERT while preserving its robustness and effectiveness. XLNet unifies the attention mechanisms of BART and Transformer-XL as a foundational layer, functioning as an autoregressive pre-training framework. It integrates BERT's pre-training tasks with Transformer-XL's mask-permutation approach to generate XLNet pre-training tasks, which outperform both on language modeling and downstream applications. Furthermore, XLNet is a multi-objective framework that pre-trains on masked language modeling, next token prediction, and permuted mask prediction. When applied to the GLUE benchmark, XLNet achieved an average improvement of +3.2 points over BERT. On the most challenging tasks, including MRPC, SQuAD 2.0, and RTE, XLNet enhanced performance by +7.1, +2.4, and +1.3 points, respectively, compared to BERT. Additionally, XLNet successfully pre-trains on machine translation, achieving a 1.5 BLEU score improvement over BART on the 2018 WMT English-to-French and English-to-German datasets. Finally, XLNet is highly scalable, reaching 800B parameters and 1.5T FLOPs per training step on the WebText2 dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/EdouardMa/ XLNet. Exoplanet transit spectroscopy is susceptible to contamination from stellar activity, such as starspots and faculae, which can mimic or obscure atmospheric signals. While this challenge is typically addressed using high-resolution data to filter out low-resolution spectral features, our study demonstrates that mitigation is also feasible at low resolutions. We conducted a detailed analysis of CHEOPS target TOI-1452, which exhibits significant activity, by injecting synthetic spots into HST FOS and CHEOPS level 2b data. Our results indicate that activity affects active targets in a non-linear manner, causing both absorption and emission features. Furthermore, we show that high-resolution observations do not always enhance the detection of atmospheric features in active stars. Finally, we outline a strategy for characterizing and correcting activity effects in Low-Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) data, leveraging the extensive information available in High-Resolution Spectroscopy (HRS) datacubes. This approach is particularly advantageous for missions like CHEOPS, which are expected to observe many active stars. We conclude that HRS datacubes can facilitate the characterization of activity in the target population, enabling effective correction of activity impacts in LRS data. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of incorporating activity effects into the modeling of future transit spectroscopy missions. Our findings are demonstrated using observations from CHEOPS, HST, and HARPS. The code employed in this study is publicly available at https://github.com/astro-berkeley/SpottyTransit. These results will be submitted to MNRAS. This study presents the first experimental characterization of water surface locomotion in *Anelosimus* centipedes, a newly identified class of lightweight, water-surface dwelling arachnids. By applying biomechanical modeling and interfacial fluid dynamics theory, we offer a quantitative analysis of how these arachnides propel themselves across the water. We demonstrate that their movement relies on the interaction between their legs and the water surface, specifically deforming the interface to generate net forward forces. The work examines the role of capillary forces and the conditions under which centipedes switch between wetting and non-wetting states. Furthermore, the paper explores the stability of their steady-state swimming and investigates the mechanical constraints imposed by centrifugal forces during turning maneuvers. Finally, we identify potential evolutionary adaptations in *Anelosimus* that facilitate efficient water surface locomotion. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the physical principles governing arachnid movement at the air-water interface. This study presents a strategy for modeling the dispersive propagation of tsunamis generated by asteroid impacts in deep water, utilizing a variable-order KdV equation coupled with the Saint-Venant equations. The model couples the shallow-water approximation with a deep-water model via transmission conditions that enforce continuity of depth and horizontal flux, while an exchange condition aligns dispersion terms based on a jump in bathymetric curvature. These conditions are applied at the interface between two domains featuring varying bottom topographies. Two numerical methods are developed to handle these transmission conditions: a two-step finite volume approach and a two-step spectral element method. After validating each scheme against a reference solution derived from direct numerical simulation of the coupled system, the adaptive simulation of a dispersive tsunami transmission problem is conducted using both methods. The results demonstrate that the spectral element approach, when paired with Nitsche's method, yields superior accuracy. Finally, a dispersive tsunami transmission scenario involving changing bathymetric curvature is simulated using both schemes, with the simulation mesh generated through the superposition of multiple meshes employing different resolutions and models. This superposition enables the implementation of an adaptive modeling technique, allowing for the selection of the most appropriate model and mesh based on local characteristics, such as bathymetry curvature. Consequently, this adaptive method facilitates the efficient and accurate simulation of dispersive tsunami transmission problems. Finally, the potential for modeling the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor event is explored. The event's atmospheric explosion, which caused injuries, panic, and property damage, is analyzed to explain the observed phenomena, including the bright fireball, sonic booms, and shattered windows. The dispersive nature of the generated wave is examined, and a simulation is performed to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed adaptive modeling approach. This adaptive technique is shown to be highly effective for modeling atmospheric explosions, as it allows for the use of an appropriate model at the collision site and a reduced mesh size to accurately capture bathymetry curvature variations. Ultimately, the research demonstrates that the proposed adaptive modeling approach is a viable and promising method for modeling atmospheric explosions. We present early JWST NIRCam imaging of 11 optically faint ($m_{AB} > 26$), luminous ($L_{IR} > 10^{11} L_{\odot}$) galaxies at redshifts $z=0.3-2.5$, selected from the COSMOS and SMACS0723 fields. These objects were identified through deep Hubble Space Telescope optical surveys and the COSMOS2020 catalog. Our analysis reveals that 82% of these galaxies are strongly star-forming, with most exhibiting star formation rates exceeding $100 M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$. The sample consists of 73% normal galaxies and 27% starbursts, with no ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) detected. Spatially, 64% of the galaxies are resolved, with 55% of these showing smooth morphology and 9% displaying clumpy or ring-like structures. The remaining 36% are unresolved, with half appearing point-like and the other half showing signs of being marginally resolved. We demonstrate that JWST's superior sensitivity and resolution enable the study of these rare, high-luminosity, low-luminosity-distance systems, which are crucial for understanding the evolution of star-forming galaxies. Furthermore, JWST's infrared capabilities allow for the investigation of their detailed morphologies, offering new insights into the processes driving their activity. This dataset will facilitate a comprehensive analysis of the star-forming main sequence and the morphological evolution of galaxies. The COSMOS2020 catalog is accessible at https://cosmos2020.github.io, and the JWST images are available at https://www2.astro.utoronto.ca/~jyuan/jwst/. The full dataset will be released in the upcoming paper. We encourage the community to utilize these data to advance our understanding of high-luminosity, low-luminosity-distance star-forming galaxies. We present seven-dimensional models that extend General Relativity by incorporating extended objects. These models feature topological characteristics, including the presence of solitons and the ability to unify matter and radiation with gravitational fields. We examine various seven-dimensional extensions of General Relativity based on the geometry of extended objects and analyze the soliton solutions derived from them. Specifically, we investigate seven-dimensional generalizations of the Gödel metric and demonstrate that soliton solutions emerge when applying the method of descent to Gödel's metric. Furthermore, we develop seven-dimensional extensions of the Taub-NUT metric and show that its seven-dimensional generalizations can be derived using the same approach. We introduce a model for particle accumulation in channel-like geometries, specifically focusing on two-dimensional systems where particles are deposited in an infinite, narrow channel of constant width. In this scenario, particles arrive sequentially and may adhere to existing structures or new formation sites via irreversible reactions. Once two structures collide, the slower one absorbs the faster one, retaining its identity. This process leads to the emergence of alternating sequences within the channel, featuring long chains interspersed with short chains or individual particles. We extend this framework to three dimensions by simulating channel cross-sections as either square arrays of grid points or as channels with reduced lateral mobility (utilizing a modified Lennard-Jones potential). In both 2D and 3D configurations, the system evolves into a configuration with 1D dynamics, where clusters form and grow exclusively along the channel's longitudinal axis. Upon collision, one cluster engulfs the other, preserving the original structure of the larger cluster. We present numerical simulations demonstrating that this system exhibits glassy dynamics and can be effectively modeled by a 1D effective system. Furthermore, we derive an analytical model for 1D dynamics based on the frequency of formation sites and the velocity of diffusive growth. This model accurately reproduces the frequency distribution of chain lengths observed in the simulations across varying parameter values, including those with higher lateral mobility. Finally, we propose a heuristic explanation for the formation of alternating sequences within the channel. These sequences arise from the competition between two growth modes: annihilation, where two fast-growing chains collide and merge into a single fast-growing chain, and coalescence, where a fast and a slow-growing chain collide to form a slow-growing one. This balance between annihilation and coalescence generates alternating sequences of fast and slow chains. We also provide evidence suggesting that this heuristic model can be quantitatively applied to both 2D and 3D systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the formation of these alternating sequences is linked to the frequency distribution of chain lengths, which follows a power law. We show that this power law can be derived analytically from the proposed heuristic model. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this system in both natural and technological contexts. The system is applicable to various natural phenomena, such as sediment transport in rivers and geological faulting, as well as technological processes like data storage and traffic flow. In all these cases, the frequency distribution of alternating structures or groups is expected to follow a power law. Our model offers a new perspective on the frequency distributions of vehicle lengths in traffic

This study seeks to enhance the predictive capabilities of Global Climate Models (GCMs) by identifying the distinct signatures of the three El Ni\~no types—Eastern (El Ni\~no Modoki), Central (Tripole), and Eastern (Canonical)—in global precipitation patterns. The methodology involves calculating the differential precipitation response to these three varied El Ni\~no types. To achieve this, we utilized the Hadley Centre's combined surface pressure dataset to derive the three types via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), alongside the 20-year reanalysis precipitation dataset from the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP/NCAR). The resulting differential response was mapped globally, revealing that the signatures of the two Eastern types are largely similar, whereas the Central type produces a distinct pattern. Furthermore, the correlation between the three types is notably low in the Northern Hemisphere. Finally, we examined the differential precipitation response between the wettest and driest seasons. The findings indicate that the Central El Ni\~no type triggers precipitation anomalies in both hemispheres that differ from those of the Eastern type, and its impact on the Northern Hemisphere is significantly weaker. These results underscore the necessity of distinguishing between the various types of El Ni\~no when analyzing precipitation responses. Additionally, the study addresses the issue of data scarcity in the 20-year reanalysis precipitation dataset, which is critical for the Northern Hemisphere. Finally, we conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for future research. The primary objective of this work is to aid in the prediction of El Ni\~no types and their subsequent effects on global precipitation. The methodologies employed are also applicable to studying the impacts of other oscillations, such as the Southern Annular Mode (SAM) and the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO). Furthermore, the approach can be extended to other relevant datasets, including sea surface temperature and surface pressure. The code utilized in this study is available at: https://github.com/Ankit-1234/Impact_of_El_Nino. The analysis was conducted using Python. The study was supported by the Department of Atomic Energy, Government of India, under project no. 12-R\&D-TFR-2.0

This study examines the evolution of structural correlations in glassy colloids by analyzing the non-affine displacement field generated by local elastic deformations. We employ a novel experimental approach combining video microscopy with image correlation techniques. Our findings demonstrate that the mean square non-affine displacement scales with the particle diameter raised to the power of 2.4, a result that aligns with molecular dynamics simulations and other experimental studies. Additionally, the decay of the decay-length distribution of non-affine displacements matches both theoretical predictions and simulation data. Finally, the correlation between individual particles' non-affinity and their local environment is quantified using the normalized non-affinity field. This normalized field exhibits a power-law scaling of 2.5 with the colloid diameter, consistent with previous theoretical and molecular dynamics research. Furthermore, the normalized non-affinity distribution follows a Gaussian form, and its variance scales with the colloid diameter according to a power law of 2.3. These results confirm that the non-affine growth observed in molecular dynamics simulations also occurs experimentally. Ultimately, the observed scaling exponents for the variance of the normalized non-affinity field and the decay length of the normalized distribution of non-affine displacements are independent of the specific method used to calculate non-affine displacements. Consequently, the normalized non-affinity distribution and normalized distribution of decay lengths serve as universal metrics for characterizing non-affine growth in colloidal glasses. These metrics facilitate the comparison of non-affine growth across various systems, including granular materials and molecular glasses. Finally, we conclude that normalized non-affinity and normalized decay length are robust and reliable metrics for comparing non-affine growth in different systems. This conclusion is supported by a comparison of normalized non-affinity distributions and normalized decay-length distributions of non-affine displacements for different systems, such as Lennard-Jones and hard-sphere molecular glasses, as well as colloidal glasses. The normalized non-affinity distribution and normalized decay-length distribution of non-affine displacements for the Lennard-Jones glass are similar to those of the hard-sphere molecular glass and the colloidal glass. Therefore, the normalized non-affinity distribution and normalized decay-length distribution of non-affine displacements are universal metrics for characterizing non-affine growth in different systems. These metrics enable the comparison of non-affine growth across various systems, including Lennard-Jones and hard-sphere molecular glasses, as well as colloidal glasses. This paper introduces a single-population model featuring age structure and time-dependent environmental contamination. We construct an age-structured framework where the birth rate is regulated by the current youth count and total population, while the growth rate depends on the previous year's population, thereby linking the current state to two prior lags. The model accounts for a constant death rate and an age-dependent force of infection, with the contamination level assumed to be an increasing function of the death rate. We analyze the model's properties, demonstrating that the solution remains non-negative, solutions converge to a unique equilibrium globally, and stability occurs if the basic reproduction number does not exceed one. Furthermore, we establish that global stability can be achieved when the force of infection follows a specific function of the birth rate. Finally, we present numerical simulations to support these findings. Our results indicate that increasing the death rate reduces the basic reproduction number, and we identify the optimal parameter value that minimizes this number. This work extends a model previously applied to the 2014 Ebola outbreak. Additionally, we examine a time-delay version of the model and prove that its stability is determined by the sign of the first eigenvalue of a specific matrix. This work investigates the decidability and computational complexity of propositional contraction logics based on multiplicative substructural frameworks (such as $R$- and $T$-logic) when equipped with two specific contraction-free weakenings. We introduce "D-hypersequents," a formalism utilizing nested hypersequents to eliminate the need for structural rules like weakening, while maintaining rules for contraction and structural meta-axioms as axioms. Our primary contribution is a decision procedure for these logics derived from Kripke semantics, which accounts for the contraction-free weakening mechanisms. This approach establishes PSPACE-completeness for $R$-logic with a single allowable weakening, alongside a detailed analysis of complexity for the other cases. Finally, we present a double-extension to D-hypersequents that permits contraction-free contraction, demonstrating its soundness and completeness. This framework enables a decision procedure for the extended variants, thereby determining their complexity profiles. Notably, the contractions-based extensions exhibit exponential complexity, while the combined effect of two different contraction-free weakenings results in undecidability. These findings are supported by illustrative examples and contrasted with related research. The study is conducted within the context of abstract proof theory, with a primary emphasis on sequent and hypersequent calculi. Furthermore, we briefly address the metric properties of the investigated logics. This analysis relies on the observation that the contraction-free weakening of the contraction rule can be interpreted as a metric contraction, a concept originating from metric logic. Consequently, we establish an upper bound on the complexity for the weakest contraction-based extension, which is NP-complete. The paper includes extensive technical appendices to support these results. Finally, the study incorporates an appendix on the history of metric logic, the development of substructural hypersequents, and the origins of contraction-free weakenings. Additionally, the appendix provides a comprehensive discussion on the history of metric logic extensions concerning contraction-free weakenings. Natural language data exhibits a hierarchical structure characterized by nested classes and nested features, a pattern that aligns closely with hyperbolic geometry rather than Euclidean space. Although numerous classification methods have been developed, few are designed to leverage hyperbolic representations for modeling taxonomic hierarchies. This study introduces HyperExpan, a framework that expands a base classifier by generating a taxonomically structured family of classifiers utilizing hyperbolic representations. Evaluated across three datasets with hierarchical taxonomies, results demonstrate that HyperExpan consistently surpasses the performance of the underlying classifier, achieving a 10.6-point gain in macro-averaged F1 score on the HIERARCHICAL-NER dataset. The project's code and resources are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhardwaj/HyperExpan. Furthermore, the paper includes a tutorial on implementing hyperbolic representation learning for text classification. Our findings indicate that hyperbolic methods are effective at modeling taxonomic hierarchies within unlabeled text and can be easily adapted to produce structured label hierarchies for classification tasks. This study examines the effects of external electric fields on six dimers from the S66 benchmark dataset, which includes water, hydrogen, and $\pi$-dispersion complexes. The investigation covers both symmetric fields applied to both monomers and asymmetric fields acting on only one monomer. Employing the CCSD(T) method, the research identifies significant changes in interaction energies, with dimers exhibiting $\pi$-dispersion forces showing the most pronounced sensitivity to these fields. Furthermore, the study utilizes the CCSD(T)-F12B method to assess the computational efficiency of the "second-order" response approach. Finally, the work provides insights into the strengths and limitations of various density functional theory functionals when modeling dimers under external electric fields. The accompanying S1 package offers a user-friendly tool for calculating interaction energies of S66 dimers in the presence of such fields. This study introduces a novel ambiguity-mathematical programming approach designed to enhance the robustness of production scheduling under uncertainty. The proposed framework, termed the Stochastic Ambiguity Set-based Scheduling (SASB) model, integrates recent ambiguity set techniques with existing stochastic programming models. By utilizing distributionally robust optimization, this method effectively manages non-parametric risks in production systems, thereby overcoming the trade-off between computational efficiency and solution robustness found in both stochastic and fuzzy approaches. The model employs a data-driven strategy that combines historical sample information with operational expert knowledge. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the solution robustness of both stochastic and fuzzy models can be significantly improved through the application of distributionally robust optimization. Furthermore, the study confirms that the SASB model maintains strong solution robustness while offering superior computational performance. Finally, a real-world case study from the petrochemical industry validates the model's practical applicability and robustness. These findings provide new insights into the robust scheduling of production processes and establish a new benchmark for evaluating solutions in this domain. Additionally, the research offers new perspectives on the theory and practice of distributionally robust optimization. The model is implemented in GAMS and made available for public use. Keywords: Production scheduling; Distributionally robust optimization; Ambiguity set; Data-driven; Expert knowledge; Expert system.

This paper introduces an STL-driven formulation for robustness in cyber-physical systems. Specification Temporal Logic (STL) is widely used to define desired behaviors for dynamic systems. We address two core questions: first, can robustness be defined for any STL formula, and second, what are the computational implications of doing so? Regarding definability, we demonstrate that while robustness is not possible for all STL formulas, it is achievable for a broad and practical subset that includes properties of significant interest. Furthermore, we establish that deciding STL robustness is PSPACE-complete, indicating a high computational complexity. Finally, we provide a robustness formulation for both signal-based and trajectory-based interpretations of STL. Finally, we validate our approach by applying it to a robotic vehicle control problem. In this scenario, we utilize the vehicle's acceleration capabilities to determine safe distances from obstacles, thereby ensuring safety robustness. Additionally, we employ the robustness value as a cost function to design a controller that optimally balances safety and progress. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of this methodology. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexfazelpour/STL-Robustness. We introduce a strategy for investigating obscure materials, such as interstellar dust, by analyzing data from various objects using a diverse array of sensors. This approach addresses the challenge of insufficient mass in individual experiments, which limits the reliability of stochastic signals predicted by certain scientific models. We illustrate the feasibility of this method by estimating constraints on interstellar dust characteristics based on a recent study of a single CubeSat. This single-satellite analysis sets limits that are nearly two orders of magnitude less stringent than those achievable with the full network. Furthermore, we provide order-of-magnitude estimates for a global network of 10,000 cubesats and 10,000 other aircraft, demonstrating that these networks could achieve constraints exceeding two orders of magnitude stronger than current bounds. Our global satellite network could constrain asteroidal dust densities up to $10^{-8}$ g/cm$^3$, while our aircraft network could limit densities as high as $10^{-5}$ g/cm$^3$. Additionally, the aircraft-based sensors offer constraints on dust with higher velocities and larger sizes than those probed by satellite experiments. We conclude that a global network of accelerometers holds significant promise for constraining obscure matter. This sub-terawatt strategy represents a substantial shift from traditional approaches, which often require megawatt-class facilities to probe obscure phenomena. We anticipate that this novel framework will inspire a new generation of experiments to probe physics beyond the Standard Model. This study examines a specific class of nonlinear diffusion equations featuring quadratic diffusion coefficients and sources within general Riemannian manifolds. The methodology relies on specialized constructions of Riemannian metrics and subsequently applies established techniques from prior research. The initial portion of the paper addresses the nonlinear equation that encompasses the Laplace-Beltrami operator, deriving multiple nonlinear gradient representations on the associated quadratic metric space by employing recent findings on Sobolev inequalities, Poincaré inequalities, and mean curvature bounds. The final section presents several representations for a more expansive nonlinear diffusion equation, distinguished by a source term that precludes the utilization of Riemannian method representations. These additional representations are constructed using diverse approaches to isoperimetric inequalities and Ricci curvature bounds. The various gradient representations established in this work hold significant utility for parabolic evolution equations associated with these nonlinear diffusion processes. Furthermore, numerous applications exist within the field of mathematical physics, including the study of the Navier-Stokes equations, the NLS equation, and the Yang-Mills equation.

The nature of compact radio sources, particularly those with angular sizes under 1 arcsecond, remains a fundamental yet unresolved issue in radio astronomy. This study investigates source properties as a function of angular size by stacking images of radio sources identified in the 20 cm FIRST survey, which were subsequently cross-matched with the 8.4 GHz WSRT survey. We analyzed a sample comprising 1,000 sources smaller than 0.5 arcseconds and 1,000 sources between 0.5 and 1.0 arcseconds, comparing them to sources larger than 1.0 arcseconds. Our findings indicate that sources smaller than 1 arcsecond exhibit flatter spectral indices, higher linear flux densities, and more complex morphologies than their larger counterparts. Furthermore, the average spectral index of the stacked sources smaller than 1 arcsecond is found to be consistent with that of known blazars. Finally, we demonstrate that the majority of these compact, dim radio sources are radio-quiet quasars. These results support the hypothesis that a significant fraction of compact, dim radio sources are extragalactic active galactic nuclei. Additionally, we show that the average size of the brightest core in a group of compact, dim radio sources is approximately 0.005 arcseconds. This value is comparable to the average size of the brightest core in blazars and is similar to the resolution limit of the WSRT used in this study, suggesting that the brightest cores of most compact, dim radio sources are unresolved by the WSRT. Consequently, we conclude that the physical sizes of these cores are comparable to or smaller than the wavelength of the observed radiation. Finally, we propose that the radio emission from these cores originates from the jet base located at the radio-quiet quasar's accretion disk. This model is supported by the observed fact that the brightest cores of compact, dim radio sources display a higher degree of polarization than the brightest cores of radio-loud radio-quiet quasas. We also note that the average size of the brightest core in radio-loud radio-quiet quasars is approximately 0.05 arcseconds, which is comparable to the resolution limit of the FIRST survey. This suggests that the brightest cores of these radio-loud radio-quiet quasars are resolved by FIRST, whereas those of the WSRT-resolved compact, dim radio sources are unresolved by FIRST. Our analysis examines the impact of boundary conditions on reflected solitons and the influence of finite-size effects on thermal noise within bosonic systems. To validate our approach, we utilize the nonlinear Schrödinger equation to model an infinite-extent, noise-free analog black hole of finite size and compare our findings with exact numerical solutions. This framework offers a valuable tool for guiding future experiments, thereby advancing our understanding of scattering phenomena in the horizon region of analog black holes. Furthermore, it establishes a foundation for investigating the complete evaporation process of these systems. Specifically, the high precision achievable with this technology could enable the first experimental observations of Hawking correlation functions. Additionally, the ease of modifying system parameters in microwave setups will facilitate a more comprehensive exploration of beyond-linear effects. Ultimately, this work paves the way for developing a scattering-based phenomenology of analog Hawking radiation. This research addresses the privacy of anonymized location data by applying an established model privacy framework to spatial point processes. Specifically, it tackles the challenge of characterizing the belief system—comprising both belief measures and their density functions—for a conditional prior, which functions as a conditional version of a prior within the Bayesian statistical model. While the existence and uniqueness of such belief systems for conditional priors are generally difficult to establish, we demonstrate that under mild assumptions, these properties are guaranteed for two specific cases: the conditional Simplex Gibbs measure and the conditional Mat\'ern type covariance random field. Leveraging these findings, we introduce computational algorithms capable of approximating the belief functions associated with these conditional Gibbs-type belief systems using only local neighborhood information from the location data. Finally, the study illustrates the theoretical results through numerical examples and confirms the practical utility of the proposed algorithms. The proofs for the theorems are provided in the appendix. The Python code for the numerical examples can be found at https://github.com/PrashanthKumarKoduri/Location-Privacy. This paper addresses the challenge of global localization for mobile robots within vast environments, a task often hindered by numerous local minima and the difficulty of matching sparse, noisy LiDAR data to 2D maps. While Normal Distribution Transforms (NDTs) effectively model uncertainty and align local scans to global maps, their computational demands are often prohibitive for large-scale applications. To overcome these limitations, we introduce NDT-Transformer, a transformer-based localization system designed for large-scale settings. This approach leverages the Normal Distribution Transform depiction to compactly represent 3D point clouds into latent tensors of arbitrary size, enabling efficient processing with state-of-the-art performance. Evaluated on both indoor and outdoor datasets, NDT-Transformer achieves localization accuracy comparable to recent methods but operates at a speed 100 times faster. The NDT depiction and accompanying code are accessible at https://github.com/autonomousvision/ndt-transformer. Furthermore, we release an outdoor dataset comprising 300 ground-truth poses across 100 pairs of point clouds in San Francisco, San Francisco Bay, and Golden Gate Bridge, intended for benchmarking localization algorithms. This dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/autonomousvision/ndt-transformer/tree/master/data. Our findings indicate that transformer-based localization is highly effective for mobile robot navigation in large-scale outdoor areas. The source code is available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/ndt-transformer. Our contributions are threefold: (i) We propose NDT-Transformer, a transformer-based localization algorithm utilizing Normal Distribution Transforms to achieve state-of-the-art results in large-scale environments with superior efficiency; (ii) We make the NDT depiction, a novel compact representation of 3D point clouds, publicly available for benchmarking; and (iii) We provide a new outdoor localization dataset comprising 100 pairs of 3D point clouds with 300 ground-truth poses. This dataset features diverse scenes from Golden Gate Bridge, San Francisco Bay, and San Francisco City, totaling over 10 million points. We anticipate this resource will facilitate the development of efficient, large-scale localization methods for future research. Our results demonstrate that transformer-based localization can effectively solve global localization challenges for mobile robots in large-scale outdoor scenarios. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is extensively employed to investigate brain organization and the neural underpinnings of cognitive and behavioral processes. Given the inherent stochasticity in experimental conditions, the variability of stimuli, and biological systems, it is essential to determine how prediction precision varies with the number of trials and the scale of the system. To address this, we developed a stochastic multisite network model that integrates structural connectivity with random fluctuations. Our findings indicate that the statistical strength of functional connectivity scales with the number of trials according to a power law, where the exponent is determined by structural connectivity and network topology. Consequently, the precision of connectivity measures is influenced by both the length of the time series and the scale of the system. Furthermore, the prediction precision of node activity increases with the number of trials and also follows a power-law scaling, with the exponent dictated by structural connectivity and network topology. These results are robust and consistently observed in both simulated data and real-world fMRI datasets. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that rs-fMRI connectivity analysis exhibits distinct characteristics compared to other stochastic systems, offering critical insights for future rs-fMRI research. Additionally, the model and these conclusions may hold broader relevance for other stochastic systems. Finally, the provided Python code is released under the MIT license and can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/Connectivity. We examine a beeping network consisting of $n$ nodes that communicate exclusively through "beeps"—simple signals sent without containing data. Each node operates in one of two power states: active or dormant. The objective is to enable every active node pair to establish a connection, defined as the ability for any two active nodes to coordinate and switch on at the same time step. Our approach involves two phases: first, each active node identifies the count of other active nodes by repeatedly changing power states; second, they leverage this information to achieve pairwise connections. We demonstrate that when the network size falls within the range $n \in [\Omega(\log^2\Delta), \Omega(\log^3\Delta)]$, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum degree of active nodes in the underlying graph, a specific algorithm can determine the node count using $O(\log\Delta)$ beeps per node over $O(\log\Delta)$ rounds. Subsequently, this gathered information allows any pair of active nodes to connect in $O(\log\Delta)$ rounds while requiring each node to beep for only $O(1)$ time steps per round. Furthermore, we prove that for node counts below $O(\log^2\Delta)$, determining the exact number of active nodes is impossible. Finally, we establish that no algorithm can achieve both $t = o(1)$ beep time per node and $r = o(\log\Delta)$ connection time per pair. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first study on energy-efficient communication in beeping networks. Our findings indicate that beeping networks can achieve connection times comparable to traditional radio networks, though they require slightly longer initialization periods. Additionally, we show that beeping networks can match the performance of radio networks in terms of beeping duration, provided they accept a modest increase in connection time. Our proposed method for determining the number of active nodes is straightforward and can be readily extended to other fundamental network problems. Finally, we outline an extension of this work to scenarios with unknown network size. In such cases, our method still determines the number of active nodes, albeit with a modestly higher connection time per pair. Crucially, this approach enables the execution of fundamental distributed tasks on beeping networks for the first time. This translingual nature renders them distinct from monolingual texts, presenting a unique challenge for machine learning applications. We demonstrate that these transition points serve as effective features for decoding mixed sentences and propose enhancing standard positional encodings by incorporating signal change information at these transition points. Our results indicate that this approach improves upon state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we present PaHiNLP, a newly curated dataset of code-mixed Hindi and English sentences annotated with transition points, which fills a critical gap in current research resources. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the phonon characteristics and superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S hydride across a pressure range of 100 to 250 GPa. We discovered that at 250 GPa, the pressure-induced van Hove singularity (VHS) of the second derivative of the total energy with respect to the atomic positions of the S atom and two of the H atoms in the H$_{3}$S unit lowers the isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha$) for sulfur from 0.28 to 0.22, while having a negligible impact on the coefficients for the three hydrogen atoms. Furthermore, by analyzing the electron-phonon coupling matrix elements, we identified that the largest contributions to $\alpha$ originate from interactions involving the optical modes of the three hydrogen atoms and the optical modes of the sulfur and one hydrogen atom. These findings indicate that the sulfur optical mode is the primary driver of the isotope effect's reduction at 250 GPa. Additionally, we computed the temperature-dependent critical temperature ($T_{c}$) for pressures between 100 and 250 GPa, revealing a peak of 208 K at 200 GPa. Our results demonstrate that the temperature-dependent $T_{c}$ is significantly influenced by the VHS; specifically, at 250 GPa, the VHS causes a sharp decline in $T_{c}$ at low temperatures. This decrease is attributed to the reduced density of states at the Fermi level, which results from the crossing of the second VHS with the fourth electron filling sub-band. Finally, we observed that the peak $T_{c}$ shifts to higher pressures as temperature increases. These results offer valuable insights for future experimental research. (C) 2021 The Author(s). This paper introduces a new approach designed to improve motion planning in scenarios featuring dynamic obstacles and obstacles with large dimensions. The core concept involves spatially constraining the robot's trajectory to reduce the impact of high-dimensional state spaces, even when these obstacles are static. This constraint is established by solving a specific optimization problem that accounts for both static and dynamic obstacles, as well as the robot's dimensions. The resulting solution is efficient and can be computed in real-time. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through two simulation cases and one experimental case. The findings indicate that the proposed method successfully generates plans that consider obstacles and the robot's dimensions, thereby avoiding collisions. Furthermore, the method is capable of generating plans for the robot to pursue a specific target. Additionally, the generated plans are free of local minima and can be computed in less than 100 milliseconds. This paper introduces a new visual relocalization approach designed for outdoor environments. Unlike traditional methods that depend on geometric constraints, our technique leverages the textural details of visual features. Specifically, we first map the textured surfaces of the surrounding environment onto a 3D point cloud to create a "surfel map," which serves as a global reference frame. Subsequently, local descriptors extracted from images are compared against the textural patterns of these surfel points using our proposed deep neural network feature representation. This method achieves a significant performance boost, increasing relocalization accuracy by 100% and improving the F1 score by 160%. Furthermore, the framework is adaptable to various feature descriptors, enabling the integration of both geometric and textural information. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in relocalization accuracy. The source code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.

This study tackles the challenge of optimizing precoding and joint user selection within multiuser MIMO downlink networks. The analysis assumes that base stations share their channel data with users but lack knowledge of user-channel links on the reverse direction. The primary goal is to ensure that selected users achieve a target data rate while maximizing the number of users served per transmission, thereby enhancing network throughput. To address this, we introduce a mixed-integer non-linear programming formulation. We then develop a low-complexity algorithm based on the mathematical program with complementarity constraints (MPCC) to identify the optimal set of user selections and precoders. Furthermore, we propose a distributed implementation of this algorithm, enabling collaborative decisions among user devices. Finally, numerical results are presented to validate the proposed method. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed algorithm effectively selects users and determines precoders, achieving a significant improvement in downlink throughput. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits strong scalability regarding the number of users and antennas, as well as low computational complexity. Notably, it can be executed in a distributed fashion without requiring channel information from the user side. In this distributed setup, users autonomously make complementarity-based choices to maximize downlink performance, illustrating the potential for collaborative decision-making in future networks. To achieve this, we designed a communication protocol that allows users to exchange necessary information for the distributed algorithm while minimizing overhead. This protocol ensures that only a subset of users communicates with the base station, thereby reducing the complexity of the distributed solution. The results confirm that the proposed protocol incurs minimal overhead and computational cost, making it highly suitable for practical deployment. Overall, this work paves the way for future collaborative decision-making in multiuser MIMO downlink systems. Additionally, the MPCC framework is applicable to other problems where decisions involve choosing between two alternatives, such as activating a subset of sensors in a distributed system. This approach is particularly advantageous in scenarios where only partial information about the environment is available. In such cases, the method can be adapted to jointly select sensors and their corresponding precoders to optimize distributed sensing performance. The proposed framework is also extendable to other collaborative decision-making problems, such as resource allocation in wireless networks. In these contexts, users can collaboratively choose resources to optimize overall network performance. Furthermore, the MPCC approach can be utilized in distributed machine learning applications, where users jointly select data samples to train a model, optimizing performance while preserving privacy. In this scenario, users would choose which samples to share with a central server for joint training, with the model subsequently used for inference.

The results indicate that for a broad class of discontinuous Markov decision processes (MDPs), the analysis remains consistent with the convergence properties of continuous MDPs. This article explores the relationship between the Vassiliev characteristic of order three and the Franko-Hatcher characteristic of order two. We demonstrate that the value of a characteristic class of order three on the Fox-Hatcher loop is proportional to the linking number of its components, with the constant of proportionality determined entirely by the characteristic class itself. Consequently, the linking number emerges as the unique non-trivial invariant of self-linked 2-component links that is either Vassiliev type or is an integral multiple of the Franko-Hatcher characteristic of order 2. Furthermore, we calculate the value of the Vassiliev characteristic of order 3 on the Fox-Hatcher loop and determine the weight system associated with the Franko-Hatcher characteristic for any natural number k, identifying it as the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2k}{k}$. Finally, we compute the weights for all natural numbers k, confirming that they are integers. This finding suggests the existence of an extended family of weighted diagrams for the Hopf link, where the weights are derived from the central binomial coefficients. Additionally, we present several examples of diagrams for the Hopf link that correspond to the weights of the characteristic class of order 3. Finally, we outline the extension of the characteristic class of order 3 to multivariable links and investigate the link between the multivariable Arakawa-Vassiliev characteristic and the multivariable Franko-Hatcher characteristic. Specifically, we show that the linking number is the sole "Vassiliev type" characteristic of a 2-variable Hopf link. Furthermore, we establish that the value of the multivariable Franko-Hatcher characteristic on the Fox-Hatcher loop is given by the central multinomial coefficient $\binom{k+k}{k,k,k}$, which is also an integer. This implies the existence of a diagram set for the Hopf link with weights defined by the central multinomial coefficients. Finally, we compute the weights for the extended family of diagrams using the multivariable Franko-Hatcher characteristic. The interplay between antiferromagnetism and nematicity in iron-based superconductors is a subject of significant interest. Although both phenomena are observed in the parent compounds of BaFe$_2$As$_2$ and FeSe, the coexistence of nematicity and antiferromagnetism remains controversial. In LiFeAs, antiferromagnetic order emerges below 17.5 K, yet recent studies have suggested a nematic phase exists between 17.5 K and 18.5 K. To investigate this, we conducted x-ray diffraction experiments on LiFeAs single crystals across a broad temperature range. Our results show that the in-plane lattice parameters remain isotropic down to 2 K, contradicting prior suggestions of nematicity. Furthermore, we detected no anomalies in the thermal expansion coefficient at 17.5 K. These findings suggest that antiferromagnetic order in LiFeAs does not induce nematicity. Additionally, we compared the thermal expansion behavior of LiFeAs with that of FeSe, observing distinct differences in their temperature dependencies. These differences may reflect variations in the electronic structures of the two materials. Overall, our data indicate that LiFeAs possesses a simple ferromagnetic lattice, with antiferromagnetism arising solely from the ferromagnetic superlattice exchange interaction. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the interplay between antiferromagnetism and nematicity in LiFeAs. (Letter) DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.125.056401. This paper presents a comprehensive global analysis of Type-II two-Higgs-doublet models (2HDM), incorporating predictions for the future $Z \to h_a h_b$ decay mode. Our numerical computations are based on numerical one-loop corrections to the $Z$-boson decay width, utilizing a dedicated numerical package. Furthermore, we integrate recent experimental constraints from LHC Run-2, including limits on the $h_w \to \gamma\gamma$ signal strength, Higgs diphoton production cross-sections, and the $Higgs \to Z\gamma$ signal strength. We also incorporate bounds derived from the muon anomalous magnetic moment and the electric dipole moment of the electron. Our study examines two scenarios: one where the light CP-even Higgs boson mass is fixed at $m_{h_w} = 125$ GeV, and another where it is treated as a free parameter. In both cases, we evaluate the $h_w \to h_a h_b$ channel, which is accessible at the Belle II detector. We compare these theoretical predictions against current experimental constraints and project outcomes from Belle II and a high-luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). Finally, we discuss the implications of potential future results on the viability of the 2HDM framework. Our findings indicate that, given the current experimental landscape, the mass of the CP-odd Higgs boson ($m_{h_z}$) is bounded below by approximately 100 GeV. Additionally, the branching ratio for $Z \to h_a h_b$ decays is constrained to be less than $10^{-5}$ across the entire parameter space. We conclude that Belle II will play a crucial role in probing the 2HDM parameter space, particularly for the $h_w \to h_a h_b$ channel, with a projected sensitivity reaching down to masses of $m_{h_z} \sim 1$ GeV. This sensitivity is achieved assuming an integrated luminosity of 10 ab$^{-1}$ and a signal-to-background ratio of 1:100. Finally, we demonstrate that a high-luminosity LHC will be essential for further exploring the parameter space, specifically for masses below 1 TeV. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/PrashantKumar2000/2HDM-Global-Fit. Our results will be updated regularly as new numerical corrections are incorporated into the 2HDM parameter space

This paper establishes a novel ill-posedness result regarding the dimensionless steady Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any given initial velocity field, there exists a perturbation of arbitrarily small norm that results in a perturbed solution with a large norm. Furthermore, our constructed counterexamples exhibit a blow-up rate of at least exponential in nature. These findings thereby complete the ill-posedness investigation for the dimensionless steady Navier-Stokes equations across all critical function spaces. Additionally, we address a related question for the dimensionless unsteady Navier-Stokes equations by constructing counterexamples exhibiting a blow-up rate of at least power-law. Finally, we compare these results with existing literature on various Navier-Stokes equations and derive new well-posedness findings for dimensionless small data. Notably, our ill-posedness examples for both unsteady and steady Navier-Stokes equations are formulated within the same critical Besov spaces. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of such a comparison between ill-posedness and well-posedness results for dimensionless Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces. Consequently, our results significantly extend the scope of prior research on the ill-posedness of the dimensionless unsteady Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces. Our approach relies on the construction of counterexamples via the nonlinear term, thereby circumventing the limitations of linearized analysis. This technique is expected to be applicable to other nonlinear partial differential equations. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research concerning the dimensionless Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces. These directions include exploring whether the constructed counterexamples possess the self-similar property, whether they yield power-law or exponential blow-up rates, and whether they can be adapted to other critical function spaces. Such an extension would further broaden the scope of previous research on the ill-posedness of dimensionless Navier-Stokes equations in critical function spaces. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive and systematic framework for investigating the dimensionless Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces, thereby advancing the field of fluid dynamics. This contribution is particularly significant given the ongoing interest in the Navier-Stokes equations within the mathematical community. Our results thus represent a substantial and meaningful advancement in the study of these equations. By offering a thorough and systematic analysis of the dimensionless Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces, our work is poised to make a lasting and significant impact on the field of fluid dynamics. We further compare this thermal compression with magneto-elastical lattice expansion caused by magnon polarization.
