We introduce two variations to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, which utilize structured Goppa codes as their matrix. The first variation employs a matrix built from extended ternary Hamming codes, while the second builds its matrix using extended ternary BCH codes. When utilizing extended ternary Hamming codes, the design achieves performance comparable to lattice-based schemes while offering smaller key sizes and faster operations. Furthermore, substituting extended BCH codes enhances the scheme's resistance to algebraic attacks. Security assessments against multiple attack vectors demonstrate that both proposed designs offer robust security guarantees. Finally, benchmarking confirms that the computational complexities for key generation, encryption, and decryption in our variants are comparable to those of many leading lattice-based schemes.

Pre-training language models (PLMs) have recently become a leading approach for numerous NLP applications. However, current PLMs typically employ a single BERT model trained on both natural language and Wikipedia. This study investigates the distinct characteristics of these two text sources and demonstrates that for specific downstream tasks, either source may be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose pre-training a more robust BERT model by leveraging multiple text sources. Specifically, we introduce the pre-training of a new Multi-Lexicon BERT (Dict-BERT) model, which utilizes various lexicons rather than relying solely on Wikipedia. Extensive experiments across various downstream tasks indicate that Dict-BERT significantly surpasses existing BERT models, particularly on small-scale pre-training corpora. The code and data associated with Dict-BERT can be accessed at https://github.com/ymcui/DictBERT. Furthermore, Dict-BERT will be made available for public use. Our findings suggest that this approach will enhance the generalization capabilities of language models. Additional details are available at https://dictbert.github.io/. We welcome any feedback. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) has recently attracted significant attention for its capacity to safeguard data privacy and user confidentiality. Nevertheless, it is widely acknowledged that VFL is not immune to privacy breaches, as various attacks have been demonstrated to cause substantial data leakage. This paper introduces a novel privacy threat against VFL known as PrVI (Pragmatic Privacy Assault), which is the first such threat to exploit the specific characteristics of data samples in vertical federations. Under this attack, the adversary infers sensitive information from a subset of local samples without leveraging transfer learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PrVI, showing that it can accurately reconstruct data from users with narrow domains and accurately predict samples from users with wider domains. Furthermore, we prove that standard VFL protocols, including differential privacy, offer little to no protection against this attack. Finally, our empirical findings indicate that horizontal domain decomposition within vertical federations amplifies the risk of data leakage caused by PrVI. To mitigate this, we propose a novel approach called $\mathsf{FP-DP-FL}$, which integrates differential privacy with federated learning on formal concept analysis to obscure the structural relationships between samples. Extensive experiments confirm that $\mathsf{FP-DP-FL}$ can effectively suppress privacy assaults in practical federated learning scenarios. Using the QCD light-cone synthesis rule, we investigate the exclusive decay process $B \to p + \text{dark antibaryon}$. In this framework, the $B$-meson is modeled as a three-quark system, while the dark antibaryon is treated as an anti-triplet of dark quarks interacting via an antineutrino. Our analysis indicates that the exclusive production of dark antibaryons in this channel is highly suppressed. This suppression arises primarily from the smallness of the $B$-meson distribution amplitude at large momentum fractions and the high virtuality of the dark antibaryon, which necessitates the use of its leading twist distribution amplitude. Consequently, dark antibaryons are more likely to be produced inclusively rather than exclusively. These findings offer valuable insights for interpreting potential signals from upcoming experiments, such as the LHCb Dark Search run. Furthermore, our results reinforce the conclusion that the LUXZETA experiment cannot rule out the dark baryon model, as it is capable of detecting dark antibaryons. Finally, we demonstrate that the ratio of signals for dark antibaryons versus dark di-mesons in $B$-meson decays could serve as a distinguishing feature to differentiate between the two dark baryon models. This ratio is predicted to fall within the range of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$. Future measurements of this ratio will provide a stringent test of the dark baryon hypothesis. Additionally, we estimate that the production cross section for the process $pp \to B + \text{dark antibaryon} + X$ is approximately $10^{-11}$ times that of the inclusive $B$-meson production cross section. This estimate relies on the assumption that the dark antibaryon is emitted via an s-channel antineutrino. Intelligent cities are evolving into complex socio-cyber-physical systems (SCPS) that integrate advanced computing, communication, and control systems with their computational infrastructure. These systems facilitate data exchange between advanced applications and advanced computing platforms, enabling advanced control systems to execute critical functions. However, the reliance on these SCPS applications and platforms introduces vulnerabilities to cyber attacks, which can disrupt operations and compromise data integrity. This paper introduces the Intelligent City Defense game, a two-player, two-player zero-sum model where one participant acts as the attacker and the other as the defender. The objective is to identify optimal strategies for both sides within a resource-constrained environment, specifically addressing the trade-off between security and efficiency. This framework is designed to be easily adaptable to various real-world SCPS applications, such as power grids, water distribution networks, and traffic management systems. The study concludes by demonstrating the game's applicability to specific SCPS scenarios. Additionally, the research highlights the existence of Nash equilibria and explores the development of learning-based algorithms to identify these equilibria. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to illustrate the game's dynamics. The findings suggest a promising avenue for future research in this domain. We investigate the thermodynamics of black holes within a chamber, focusing on how the horizon structure and heat capacity evolve with temperature. Our results indicate that the presence of a chamber alters the Hawking--Page phase transition temperatures for both nonrotating and extremal charged black holes, thereby influencing the system's thermal stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that extremal charged black holes possess two distinct large horizon phases: one resembling an large nonextremal horizon and another characterized by an even larger horizon. These newly identified phase transition scenarios open several avenues for future research. Finally, we suggest that these findings are crucial for comprehending the physics of a global AdS space enclosed by a chamber. Additionally, our framework offers a potential pathway for investigating the holographic connection between field theory and gravity in global AdS settings. This specific aspect holds significant promise for advancing our understanding of the holographic renormalization group flow. Finally, we highlight that our findings offer a new perspective on the recent developments regarding the island conjecture and the calculation of entropy for AdS systems with boundaries. Specifically, we show that the entropy of charged AdS systems within a chamber can be derived using the island formula. Moreover, our calculations reveal that the entanglement entropy between the matter field and the gravitational sector is not negligible. Consequently, the island conjecture must be reevaluated in the context of a bounded AdS system. Although deep learning has significantly advanced the fields of natural language processing and information retrieval, it is highly susceptible to noisy labels. While existing methods for data retrieval under label noise primarily target image datasets, the paper addresses this gap by proposing a solution specifically for the document domain. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness across diverse real-world applications. However, their performance often suffers in real-life scenarios characterized by limited labeled data and a vast volume of unlabeled information. To address this, we introduce a novel semi-supervised framework designed to leverage unlabeled nodes by enhancing the quality of their synthetic labels. Our strategy involves two key components: (1) the strategic utilization of a high-confidence subset of unlabeled nodes to refine pseudo-labels for the broader unlabeled pool, and (2) the application of data augmentation on nodes with low-confidence labels to generate synthetic confidence data. Experimental results indicate that our approach significantly boosts GNN performance, achieving a 20% gain over the best baseline when training on just 1% of labeled data. Chain event graph models have recently been developed to address generalized versions of partial order Markov models. While various parametric and non-parametric methods exist for fitting these models to data, this paper introduces a novel approach for selecting chain event graphs as the most probable explanations based on observed data within a Bayesian framework. We present a general algorithm that identifies the set of optimal chain event graphs by applying the projected smoothing operator to the posterior distribution of this set. This method ensures that the resulting posterior distribution remains concentrated on this set. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of our selection algorithm using a real-world dataset. The demonstration confirms the model's ability to capture complex dependencies in the real data, as evidenced by the partial order Markov properties estimated from the selected chain event graphs. Additionally, we show that the posterior distributions of this model family possess specific properties, such as total positivity, which significantly accelerate the algorithm's performance. Finally, we provide a comprehensive simulation study that validates the algorithm's efficiency and accuracy. The code required to replicate the simulations and the example application is available at: https://github.com/maartensl/CEGselection. We introduce a dynamic with damping and a regularization term that mirrors the well-known Tikhonov regularization used in tikhonov regularization problems. Specifically, for any initial condition, this dynamic generates a piecewise absolutely continuous trajectory that strongly converges to the minimum norm element within the solution set. Our primary contribution lies in the rate of convergence: under a mild technical assumption regarding the initial condition, the trajectory achieves a convergence rate of $o(t^{-2/3})$ (where $t$ denotes the time variable). This result is optimal within the class of time-dependent convergence rates. Furthermore, when the initial condition belongs to the set of elements that strongly converge to the minimum norm solution, we demonstrate that the trajectory converges strongly to this minimum norm element with the optimal algebraic rate $O(t^{-2/3})$. These findings apply to both undifferentiated and differentiated dynamical systems. Finally, we illustrate the efficacy of this approach through several numerical experiments. Notably, we observe that, in many practical scenarios, a significantly smaller Tikhonov regularization parameter is required to achieve a satisfactory solution compared to standard methods. Additionally, we highlight that the undifferentiated approach offers the advantage of not requiring the computation of the Hessian matrix. Finally, we establish the strong convergence of trajectories generated by a certain class of underdamped mechanical problems with regularization toward the minimum norm solution. In this context, convergence rates are also derived, albeit with a less favorable exponent. These findings extend naturally to frictional regularized problems, where trajectories converge strongly to the minimum norm solution. However, it is important to note that rates of convergence are not guaranteed in this specific case. The theoretical results presented herein are applicable to a broad spectrum of problems, including those involving nonlinear operators, set constraints, and Tikhonov-type functionals. The latter category encompasses a wide range of applications, such as the Tikhonov regularization problem, the total variation regularization problem, the trace norm minimization problem, the nuclear norm minimization problem, and the low rank matrix recovery problem. Furthermore, the framework extends to scenarios where the Tikhonov functional is replaced by a more general Bregman function. In this generalized setting, the trajectory converges strongly to an element with the minimum norm, though the resulting rates may be suboptimal. This work extends the findings of [1-3]. This paper investigates the wall-following task, which involves a robot moving along a wall without collisions. While the vast number of possible wall-following behaviors (WFBs) has previously been underestimated, we now provide a complete and accurate classification of these behaviors based on their dynamical characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the state transition diagram (STD) of a WFB is determined by the state transition rules (STRs) of its constituent dynamic subsystems (DSs). Consequently, we derive the specific sequences of DSs required to form a complete WFB. Finally, leveraging the derived (in)equalities, we establish the growth rate of WFBs and identify a lower bound for the number of states in an WFB given a specific STR. These findings offer a comprehensive framework for designing wall-following robots and facilitate a systematic analysis of the diverse WFBs they can exhibit. Additionally, our research offers a general methodology for analyzing sequences of dynamical systems, with potential applications extending beyond wall-following robots. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through simulations.

Kinetic energy driven superconductors, including cuprates and iron-based compounds, are expected to exhibit anomalous microwave conductivity. This study presents a model for such materials featuring a low density of extended defects, which are anticipated in the growth fronts of single crystals. The model demonstrates that microwaves can penetrate these materials deeply, penetrating further in underdoped samples and within the pseudogap phase. In regimes where conductivity is low, microwave power dependence becomes significant, leading to a transition from metallic to insulating behavior. This model aligns with existing experimental data. We predict that materials with a low defect density will display distinct signatures of kinetic energy driven superconductivity, including diverging penetration depth at the pseudogap temperature and a shift from insulating to metallic conductivity at high microwave powers. These predictions are particularly promising for single crystal cuprates, which possess growth-free growth fronts and possess high purity. Additionally, we propose that the microwave conductivity of realistic materials with defects will be suppressed relative to pristine superconductors, an effect that is more pronounced in underdoped samples. Finally, we suggest that the penetration depth will be reduced due to microwave power, with a more pronounced effect in underdoped samples. These findings may also be observable in materials with a high density of defects. Ultimately, our results indicate that the microwave conductivity of kinetic energy driven superconductors is highly sensitive to both microwave power and doping level. This sensitivity could serve as a critical tool for characterizing the superconducting gap and the pseudogap phase. Furthermore, measuring the penetration depth as a function of microwave power offers a unique method for distinguishing between the cuprate phase diagram models involving a pseudogap and one without. This distinction relies on the contrasting predictions regarding penetration depth and microwave conductivity within the pseudogap phase. Finally, we outline a pathway to achieve the ultimate precision in measuring the penetration depth of superconductors. This approach involves measuring the penetration depth in both normal and superconducting states and calculating their ratio. Such a method would enable the direct observation of potential divergence as the temperature approaches the pseudogap temperature. Additionally, it would allow for the detection of power-dependent penetration depth, providing a means to differentiate between the BCS and $d$-wave superconducting gap symmetries. The proposed methodology is applicable to a wide range of superconducting materials. Furthermore, we note that the penetration depth of kinetic energy driven superconductors is likely to be reduced by microwave power, a phenomenon that may be more pronounced in underdoped samples

This paper provides an overview of the long-term behavior of bounded domains evolving according to the crystalline-like average curvature (CtAC) law, which represents the most anisotropic curvature flow, alongside its associated wedge flow variant. We demonstrate that the flow exhibits distinct characteristics compared to more isotropic curvature flows or those with lower anisotropy, particularly in how it handles singularities. The primary focus is on the blow-up dynamics of the CtAC flow, which differ markedly from those of the wedge flow. Specifically, we establish that the CtAC flow can develop singularities at interior points away from corners, a phenomenon absent in the wedge flow. Furthermore, we establish the scale-invariance of the CtAC flow and derive the corresponding self-similar blow-up solutions. Finally, we examine the interaction between these self-similar blow-up solutions and the flow, revealing that the blow-up rate is slower than in wedge flow, thereby highlighting the distinct nature of the CtAC flow. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The CtAC flow is the most anisotropic curvature flow, whereas the wedge flow is the next most anisotropic; the latter has been previously studied in arXiv:2001.00308 and arXiv:2001.00309. The results presented here demonstrate the unique blow-up behavior of the CtAC flow, which contrasts with that of the wedge flow. The study of anisotropic curvature flows is driven by the hypothesis that they may admit singularity types not observed in isotropic flows, a hypothesis that the CtAC flow appears to validate. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 offers a review of the results from our earlier works on wedge flow; Section 3 presents the CtAC blow-up results, with Subsection 3.1 detailing the flow's scale invariance and Subsection 3.2 describing the blow-up dynamics; Section 4 investigates the interaction between the flow and the self-similar blow-up solutions, with Subsection 4.1 addressing the case of $m=1$ and Subsection 4.2 covering the $m>1$ scenario; and Section 5 concludes with a discussion of the results. We derive the scaling limit of conditionally uniform $s$-loop eroded annuli as the annulus degenerates to a disk, demonstrating convergence to uniformly $s$-erased SLE$(8/3,\rho)$ on the disk. This finding confirms the conjecture proposed by Lawler and Vuong [Ann. Probab. 48 (2020), no. 4, 1421--1452] and aligns with the scaling limits predicted by the double scaling limit of two-dimensional Colored Tensor Models. Furthermore, we apply this result to investigate the nesting structure of SLE loops. Our analysis reveals that the nesting structure of SLE$(8/3,0)$ matches that of uniform disks, thereby corroborating the first author's recent conjecture [arXiv:2009.00010]. Additionally, we elucidate the relationship between uniformly $s$-erased SLE$(8/3,\rho)$ and Liouville Quantum Gravity. Specifically, we demonstrate that conditioning a Liouville Quantum Triangle [arXiv:2009.00010] to have infinite area in a specific direction—constrained by an infinite geodesic arc—yields an object conformally equivalent to uniformly $s$-erased SLE$(8/3,\rho)$ on the disk. This construction also accounts for the fractal structure of uniform $s$-erased SLE$(8/3,\rho)$ on the half-plane, thereby extending the known result regarding the fractal structure of uniform SLE$(8/3)$ on the half-plane. Finally, we compute the scaling exponent of the outer boundary of conditionally uniform $s$ loop erasures on degenerating annuli, which yields a new formula for the scaling exponent of $s$-erased SLE$(8/3,\rho)$ on the half-plane. This result extends the known exponent of $s$-loop erasures of SLE$(8/3)$ on the half-plane and enables the calculation of the scaling exponent for uniform $s$ loop erasures of SLE$(8/3)$ on the half-plane. Furthermore, we prove that the scaling exponent of conditionally uniform loops on an annulus is given by the minimum of the scaling exponents of loops on conditionally uniform annuli and conditionally uniform SLE$(8/3,0)$ disks. We propose a solution to the dark matter problem by integrating a curvaton field with a non-minimal coupling to curvature into the standard curvaton model. In this framework, the effective curvaton potential evolves over time, driving inflation into a rapid exponential phase. This dynamic generates dark matter candidates known as dark fermions, which possess a suppressed mass and exhibit renormalization group (RG) running. The curvaton subsequently decays into these dark fermions, with the final effective curvaton potential determining the resulting dark matter density. We demonstrate that the curvaton mass can be tuned to match the observed dark matter density. Furthermore, the non-minimal coupling to curvature induces an effective non-linearity in the dark matter potential, causing the mass to run. This behavior is quantified by the anomalous dimension, which can reach values as high as 5. Our findings indicate that the density of dark matter particles is highly sensitive to the RG running, with the dark fermion mass decreasing as the anomalous dimension increases. Consequently, the dark matter density can be adjusted to align with observational data. Finally, we examine the implications of our model for future space-based gravitational wave detectors. In this context, the curvaton plays a crucial role in determining the spectral density of the dark matter halo. Educational institutions are increasingly adopting various analytical techniques to investigate student outcomes and instructional methods. This study introduces a latent variable model that integrates multiple data sources to investigate academic trajectories. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon control framework utilizing differential games. The proposed method offers two distinct control strategies: one for the lead vehicle and another for the following vehicles. The differential games approach enables the lead vehicle to minimize fuel consumption by selecting an optimal trajectory, accounting for the self-interested nature of other road users. Following the differential equation for the lead vehicle's position, the position of each subsequent vehicle is determined based on the preceding vehicle's position and the solution to the associated differential game. This proposed control strategy effectively reduces fuel usage for the lead vehicle and the third vehicle in the platoon while maintaining a safe inter-vehicle distance. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of the discount factor on the objective function of the differential games, demonstrating its ability to model the selfishness of vehicles within the platoon. Finally, the paper provides an analytical solution to the differential games and validates the effectiveness of the proposed control system through computer simulations. The simulation results indicate that the method successfully achieves the lead vehicle's objective of minimizing fuel consumption. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the discount factor significantly influences fuel consumption, allowing for the optimization of the lead vehicle's performance by selecting an appropriate value for this parameter. The simulation outcomes also show that the proposed system maintains the required inter-vehicle distance throughout the trip. These findings confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving the lead vehicle's objective. Additionally, the results illustrate that the proposed system outperforms the existing one by reducing fuel consumption for both the lead and third vehicles in the platoon. This improvement is achieved without compromising safety, as evidenced by the maintenance of the specified inter-vehicle distance during differential games control. Consequently, the proposed approach is deemed effective for the differential games control system. The findings also suggest that the proposed system can be extended to optimize the platoon arrangement by employing differential games control for multiple lead vehicles simultaneously. Future research will explore the application of differential games control to optimize platoon arrangements for the entire fleet. This paper serves as a foundational step toward implementing differential games control in vehicle platoons. The presented findings offer a basis for future research on utilizing differential games for platoon control. It is a well-known phenomenon that including interaction terms in a regression model can result in misleading inferences regarding main effects. This occurs because selecting no interaction terms may yield an invalid inference procedure, whereas inferring that no interaction effects exist without testing for them can be misleading. To address this, we introduce a sequential testing framework designed to prevent interaction effects. The method's steps are: (1) test the null hypothesis of no interaction; (2) perform model selection excluding interaction terms; and (3) infer confidence regions for all main effects. We demonstrate that this approach yields valid inference for main effects and illustrate its application with a simulation study. Furthermore, we apply the method to a case study examining the relationship between air pollution and mortality in the United States. The framework is implemented in the R package `avoidinter`. We present a comparative study of the spin dynamics in a chiral honeycomb Heisenberg antiferromagnet across amorphous, single-crystalline, and polycrystalline samples. By employing inelastic neutron scattering and numerical simulations, we analyze the evolution of spin excitations and the system's proximity to a chiral spin liquid ground state. Our findings indicate that structural disorder does not hinder access to the chiral spin liquid phase; in fact, it may facilitate it. We suggest that the enhanced stability of the chiral spin liquid phase in amorphous samples stems from residual couplings to out-of-plane modes, which are more prevalent in disordered materials. Consequently, these specific samples exhibit longer lifetimes for the topological order characteristic of the chiral spin liquid. This research underscores the critical role of sample quality in determining the stability of topological quantum matter. Furthermore, it establishes the necessary conditions for the chiral spin liquid phase, paving the way for its realization in other materials through controlled disordering. Finally, our results underscore the significance of the amorphous sample in advancing the field of topological quantum matter. This is because the robustness of the chiral spin liquid phase against disorder in this sample suggests that the boundary between the H3 chiral spin liquid and the frustrated ferromagnetic phase is unusually close in the amorphous material, thereby offering a promising route to explore the phase diagram of the H3 Hamiltonian. This proximity can be achieved either by fine-tuning the Hamiltonian or by selecting a material with a naturally proximate phase diagram. Both strategies hold significant potential for discovering new quantum spin liquid materials. To illustrate this, we examine the phase diagram of the chiral honeycomb Heisenberg antiferromagnet in the related compound Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the viability of a chiral spin liquid ground state in both polycrystalline and amorphous samples. The polycrystalline sample displays a phase diagram comparable to that of single crystals, whereas the amorphous sample exhibits a phase diagram that is distinct from both. This discrepancy arises from the competition between the H3 chiral spin liquid and the ferromagnetic phase, which is influenced by out-of-plane coupling. In the amorphous sample, the out-of-plane coupling is stronger, stabilizing the ferromagnetic phase and shrinking the chiral spin liquid phase. This paper introduces a class of algorithms designed to efficiently calibrate large-scale radio interferometric datasets. Our approach leverages the Fourier transform properties inherent in data cubes generated by an N-antenna array arranged in a regular 2D grid. Specifically, we demonstrate that for baselines following a specific trajectory, the calibration matrix can be applied to a data cube via two rapid Fourier transforms. This capability enables the rapid modeling of complex instrumental errors, such as antenna gain fluctuations and primary beam structure, even when these effects exhibit non-local variations across the field of view. By restricting the problem to data cubes where source emission is confined to a limited solid angle, we develop an iterative algorithm that achieves ${\cal O}(N\log{N})$ scaling with respect to the number of antennas, alongside linear scaling relative to the data cube's size. We validate this method using an array of approximately 1000 antennas and show that the algorithm converges within a small number of iterations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can be parallelized, allowing for linear scaling of the computational time per iteration based on the number of available processors. Finally, we illustrate the method's effectiveness by successfully correcting primary beam and gain variations in a data cube from the SKA pathfinder array, MOPRA. This achievement required correcting for a primary beam with a half-power beam width of roughly 10 arcminutes and gain variations reaching 100% across the field of view. The rapid convergence of the algorithm was confirmed even under these extreme conditions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rgregory22/CalibrationMethods. We introduce a new method for diversifying portfolio distributions, utilizing an autoencoding conditional generative adversarial network. This approach is designed to handle financial time series data that frequently lacks normality and log-normality. By encoding financial time series into a specific distribution and simultaneously training to decode from that distribution back into the original series, the method successfully retains the statistical properties of the original data. Empirical results demonstrate that the distribution produced by our model achieves higher diversification and comparable returns relative to the Merton model. Furthermore, we show that the model can be effectively applied to individual time series without requiring pre-training on a large corpus of data. Finally, our analysis reveals that the autocoder component of the model functions similarly to a wavelet transform. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexeykolesnikov/Portfolio-GAN. We provide the analytical expression for the polarized transition function $A_{gq}(N)$ in the variable flavor number scheme at third order in $\alpha_s$, specifically for the cases where the flavor number is $N_f=4$ or $N_f=5$. This function plays a critical role in the variable flavor number scheme by governing the transformation of parton distribution functions between different flavor thresholds, while also influencing the calculation of polarized PDF evolution and the interpretation of polarized structure function data. To the best of our knowledge, the polarized $A_{gq}(N)$ has not previously been computed at $O(\alpha_s^3)$; we have now completed this calculation and will publish the results in a forthcoming paper. Additionally, we present numerical evaluations of $A_{gq}(N)$ for both $N_f=4$ and $N_f=5$ that can be utilized for phenomenological studies. Finally, we compare our findings with the $N_f=4$ component of the polarized gluon to quark transition function derived in a prior work. This study demonstrates the application of Bayesian artificial networks (Bayesian ANs) for classifying gamma-ray blazar sources within the Fermi-LAT 3FGL catalog. We utilized the publicly available XMM-Newton BLAZAR database to derive X-ray data for 3FGL sources, cross-referencing them with radio data from the NVSS catalog. Our methodology involved training Bayesian ANs using 3FGL sources with established radio and X-ray counterparts. The resulting models were applied to classify 3FGL sources, and the accuracy of this approach was validated against observations. Furthermore, we examined the posterior probability distributions of the Bayesian AN parameters to identify the characteristics of radio and X-ray BLAZAR sources. This research offers a novel perspective on the radio and X-ray properties of Fermi-LAT BLAZARs. Ultimately, we conclude that Bayesian ANs serve as an effective tool for classifying 3FGL sources. Additionally, we propose that radio and X-ray properties can be estimated by examining the prior and posterior distributions of Bayesian AN parameters. These findings may assist astronomers in understanding the nature of BLAZAR sources. Additionally, we derive an inclusion relationship regarding the tensor products of two graphs based on their adjacency spectra. In this context, we demonstrate that $0$ is always an eigenvalue of the spectral radius of the tensor product of two graphs, and we provide an explicit formula for the spectral radius of such a tensor product when the graphs involved are bipartite. This white paper outlines the case for an orbital space telescope designed to conduct high-resolution spectroscopy and imaging across the ultraviolet, blue, and near-infrared spectrum. The primary scientific justification stems from the significant gaps in our current knowledge of the early Universe, which can be effectively addressed by an instrument offering a broad wavelength range, wide field of view, and high-resolution imaging alongside high-throughput spectroscopy. Furthermore, the paper details the technology readiness levels of the proposed instrument and supporting technologies, demonstrating that a high-resolution spectrograph is achievable with existing capabilities, while other technologies are at various stages of development. The proposed telescope is envisioned as a partnership between ISRO and NASA, leveraging NASA's expertise in high-resolution spectroscopy and high-performance computing, alongside ISRO's robust space telescope program. This collaboration would enable the project to move forward as a joint mission. Additionally, the paper addresses the necessary ground-based support infrastructure, including advanced ground-based spectroscopy and the need for a dedicated astronomy supercomputing facility in India. Finally, the paper concludes by identifying the steps required to initiate the mission, such as establishing a joint task force and organizing a series of joint workshops to foster collaboration between the two agencies. Overall, the authors believe that the proposed joint mission is highly feasible and that initiating the process to bring it to fruition is of paramount importance. We hope this document inspires the Indian astronomical community to work together to realize this ambitious joint space mission. The full text is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02005. This study investigates natural cubic splines for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials. We propose a regression framework utilizing natural cubic splines to model the relationship between longitudinal biomarkers and time. The clinical focus centers on assessing the impact of trial drugs on these markers. Our methodology includes developing score tests for hypotheses regarding treatment effects and the treatment-by-spline-knot interaction. To enhance robustness, we create weighted least squares estimators that are resistant to outliers. Furthermore, we establish significance tests for treatment effects, offering a weighted least squares approach that achieves robustness against outlying treatment effects. Through simulations, we evaluate the performance of these hypothesis tests and demonstrate that our weighted treatment effect estimator yields more robust results than the standard estimator. Finally, we apply this technique to data from the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study (ADCS) 356 trial. Our analysis reveals that the drug significantly slows cognitive decline, with the magnitude of this effect varying across the trial's duration. Additionally, the drug demonstrates a significant effect on the primary outcome at specific time points, though not consistently throughout the study. These findings align with previous conclusions drawn from the same trial. The proposed methods are accessible via the `SplineFit` package on CRAN. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease, clinical trials, natural cubic spline, score test, weighted least squares, treatment effect. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 62F10, 62J10.

We present a method for optimizing the "penalty action functional" to identify dominant transition pathways. This global strategy identifies paths that balance minimal action with minimal departure from the natural system dynamics, thereby revealing multiple transition routes. The technique is validated through an activation problem and a realistic scenario involving the denaturation of the protein chymotrypsin inhibitor 2. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications across various fields. These results indicate that penalty functional optimization serves as a complementary approach to other transition path sampling variants, offering a straightforward global optimization framework that prioritizes accessibility and interpretability. These findings stem from a collaboration with the theoretical and computational groups at the University of Minnesota and the Max-Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems. Specifically, this work expands upon the study by S. Chen, C. Dellago, S. B. Headrick, S. Ma, J. D. Gezelter, and C. A. Broedersz, published in J. Chem. Phys. 156, 124103 (2022). The latter research was driven by the initial insight regarding the penalty functional's behavior as a transition path optimizer, an idea proposed by C.A.B. during his tenure at the Max-Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems in Dresden. Additionally, S.C., C.D., and J.D.G. contributed to developing a practical implementation of this approach. C.D. and S.C. collaborated on the application to chymotrypsin inhibitor 2, while S.C., S.M., and J.D.G. utilized the penalty functional to explore multiple paths in protein unfolding. Finally, S.C., J.D.G., and C.A.B. conducted benchmarking of the penalty functional against other transition path sampling variants. These contributions were integral to the development and refinement of the method, which has now been widely applied to investigate multiple transition routes in diverse systems. The resulting theoretical and computational advancements have significantly enriched our understanding of how systems traverse various transition routes, offering new avenues for targeted control and intervention. The theoretical and computational groups at the University of Minnesota and the Max-Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems have fostered a vibrant exchange of ideas that has driven these significant advances. We are deeply grateful for the stimulating discussions and collaborations that have contributed to this progress. We extend our sincere thanks to all members of both groups for their invaluable input and support. We are particularly indebted to our colleagues, whose insights and contributions have been instrumental in advancing this field

By employing a novel parabolic extension of the Alexandroff maximum principle, we derive new Alexandroff-Yau-Harnack inequalities. These findings not only extend the previously established $S$-type and Kohn-McKean estimates but also offer a more streamlined proof for the Kohn-McKean estimate. Furthermore, we utilize the Kohn-McKean method to address an open question regarding parabolic complex Monge-Ampère equations. Additionally, our methodology offers a more concise and effective approach to the Kohn-McKean estimate compared to the original formulation. Finally, we provide a novel application of these $L^{\infty}$ evaluations to the regularity analysis of the parabolic Monge-Ampère equation. Specifically, we demonstrate that if the initial data $u_0$ and the boundary value function $\varphi$ belong to $C^{1,1}$, then the solution $u$ is guaranteed to be in $C^{1,1}$. This demonstrates that the Kohn-McKean estimate serves as a potent instrument for examining the regularity of parabolic complex Monge-Ampère equations. Additionally, the techniques employed in this work may hold potential for other applications. This study investigates the computational and logical characteristics of two classes of (multi-variable) functions mapping $\mathbb{N}^p$ to $\mathbb{N}^q$: \mbox{SubReg}, comprising all sub-regional functions, and \mbox{SubReg$_0$}, which includes those sub-regional functions vanishing outside a bounded domain. We demonstrate that SubReg$_0$ constitutes a boolean algebra and identify $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^{2k}$ as its free generator. Furthermore, we establish that SubReg and SubReg$_0$ are recursively equivalent, with a polynomial-time reduction existing from the former to the latter. Regarding lambda-calculi, we define $\lambda_{\mathsf{subreg}}$ and $\lambda_{\subreg0}$, the fragments of the lambda-calus of functions capable of interpreting all functions in SubReg and SubReg$_0$, respectively. We provide characterizations of these fragments based on their normal forms and the simplest functions within them. Additionally, we introduce $\lambda_{\subreg}$ and $\lambda_{\subreg0}$, fragments derived from the typed lambda-calus of functions by restricting to types $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^{2k}$ and $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}^k$. The primary findings of this work are that each of the four identified fragments is functionally complete for its corresponding class of functions. Finally, we offer characterizations of $\lambda_{\subreg}$ and $\lambda_{\subreg0}$ through their most expressive types and the $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$-valued functions representable within them. The research also features several examples and counter-examples. Notably, the fragment $\lambda_{\subreg}$ is shown to be reducible to the lambda-calus of functions and SubReg to the class of E-regular functions, yet no such reductions exist for $\lambda_{\subreg0}$ or SubReg$_0$. The paper concludes with several open questions. **Keywords:** lambda-calculi, boolean algebras, regular functions, typed lambda-calculi. **MSC 2010:** 03D15, 03D20, 03D60, 03E30, 03E72, 03B72

This text serves as a technical appendix focused on nonstandard integration theory. It briefly outlines the motivations and fundamental principles of the Stratonovich integral, which are essential for understanding the construction of conditional distribution flows. Additionally, it demonstrates the equivalence between the Stratonovich and Itô integrals when applied to a specific class of functionals. These concepts are vital for comprehending Itô calculus, as well as for the associated theoretical and practical challenges. This study examines the geometry of certain metric spaces associated with specific metric groups. We present examples of hyperbolic groups, including those arising from free class groups of hyperbolic groups and certain K-theory groups of free groups, that are not Sturmian. Additionally, we offer metric space examples that fail to possess the properties of either hyperbolic or Sturmian spaces. Our analysis relies on the properties of geodesic bicombings and the asymptotic behavior of geodesic triangles. The paper concludes with several open questions. Notably, we demonstrate that a proper length space equipped with a geodesic bicombing exhibits properties closely resembling the cone structure found in hyperbolic spaces. Furthermore, we establish that every one-complex geodesic space is Sturmian and contains a finite graph as a subspace under a Gromov-hyperbolic embedding. These findings provide a framework for constructing new examples of hyperbolic and Sturmian metric spaces. The construction of hyperbolic groups via their class groups was inspired by the work of J. Meier. We extend this approach to certain K-groups within the context of graphs. Additionally, we construct examples of hyperbolic groups that are not finitely presented by utilizing metric spaces that are neither hyperbolic nor Sturmian. This study tackles cross-domain text-to-SQL by introducing an Auxiliary Task Learning (ATL) approach that employs a two-stream framework. The initial stream performs standard text-to-SQL mapping, while the secondary stream executes an auxiliary task learning stream (ATLS) dedicated to query understanding. The ATLS leverages query annotations to generate queries with varied complexities, thereby serving as an auxiliary process to facilitate cross-domain text-to-SQL mapping. Empirical evaluations across two benchmark domains, Spider and DBpedia-EntityLink, demonstrate that our ATL S framework achieves competitive performance relative to existing methods. Furthermore, our analysis of the model's behavior and performance reveals that the proposed ATL S approach offers a promising avenue for advancing cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/EECDSQL. Additionally, we present a novel dataset, Cross-Domain-SQL-1K, which integrates queries from two distinct domains, Spider and DBpedia-EntityLink, available at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/Cross-Domain-SQL-1K. We anticipate this resource will prove valuable for enhancing cross-domain text-to-SQL research. Finally, we illustrate how our method can be utilized to generate queries with diverse complexities, offering a potential solution for aiding query understanding. The accompanying paper details the methodology, dataset, and results, with the full study accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03509. We hope this work will contribute meaningfully to the field of cross-domain text-to-SQL. Our methodology addresses the challenge where queries across different domains exhibit varying levels of complexity, a factor that significantly impacts cross-domain text-to-SQL performance. By utilizing auxiliary task learning, we demonstrate how to mitigate the effects of query complexity in this context. The paper explores methodologies, datasets, and results, with the full study available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03509. This work addresses the issue of queries having diverse complexities across different domains, a factor that greatly influences cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks. This paper introduces a new Information-Focused Risk-aware Model Predictive Control (IFFMPC) framework designed for secure navigation in multi-robot systems within uncertain environments. The approach utilizes a multi-layered cost function to prioritize the reduction of uncertainty in both the robot's position and orientation. The initial layer employs a risk-aware uncertainty reduction function, utilizing set-valued information filters to quantify uncertainty reduction across position and orientation. Subsequently, the second and third layers apply model predictive control to generate a risk-aware trajectory that minimizes total uncertainty reduction while ensuring safe navigation. This method is applicable to systems where position and orientation are coupled, allowing robots to dynamically select their uncertainty reduction focus based on environmental conditions. The study demonstrates the efficacy of IFFMPC through simulation results featuring three robots navigating an uncertain setting. Additionally, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of the framework's stability and convergence properties. Finally, the proposed approach is benchmarked against two alternative strategies, revealing that IFFMPC outperforms the alternatives by generating more appropriate uncertainty reduction decisions in uncertain settings. A theoretical analysis of the IFFMPC framework is included in the appendix. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/IFFMPC. Non-orthogonal sequence design is essential for grant-free massive connectivity, aiming to create a large set of sequences that maintain distinguishability despite inherent design constraints. This study introduces a novel two-stage genetic sequence designer. In the first stage, a genetic algorithm generates a diverse collection of initial sequences. The second stage involves mapping these collections to hypercubes of Hamming space via an isometric transformation; subsequently, a second genetic algorithm refines the sequence collection by optimizing the representation of the hypercube's corners. The performance of this proposed designer is evaluated based on the trade-off between the size of the generated sequence collection and the minimum Hamming distance between them. Simulation results demonstrate that, for a fixed minimum Hamming distance, the proposed designer produces significantly larger sequence collections compared to four existing methods. Furthermore, when compared to a random generator, the proposed approach achieves superior results in both maximum sequence size and minimum Hamming distance. Finally, experimental evidence confirms that utilizing the proposed designer leads to substantial gains in detection probability and reduces the required transmission power by 10 dB within grant-free grant-free massive machine type communication systems. Additionally, the detection probability of the proposed sequences exceeds that of existing methods by 10% to 20%. The design algorithm is implemented in Python and is publicly accessible. This study examines various approximations for modeling humid air, focusing on equations of state and constitutive relations for humid air vapor. The analysis evaluates the thermodynamic coherence of these models and identifies a thermodynamically consistent variant of the ideal gas law for mixed vapors. Additionally, the parametric law is enhanced to increase its thermodynamic coherence and practical utility. The paper concludes by formulating thermodynamically coherent sets of constitutive equations for humid air, derived from both the Zamfirescu equation of state and the parametric law. Finally, the applicability and accuracy of each set are assessed based on their respective domains of validity. The research confirms the practical relevance of these new models and explicitly defines their limits of validity. A key advantage highlighted is that the proposed thermodynamically coherent set for humid air can be readily adapted for use as an equation of state for other mixed ideal vapors. This capability is achieved by adjusting specific model parameters based on the specific enthalpy and temperature of the vapor mixture. Consequently, this approach significantly simplifies the modeling process for mixed ideal vapors. All equations of state and constitutive sets for humid air are provided in both dry-bulb temperature and specific humidity forms, as well as in absolute temperature and molar fraction forms. Furthermore, the derived Zamfirescu-based equation for mixed ideal vapors is the first to achieve both forms, a significant improvement over prior versions of the Zamirescu equation that were only available in temperature and mole fraction form. Additionally, the parametric law equation for mixed ideal vapors is presented for the first time in both absolute temperature and molar fraction form, whereas previous versions were limited to the temperature and mole fraction variant. To support these findings, the validity ranges for each equation of set are illustrated through plots of the relative error in specific heat capacity as a function of temperature. These graphs demonstrate the accuracy of the equations across their respective validity ranges. The determination of these ranges relies on the maximum relative error, a criterion that is both simple and practical. Finally, the methodology for calculating the thermodynamic properties of mixed ideal vapors using the proposed equations is also established. This approach allows for the determination of validity ranges for the Zamfirescu equation and its parametric law equivalent when applied to other mixed ideal vapors. The concept of the sum of two matroids is extended to define the \textit{subalgebra} and \textit{generated subalgebra} of a matroid. This paper outlines the fundamental properties and characteristics of these structures. A matroid defined on a universal set $\Omega$ is termed \textit{closed} if its independent sets constitute a subalgebra of all $\emptyset,\Omega$-partitions. The text demonstrates that every matroid possesses a maximal closed submatroid, which serves as the analog to the commutator of a group. Furthermore, the \textit{commutator rank} of a matroid is defined as the rank of this maximal closed submatroid. The work also investigates the properties of matroids with a commutator rank of $0$ and $1$, and explores the $\text{GL}_2(\mathbb{F})$-invariant of matroids, specifically examining its relationship with the commutator rank. A key finding is that the commutator rank equals $0$ if and only if the matroid is representable over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The paper concludes by listing several questions and conjectures for future research. This study forms part of the author's PhD thesis, with related work detailed in \cite{Borovikov2021}. Additional context can be found in \cite{Borovikov2020}. The terminology and notation are derived from \cite{Borovikov2020}. The author's contact email is borovikov.i.a.\ at gmail.com. This paper introduces a new method for dialogue state monitoring (DSM) in dialogue systems. Our approach models the uncertainty of automatic speech recognition (ASR) and natural language understanding (NLU) within spoken dialogue using Word Confusion Networks (wCNs) and feature engineering, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first instance of modeling wCN uncertainty for effective DSM. We conducted experiments on the CASINO dialogue system platform, which supports multiple domains and tasks. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating ASR and NLU uncertainties in DSM significantly enhances correction performance. Furthermore, the proposed method surpasses existing techniques in accuracy while reducing latency and computational complexity. Finally, we evaluate the robustness of our approach across varying ASR confidence levels and input perturbation levels. These results underscore the method's effectiveness and robustness for practical application in real-world dialogue systems. This paper introduces a mathematical model for the minimal intricate structures within universal entry frameworks, which include mathematical, physical, and linguistic systems. The concept of "intricacy" is derived from the complexity of logical networks, specifically through the complexity of their nodes and the complexity of the connections between them. Nodes are characterized by the minimal number of bits required to represent their states, while the complexity of a connection refers to the minimum bits needed to define the relationship between two nodes. We demonstrate that structures achieving minimal intricacy in universal entry frameworks are remarkably simple, consisting of a single node with internal connections. The inherent complexity of these nodes is determined by the framework's alphabet size, a parameter that varies across different systems. Furthermore, the complexity of the connections between these nodes is governed by the relationships defined within the framework. Finally, we discuss the significance of intricacy as a measure for the minimum resources required to implement a universal machine for each framework. The results indicate that minimal intricacy corresponds to minimal resource consumption in mathematical machines, moderate consumption in physical machines, and substantial consumption in symbolic machines. Consequently, the concept of intricacy provides a quantitative basis for explaining the hierarchy among mathematical, physical, and symbolic machines. This approach offers a new perspective on the Hierarchy Problem in modern physics, suggesting that the hierarchy may arise from the fundamental differences in the intricacy of universal entry frameworks. Intricacy serves as a new physical quantity that can be applied to characterize the properties of matter and energy. Additionally, we propose that the minimal structures of universal entry frameworks represent a new state of matter, which we term "universal matter." We outline the properties of this matter and suggest that it may be a viable candidate for dark matter. Finally, we conclude that the intricate nature of universal matter provides a potential solution to the problem of matter-antimatter asymmetry. A detailed analysis of these results will be presented in a future publication. This study presents a comparative analysis of turbulence data from JET discharges with and without a toroidal field ripple. This comparison is essential for distinguishing between the two primary theories regarding Palm Tree Modes (PTMs): the shear-tearing mode theory and the turbulence theory. The analysis utilizes high-resolution, non-invasive diagnostics, specifically the JET Imaging Reflectometry (JIM-R) and the JET Edge Scanning Reflectometry (JESS-R), to investigate the PTM's structure, phase, and radial wavenumber. Our findings indicate that PTMs are small-scale turbulence structures, with radial wavenumbers aligning closely with E × B vortices. Additionally, we observed that PTMs exhibit a strong correlation with edge turbulence, suggesting they may represent a specific manifestation of Edge-Localized Modes (ELMs) on a smaller scale. Finally, we demonstrate that the phase of PTMs is consistent with the existence of a large-scale mode. Collectively, these results support both the turbulence and shear-tearing mode theories, implying that Palm Tree Modes likely arise from the interaction between small-scale turbulence and large-scale magnetic perturbations. Furthermore, we show that a simple model based on the linearization of the MHD energy principle can account for the observed characteristics of these modes. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future research. This work is based on research conducted during the author's PhD thesis at the Max-Planck-Institut für Plasmaphysik, Garching, Germany. Continual learning (CL) aims to master a sequence of tasks without forgetting prior ones, a capability essential for the ongoing updates of deep neural networks in real-world scenarios. Recently, CL research has increasingly focused on leveraging pretrained models, particularly those pretrained on large-scale data like ImageNet, to enhance performance. However, this trend introduces new challenges, such as catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning and suboptimal results compared to training from scratch. To address these issues and question the efficacy of using pretrained models, we propose a straightforward baseline that matches the performance of leading methods while being easier to implement. Our approach employs a simple fine-tuning strategy to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, eliminating the need for complex rehearsal techniques or dynamic network architectures. Furthermore, our baseline outperforms other methods even when the latter use pretrained models and intricate regularization strategies. Additionally, extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results even when fine-tuning on ImageNet, a resource often considered a prerequisite for success in CL. The implementation is available at https://github.com/ChenYixuan0719/straightforward-cl. Finally, we hope our baseline will inspire the community to reevaluate the necessity of relying on pretrained models in continual learning. All code and data required to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/ChenYixuan0719/straightforward-cl. Chen Yuanfeng is the corresponding author. This study addresses the task of identifying hate speech across three social media platforms—Facebook, Twitter, and Reddit—using multiple modalities: text, images, and user profiles. To enhance model interpretability and enable more effective countermeasures against hate speech, we incorporate three explanation techniques into our framework. Furthermore, we introduce a novel dataset of user-generated comments annotated with self-reported reasons for posting, allowing us to assess whether our classifications align with users' own motivations. Finally, we analyze the strengths and limitations of integrating these reason-based annotations into classification systems. The code and data for this work are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/understandable-hate. Our results demonstrate a strong correlation between a model's performance and the prevalence of reasons matching its outputs, indicating that comprehension of user intent is crucial for successful classification. Additionally, we find that our explanation methods reveal a significant disparity in the reasons cited on Facebook compared to Twitter and Reddit. Finally, by fine-tuning a pre-trained BERT model with reason-based data, we show that BERT-based architectures can be trained to identify the reasons behind user comments. These findings offer new avenues for leveraging reason-based information in hate speech classification and suggest promising future research directions for natural language processing. This study examines heterogeneous networks linking excitatory and inhibitory Type-I neurons, analyzing how power-law degree distributions influence both average firing rates and oscillatory dynamics. Utilizing the mean-field approach, we derive conditions for the coexistence of active and quiescent states, oscillatory versus resting states, and the onset of local field potential (LFP) oscillations. Our findings indicate that networks featuring power-law degree distributions can sustain stable oscillations across a broad spectrum of average firing rates, a property attributed to the presence of highly connected hub neurons. These results align with experimental data showing that hub cells in the hippocampus exhibit higher average firing rates than non-hub cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that networks with power-law degree distributions maintain stable oscillations even when perturbed by external inputs, a trait linked to the robustness of hub cells against perturbations. Finally, our predictions regarding LFP stability in perturbed networks are supported by recent experimental evidence. These insights offer a potential explanation for the prevalence of LFP oscillations in the healthy brain. Additionally, we show that networks with log-normal degree distributions also support stable oscillations, consistent with the observation that log-normal distributions often emerge as the limit of power-law distributions under specific growth dynamics. This suggests that both power-law and log-normal degree distributions are plausible in biological systems. Consequently, networks with these types of degree distributions may facilitate the emergence of LFP oscillations, thereby enhancing the brain's computational capabilities. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for understanding the effects of hub cell loss in epilepsy. Our analysis reveals that hub cell loss can disrupt LFP oscillations, potentially explaining the reduced LFP power observed in patients with hippocampal sclerosis. This underscores the critical role of hub cells in maintaining LFP oscillations. Overall, our findings highlight the significance of hub cells in both healthy and pathological brain conditions. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of the mean-field approach in studying large-scale brain networks, as it enables the investigation of complex networks with power-law or log-normal degree distributions without relying on the unrealistic assumption of a mean-field degree distribution. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel perspective known as antagonistic patch creation. This approach aims to generate repair code that can differentiate between correct and incorrect executions of a program. The capability region (CR) of a graph is defined as the union of the spectra of all its subgraphs. This concept was recently explored in the paper "On the capability region of a path graph" within Linear Algebra and its Applications, which demonstrated that the CR of a path graph $P_n$ forms a line segment connecting the spectra of $P_1$ (a single vertex) and $P_2$ (two connected vertices). This article generalizes those findings in two significant ways. First, we examine graphs with non-negative entries, proving that their capability region is convex—a property not necessarily true for general graphs. This finding enables the construction of a novel family of matrices, denoted $A_{k,n}$, whose capability region is precisely the line segment connecting the spectra of $A_{k,1}$ and $A_{k,2}$. Second, we investigate the continuous capability region (CCR), defined as the set of spectra for all possible continuous deformations of a graph. We establish that the CCR of $A_{k,n}$ is the entire complex plane, a stark contrast to the bounded, one-dimensional CR. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of matrices with a CCR equal to the entire complex plane and demonstrate that the CCR of a matrix is invariant under matrix similarity. The study begins with the definition and fundamental properties of the CR and CCR, followed by an outline of the paper's structure. Section 2 addresses the convexity of the CR for graphs featuring non-negative entries. In Section 3, we define the CCR and present methods for calculating it, starting with grid graphs. The final section introduces the concept of the continuous deformed spectrum, which is essential for understanding the CCR. Finally, in Section 4, we analyze the specific case of graph capability regions by linking the eigenvalues of a graph matrix to the roots of a corresponding polynomial. This approach yields the exact capability region for a specific class of matrices and, more broadly, allows for the calculation of the CR for matrices where the degree of the characteristic polynomial does not exceed 2. The capability region of a matrix is defined by the union of the spectra of all its submatrices, and the techniques developed in this work are applicable to the study of such regions. The collision architecture of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions is analyzed through the evolution of the equation-of-state (EoS). This work introduces 3-dimensional flow examination (3DE), a new diagnostic tool designed to investigate collision dynamics and the quark-gluon plasma EoS. 3DE is modeled using three orthogonal planes: the reaction plane, the symmetry plane, and the vertical plane. The methodology is first validated using ideal hydrodynamic simulations of Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV, followed by an analysis of experimental data. Homicide rates in Brazil have historically been used as indicators of social instability. While numerous studies have analyzed these rates using methods like principal component analysis, factor analysis, and spatial econometrics, they often overlook the spatial heterogeneity inherent in the data. This study examines the spatial distribution of homicide rates across Brazil's Goias province between 2002 and 2014, analyzing how specific socioeconomic and environmental factors influence these rates. By employing a spatial lag regression model, the research identifies distinct clusters of high and low homicide rates. The findings suggest that the spatial lag model is effective for this analysis, revealing that homicides are concentrated in specific municipalities within Goias. Furthermore, the study confirms the impact of various socioeconomic and environmental variables on these rates. Ultimately, this approach offers valuable insights for policymakers by highlighting the spatial characteristics of the data. Additionally, a comparison with a standard fixed effects regression model demonstrates the superior performance of the spatial lag model. The code for all analyses is publicly accessible. A detailed comparison with other spatial and non-spatial models is provided in our working paper (Vieira et al., 2019). Given Goias's significant role in Brazil's homicide landscape, this research holds particular relevance for the country. Furthermore, the authors have committed to replicating this study in other Brazilian provinces, such as Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, to extend these findings. This paper investigates the convergence properties of an accelerated stochastic gradient descent (SGD) method, a topic that has received limited attention in prior literature. Specifically, this study focuses on a rapid SGD variant, previously explored in \cite{balsubramanian2017}, which employs a larger step-size than conventional SGD to achieve comparable convergence rates. This approach is particularly advantageous for processing audio data, given its inherent non-stationarity and sparsity. Furthermore, we propose modifications to stochastic gradient descent and accelerated stochastic gradient descent to enhance their suitability for audio streams characterized by varying sampling rates. These adjustments involve reweighting gradient estimates to ensure robust convergence across different sampling frequencies, thereby maintaining a consistent convergence rate regardless of the audio's sampling speed. This reweighting strategy effectively mitigates biases introduced by irregular sampling frequencies. Additionally, we examine a rapid SGD variant that achieves convergence rates equivalent to standard SGD while operating at a significantly faster pace. Our findings indicate that both the standard and accelerated SGD variants converge robustly under different sampling frequencies, with performance scaling linearly relative to the sampling rate. Finally, we present numerical results that validate our theoretical analysis. **Background:** The integration of free-breathing motion correction with respiration correction is essential for high-quality, reproducible 4D (3D+respiration) MRI of the body. This study evaluates the feasibility of free-breathing motion correction in 4D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) MRI for the abdomen, pelvis, and breast.

**Methods:** Fifteen healthy volunteers underwent free-breathing 4D T2-weighted 3D T2-TSE scans targeting the liver, pelvis, and breast. A single-shot 2D phase-contrast navigator was employed for motion correction, while respiratory gating ensured consistent coverage of the region of interest (ROI). The resulting free-breathing volumes were retrospectively corrected to generate reproducible 4D volumes. Image quality and coverage were assessed using a 5-point scale.

**Results:** Free-breathing motion correction successfully produced reproducible 4D volumes in 95% of cases. When respiratory gating was applied, 100% of 4D volumes exhibited complete coverage of the targeted organs.

**Conclusion:** The study demonstrates that free-breathing motion correction combined with respiratory gating yields complete coverage in 4D T2-weighted 3D T2-TSE MRI for the liver, pelvis, and breast. This free-breathing approach is equivalent to breath-holding techniques and offers superior reproducibility. Furthermore, the free-breathing motion correction method is generalizable to various pulse sequences and can be combined with other correction strategies, such as respiratory gating.

**Key Words:** MRI, Turbo spin-echo, Respiration correction, Motion correction, Free-breathing.

Model compression techniques have long been employed to reduce the computational footprint of deep neural networks, a necessity for deploying high-performance models in resource-constrained environments. Among these approaches, knowledge distillation stands out for its ability to transfer expert knowledge from a large teacher model to a compact student, yielding superior performance. However, existing distillation methods often overlook the internal data flow within the student, a factor that significantly influences its learning trajectory. This work presents a data flow-preserving knowledge distillation method that maintains the internal data flow of teacher convolutional layers when training student models. By aligning the internal representations of teacher convolutional kernels with those of student filters, this approach ensures that the student retains a flow structure similar to the teacher's, thereby enhancing out-of-distribution generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a 1.0% increase in top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with a reduced student model size, and a 2.0% gain on CIFAR-100, all while maintaining the same input-output structure. Pastoralists frequently reside in regions beyond their livestock grazing lands, a situation that can lead to unauthorized grazing despite conservation initiatives. This study investigates the ecological consequences of such non-resident grazing on dry-land vegetation using a dry-land plant dynamics model that incorporates both resident and non-resident grazing, analyzed via local stability and bifurcation methods. The research identifies two key thresholds: the eigenvalue threshold and the bifurcation value. Through numerical simulations, the dynamics of the system under non-local grazing pressure are explored. The findings indicate that non-resident grazing can trigger various ecological transitions, including plant extinction, the loss of stability in plant populations, and a decline in the average number of coexisting plant species. These results underscore the necessity of engaging local communities in land management decisions and the importance of monitoring plant diversity to assess the impact of non-resident grazing activities. Additionally, the study offers several recommendations for conservation efforts aimed at mitigating the effects of non-resident grazing. Finally, this research contributes to the broader understanding of how human activities influence dry-land plant dynamics. Future work will focus on expanding the model to include competition between plants and functional responses for herbivores, alongside an investigation into the effects of climate change. CountSketch is a widely used method for estimating the $\ell_2$ norm of high-dimensional vectors. Although the sketch size is typically selected based on the target accuracy, the resulting error bounds fail to hold for all possible samples from the distribution. This shortcoming is particularly problematic in adaptive learning scenarios, where a learner must guarantee that the sketch remains sufficiently accurate at every step. To address this, we introduce a refined analysis of CountSketch that accounts for a specified number of adaptive queries, ensuring accurate estimates at each step. This analysis demonstrates that a slightly larger sketch is necessary to ensure with high probability that all estimates remain within the desired range. We establish that this revised analysis is optimal and provide a lower bound indicating that a larger sketch is indeed required to maintain accuracy for every sample in the adaptive learning setting. Furthermore, we extend these results to the online learning context. Finally, we present a lower bound for the general problem of $\ell_2$ norm estimation under adaptive queries, which surpasses the bounds previously established by Orlovsky et al. [2019]. Our findings indicate that, in the worst-case scenario, CountSketch requires a sketch size of $\Omega(\log^2 n \cdot \log^2 T)$ to ensure accurate estimates for $T$ adaptive queries with high probability. Additionally, we explore the application of CountSketch to the heavy-tailed streaming problem, showing that our analysis yields a competitive algorithm for this task. Income distribution is a fundamental aspect of economic systems. This paper examines a two-agent economic model featuring brokers. Our theoretical framework establishes a foundation for the hypothesis that brokers enhance income, and numerical simulations indicate that agents interacting through brokers achieve higher earnings. Furthermore, we propose that both-rich and rich-poor income distributions can arise depending on the specific parameters. The model incorporates brokers within the Vicsek-like agent-based framework, which is grounded in statistical physics. We contend that income can be modeled as the time-average velocity of agents. The study also addresses the issue of breaking the zero-average-velocity constraint. We demonstrate that income distributions follow a power-law law, and both the income-brother correlation and income-agent correlation are positive. Additionally, we found that the income-brother correlation is stronger than the income-agent correlation. These results suggest that brokers play a significant role in an agent-based economic model. Finally, we note that both the income-broker and income-agent correlations exhibit a power-law relationship with income. Overall, this research indicates that brokers are crucial for agent-based economic models. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the theoretical background, while Section 3 details the results, and Section 4 provides the conclusion.
