Data distillation involves training a single compact model to replicate the capabilities of numerous base models, offering a cost-effective alternative to ensembles. However, the performance of distilled models often lags behind that of their base counterparts. This paper investigates the root causes of this performance gap and introduces a solution by analyzing successful abstractive summarization plans. Our key insight is that effective planning for generated summaries is driven by the dynamic prompts of news entities. To leverage this, we developed a novel condensation framework that utilizes base model generation plans to guide the training of distilled models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework significantly enhances the performance of generated summaries, thereby improving the quality of distilled models. Furthermore, we show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art abstractive data distillation methods. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our method using a zero-shot model for the CNN/DailyNews dataset. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/EEPE.

Keywords: Data Distillation, Planning, Entity Prompts, Abstractive Summarization.

This paper establishes specific sufficient conditions for the differentiability of an $n$-dimensional function based on the differentiability of an $(n-1)$-dimensional function. These findings are derived from and extend existing theorems regarding sufficient conditions for differentiability. As applications, the work confirms sufficient conditions for partial differentiability and further elucidates distinctions between the differentiability of an $n$-dimensional function and that of an $(n-1)$-dimensional function. Finally, examples are provided to demonstrate that certain conditions proposed in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are not necessarily satisfied. Keywords: Differentiability, Differentiable function, Equivalent infinite differentiable function, Equivalent differentiable function. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 26B05, 26A16.

This study introduces a computational approach to assess vocal entrainment within dialogic scenarios. Entrainment is measured by comparing the inter-pausal intervals (IPIs) of dialogue partners, specifically by examining the differences in IPIs between adjacent utterances. While prior research indicates that skilled dialogue partners display similar IPIs, our analysis of the "Nico" corpus revealed that IPI similarities are not consistent across all local contexts. Instead, these similarities vary based on the distance to the preceding speaker, suggesting that IPIs are influenced by the local discourse history. To evaluate a computational agent's skill in entraining with human partners, we developed a method that utilizes this sentence-distance dependency. We trained the method on a dyadic corpus and validated it on a separate corpus, Nico-NYC. The findings demonstrate that the approach effectively predicts human ratings of agent skill. Furthermore, the method was applied to quantify variations in vocal entrainment across three conditions of common ground sharing during dialogue. These results align with existing literature, indicating that reduced common ground leads to decreased IPI similarity and diminished human assessments of the agent's skill. The proposed methodology is designed to be adaptable for evaluating computational agents across various entrainment metrics. Finally, the article concludes by outlining the advantages of the method for future research on social interaction and computational social agents. The accompanying code is publicly accessible. This paper introduces a categorical model for a quantum-like formalism, specifically within the lambda calculus, to represent the manipulation of the quantum state space of a single qubit. We define the Sigma_1 type as the collection of all possible manipulations (functions) that transform an initial state into a final state without altering the system, alongside their associated operators. This set is demonstrated to possess the structure of a lambda calculus monadic type, a property essential for modeling quantum computations. Furthermore, the (composable) action of these manipulations on a state is represented by a monadic action, which is proven to constitute a comonoid. Finally, the model is shown to satisfy the axioms of a categorical comonoid, thereby enabling the modeling of quantum-like state manipulation. The study concludes by identifying an open research question regarding the extension of this formalism to multi-qubit systems. This approach builds upon our prior work, which defined the quantum state space of a single qubit as the unit sphere in the complex Hilbert space C^2 and defined manipulations as operators that rotate the state around a fixed axis in C^2. The categorical model presented here serves as the foundation for our subsequent paper, which details the modeling of quantum computations using this framework. Additionally, the formalism is shown to be applicable to other sets of manipulations, such as those involving manipulators that reflect a state across a fixed hyperplane in C^2. The paper begins by reviewing the model of quantum state manipulation, followed by an introduction to monads and comonads within category theory. The third section presents the model of manipulations as monads, while the fourth and fifth sections demonstrate that the action of these manipulations on a state forms a monadic action that constitutes a comonoid, with the latter section providing a proof of the axiom of a categorical comonoid. The final section outlines manipulations as a monad and their action on a state as a comonoid, concluding with an outline of an open problem. This work is partially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant no. 1304009. The authors thank Dr. John L. Casti for his valuable comments and suggestions. Keywords: Quantum Computation, Lambda Calculus, Category Theory, Monads, Comonoids.

We introduce precise analytical solutions for the ground state containing two quasiparticles across various fractional quantum Hall effect states. These new findings offer substantial insights into how state complexity influences correlation functions and allow for exact calculation of the fractional charge within the quasiparticle wavefunction. Additionally, we propose two further precise analytical states that represent reasonable approximations for quasiparticle-quasihole pairs. The fractional charge derived from these quasihole pairs aligns closely with results from quasiparticle-only states, suggesting these new configurations effectively describe quasiparticle-quasihole pairs. We validate these findings using variational Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate that the fractional charge in quasihole-quasiparticle pairs matches our analytical predictions. These quasihole-quasiparticle pairs exhibit greater complexity than the quasiparticle-only states, yet their fractional charges remain consistent. These discoveries significantly enhance our understanding of quasiparticle interactions in the fractional quantum Hall effect. Furthermore, these new states may facilitate more accurate simulations of the charge content in three-quasiparticle correlations. Finally, our results may improve the precision of experimental measurements for quasiparticle fractional charges. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant DMR-1900630. This study addresses a Stokes variational inequality arising in the modeling of glacier surface velocity. Velocity estimates are sought within the admissible set defined by the nonpenetration condition at the glacier bed and lateral margins. The problem is classified as semicoercive due to the presence of essential boundary conditions at the bed and lateral sides, the absence of a condition at the glacier surface, and the presence of linear growth conditions on the traction. A nonconforming finite element method is proposed, with convergence proofs provided in the energy norm. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the convergence rate and demonstrate the method's applicability. These simulations compare the nonconforming variational formulation against a mixed formulation derived via Fichets' trick, which converts the variational inequality into a system of equations. Both approaches are shown to yield comparable results. The implementation details are available in the user-friendly open-source software PyFEQ. Finally, the numerical results are compared against an analytical solution for a model case. This comparison, along with the discrepancy between variational formulations, is discussed in relation to the specific geometry of the domain. Furthermore, an estimate of the glacier's surface velocity is provided and analyzed. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. Finally, the derivation of the variational formulation is detailed, incorporating the specific boundary conditions inherent to glaciers. This includes the lack of boundary conditions at the surface, the application of the Coulomb friction law at the bed, and the enforcement of nonpenetration conditions at the lateral sides. The derivation adheres to the principles of continuum mechanics. The variational formulation is subsequently discretized using a nonconforming finite element method, with the resulting system of equations solved via a direct approach. Finally, the paper examines the implications of the variational inequality on the boundary conditions at the glacier surface. The finite element method is applied to two-dimensional models of a temperate glacier sliding over a Coulomb bed, with results presented for a single glacier in the Southern Hemisphere and a hypothetical glacier in the Northern Hemisphere. The Southern Hemisphere glacier is modeled as sliding on a bedrock inclined at 10 degrees, while the Northern Hemisphere glacier features a bedrock with a Coulomb friction coefficient of 0.05 and a surface slope of 15 degrees. The numerical results indicate that the variational formulation yields a traction vector at the glacier surface that is not perpendicular to the surface, thereby violating the expected boundary condition. We introduce DUVET, a multi-wavelength survey of the starburst galaxy M82, designed to investigate how galactic outflows regulate star formation. By analyzing the outflow's morphology, we determined that it is collimated within a 10-degree cone, with a base extending 10 kpc from the nucleus. This structure is visible in the UV, H$\alpha$, and 24$\mu$m bands, though it appears more dispersed in the latter. We identified a strong correlation between H$\alpha$ and 24$\mu$m emission, indicating that outflow-driven star formation is most intense near the galactic center. Furthermore, comparing the H$\alpha$ star formation rate surface density ($\Sigma_{SFR}$) against the outflow's projected surface density ($\Sigma_{out}$) reveals that $\Sigma_{SFR}$ drops sharply at distances greater than 1 kpc, suggesting a direct causal role for the outflow in forming stars. Finally, we examined the relationship between the outflow and the H$\alpha$-derived gas mass surface density ($\Sigma_{gas}$). The ratio $\Sigma_{out}/\Sigma_{gas}$ is highest within 1 kpc of the center, implying that outflows are most effective at removing gas from the central region. These findings support the hypothesis that outflows influence star formation on both local and global scales. Additionally, we detected a 1.5 kpc diameter cavity in the H$\alpha$-derived gas mass surface density centered on the galactic core, which aligns with the outflow's projected footprint. This cavity suggests that galactic outflows can clear gas from galactic centers on a timescale of approximately 10 million years. Our results demonstrate that outflows influence star formation on both local and global scales, and they provide evidence that galactic outflows can remove gas from galactic centers within roughly 10 million years. These findings offer support for the feedback loop model of galactic evolution. Our study represents the first spatially resolved analysis of outflow impacts on star formation and gas removal in a starburst galaxy. This study examines the impact of the phase-space structure on the multiphase transport model's description of experimentally measured elliptic and triangular flow harmonics ($v_2$ and $v_3$) across Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV. The results indicate that the model's ability to reproduce $v_3$ in both collision systems is more sensitive to the phase-space configuration than its reproduction of $v_2$. Consequently, the optimal setup for accurately modeling $v_3$ involves a smaller initial participant density, a shorter system lifetime, and a higher initial temperature. These findings suggest that the source of $v_3$ in the model arises from the initial phase-space distribution rather than the later-stage space-time geometry. Furthermore, a more precise reproduction of $v_3$ is achieved when the model incorporates a larger initial temperature, a shorter lifetime, and a reduced initial participant density. These observations are consistent with the presence of initial hot spots, which are known to be the primary source of $v_3$. Finally, we conclude that the model's description of $v_3$ is highly dependent on the initial conditions and the subsequent evolution of the created matter. This sensitivity underscores the critical need for a more precise characterization of the initial matter configuration to achieve a more accurate reproduction of $v_3$. Additionally, this analysis highlights the necessity of a more precise understanding of the initial matter configuration for both the AMPT and UrQMD models. Specifically, the AMPT model should be adjusted to generate a higher initial temperature and a smaller participant density. In contrast, the UrQMD model, which already produces a higher initial temperature and lower participant density, requires only a slight reduction in lifetime to accurately reproduce $v_3$. These conclusions are supported by the fact that both models are capable of reproducing the experimentally measured $v_2$. This work demonstrates that the same initial conditions can simultaneously reproduce both $v_2$ and $v_3$, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the AMPT and UrQMD initial conditions. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the initial conditions in both models are more precise than previously assumed. This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that the model successfully reproduces both $v_2$ and $v_3$ under the same initial conditions. This paper introduces a new class of simultaneously actuated and deployable robotic structures, designed to perform multiple tasks through coordinated motion of both structure and end-effectors. These structures are engineered for manufacturing simplicity, featuring planar, polygonal cells constructed from linear links and actuators alongside point masses. The proposed design methodology involves defining a target configuration, subsequently deriving the specific geometry and actuation requirements to achieve it. The study presents the design and analysis of a 3-DOF structure, demonstrating its ability to transition from a compact, flat state to a three-dimensional arrangement. This example is developed to be both easily manufacturable and easily to deploy, with the capability of covering a 3D arrangement of three sensors. The paper provides design and analysis for this example, along with generalization and numerical results. Keywords: deployable structures, deployable mechanisms, deployable robots, deployable space structures, deployable sensor networks, deployable robots, deployable mechanisms, deployable structures.

Recent research indicates that pre-training semantic segmentation models on monocular depth estimation tasks yields better performance than common pre-training on dense labels using supervised scene reconstruction. To further explore this finding, we conducted an extensive and direct comparison between these two pre-training strategies across various models and datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that the superior outcome of depth assessment compared to supervised scene reconstruction is likely due to the latter being less challenging. Furthermore, we propose a more difficult pre-training task that outperforms both approaches. Finally, we analyze the underlying reasons for these results and present insights that may inform future research in self-supervised learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepDriveLab/MDS. *Equal contribution. $\dagger$Corresponding author.

Let $\mathcal{B}$ denote the class of analytic functions $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+...$ in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}:=\{z\in \mathbb{C} : |z|<1\}$ that are bounded by a Bohr radius $\rho(\mathcal{B})$. In this paper, we extend the Bohr radius concept to ${\mathcal{SH}}_{\mu,\gamma,\lambda}^{p}[A,C,\phi,\phi_1]$, a newly defined subclass of normalized $p$-valent log-harmonic mappings that are strongly starlike of order $\rho$. Our primary finding is that $\rho({\mathcal{SH}}_{\mu,\gamma,\lambda}^{p}[A,C,\phi,\phi_1])=\min\{1,\frac{1-C}{1+A}\}$, which is sharp. Furthermore, we derive the explicit Bohr radius for the class of strongly spiral-like log-harmonic mappings $ {\mathcal{S}}_{\mu,\gamma,\lambda}^{p}[A,C,\phi,\phi_1]$. Additionally, we establish the Bohr radii for starlike and convex combinations of normalized $p$-valent log-harmonic mappings. Finally, we provide an upper bound for the Bohr radius of the class $ {\mathcal{SH}}_{\mu,\gamma,\lambda}^{p}[A,C,\phi,\phi_1]$. These results generalize numerous existing findings in the literature. The mathematical tools employed include the area theorem, Cauchy's integral formula, and inequalities. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, offering robustness against outliers and capacity to detect monotone relationships. However, calculating the exact value of Kendall's tau becomes computationally prohibitive when dealing with datasets containing more than a few hundred data points. Consequently, researchers typically rely on Monte Carlo approximations to estimate the p-value for testing the significance of Kendall's tau. This study introduces a collection of methods designed to determine the exact or highly accurate p-value with a controlled failure rate, even for large-scale datasets. These approaches are grounded in techniques for reducing sample size, including the nearest neighbor chain algorithm, and utilize the concept of effective sample size. The proposed methods are evaluated through simulations and case studies focused on climate change. Additionally, all methods are implemented in the R package `kendalltest`. Finally, a web-based application named `kendalltest.org` allows users to easily access the package's functionality. This paper introduces a suite of algorithms for calculating the exact distribution of Kendall's tau, enabling robust hypothesis testing and confidence interval estimation. These methods rely on computing the effective sample size, a metric that quantifies the maximum number of pairwise comparisons necessary to estimate population parameters within a specific tolerance. The efficiency of these approaches was validated using datasets from climate change research. The implementation is available in the R package `kendalltest`, with a user-friendly web interface provided by `kendalltest.org`. These tools enable users to compute exact p-values for permutation tests of Kendall's tau, determine confidence intervals for population Kendall's tau, and assess the accuracy of common approximations. The methodology employs pairwise coarsening, drawing inspiration from the nearest neighbor chain algorithm, to reduce the count of pairwise comparisons. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings of effective sample size and its application to inferential tasks involving Kendall's tau. Furthermore, it demonstrates how to calculate population Kendall's tau and its distribution exactly, even when the effective sample size is unknown. The study also addresses scenarios where data are missing at random, allowing for the estimation of population Kendall's tau by conditioning on observed data. Finally, the paper illustrates how to leverage network structures to reduce the number of pairwise comparisons needed to estimate population Kendall's tau. The computational implementation was developed using the R packages `kendalltest` and `kendalltestR`, alongside the `kendalltest.org` web application. The rise of autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems has spurred significant research into the intersection of artificial intelligence and wireless communications. However, processing vast amounts of data at individual edge nodes often fails to capture comprehensive traffic patterns, while centralizing all data at cloud servers incurs high costs and latency. A more effective solution involves aggregating information through intelligent edge nodes, such as roadside units (RSUs), to facilitate joint model training. Nevertheless, this collaboration introduces privacy risks, as RSUs may exploit shared data to infer sensitive user information. To address this, we propose a unified framework that enables intelligent cooperation among all edge nodes—including vehicles, RSUs, and base stations—while ensuring privacy protection. This framework integrates various privacy-preserving techniques, including federated learning, differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, and blockchain, to harmonize security and privacy mechanisms. We validate the framework's effectiveness using a simulated vehicular network, demonstrating that it can successfully balance performance and privacy. Our results indicate that the framework can enhance model accuracy by up to 10% compared to standalone privacy methods. The framework is available for download at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenLi1999/PPP-Edge-Intelligence}. Furthermore, our preliminary findings suggest that large-scale pre-trained language models can be processed via edge intelligence with only a 1.5% reduction in accuracy relative to central cloud processing. These insights are detailed in our preprint paper, which can be accessed at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10010}. Our goal is to foster interdisciplinary research by bridging artificial intelligence and wireless communications. We invite interested researchers to contact us at chenchen.li@ntnu.no. This paper introduces a new family of Euler surfaces defined by the equation $y^2 = f(x)$, where the polynomial $f(x)$ has degree six or eight and includes constant terms. The study examines the conditions under which these surfaces remain smooth and computes their key invariants, such as genus, Euler-Poincaré characteristic, Poincaré polynomial, and zeta polynomial. Additionally, the Euler characteristics and braid groups associated with these surfaces are determined. The authors further explore methods for constructing similar Euler surfaces from more general polynomials. The paper concludes with a discussion of specific examples, including cases where $f(x)$ is a product of polynomials and when $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree eight with non-zero constant terms. Finally, the text presents formulas for the Euler-Poincaré characteristic, Poincaré polynomial, and zeta polynomial of the resulting surfaces. This study integrates a logistic growth function featuring a strong Allee effect with a Holling type-II predator prey response function to investigate the dynamics of a predator-prey system. The model is formulated as $\frac{dx}{dt}=bx\left(1-\frac{x}{K}\right)-\frac{cdx}{1+adx}\left(1-\frac{y}{\theta}\right)$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}=d\theta f\left(1-\frac{1}{1+adx}\right)\left(1-\frac{y}{\theta}\right)\left(1+\frac{y}{\phi}\right)\frac{dx}{dt}+K\left(1+\frac{dy}{dt}\right)$, where $x$ and $y$ denote prey and predator populations, $b$ represents the intrinsic prey growth rate, $K$ is the carrying capacity, $d$ is the predator's attack rate, $a$ is the half-saturation constant, $\phi$ is the extinction density, $\theta$ is the predator's Allee threshold, $f$ is the predator's intrinsic growth rate, and $\lambda$ is the predator's death rate. Analysis reveals that when $0<\phi<K$, the system's dynamics are significantly altered. Specifically, a saddle-node bifurcation occurs at $x_{s}=\frac{1}{2}\left(K-\phi\right)$, resulting in a saddle point and an unstable node. Additionally, a Hopf bifurcation occurs at $x_{H}=\frac{adK\phi}{\left(1+ad\phi\right)\left(1+adK\right)}$, marking the transition to a stable focus. The model demonstrates various behaviors, including extinction, persistence, stable coexistence, stable limit cycles, and chaotic dynamics. Numerical simulations are provided to illustrate these outcomes. These findings hold significant implications for managing both pest populations and their natural predators. Furthermore, the study examines the system's extinction and persistence criteria, the existence of a limit cycle, and the conditions under which periodic solutions emerge. These results are validated through numerical simulations. This research contributes to the understanding of species interactions and aids in the development of sustainable management strategies for both prey and predators. The proposed model is anticipated to be valuable for ecological studies and conservation efforts. This paper introduces a novel pivot simplex approach for solving any linear programming problem, derived from a generalized version of the L-shaped method proposed by Birge and Louveaux in 2011. The study establishes an optimization limit for the generated sequence of simplexes, set at $n+1$, where $n$ represents the number of non-basic variables in the initial basic feasible solution. Additionally, the article presents a termination criterion and a method for identifying a sub-optimal basic feasible solution. Finally, an algorithm is proposed to construct the initial basis. Through illustrative examples, the authors demonstrate the application of this technique, including the use of the specific algorithm for generating the initial basis. The paper concludes with remarks and suggestions for future research. The proposed strategy is anticipated to be highly effective for large-scale linear programming problems, offering rapid convergence, minimal computational effort, and optimal basic feasible solutions. Furthermore, this method is expected to be valuable in fields involving large-scale linear programming, such as operations research, management science, and economics. The authors hope their findings will contribute to the advancement of mathematical sciences. This work presents leading-order predictions for top quark plus jet production at the LHC, specifically examining the extraction of the top quark mass from $t\bar{t}$+jet events. A primary objective is to assess the stability of the extracted mass value against variations in the five-gluon jet emission profile. We demonstrate that off-shell effects are substantial and that ignoring them can lead to a shift in the reconstructed pole mass of approximately 1 GeV. Furthermore, we show that these off-shell and other non-perturbative corrections can be effectively modeled by adjusting the gluon jet energy within our parton shower. Finally, we quantify the sensitivity of the extracted pole mass to jet kinematic selections and establish the current precision limits for this measurement. To achieve a precision of $\mathcal{O}(500 \text{ MeV})$, a data sample of at least 300 $\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ is required. Additionally, we observe that the extracted pole mass is highly sensitive to the jet energy cutoff used in the reconstruction algorithm. This dependence is resolved by implementing a correction that accounts for the energy lost to soft gluons, which are typically below the cutoff threshold. Incorporating this correction reduces the energy dispersion of the extracted pole mass by a factor of three. Ultimately, we conclude that the precision of the pole mass extraction from $t\bar{t}$+jet data is currently limited by the energy dispersion of the jet system. The advent of photorealistic deepfake images and video has prompted significant concerns regarding their potential exploitation. A primary concern is the absence of visible indicators to distinguish deepfakes from genuine media. To address this, researchers have developed various countermeasures to detect these fakes. However, the continuous evolution of deepfake generation techniques necessitates that countermeasures remain robust and generalizable. Consequently, researchers increasingly rely on vision transformers, which demonstrate superior generalization capabilities compared to convolutional neural networks. This study investigates the efficacy of vision transformers in detecting face deepfakes. We assess the performance of pre-trained models across three prevalent deepfake methods: Face2Face, DeepFakes, and FakeClean. Our findings indicate that vision transformers achieve state-of-the-art results across all three datasets. Furthermore, we analyze the feature representations of these models to elucidate their operational mechanisms. Finally, we explore the efficiency of pre-trained vision transformers specifically for the task of detecting deepfake faces. To our knowledge, this represents the first research effort to address the efficiency of pre-trained vision transformers in the context of face counterfeit detection. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has recently become a promising approach for developing autonomous vehicles, with researchers focusing on creating transferable DRL models capable of handling unseen scenarios. However, the significant domain gap between simulated environments and real-world conditions hinders the practical deployment of these models on actual self-driving cars. This study investigates a specific domain adaptation challenge: enabling a model trained on a driving simulator to operate effectively on a scaled-down, vehicle-like testbed. The proposed framework utilizes a single, shared deep neural network architecture across both domains, facilitating the transfer of model parameters from the simulator to the testbed. Experiments conducted on a third-party autonomous driving simulation platform demonstrate that this model can successfully navigate various general driving scenarios, including intersections, roundabouts, and curves, within a simplified vehicle environment. The findings indicate that the framework significantly enhances the generalization capabilities of deep reinforcement learning models across different domains. Furthermore, the model achieves an average success rate of 80% on the testbed for previously unseen scenarios. These results validate the framework's effectiveness in addressing domain adaptation challenges for self-driving vehicles and offer a foundation for future research in this area. Asynchronous parallelization has become a standard approach for accelerating multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). However, this method introduces evaluation time bias, where algorithms often favor short-running objectives, thereby compromising solution quality. Current mitigation strategies are limited and typically rely on maintaining a shared population across all objectives, which hinders their applicability to hierarchical multi-objective optimization (HMO). This paper introduces a novel parent selection mechanism designed to eliminate evaluation time bias in asynchronous parallel HMO without constraining population or eligibility list (EL) sharing policies. The core concept involves constructing frequency vectors that track the historical achievement frequency of solutions, thereby enabling the algorithm to identify those most likely to yield high-quality results. By integrating these frequency vectors into the selection process, the proposed mechanism effectively addresses evaluation time bias. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach successfully mitigates the aforementioned bias and significantly enhances solution quality. Furthermore, the method is general and can be adapted to various existing asynchronous parallel MOEA designs. Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence confirm that the proposed mechanism improves the convergence and diversity of the obtained solutions. Additionally, the method is available in the PyMOEO library for hierarchical multi-objective evolutionary optimization. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous computer vision tasks, yet acquiring and annotating sufficient training data for specific applications often proves difficult. A promising solution involves transferring knowledge from large-scale image datasets, a capability facilitated by deep network architectures. This study examines a scenario where transfer is necessary due to distinct domain shifts, such as those caused by variations in imaging systems or acquisition conditions. We evaluated three domain transfer techniques: standard fine-tuning, data augmentation, and subnetwork extraction. Our experiments reveal that fine-tuning and data augmentation yield comparable performance, while subnetwork extraction fails to improve results. Furthermore, fine-tuning and data augmentation enhance performance when applied to subsets of 10% or 20% of the target data, provided the source and target domains are similar. Conversely, these methods offer no significant advantage if the source and target domains differ substantially. Finally, we observe that fine-tuning and subnetwork extraction tend to overestimate domain adaptation effectiveness in cross-fold evaluations, a bias that is mitigated by employing a cross-fold experimental design. These findings are robust and generalizable across various datasets, tasks, and network architectures. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexanderkopp/domain-assessment. This work was presented at the 2018 European Conference on Computer Vision. Additionally, it was featured in the Domain Adaptation and Domain Generalization Challenge at the 2018 Joint European Conference on Artificial Intelligence and the 2018 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. The challenge involved radiology and wildlife monitoring domains, and the evaluation was conducted by a committee of four experts. Our results indicate that the source and target domains in this challenge are sufficiently similar to justify knowledge transfer. Specifically, fine-tuning and data augmentation improved classification accuracy for fine-grained bird species, whereas transfer via network weights did not. We provide explicit formulas for counting arcs in the affine plane $\mathbb F_q^2$, distinguishing between arcs that can and cannot be extended. For the $2$-extendable case, we establish a combinatorial identity linking this count to the total number of arcs. Additionally, we introduce and calculate the number of arcs in a specific class known as multiplicative arcs. Our findings are extended to the scenario where the field $\mathbb F_q$ is replaced by a subset $S \subset \mathbb F_q$ with size $s$. We derive exact or asymptotic bounds for these partial arcs, demonstrating that their properties closely resemble those of arcs over the complete field. Finally, our results generalize to higher dimensions, enumerating arcs and non-singular surfaces in $\mathbb F_q^d$ for $d=2,3$. In these settings, we prove combinatorial identities connecting the counts of extendable arcs and surfaces to the total counts of such objects. Our work also establishes asymptotic estimates for $(S,\cdot)$-multiplicative arcs and surfaces. For $d \geq 3$, we further extend the analysis to weighted arcs and surfaces, deriving asymptotic bounds for the number of extendable weighted arcs and surfaces of fixed multiplicity $m$. These results hold true for partial multiplicative structures defined on subsets $S$ and $T$ of $\mathbb F_q$. We conclude by deriving asymptotic estimates for $(S,\cdot)$-multiplicative arcs and surfaces, confirming that they exhibit similar characteristics to their full-field counterparts. Our conclusions are supported by numerical evidence. Additionally, we offer asymptotic estimates for arcs within multiplicative Cayley graphs, and we extend these findings to weighted arcs in multiplicative Cayley graphs, as well as to surfaces within both multiplicative and additive structures. We report a serendipitous gravitational lensing discovery involving the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420, which exhibits multiple lensed arcs and two substructures, designated as DS1 and DS2. By analyzing the convergence map, we determined the physical properties of these substructures. Our findings indicate that DS1 is likely a dark matter halo with a mass of $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.4} \times 10^{13} M_{\odot}$ located at $0.17^{+0.05}_{-0.04} r_{500}$, while DS2 corresponds to a halo mass of $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.4} \times 10^{12} M_{\odot}$ at $0.35^{+0.08}_{-0.06} r_{500}$. Additionally, we identified a subclump in the X-ray surface brightness profile that aligns with the substructure at 0.35 r500. This subclump's X-ray luminosity is estimated to be $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.4} \times 10^{43}$ erg/s, with a 90% confidence level that it is not a chance alignment. The presence of substructures in both the X-ray profile and mass distribution suggests that the accretion history of RXCJ0232.2-4420 is more complex than previously understood. Furthermore, the mass distribution of the substructures remains largely unaffected by the cluster's merging activity. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings regarding the cluster's formation and evolution. This study underscores the value of combining gravitational lensing with X-ray observations for investigating galaxy cluster substructures. Future research should employ more sophisticated techniques to analyze substructure properties and their impact on the cluster's evolution. Additionally, we recommend further studies to explore the relationship between substructures and the cluster's accretion history. Ultimately, RXCJ0232.2-4420 serves as a valuable case study for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. Weakly-interacting massive particles (WIMPs) have served as the leading candidate for dark matter for the past three decades. This review examines the current experimental landscape of direct detection, summarizing the achievements and constraints established by existing experiments. It then outlines the experiments currently under construction, before concluding with a perspective on the future of the field. While direct detection has not yet identified WIMPs, it remains the only viable method to test the full range of WIMP parameter space, particularly for masses exceeding a few tens of GeV. Consequently, direct detection must continue its pursuit of WIMPs. Furthermore, even if future experiments were to rule out the traditional WIMP paradigm, the WIMP framework offers a flexible structure that can be readily adapted to incorporate novel ideas beyond the standard model. Thus, the quest for WIMPs is, in effect, a broader mission to discover new physics. This article is part of an issue dedicated to 30 years of searching for dark matter. We demonstrate that a network of naming agents reaches a stable equilibrium where the entire system adopts a single sign for a given concept, even though the opposite sign also circulates. This outcome stems from a linguistic consistency rule, which dictates that agents prefer adopting words that maintain consistency relative to their existing vocabulary. To illustrate this mechanism, we introduce an extension of the standard naming game that incorporates migrating agents. Our analysis of this model reveals that the equilibrium state functions as a dynamic saddle point. Furthermore, we show that such a saddle point can emerge naturally without any consistency principle if communication is restricted to a specific subset of agents. Finally, we explore how the attraction basins of this saddle point are influenced by the network's topology and by parameters governing the spread of pure noise and inconsistency. These findings underscore the critical roles of both topological structure and linguistic consistency in the stability and robustness of emergent linguistic systems. Additionally, the consistency principle offers a potential explanation for why certain linguistic regularities persist across various communities. This insight is particularly valuable for linguistic engineering initiatives, such as the Interplanetary Social Network (IPSN), which aim to develop natural languages for interplanetary communication. We conclude by outlining an algorithm designed to construct languages that maximize consistency. (This paper is partially based on a preprint available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.00010.) Keywords: Naming games, emergent languages, linguistic consistency, network topology, linguistic engineering. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a promising method for addressing inverse problems by embedding physical knowledge directly into the solution process. However, recent research indicates that PINNs often converge slowly and may become trapped in local minima, particularly when dealing with functions exhibiting spectral bias. This study demonstrates that incorporating a physics-informed momentum method can mitigate these challenges and enhance solution quality. The findings are supported by numerical experiments across various inverse problems, including heat transfer, diffusion, and Laplace equations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexei-tikhonov/pinns-momentum. Furthermore, this work has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics. Our contributions include: (i) a novel optimization approach for PINNs that integrates a momentum method, (ii) a demonstration of the momentum method's efficacy in reducing local minima and improving both training speed and accuracy, (iii) an analysis of how momentum influences the algorithm's behavior, and (iv) a comparison of solutions generated with and without the momentum method using multiple test cases. Additionally, numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method is effective for both inverse problems and in forward scenarios. The accompanying GitHub repository provides a user-friendly implementation of the physics-informed momentum method for PINNs. The comprehensive code for all tests and analyses is available on arXiv under the title "Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Momentum," which is accepted by the JCAM. We investigate the stability of waves connected to each other through nonlinear internal forcing, modeled within a fluid medium that features spatially varying Kelvin-Voigt attenuation. This system is mathematically represented as a dissipative Schrödinger system, where one component experiences attenuation while the other remains undissipative due to the fluid's shear coupling. We assume that nonlinear cross-coupling occurs solely in the undissipative component and that attenuation is a localized function. Under these conditions, we demonstrate local stability for both standing and traveling waves. Furthermore, we provide additional findings regarding the influence of cross-coupling, nonlinearity, and attenuation on stability. These insights are particularly relevant to atmospheric science, as they help clarify the conditions enabling the propagation of gravity-inertia waves from the mesosphere into the upper atmosphere. Specifically, our analysis indicates that stability is preserved when attenuation is confined to narrow regions and when molecular viscosity is negligible. Finally, we support these conclusions with numerical simulations of damped coupled waves. Additionally, we extend our methodology to address stability for weakly damped waves subject to nonlinear effects and local forcing. In this scenario, we derive a modulation equation for the slowly evolving wave envelope and prove stability under assumptions of small dissipation and weak cross-coupling. This approach is applicable to modeling stratospheric tides, which are critical for understanding the dynamics of the upper atmosphere. The envelope evolution is governed by a dissipative Schrödinger equation that incorporates both local molecular viscosity and gravity wave forcing. We also examine the stability of standing and traveling wave solutions to this equation, highlighting the significant impact of transverse molecular viscosity on stability. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations of weakly damped, locally forced waves. Our results align with recent observations of tidal phase shifts caused by mesospheric gravity wave forcing and with numerical simulations of tidal dissipation resulting from gravity wave drag. These phenomena are quantified by the small molecular viscosity and the gravitational drag coefficient, respectively. Our analysis indicates that stability is maintained when either the molecular viscosity or the drag coefficient is sufficiently small. In the concluding section, we discuss the broader implications of our findings for atmospheric modeling. In particular, we address the longstanding question of whether gravity waves can persist over long distances in the atmosphere. Our analysis confirms that such propagation is possible, provided that attenuation is restricted to localized regions. This conclusion is supported by numerical simulations of linked waves with nonlinear effects and attenuation. Data compression is a ubiquitous method for reducing information volume, typically designed to be reversible for standard data. However, compressing quantum data often yields a reduced probability of successful decompression. This study identifies such compression-induced nonreversibility within the optical domain. We demonstrate a quantum compression algorithm for single photons using an interferometric setup and show that when the compressed state corresponds to a nonclassical photon number, the corresponding decompression protocol exhibits a success probability strictly less than unity. Furthermore, we establish a link between this phenomenon and the nonreversibility characteristic of nonlinear amplification. Collectively, these findings offer valuable insights for quantum information processing involving photonic states. Additionally, our results indicate that certain instances of quantum compression cannot be attributed to quantum friction. Finally, we discuss the implications of our work for the broader field of quantum thermodynamics. Our experimental details and code are accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7100000. This study introduces minimax problems involving the sum of translates and establishes novel upper and lower bounds for these functions. Specifically, we resolve a longstanding conjecture by Baranov and Timan from 1998 for minimax problems with an odd number of terms. Furthermore, for a broad class of functions, we derive new upper and lower estimates for Fenton-type problems. These findings yield significant results for the Baranov--Timan problem, providing new lower bounds for translate sums with large support and fresh upper bounds for translate sums composed of sines and cosines. Additionally, we demonstrate that the functions $f(x)=\sin x+\sin\sqrt{2x}+\sin\sqrt{3x}$ and $g(x)=\sin x+\sin\sqrt{2x}+\sin\sqrt{3x}+\sin\sqrt{5x}$ are optimal. The proofs utilize techniques from harmonic analysis, including Fourier analysis, orthogonal polynomials, and operator theory. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research. This work honors the memory of Zigmunt Baranov and his significant contributions to the field of almost periodic functions. We introduce a direct detection experiment designed to identify spin-dependent (SD) dark matter-nucleon interactions using a $^{6}$Li target. This setup employs a $\sim$100 kg $^{6}$Li target, where nuclear recoil signals are measured via the conversion of recoil energy into heat. The experiment will accumulate a dataset of 10 years, achieving an exposure of $\sim$100 kg-years. We estimate that this configuration will reach a sensitivity of $\sim$100 fg/cm$^2$ for dark matter cross sections with a mass of $\sim$10 GeV/c$^2$, corresponding to a significance of $\sim$3$\sigma$. This sensitivity represents an improvement of two to three orders of magnitude compared to current state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a complementary experiment utilizing a natural lithium target could achieve $\sim$3$\sigma$ significance sensitivities of $\sim$1000 and $\sim$10000 fg/cm$^2$ for the proton and neutron spin-dependent cross sections, respectively. These benchmark sensitivities are expected to remain unattainable for the foreseeable future with other existing or planned experiments. We conclude that a positive detection in a $^{6}$Li-based experiment would necessitate the construction of a lithium target experiment to confirm the nature of the dark matter-nucleon interaction. Conversely, null results from such a lithium-based setup would impose stringent constraints on the spin-dependent proton scattering cross section, thereby limiting the potential yield of $^{6}$Li targets. This scenario would strongly motivate future efforts to develop advanced target materials capable of outperforming $^{6}$Li in sensitivity to dark matter spin-dependent interactions. We anticipate that the scientific community will soon initiate the design and development of such advanced target experiments. Finally, we outline the necessary steps to advance the lithium target concept from the current R&D phase to the construction of a full-scale experiment. These steps include securing funding for R&D and demonstrating technical feasibility, as well as recruiting an experienced project manager to lead the initiative. We strongly encourage the scientific community to pursue the development of a lithium target experiment to ensure that future direct detection experiments remain competitive in probing the parameter space of spin-dependent dark matter interactions. This paper introduces Hoare Logic extended with natural language, a formalism designed for the validation of imperative programs specified in natural language. Building on the Hoare Logic for Kleene Sequence and the Strawson Description Theory for classical description logic, this approach enables the formal validation of programs and their natural language specifications. The paper provides a series of examples demonstrating valid and invalid program judgments, followed by discussions on potential applications and future research directions. Specifically, this work serves as a foundational step toward automated validation of imperative programs from descriptive forms of natural language that do not rely on formal semantics. It also aims to stimulate further research into the formal validation of other imperative constructs and the development of formalisms that extend beyond classical description logic. Finally, we present an experimental implementation of the proof system, which is available as open-source software. This tool supports the validation of programs written in English using the Coq proof assistant and can be accessed at https://github.com/tpereira/Coq-naturalHoareLogic. The source code for this tool is also provided in the accompanying appendix. The paper concludes with a discussion of the differences between the tool's implementation and the theoretical framework presented. Notably, the tool employs a more expressive description logic than that proposed in this work, and its sound proof system relies on additional axioms that extend classical description logic. These axioms are detailed in a separate publication, which also addresses the various design choices made during the tool's development. Additionally, we have released a new version of the tool that incorporates the examples from this paper, supports validation in French, and offers a more user-friendly interface. This updated version can be found at https://github.com/tpereira/Coq-naturalHoareLogic/tree/nhlgv2. The tool's validation procedure requires the use of informal ontologies, a topic that will be explored in future work. Overall, the tool successfully demonstrates the feasibility of validating imperative programs using descriptive natural language. However, it does not support the validation of programs defined using the procedural natural language found in requirements engineering, as addressed by the NL4RE formalism. Supporting NL4RE specifications remains a significant area for future research. To initiate this direction, we have begun work on sound and complete natural language Hoare Logic for NL4RE, which is detailed in a separate publication. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replica state machine designed for cloud environments, featuring a streamlined protocol that reduces communication and latency compared to other BFT systems. It has been deployed in production at Google and GCP to manage large-scale distributed data services. However, Canopus currently relies on the assumption that all replicas remain responsive throughout the system, an assumption that is both unrealistic and costly to validate. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus capable of tolerating both failures and Byzantine behaviors in real-time. We also present a novel, distributed algorithm to verify the BFT property of an RCanopus deployment, ensuring that the majority of replicas are responsive at any given moment. We have integrated this verification process into a new deployment tool for RCanopus. Experimental results indicate that RCanopus maintains comparable performance to Canopus. Furthermore, we conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the success probability of RCanopus, demonstrating that its reliability is sufficient to satisfy practical system needs. Finally, we outline strategies for configuring and operating Canopus to ensure that the majority of replicas remain responsive. By following these guidelines and utilizing the new RCanopus deployment tool, Canopus users can effectively manage replica state and guarantee BFT properties with minimal overhead. Additionally, we have developed a generic library that enables any Canopus-based system to verify the BFT nature of their deployments. This library is designed to be easily adaptable for specific use cases and can be integrated into any Canopus-based system with straightforward modifications. This work is released as an open-source project under the Canopus repository. Our findings suggest that Canopus should be extended to support the toleration of non-responsive replicas, a capability that would significantly benefit the broader community. We have made this extension available as an open-source project within the RCanopus repository. This study examines the mechanical properties of lipid membranes within the context of molecular dynamics simulations. We develop and apply two distinct theoretical frameworks to estimate the average in-plane pressure, serving as the foundation for calculating the bending modulus. The first framework, an extension of the classical approach by Irving and Kirkwood, determines pressure by averaging inter-particle forces across a volume. The second, a novel theoretical method, calculates pressure based on the time average of pressure tensor time-correlation functions. Our findings indicate that the bending modulus is significantly influenced by both the type of lipid and the extent of cholesterol incorporation. Furthermore, our theoretical results align well with existing literature, and the computational cost for these calculations remains comparable to that of standard structural analysis. This study presents a catalog of the most energetic cosmic rays recorded during the initial year of Phase I at the Pierre Auger Observatory, spanning events with energies exceeding 7×10¹⁹ eV up to the highest energies detected. The Auger Collaboration's previous catalog, which covered the full Phase I dataset, is also included for comparison. We compare the celestial distributions of events in both catalogs against various isotropic and anisotropic models. Additionally, we examine the characteristics of events with energies above 3×10²⁰ eV, known as the ultra-high energy events. The analysis reveals that the energies of the events comprising the two most energetic catalogs are statistically indistinguishable. The most energetic event in our list, designated Event 1970, is identified as the well-documented "Shower 794." The second and third most energetic events, Event 7457 and Event 1947, are identified as previously documented events previously known as "Event 279" and "Event 227," respectively. The third and fifth highest energy events, Event 7947 and Event 1977, are noted to be significantly displaced from the Great Attractor and the Sgr A* region, respectively. The ultra-high energy events, Event 2347, Event 1837, and Event 1961, are found to be aligned with the Great Attractor, the Sgr A* region, and the Virgo Cluster, respectively. Furthermore, the ultra-high energy events exhibit a lack of correlation with the Great Attractor, the Sgr A* region, the Virgo Cluster, or the Perseus Cluster. The highest energy events also show no correlation with the direction of the galactic center. The angular dispersion of the ultra-high energy events is consistent with the angular dispersion observed in the entire Phase I data sample. The angular dispersion of the three highest energy events is found to be smaller than that of the Phase I sample. The angular dispersion of the three highest energy events is also smaller than that of the sample excluding the highest energy event. The angular dispersion of the three highest energy events is also smaller than that of the sample excluding the two highest energy events. The angular dispersion of the fifth highest energy event is found to be smaller than that of the Phase I sample. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications; however, their internal decision-making processes often remain opaque, particularly regarding the reliability of their predictions. While Monte Carlo (MC) dropout offers a common approach to estimate uncertainty in deep networks, it suffers from poor calibration. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, which employs Bayesian deep learning to achieve better-calibrated uncertainty assessments. By utilizing variational dropout, BayesOD approximates the Bayesian framework of deep detectors efficiently, maintaining performance comparable to MC dropout-based methods. Experimental results on the COCO dataset demonstrate that BayesOD significantly outperforms MC dropout in both detection accuracy and uncertainty calibration. Furthermore, evaluations on the Oxford Pet dataset highlight its effectiveness in generalizing to unseen categories. Finally, an assessment of medical pet images underscores BayesOD's utility in medical computer vision tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/BayesOD. Given that object detection is a foundational task in computer vision, BayesOD is expected to find extensive applications across various domains. This study addresses traffic prediction using data from inductive loop detectors, focusing on determining future flow for each detector over the next 15 minutes based on the last 60 minutes of flow and speed. We introduce a novel segmentation approach that groups detectors into clusters sharing similar traffic trajectories, identified as segments with high statistical significance. For each segment, we develop a corresponding traffic model to forecast flow for every detector within that cluster. We demonstrate the efficacy of our segmentation and prediction methods through both statistical evaluations and an analysis of a real-world case study. The results indicate that our approach outperforms established point-to-point prediction methods, which do not account for the intra-flow demand between detectors. Additionally, we show that flow prediction can be accurately derived from both flow and speed measurements. Consequently, this approach extends prior results by proving that if a theory $T$ models a theory $S$ and $S$ is consistent, then $T$ itself must be consistent. This outcome is achieved through a straightforward application of the new rewriting rules to the axioms of first-order logic. Furthermore, the study confirms that the $S$-translation of Herbrand's theorem holds for this class of rewriting rules. As an illustrative example, the paper shows that if a theory $T$ models both first-order logic and the theory of a specific structure $M$, and if the axioms describing $M$ are interpretable within $S$, then $T$ possesses a model that interprets $M$. This study introduces a multiple convolutional neural network framework designed to enhance the accuracy of classifying computer-generated segmentations of the hippocampus in MR images for both epileptogenic zones and Alzheimer's disease. The framework was evaluated using a dataset of 3D T1-weighted head MR scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), involving 100 patients with epilepsy and 100 individuals with Alzheimer's, who underwent hippocampus segmentation via the Hippocampus Automatic Labeling (HAL) method. The findings indicate that the developed framework significantly enhances correctness rates in hippocampus partitioning for epileptogenic zones and Alzheimer's disease. Furthermore, the developed multiple convolutional neural network has shown improved correctness rates in hippocampus partitioning for both conditions. This study presents results from a Monte Carlo simulation of crewed spacecraft at Low Earth Orbits (LEO) exposed to the modulated flux of cosmic ray secondary particles. The simulation tracks the propagation of these particles through the vessel structure and into human tissue, calculating absorbed doses in various organs. The simulation model was validated against existing experimental data. Calculations were performed for LEO altitudes ranging from 200 to 800 km, incorporating solar activity conditions during solar maximum and minimum. The vessels were modeled as spheres and cylinders with aluminum and galactic radiation shielding thicknesses of 0, 10, 20, and 30 g/cm². Results indicate that at 400 km, the average annual absorbed dose for unshielded occupants is approximately 100 mSv during solar maximum and 400 mSv during solar minimum. For a 10 g/cm² shield, the average annual absorbed dose is approximately 10 mSv during solar maximum and 40 mSv during solar minimum. The ratio of organ-specific doses to whole-body doses remains nearly constant across all organs and shielding configurations. Consequently, the dose to the blood-forming organs can be used to estimate the dose to other critical organs, such as the brain, eyes, and skin, with an accuracy of about 20%. This relationship is expressed as D(Organ) = k × D(Blood-Forming Organs), where the organ-specific coefficients (k) are 1.1 for the brain, 2.5 for the lens of the eye, and 1.5 for the skin. The coefficients for the thyroid and breast are both 1.0. The data for the brain, eye lens, skin, and blood-forming organs are available at http://www.astro.rug.nl/~j.j.k.van.den.bossche/LEOdata. The probability of cataract formation is roughly 10% for unshielded crew and 1% for shielded crew. The probability of skin erythema is approximately 100% for unshielded crew and 10% for shielded crew. The astrosphere, a region dominated by the solar wind and pressure from the escaping star, is anticipated to significantly alter the characteristics of interstellar matter. However, the specific impacts of this escape on extinction, emission, and polarization remain uncertain. This study aims to determine how astrospheric conditions influence the properties of interstellar dust grains, focusing on dust and PAH particles within the "sparse" phase of the interstellar medium (ISM), which exhibits low density and high turbulence. We present a novel model that integrates astrospheric effects into astrophysical simulations. Our approach employs a self-consistent, time-dependent treatment of grain charging, heating, and radiation emission, alongside a polarizability-based polarization model. We demonstrate that astrospheric effects are most pronounced in the low-density ISM, resulting in larger extinction and polarization values, as well as distinct spectral features in emission. Furthermore, we show that these effects cause astrospheres to appear redder than the surrounding ISM. Finally, we outline the implications of our findings for interpreting observations of star-forming regions and the heliosphere. Our model is available as a Python package named \texttt{Astrodust+PAH}. \texttt{Astrodust+PAH} is a multi-purpose tool designed to calculate dust extinction, emission, and polarization across a wide range of astrophysical scales, from the solar system to cosmology. It incorporates astrospheric effects on grain properties, charging, heating, and polarization, while also modeling astrospheric ionization and the ion-molecule chemistry of PAHs. The package is highly extensible, allowing users to define custom grain size distributions, compositions, and extinction cross-sections. This work is based on the \texttt{Astrodust+PAH} modeling framework, which is detailed in a companion paper. \texttt{Astrodust+PAH} can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/astrodustpy/astrodust_plus_pah}. This research was conducted using the \texttt{AstroPy} Python package, which is now available at \url{https://www.astropy.org}. \texttt{AstroPy} is a collaborative project supported by the Scientific Computing and Data Science Core at the University of Central Florida. We report the detection of a massive planet within a disk surrounding the young, extremely low-mass star CIDA 1, which has a mass of 0.017 solar masses and a spectral type of M6. Our analysis of high-contrast imaging data from the VLT/SPHERE instrument, combined with ALMA observations, reveals a point source at 100 au with a mass of 10 Jupiter masses. Additionally, we identified a disk structure with a radius of 100 au and a width of 20 au, exhibiting a temperature of 100 K and a surface density of 10 g/cm². The presence of this massive planet in the disk is consistent with the observed disk properties and the planet's migration from the disk edge toward the observed position. This system is significant because it demonstrates that giant planets can form around very low-mass stars, and it is the second such disk-planet system identified around an extremely low-mass star. This finding supports the hypothesis that giant planets can emerge from the collapse of the outer disk regions of these young stellar objects. Furthermore, the disk's properties align with those of other disks around extremely low-mass stars, suggesting a potential link between these stellar characteristics and disk attributes. Finally, the planet's location and mass indicate that it is gravitationally interacting with the disk, which may influence the disk's evolution. This study underscores the necessity of investigating both the disks and companions of extremely low-mass stars to better understand the relationship between stellar mass and the conditions necessary for planet formation. Our findings are based on observations from the ESO VLT/SPHERE and ALMA facilities. This study examines the game "Lights Out" played on a two-dimensional $m \times n$ grid. The objective is to extinguish all lights by pressing them; each press toggles the state of a light along with its direct vertical and horizontal neighbors. We determine the fewest moves required to reach a "all off" state from any "all on" starting configuration, demonstrating that this number does not always equal $m \times n$. Leveraging the properties of Kronecker products, we construct the specific matrix representing this optimal solution. Additionally, we explore a variant of the problem where the initial configuration is random, analyzing the expected number of moves needed to solve it. Finally, we investigate the probability that a random configuration on an $m \times n$ grid is unsolvable, and we numerically estimate the average length of the shortest sequence of moves for random configurations on a $5 \times 5$ grid. Our findings indicate that for a $5 \times 5$ grid, the expected number of moves is approximately 26.6. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to higher dimensions, showing that for an $m \times n \times \dots \times n$ grid, the maximum number of moves needed to solve the game is $m \times n^2$. We also provide a characterization of unsolvable configurations for this generalized game. For a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ grid, we calculate the proportion of unsolvable configurations as $127/256$, and we offer a conjecture regarding the proportion of unsolvable configurations for a $3 \times 3 \times 3$ grid. Finally, we compute the number of unsolvable configurations for a $2 \times 2 \times n$ grid for small values of $n$ and propose a conjecture for the general case. Our research suggests that as the grid size grows, the proportion of unsolvable configurations approaches 1. Specifically, for an $n \times n \times n$ grid, we conjecture that the proportion of unsolvable configurations is approximately $1 - \frac{1}{2^{3n-2}}$. This conjecture is supported by numerical evidence for $n \leq 5$. We also extend the analysis to $2 \times n$ grids, finding that the proportion of unsolvable configurations is $1 - \frac{2^{n+1} + (-1)^n}{3 \cdot 2^{2n-1}}$.

This study introduces a new Variational Image Partitioning (VIP) model integrated with Image Reconstruction (IR) to recover high-fidelity images from incomplete data. Unlike traditional methods that treat image recovery and segmentation as separate steps, this model integrates both processes into a unified framework. Specifically, the method reconstructs images within data-driven bounds by estimating latent variables that define the image's partitioning structure. The proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance in handling nonconvex data likelihoods, making it particularly effective for low-dose CT and compressed sensing applications. Furthermore, the approach is capable of generating either binary or continuous segmentation maps alongside the reconstructed images. Experimental results confirm that the method produces high-quality image reconstructions and segmentation outcomes. Additionally, the model was extended to support multi-modal imaging, successfully producing multi-modal reconstructions accompanied by robust segmentation maps. Theoretically, the algorithm is proven to converge to a Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) point of the model, and numerical experiments further validate the convergence of the algorithm itself. Finally, the method was evaluated on both simulated and real-world datasets, yielding promising outcomes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongtao1993/VIP_IR. The standard implementation of AI's interval domain employs a two-phase approach: a rising phase where the information lattice is truncated to ensure the width condition holds, followed by a falling phase where widened results from the rising phase are projected back onto the original lattice to restore the $Fix^+$ leastness property. This paper introduces a novel three-phase framework that decouples these phases, enabling multiple falling phases to occur after a single rising phase. We validate this approach using an implementation of the interval domain for control-flow analysis, which demonstrates superior efficiency compared to traditional two-phase methods. Furthermore, we generalize this framework to arbitrary AI procedures and its original formulation by defining a new concept of $f$-stability for information elements. Finally, we provide a theoretical characterization of the framework's optimality. The provided Python code includes implementations of both the two-phase and three-phase approaches, along with experimental results comparing their performance. These results confirm the framework's effectiveness and highlight the three-phase approach as a new, more efficient method for controlling lattice widening. The complete code is available at \url{https://github.com/ai2024phases/ai2024phases}. Our GitHub repository also offers a Python package, \texttt{ai2024phases}, which can be installed via pip. Topological phonon materials have recently attracted significant attention due to their promising applications in sensing, energy harvesting, and nanotechnology. However, phonon topology in ceramics has remained unexplored, largely because phonon resonances are difficult to detect in these systems. In this study, we experimentally identify topological phonon modes in the acoustic branch of the complex oxide ceramic YbOs. The emergence of these topological modes is governed by the emergence of phonon resonances, which are regulated by an ultrafast laser. This research establishes a new class of tunable topological phonon systems, thereby expanding the frontiers of both phonon and oxide physics.

Outlier detection is a critical component of data mining, yet it remains difficult due to the heterogeneous nature of outliers and the scarcity of labeled data. This paper introduces a rapid, data-driven outlier detection framework grounded in metric space methodology. The approach is highly efficient, utilizing a metric-based distance function to measure similarity between data points and outliers, with the MIND index serving as a representative example. The proposed framework comprises two main components: first, the construction of a proximity graph where data points are linked to their nearest neighbors, and second, the identification of an isolated node within this graph that is least connected to others. We demonstrate that the resulting index is both accurate and scalable, performing effectively across diverse datasets. Furthermore, the index exhibits data-driven adaptability, adjusting to varying degrees of outlierness. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets confirm that the index significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of scalability and accuracy. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/MOOH. Our findings indicate that this index is particularly effective for datasets with high levels of outlierness. Future research will explore the application of metric space methods in other data mining domains, such as clustering and classification. Additionally, we plan to extend the index to handle high-dimensional data, thereby broadening its applicability to a wider range of datasets. Finally, we intend to investigate the impact of noise on outlier detection using metric space methods and develop strategies to mitigate noise effects. This study aims to lay the groundwork for future research on metric space-based outlier detection. Finally, we acknowledge the valuable contributions of all individuals involved in this research. We appreciate their time, effort, and insights, which have been instrumental to our work. We look forward to collaborating with them in the future. We construct solutions for kinetic equations governing reversible enzyme processes, utilizing an iterative scheme built upon the approximate steady-state approximation. In the initial iteration, this yields the well-known equation for the reversible reaction $E+S \rightleftharpoons ES \rightleftharpoons E+P$. For subsequent iterations, the approximate concentrations of the reaction components are determined by integrating these enzyme and reaction rate equations. Furthermore, this approach generates approximate laws for the time evolution of the system's key quantities, such as the conversion of $S$ into $P$. The validity of these approximate evolution laws is supported by both analytical and numerical evidence. Additionally, these findings can be interpreted as an approximate validity of the quasi-steady-state approximation for reversible enzyme processes, a topic that has received limited attention in the literature. Finally, we provide numerical simulations of the kinetic equations for a specific reversible enzyme process, which can be utilized for educational purposes. This simulation demonstrates that the proposed method generates accurate approximate solutions for the kinetic equations. Current review-based product recommendation systems often neglect the interdependence between a user's specific sentiment toward a product and the product's sentiment toward that user's review. To address this, we introduce the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which explicitly models this mutual relevance. The model comprises two interactive subnetworks: one aggregates review representations based on the product's sentiment toward the review, while the other fuses user representation with specific review content, guided by the user's sentiment relevance to the product. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an 8.3% to 11.5% increase in Recall@20 and a 5.1% to 7.4% improvement in Mean Reciprocal Rank@20. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/SIFN. Additionally, we have released the Amazon Review and Customer Reviews datasets to support the community. The data can be retrieved from: https://drive.google.

Data augmentation is a widely adopted strategy for enhancing neural network performance, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. This paper examines a code-switching approach designed to increase dataset diversity by generating out-of-domain samples through lexical substitutions. Our primary contribution lies in applying this technique to Arabic-English code-switched text, which presents unique challenges due to the absence of word boundaries and a lack of effective tools for accurate and efficient substitution. We evaluate various substitution tools and present experimental results demonstrating that our method successfully boosts performance on micro-blogging classification tasks. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of this approach within domain adaptation contexts. Given the significant impact of code-switching on global communication, our findings offer valuable insights for future research in this area.
