This note demonstrates that no precompact subgroup of the diffeomorphism group of a compact hyperbolic surface, equipped with the precompact open set topology, induces a Roelcke precompact topology. Consequently, the precompactness results established by Bader, Monod, and Tsoi regarding the homeomorphism group of a compact metric space do not necessarily extend to the diffeomorphism group under sufficiently smooth metrics. Our argument relies on the fact that the space of diffeomorphisms for such a surface, when subjected to the compact-open topology, contains a copy of the compact-open topology itself. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the precompact groups within Diff([0,1]) subject to the compact-open topology exhibit Roelcke precompactness if and only if they are compact. The strategies employed here are anticipated to be applicable in broader contexts. Specifically, we show that the group of all compactly supported homeomorphisms on [0,1], along with its subgroups of even extensions and those fixing 0 and 1, are all Roelcke precompact. Additionally, the maximal precompact subgroup of this space under the compact-open topology is compact. These findings indicate that the techniques utilized by the authors of [BBMT20] cannot be applied to the diffeomorphism group of a compact Riemannian manifold under any specific Riemannian metric. Finally, we provide examples of precompact groups of diffeomorphisms on the circle that are not Roelcke precompact. One such example is the group of all diffeomorphisms vanishing to infinite order at 0, which is both precompact and minimal Roelcke precompact. The other example consists of diffeomorphisms where the logarithm of their derivative constitutes a non-positive function with compact support. The latter example is minimal Roelcke precompact; its construction draws upon the theory of amenable group actions on manifolds. This latter example is constructed from a family of precompact groups of homeomorphisms on [0,1] that are not Roelcke precompact. The maximal precompact subgroup of these homeomorphism groups is compact. We also examine the case of strictly positive functions and identify a precompact group of homeomorphisms on [0,1] that fails to be Roelcke precompact. We investigate connectable branes arising from the generalized $\lambda$-deformation of group manifolds. These branes are connectable precisely when the 1-form $J$, which defines the $T$-duality invariant, is either closed or satisfies $\iota_{\xi}J=0$ for the Killing vector $\xi$ associated with $T$-duality. Furthermore, if $j$ denotes the 2-form on the dual group manifold, $J$ is closed if and only if $j|_{\mathcal{B}}=0$ on the brane; under this condition, the geometry of the connectable brane within the deformed background can be determined. Finally, we present specific examples of these branes. One class corresponds to standard examples found in standard $T$-duality on rigid Lie algebras, while another consists of examples unique to the generalized $\lambda$-deformation that cannot be obtained via standard $T$-duality. Notably, the geometry of these connectable branes on rigid Lie algebras includes non-geometric types, such as Newton-Cartan geometry. Additionally, on solvable Lie algebras, connectable examples exhibit solvable geometry, with some being null and others possessing non-vanishing torsion. A significant feature of these connectable branes is that their geometry is entirely determined by the choice of $J$. Finally, we identify a correspondence between connectable branes in the standard Wess-Zumino-Witten model and those that are closed under $J$ in the deformed model. This suggests that the geometry of a connectable brane in the deformed background can be understood through its counterpart in the original model. This finding is particularly interesting because it implies that the novel, non-geometric examples found in this paper would not appear if the $\lambda$-deformation were restricted to rigid Lie algebras. This result also indicates that the correspondence between connectable branes in the rigid Lie algebra case and those in the solvable Lie algebra case is more significant than previously thought. This suggests that connectable branes in the $\lambda$-deformed case may be described using generalized geometry, and that such a description could be derived from the theory of Courant algebroids. We introduce a new tetrakis-snub dodecahedral subdivision, termed the "tetrahedral mesh," which is specifically designed to cover arbitrary hex meshes for finite element analysis. This procedure is fully automated, functioning as a script within the open-source software Gmsh. The resulting tetrahedral meshes, achieved through Delaunay refinement, consistently attain a quality index of at least 0.45, with an average index of 0.62. Furthermore, we provide theoretical and numerical evidence demonstrating that the optimal tets/hex ratio for this method is exactly 58, a figure that aligns with prior numerical observations. This ratio is derived from a novel formula for the fundamental group of a Heegaard splitting of a 3-manifold. Additionally, the paper includes supplementary findings on this formula. Our results indicate that 58 is the maximum number of tetrahedra required to subdivide a single hexahedron while maintaining a quality index of 0.45 or higher, a number that also represents the count of vertices in the smallest regular polytope in dimension 4. Finally, we discuss the relationship between Heegaard splitting theory and mesh generation. This work was partially supported by the ANR project "TetGen" (Grant ANR-18-CE40-0021). Although recent advancements have significantly improved performance, the field still encounters numerous noisy and ambiguous cases. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages a knowledge graph (KG) to enhance RE. The inherent discontinuity of value functions and policies in many reinforcement learning (RL) settings complicates their deployment in safety-critical environments. To address this, we propose replacing discrete policies with coarse-grained policies, which are Borel-measurable when defined over a metric space. We present a coarse-grained continuity concept applicable to any RL problem in a metric space, tailored to the specific needs of the application. We demonstrate that under appropriate metric selection, both approximate dynamic programming and approximate policy iteration yield coarse-grained continuous solutions. Furthermore, we introduce the first general policy optimization framework capable of producing coarse-grained continuous outcomes, even under function approximation. Additionally, we introduce the policy-continuous Borel-actionable Markov decision process, a novel Markov decision process variant designed for coarse-grained continuity, and establish the existence of value function continuity for problems satisfying this condition. Finally, we present a general framework for constructing coarse-grained continuous RL solutions across various problem types by appropriately selecting the metric. Experimental results indicate that solving RL problems using induced metrics results in models suitable for safe deployment. The human brain's ability to categorize objects into animacy and categorize them based on shared attributes is fundamental to social and daily functioning. This study investigates the neural mechanisms underlying this capacity by examining the ventral temporal cortex's role in object categorization. By analyzing the relationship between brain activity and animacy, we demonstrate that the ventral temporal cortex encodes animacy through distributed, high-dimensional representations. Furthermore, we reveal that this region's animacy encoding is enhanced by its sensitivity to item-specific details, a finding supported by computational modeling of cortical representations. Finally, our research confirms that the ventral temporal cortex's ability to encode animacy is intrinsically linked to its function in object recognition. Collectively, these findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how the ventral temporal cortex supports animacy categorization and the associated neural mechanisms. This study introduces a new, robust filter designed to eliminate numerical noise from mesh-based simulations in physics-informed mathematical frameworks, such as the finite element method. Unlike conventional filtering methods that rely on arbitrary noise suppression techniques, our approach is grounded in the rigorous properties of convex optimization. This ensures that the filter maintains key characteristics of the underlying operator, including linearity, symmetry, and spatial support. Furthermore, the method is versatile and can be effectively applied to both linear and nonlinear partial differential equations. Finally, the paper validates the proposed filter through representative examples across linear and nonlinear scenarios. Notably, the method demonstrates superior performance by robustly sharpening solutions to the 2D Burger's equation and effectively reconstructing the Mandelbrot set. These capabilities highlight the filter's significant potential for enhancing the visualization of 2D and 3D data within computational science and engineering. Additionally, all code required to replicate the examples is publicly accessible. Source Code: https://github.com/abhishekdeshmukh/arrangement-preserving-filter. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are characterized by high-frequency, low-amplitude signals that emerge during the hard-intermediate state. This study employs the Insight-HXMT observatory to investigate the evolution of the type-C QPO in MAXI J1535-571, focusing on the spectral evolution of the high-frequency band. The analysis reveals that the type-C QPO gradually develops and intensifies, eventually stabilizing at a constant intensity and frequency. Furthermore, the spectral evolution indicates a decline in the corona's size and internal electron scattering optical depth. These findings suggest that the type-C QPO forms progressively, with its intensity and frequency linked to the corona's size. Additionally, the spectral evolution points to a shrinking corona, supporting the scenario where type-C QPOs arise from changes in corona size. Finally, the frequency of the type-C QPO is likely governed by the size of the corona. These results are consistent with previous studies of MAXI J1535-571. Overall, this research provides robust evidence that the size of the corona regulates the type-C QPO. The Insight-HXMT data will facilitate further investigation into the type-C QPO formation scenario. Future studies should aim to observe more type-C QPO sources to validate the relationship between QPO intensity, frequency, and corona size. This paper introduces a new approach to transfer empowerment, designed to generate a social intrinsic motivation that drives two learning robots to react to each other's behaviors in a mutualistic way. The underlying hypothesis is that an intrinsic motivation derived from transferring empowerment between partners enables them to reliably respond to one another's actions. To validate this, the method is applied to two distinct experiments: a simple pursuit task and a complex locomotion task involving two quadrupedal robots. Evaluation metrics include the duration of mutualistic behavior, the diversity of learned policies, and the variety of behaviors discovered. The results demonstrate that the proposed mutualistic motivation successfully achieves dependable reciprocal responses between the robots across both tasks, outperforming alternative intrinsic motivation techniques in terms of the richness and variety of the resulting behaviors. Furthermore, the new method facilitates the learning of reciprocal responses that were impossible to achieve through other means, such as pre-training or the application of other reciprocal intrinsic motivations. These findings suggest that the transfer empowerment-based intrinsic motivation offers a promising avenue for enabling learning agents to exhibit rich and diverse behaviors, including reciprocal responses, without relying on techniques like pre-training or additional training objectives. Additionally, the approach exhibits sample efficiency, allowing robots to master these complex behaviors within a relatively short training period. Finally, the paper discusses the method's potential for application in human-robot teams. A video showcasing the results is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. Spectroscopy is a powerful technique that analyzes how light interacts with matter to identify substances. However, practical challenges often hinder its use, such as the inability to physically access the target material, constraints on measurement duration, or a lack of prior knowledge about identity. This study introduces a machine learning approach designed to identify substances from spectroscopic data using a single reference material. The method employs a contrastive learning architecture trained via Ray tracing to simulate spectroscopic interactions for any material within the OpenMXD database. Testing on only 20 real materials from the database, the approach successfully identifies all substances in a one-vs-one classification setting, achieving an F1 score of 0.99. Furthermore, the method generalizes effectively to unseen real-world materials, accurately identifying 75% of substances in a one-vs-many classification scenario. These results demonstrate the method's potential for both substance identification and classification. Additionally, the study highlights how physics-based simulation can facilitate data augmentation, enabling the training of machine learning models for scientific applications. The code and data supporting this study are available at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/One-Shot-SpecMaterial-Identification. Lie 2-algebras serve as categorical extensions of Lie algebras. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of their structure, along with related concepts such as strict Lie 2-algebras, Lie 2-groups, and the  categorical analogues of nilpotent and solvable Lie algegebras. As higher-categorical versions of these traditional Lie algebra properties, we emphasize categorification throughout the discussion. Additionally, we present specific examples of Lie 2-algebras drawn from differential geometry and group theory. Finally, we sketch a potential path toward a higher-categorical analog of the Lie algebra associated with a Lie group. The text includes exercises of varying degrees of difficulty to support educational purposes. Furthermore, we have incorporated material into a corresponding Jupyter notebook, which can be accessed via this link. The notebook also features an appendix providing detailed solutions to the exercises. Our work builds upon the foundational research of Caramello, Schreiber, and Schreiber, as well as the book by Caramello, Schreiber, and Schreiber. We extend our gratitude to these authors for their significant contributions to the field of higher-categorical Lie theory. This survey aims to provide a accessible introduction to Lie 2-algebras for a broader mathematical audience. Keywords: Lie 2-algebra, Lie group, Nilpotent, Solvable, Categorification, Higher-category.

We introduce a new end-to-end descriptor matching approach that operates without relying on keypoint detectors. Our method utilizes a global feature map derived from a convolutional neural network to identify corresponding descriptors. Unlike traditional methods, our descriptors are free-standing and depend solely on global context rather than being centered around specific keypoints. A transformer-based transformer-local cross-attention mechanism enables the integration of local features with global semantic context. Furthermore, a transformer-transformer cross-attention module facilitates the mutual enhancement of global and local features. This architecture yields two primary advantages: first, local features are independent of keypoints, enhancing robustness against invariance-breaking transformations; second, global features are refined by local features, boosting overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate that LoFTR achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks, including the Oxford5k, Oxford50k, and MS LoL datasets. Additionally, LoFTR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the KITTI-300 dataset for visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) by over 10%, while offering a 3x speed improvement through reduced computational complexity. The LoFTR method is available at https://github.com/lucasb12/LoFTR. Supplementary material can be found at https://lucasb12.github.io/LoFTR. Keywords: Keypoint-free Local Descriptor Matching, Transformer-based Local Attribute Matching.

This study examines the bias inherent in the two-point running mean averaging technique used to derive vector magnetic field measurements from the Hinode/SOT's $1700\,\mathrm{\AA}$ filter. By analyzing synthetic data, we demonstrate that this bias stems from the method's reliance on the assumption of spatial homogeneity, which fails to account for the solar photosphere's inherent vertical gradients. We introduce a new approach called Inferred-Point-Averaging (IPA), which demonstrates superior performance compared to two-point running mean methods. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness of IPA using Hinode data, confirming its ability to accurately capture magnetic field variations with a spatial scale of approximately $100\,\mathrm{km}$. Our findings indicate that the bias present in two-point running mean measurements can be effectively eliminated through the application of IPA. Additionally, we show that the enhanced spatial resolution achieved by IPA allows for a more precise determination of magnetic field inclinations, thereby improving the accuracy of derived quantities such as magnetic field strength and flux. These results are particularly significant for investigating the three-dimensional structure of the solar atmosphere. We conclude that IPA serves as a more reliable method for inferring magnetic field values from Hinode observations than traditional two-point running mean techniques. Our data and code are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/IPA. Future research will explore the application of IPA to other data sets. Ultimately, the methodology presented in this paper can be adapted for other cases where forward models rely on the assumption of spatial homogeneity. This includes scenarios involving the averaging of non-linearly distributed data, such as the mean of a distribution of vectors or positive-definite matrices. In these contexts, the bias identified here may similarly impact the accuracy of the inferred distributions. The Independent Demand Side Control (IDSControl) framework is introduced to mitigate the environmental impact of electricity generation through the management of real-time electricity demand. IDSControl comprises two primary modules: Energy Usage Planning (USPlan) and Real-time Load Charging (RTCControl). USPlan determines the most energy-efficient daily usage schedule, while RTCControl executes these plans by adjusting user devices in real-time based on current load conditions. To address the RTCControl challenge, we propose the Collective Game Method (CGM), an algorithm designed to achieve the Nash equilibrium of a specific game-theoretic model. This model incorporates a cost function that accounts for both individual expenses and collective benefits, such as the reduction in total electricity generation costs. Simulation results using actual user data demonstrate that IDSControl, when implemented with CGM, achieves an optimal solution characterized by a fair distribution of costs and benefits among participants. Furthermore, it is concluded that IDSControl offers substantial environmental advantages, including a significant reduction in carbon emissions. Finally, the feasibility of applying IDSControl to other real-time demand-side load balancing problems is discussed. This study investigates charged black strings within Rastall theory, determining their existence and analyzing the impact of the Rastall parameter $\xi$ on their geometry. By applying the first law of thermodynamics, we examine the stability of these systems across various scenarios, including both anti-de Sitter (AdS) and flat spacetime backgrounds. Furthermore, utilizing the generalized Hawking temperature and the modified dispersion relation, we calculate the Hawking radiation power and establish the criteria for its validity. Our results indicate that when $\xi<1$, the influence of the Rastall parameter on Hawking radiation is negligible. However, in the case of a thick black string, the Hawking power is significantly amplified if $\xi>1$. Conversely, for a thin black string, the power is markedly suppressed when $\xi>1$, whereas it remains unaffected by the Rastall parameter if $-1<\xi<1$. Finally, we demonstrate that all black string solutions undergo complete Hawking evaporation within a finite timeframe. These findings suggest that the phenomena of thin and thick black strings, along with their stability characteristics, are contingent upon the value of $\xi$. Additionally, the study confirms that the Rastall parameter can either enhance or diminish Hawking power, thereby accelerating or decelerating the evaporation process of charged black strings. These conclusions are consistent with prior findings regarding uncharged black strings. Finally, we illustrate the stability of the system through graphical representations of Hawking radiation power as a function of $\xi$. These results align with earlier studies on nonrotating black strings and contrast with those concerning rotating black strings. This work also complements related research on the Hawking radiation of charged black strings in Rastall theory, where a modified dispersion relation was not employed. Ultimately, the findings of this paper contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of black strings in modified gravity frameworks. Focusing on Borel sets $\omega$ that are symmetric around $1/2$, we demonstrate that $\mu_f(\omega) \ge 1/2$ holds for every unit vector $f$, with equality achieved if and only if the spectrum of $U$ restricted to $\omega f$ is uniform on $\omega$. Furthermore, we establish that $\lim_{N\to\infty} \|E_N f - E_M f\| \to 0$ in the weak operator topology as $|N-M| \to \infty$ for any $f$, provided $\mu_f$ is not the Dirac measure $\delta_{1/2}$. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for $\mu_f(\omega)$ applicable to general symmetric sets $\omega$, which approaches $1/2$ when $\omega$ is nearly entirely contained within $(0,1) \setminus \{1\}$. Stars with metallicities $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ are scarce and difficult to identify, particularly in regions of the colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) dominated by numerous intermediate-age metal-rich stars. This study introduces a method for detecting these metal-poor stars using low-resolution blue ($430\text{--}450\, \textrm{nm}$) and red ($847\text{--}870\, \textrm{nm}$) spectra from the Gaia mission. By analyzing a sample of 1,000 G-type dwarfs with $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ from the Gaia Early Data Release 3 (GDR3), we developed a machine learning classifier based on spectral features. When applied to a test sample of 10,000 G-type dwarfs from GDR3 with $[Fe/H] < -1.5$, the method achieves a 90% true positive rate for stars with $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ and a false positive rate of 0.1%. This represents a fourfold improvement over the metallicity cuts used in the GDR3 catalogue. The results indicate that approximately 1,000 stars with $[Fe/H] < -2.5$ were missed in the GDR3, and we have identified 100 of these candidates within the test sample. These findings suggest that low-resolution Gaia spectra are highly effective for detecting the most metal-poor stars. The code used in this study is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/tperez1987/gaia_mlp}. This approach can be applied to future Gaia data releases, significantly enhancing the completeness of the catalog of metal-poor stars. The inclusion of these newly identified candidates in upcoming releases will greatly aid our understanding of the early chemical enrichment of the Galaxy. Fire intensity is a critical metric for evaluating the impact of wildfires on human life, property, and the environment. This study introduces a novel approach to predict and assess the intensity of seasonal worldwide wildfires. By leveraging the extensive MODIS active fire dataset, we decompose seasonal active fire counts into intensity components based on their temporal patterns. The temporal distributions of these components are subsequently modeled using neural networks, which are trained to predict intensity across varying land cover types. The results indicate that fire intensity is highest in barren/rocky and sparse vegetation areas, followed by cropland and barren/rocky zones, and is lowest in forest and urban areas. To better understand how complex language is, researchers utilize various metrics designed to capture linguistic complexity. However, the underlying assumptions of these metrics and their correlation with one another remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates the relationship between grammatical complexity and two widely used complexity scores: type-token ratio and syntactic complexity. By analyzing corpora across four morphological typologies—agglutinative, fusional, isolating, and polysynthetic—we calculate these metrics and examine their interrelationships. Our findings indicate that the type-token ratio correlates with morphological complexity only within specific corpora, while syntactic complexity demonstrates a consistent negative correlation. Finally, we validate these results using typological indicators of grammatical complexity, such as absolute and relative clause frequency. This research advances the field by offering a comprehensive comparison of complexity metrics and identifying the specific conditions under which they effectively measure linguistic complexity. Furthermore, it underscores the necessity of developing additional metrics to provide a more nuanced understanding of how complex language structures function. We investigate the potential of gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters to pinpoint small-scale gravitational amplifiers, thereby establishing a robust observational constraint on self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). By analyzing the lensing map of Abell 2744, we identified 11 lensed arcs with redshifts exceeding 2, situated near the subhaloes of satellite galaxies. We developed a novel method to detect these subhaloes by utilizing the centroid shifts of the arcs. Our results indicate that these subhaloes possess larger mass concentrations than predicted by $\Lambda$CDM simulations, a discrepancy that can be attributed to the interaction between dark matter particles and galaxy stars. Specifically, we find that a cross-section of $\sigma/m = 0.01$ cm$^2$/keV aligns with our observations. This finding demonstrates that arc centroids offer a precise probe for dark matter--baryon interactions on small scales. Furthermore, the detection of subhaloes with significant mass implies that SIDM models must account for a substantial fraction of dark matter residing in subhaloes, suggesting a low self-interaction cross-section. Consequently, our findings suggest that the widely accepted "core--cusp" explanation for SIDM is insufficient. We conclude that a low cross-section, $\sigma/m \sim 0.001$ cm$^2$/keV, is necessary to simultaneously satisfy both our observational results and the core--cusp hypothesis. Finally, we demonstrate that a self-illuminating dark matter model, in which dark matter particles absorb and re-emit starlight, can naturally account for the presence of these subhaloes. This model inherently satisfies the core--cusp and subhaloe abundance problems, while also offering a solution to the missing satellites problem. We propose that the arc centroids represent the first direct evidence supporting this self-illuminating dark matter scenario. The identification of these substructures and the resulting evidence for dark matter--baryon interactions represent a significant advancement in lensing research. In display advertising, bidding for impressions is a critical decision that directly impacts budget allocation. This paper introduces a new budget allocation mechanism designed to adapt to fluctuating bid prices while accounting for bidding risks. Unlike traditional methods that merely respond to price changes, our approach incorporates risk awareness and ensures strict adherence to budget constraints. Wigner negativity is a fundamental characteristic of Wigner functions that enables witness-based quantum enhancements in various computational and communication tasks. Although it is established that wigner-negative quantum states offer an advantage in quantum transport, the link between such advantages and wigner-negative quantum guidance remains unclear. This study investigates the quantum transport of both wigner-positive and wigner-negative quantum guidance, demonstrating that wigner-negative quantum guidance is essential for achieving quantum enhancement during particle transport. Furthermore, the results show that the quantum enhancement provided by wigner-negative quantum guidance surpasses that of wigner-negative classical velocity distributions possessing identical negative capacities. These findings provide a fresh perspective on the role of wigner negativity in quantum transport and offer critical insights for designing information carriers capable of optimizing quantum transport performance. Additionally, the study examines the connection between wigner negativity and interference in quantum transport, revealing that while both wigner-positive and wigner-negative quantum guidance distributions can generate interference, wigner-negative distributions produce more significant interference, thereby contributing more substantially to quantum enhancement. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols leverage the principles of quantum physics to establish a secret key between two parties, typically labeled Alice and Bob, who share a secret known only to them. This study presents a precise and efficient approach for calculating security bounds when utilizing non-uniform random sources for privacy amplification within QKD systems. Our proposed method is exact, meaning it correctly determines the finite-block bound for randomness extraction during privacy amplification. By combining this technique with bound entanglement, we demonstrate that the fundamental laws of physics can enable secure key distribution even in scenarios where the no-key theorem previously deemed communication impossible. Furthermore, we derive the exact randomness extraction bound for the finite version of the E91 protocol, revealing that the randomness rate can achieve a maximum of 1 bit per signal under specific conditions. These findings hold significant potential for enhancing the security and practicality of QKD technologies. Additionally, we introduce a software library for QKD bound calculation, which supports various protocols including BB84, EB91, EB91-variant, EB91-QEC, EB91-QEC-variant, and GC04. The library is available at https://github.com/Quantum-Computing-Group-2020/QKD_Bound_Calculation. This study examines Feller diffusions, defined as weak solutions to the stochastic differential equation $dX_t=\mu(X_t)dt+\sigma(X_t)dW_t$ within the interval $[0,+\infty[$, subject to the boundary condition that the diffusion does not escape. The analysis centers on identifying boundary classifications, the criteria for the uniqueness of the Feller diffusion, the concept of nonuniqueness, and methods for constructing multiple solution paths from a single path. These theoretical findings are illustrated through specific examples, including the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross diffusion, for which a novel sampling distribution is derived. Furthermore, the work presents a family of diffusion processes that remain constant outside a specific sub-interval, examining their boundary types, conditions for uniqueness, and the application of solution path combination. This framework enables the explicit description of a wide range of weak solutions to the SDE. Finally, a sampling distribution is established for the sub-interval where the diffusion exhibits non-degenerate diffusion, contingent upon the existence of a solution to a specific integral equation. The paper concludes with an appendix providing proofs for several lemmas. This research was conducted as the author's doctoral thesis at the University of Oxford. Additionally, the author acknowledges a significant contribution by Dr. J. van de Linde, who identified an error in the derivation of the sampling distribution for the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross diffusion; Dr. van de Linde subsequently provided a corrected derivation, which has been incorporated into this paper. We investigate the evolution of spin-dependent dark energy within the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker framework using a kinetic theory approach. In this model, dark energy is represented as a dark fluid composed of spin-1/2 particles interacting via a dark photon, with dark matter and dark matter-like matter (both dark and visible) treated as the most abundant species. Our analysis reveals that dark matter can be polarized by dark matter-like matter through their dark photon-mediated interaction, whereas dark matter cannot. Consequently, the dark photon acquires a non-zero polarization vector that deviates from standard electrodynamics. This altered field dynamics significantly influence the cosmological evolution of dark matter, dark matter-like matter, and the dark photon itself. Specifically, at late times, the self-interacting dark photon can either accelerate or decelerate the expansion of the universe, contingent on the dark matter-like matter's equation of state. Furthermore, we find that dark matter-like matter behaves similarly to dark matter but with opposite sign, implying that dark matter-like matter is antipodal to dark matter in terms of its cosmological effects. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for the formation of dark matter halos. Our results indicate that dark matter can become gravitationally bound to form halos even when dark energy density exceeds that of dark matter, a scenario that contrasts sharply with the $\Lambda$CDM model. These findings suggest that spin-dependent dark energy offers a viable explanation for the early formation of galaxy clusters. Additionally, our study demonstrates that the self-interacting dark photon can be gravitationally trapped within dark matter halos, a feature absent in standard electrodynamics. This suggests that dark matter within halos may exhibit anomalous behavior, such as a density profile that deviates from the Navarro-Frenk-White profile. Finally, we outline the observational signatures of this model and discuss its testability. Our analysis shows that the expansion history of the universe, as measured by Type Ia supernovae, can distinguish between our model and $\Lambda$CDM. Furthermore, the expansion history inside dark matter halos, as observed through strong lensing, offers another potential avenue for testing this model against the standard cosmological paradigm. This paper examines Faulhaber's original formulation of the Faulhaber formula for odd powers, alongside a demonstration of how the formula for even powers can be derived from the odd case. It also explores the role of Faulhaber's auxiliary formula in connecting roots and coefficients of polynomials, clarifies the origins of the graphs Faulhaber presented to illustrate his findings, and investigates the sources of the examples provided. Furthermore, the paper offers a brief overview of a letter from L. Schwartz to J. M. Borwein, which includes a modern proof of the Faulhaber formula that generalizes both Bernoulli's and Euler's approaches. Finally, it presents a brief commentary on the historical context surrounding the formulation of the Faulhaber formula. The primary source for this study is the Faulhaber manuscript titled "Entdeckungen betreffend die Potenzen der ungeraden und geraden Zahlen," now housed in the German National Library in Weimar. This document was recently translated and annotated by the author as part of their doctoral thesis, "Christophorus Henricus Faulhaber: His Life and Mathematical Work," completed at the University of Alberta in 2009. Additional references are included for the historical context provided. The paper is written in English but incorporates German terms and phrases where appropriate. This paper introduces a delay-enhanced version of the widely used traditional zero-differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM). By exploiting the memory inherent in the equivalent baseband model, the proposed method achieves performance comparable to zero-differential detection while retaining key advantages such as all-digital operation, full delay diversity support, and computational efficiency similar to that of differential Phase Shift Keying (PSK). Furthermore, the method is flexible enough to be applied to any CPM scheme that possesses a valid root raised cosine (RRC) representation in the baseband domain. Numerical results confirm that the proposed approach matches the bit error rate (BER) performance of standard zero-differential schemes and significantly surpasses the performance of zero-differential PSK. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that the proposed method supports both symbol-based and bit-based spacing, with the latter offering superior BER results. Finally, the analysis indicates that the RRC filter in this method is more effective at suppressing inter-symbol interference (ISI) than the RRC filter used in differential PSK. Consequently, the proposed approach is particularly well-suited for high-order CPM configurations, where the RRC filter's ability to handle high-order symbols is crucial for performance. This makes the method ideal for symbol-based spacing techniques, which are currently the leading solution for delay diversity in CPM systems. Reward learning seeks to derive explicit reward functions from observed state-action-value data, enabling the training of optimal policies. However, existing methods often suffer from inefficiency in generating reward samples and the unnecessary computation of gradients across all state-action pairs during reward optimization. This paper introduces VACOR, a visually assisted and colorized cluster reward learning method. VACOR first segments the state-action space into numerous clusters, then generates visual-aided, colorized reward samples for each cluster to accelerate the reward learning process. Subsequently, it employs a gradient-based approach to learn rewards for every state-action pair. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate that VACOR achieves superior sample efficiency compared to other cluster reward learning techniques. Configuration functions serve as nonlocal generalizations of the Dirac $\delta$-function, offering nonperturbative insights into the structure of elementary particles. This work investigates the properties of nucleon configuration functions within noncommutative space-time, utilizing a model developed by J. Praschifka and T. Wilz. The study demonstrates that these functions are sensitive to the space-time noncommutative scale, which is quantified by the parameter $\theta^{\mu\nu}$. Furthermore, the analysis confirms the existence of a nonlocal structure within the nucleon. Finally, the paper establishes a specific relationship between baryon number and these configuration functions. The findings suggest that the intrinsic nonlocality of the nucleon is independent of the spatial separation induced by noncommutative geometry. Unimodular quantum field theory, which relies on a nonlocal action formulated in noncommutative space-time, serves as the theoretical framework for this study. This method enables the derivation of the classical equation of motion for the baryon field, thereby defining its configuration function. The paper concludes by discussing the potential implications of these results for the substructure of the nucleon. Additionally, it presents a solution to the problem of localizing the baryon charge in a baryon, addressing the issue of baryon charge leakage from the nucleon. Finally, the study explores the possibility of modeling the N-$\Delta$ transition current as a nonlocal function of the configuration functions. This approach offers a solution to a problem previously addressed by J. Praschifka and T. Wilz through the construction of an interpolating field between the nucleon and the $\Delta$-isobar. The work also examines the potential implications of these findings for the internal structure of the nucleon. Finally, the study explores the possibility of a finite size effect within the nucleon, a concept previously investigated by T. Wilz and J. Praschifka. This analysis is based on the properties of the nonlocal action, which is constructed from the configuration functions. Ultimately, the findings indicate the presence of an internal structure within the nucleon. These results may contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the nucleon's structure. The discussion is grounded in the framework of unimodular quantum field theory, which posits that the classical action is nonlocal in space-time, a concept derived from the quantization of noncommutative space-time. We investigate topological and frustrated extensions of the standard $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code, which typically exhibit a non-local topological ground state degeneracy on a plane. Our analysis of the energy gap and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ string order parameter reveals that non-local topological order can transition into local order, occurring either through a second-order phase transition accompanied by string order or via an infinite-order transition at a self-dual point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these models display stable topological edge states on a half-space. Notably, the topological fringed phase is characterized by long-range string order and a single dominant string order parameter, which remains stable against local perturbations. Additionally, we find that these models support chiral Majorana edge modes, with their handedness determined by the model's parameters. Finally, we explore potential physical implementations of these topological phases using Majorana qubits. This research was conducted within the framework of the TopQubit project, which aims to investigate, simulate, and utilize topological qubits based on Majorana fermions. Specifically, we propose a path toward achieving the fringed phase using topological qubits constructed from superconducting circuits. The topological nature of these fringed phases is confirmed through the explicit construction of their string order parameters and entanglement spectrum. Finally, our analysis indicates that the toric code's phase diagram can be significantly enriched by incorporating both local and non-local interactions. These fringed phases represent a distinct type of topological order that coexists with long-range order, representing a new state of quantum matter. We examine a hybrid model combining a symmetric Wigner random matrix and a Hermitian random band matrix, where the latter's band width scales with the rank of the former. This setup creates an "intricate" interaction between the two components. We demonstrate that the sigma-model approximation for this system is equivalent to that of a Hermitian random band matrix alone. The distinction between the models disappears because the first model contains no chiral symmetry, a property that is atypical for summands that are merely Wigner random matrices. The second model's sigma-model approximation is well-documented in the literature, featuring a continuous spectrum and a self-energy that grows with band width. Consequently, the primary conclusion is that a Wigner random matrix with an intricately dependent rank can induce a self-energy in random band matrices, thereby altering the density of states. Furthermore, we note that the sigma-model approximation for the second model is not universally applicable; it fails for narrow-band matrices, where a distinct approximation is required. This distinction is significant because the density of states for narrow-band matrices remains unaffected by the presence of a chiral symmetric Wigner random matrix. Finally, we discuss the model's relation to the SU(N) gauge theory of two-dimensional gravity. The SU(2) case corresponds to the first model, while the latter model resembles a two-dimensional gravity theory with a negative cosmological constant. The negative cosmological constant model is a supersymmetric version of the first model, which itself is a supersymmetric variant of a model previously studied in physics literature. The supersymmetric variants of both models share the same sigma-model approximation. The band matrix in the second model is sparse, whereas the band matrix in the first model is not. The sparsity of the second model's band matrix is the critical factor that allows the sigma-model approximation to hold. The density of states for the second model is characterized by a power-law tail, which is less pronounced than that of a Wigner semi-circle distribution. The model's parameters are defined by the band width, matrix dimension, and a single coupling constant. The sigma-model approximation for the second model is derived from a saddle-point approximation, which is valid only in the large-N limit. The density of states for the second model is determined by the large-N limit of the free energy of 2D gravity with a negative cosmological constant. Recent research indicates that conversational agents achieve state-of-the-art results in Conversation Understanding tasks by leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT. However, these models are typically pre-trained and fine-tuned using turn-level data, which fails to capture the natural flow of human interactions. This study introduces an agent-based pre-training method that incorporates various levels of interaction context to better model human communication patterns. Specifically, we develop four datasets—two each for training and testing—by integrating existing resources. These datasets offer Agent-based Pre-training (AP) objectives featuring multi-level context integration and incorporate interaction-level structural information. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed pre-training approach surpasses BERT in almost all areas of conversation understanding. Furthermore, an analysis of structural information reveals that BERT lacks an effective mechanism for capturing the structural details of conversational contexts. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our approach and datasets within the field of Computational Social Science. The datasets and code are accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Agent-based-Pre-training.

The effectiveness of machine learning (ML) is primarily determined by its interpretability. However, most existing research focuses on enhancing the performance of ML models at the cost of interpretability. This paper introduces a framework for evaluating the interpretability of data-driven algorithms through the lens of human learning. We argue that algorithmic learning mirrors human learning in two key ways: (1) humans acquire knowledge by learning from data, and (2) human learning exhibits cognitive intricacy, meaning the effort required to learn varies and is contingent on the specific learning task. Based on these principles, we develop a framework to assess the interpretability of data-driven algorithms, proposing the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CogS) as a metric for this evaluation. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by examining the interpretability of association rule mining algorithms across various CogS values. Our findings indicate that higher CogS scores correspond to lower algorithmic interpretability. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study to assess the interpretability of data-driven algorithms based on human learning principles. The proposed framework offers a novel approach to evaluating algorithmic interpretability and provides valuable insights for guiding future research in this domain. This paper introduces a new parameterization for the Poisson process used to model extreme values, defined by the transformed interarrival times and the threshold level. We demonstrate that these transformed interarrival times are independent and identically distributed according to a unit Weibull distribution, characterized by shape and scale parameters. This new formulation offers several advantages: the transformed interarrival times are non-negative, the unit Weibull distribution possesses a clear physical interpretation, and the parameters utilize a natural scale. Furthermore, we derive the prior predictive distribution and show that the prior remains insensitive to variations in scale parameters. From a computational perspective, we establish that the resulting posterior distribution is easy to sample from. Finally, we apply this method to analyze wind speed data, comparing the results with those obtained using the standard Poisson process parameterization. A comprehensive R package is also available to facilitate this analytical approach. All methods and code are implemented in R. This study theoretically examines the problem of minimizing the average (or effective) cross-section for neutron capture, scattering, and fission among nuclear targets, utilizing the isotropic transmission theory. We consider nuclear target areas where these average cross-sections remain stationary with respect to small, arbitrary variations in the boundary. Such regions may potentially serve as optimal nuclear targets for specific applications, including nuclear reactor design and nuclear astrophysics. The analysis focuses on both incompressible and compressible nuclear substances. For incompressible substances, the resulting equations are solved using the method of Lagrange multipliers. In the case of compressible substances, an additional variational problem is formulated to derive equations governing the average mean free path. Numerical solutions to these equations are obtained via the Newton-Raphson method. We propose that nuclear areas with stationary values of average cross-sections could act as effective targets; consequently, we explore various practical scenarios, such as minimizing neutron capture in a nuclear target. Furthermore, practical formulas are derived for calculating the average cross-section of a capture region, and the theoretical findings are compared with experimental data. The article concludes with a discussion of the practical implications of these results. Additionally, the computational aspects of the proposed mathematical model are addressed, with numerical solutions for the average cross-sections of capture and fission regions calculated and compared against experimental data. Finally, the problem of minimizing the average cross-section for neutron capture is practically resolved using the proposed mathematical model. A new equation for the average mean free path is introduced, and practical formulas for computing the average cross-section of a capture region are derived. The article also presents practical solutions to the mathematical problems solved, alongside numerical results for the average cross-sections of capture and fission regions. Finally, the paper addresses the practical application of minimizing the average cross-section for capture within a nuclear target. This is achieved by solving the mathematical model using the Newton method and comparing the results with experimental data. Furthermore, practical formulas for calculating the average capture cross-section are derived, and the obtained results are compared with available experimental data. The article also discusses the practicality of minimizing the average cross-section for a capture region, which is accomplished by solving the mathematical model via the Newton method and comparing the outcomes with experimental data. This paper outlines our system for the Commonsense Knowledge (COMET) task at ACL Natural Language Processing (NLP) 2020. COMET involves three subtasks centered on common sense knowledge: Metonymy Resolution (MR), Concept Generation (CG), and Metonymy Target Identification (MTI). We evaluated our systems across all three subtasks. Our approach for Metonymy Resolution leverages a recently introduced symbolic knowledge base, while our systems for Concept Generation and Metonymy Target Identification combine state-of-the-art neural models with common sense data from this knowledge base. Our results demonstrate that integrating a rich commonsense knowledge base with neural methods yields a substantial performance boost, particularly in NLP subtasks involving metaphor resolution. Additionally, we detail the comprehensive construction of the common sense knowledge base, which synthesizes outputs from multiple existing resources. This base offers extensive coverage for the subtasks addressed, and we also examine its broader applications in knowledge acquisition and graph completion. Finally, we discuss the evaluation metrics and provide a detailed analysis of system performance. Our approach achieved state-of-the-art results for two subtasks and competitive scores for the remaining one. Specifically, in Metonymy Resolution, we significantly outperformed prior state-of-the-art methods by 10.5% in F1-score. For Concept Generation, we secured the state-of-the-art score with 61.1% accuracy, improving upon the previous best score of 57.7%. In Metonymy Target Identification, our system matched the state-of-the-art micro-averaged F1-score of 60.1%. Furthermore, we detail the annotation guidelines used for the subtasks, the challenges encountered during annotation, and the resulting quality of the gold standard. Finally, we explore the potential of our knowledge base for knowledge acquisition and graph completion, highlighting its utility in these broader contexts. Our knowledge acquisition pipeline successfully recovers 85.7% of gold edges, while our graph completion pipeline achieves an F1-score of 70.2%. Overall, our results indicate that symbolic common sense knowledge can greatly enhance state-of-the-art NLP systems. Our system is available at: https://github.com/DeepMind/comet-atomic-2020. The code and data used in this paper can be found at: https://github.com/DeepMind/comet-atomic-2020. Our knowledge acquisition pipeline is available at: https://github.com/DeepMind/comet-atomic-2020/tree

Hi-GAL is a survey designed to map the interstellar medium (ISM) within the solar neighborhood, covering a 1600 square degree area at the Galactic plane ($|b| \leq 10^{\circ}$) across three far-infrared bands: 850, 1600, and 2500 microns. This study details the data reduction pipeline for the Hi-GAL survey, which processes data from the SCUBA-2 heterodyne bolometer array situated at the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) in Hawaii. The pipeline incorporates all necessary data reduction steps, including radiometer equation calculations, flagging, time-ordered file creation, map generation, and map cleaning. Additionally, it performs on-the-fly cleaning of data streams and offers a suite of tools for map analysis. A primary objective is to facilitate the rapid generation of large-scale maps, such as those covering the entire survey area, alongside smaller maps focused on specific regions. The Hi-GAL pipeline is an adaptation of the SCUBA-2 pipeline developed by the Science Data Centre (SDC) at the University of Cambridge. We outline the pipeline's features and describe specific modifications made to suit the Hi-GAL survey. Furthermore, we present a series of maps generated from archive data to demonstrate the pipeline's capabilities. These range from single-field maps of the Taurus and Ophiuchus star-forming regions to multi-field maps of the entire survey area. A web-based interface is available to view and download the maps produced by this pipeline. The paper concludes with a discussion of the maps and their applications. A companion study will address the calibration of Hi-GAL maps. The Hi-GAL pipeline is accessible via a public repository at https://github.com/Hi-GAL/Hi-GAL-pipeline. The current version is release 2.0.0, which is fully compatible with data from all Hi-GAL observations. Version 2.0.0 is distributed as a standalone package that can be installed on any machine. Users can either install the package or clone the repository and execute the scripts directly. This approach allows users to access the latest development version, although it may not be entirely compatible with all data. We provide a user guide and tutorials on using the pipeline to generate maps. The current version is highly modular, allowing users to run individual tasks or a complete reduction on data. We also discuss the pipeline's internal tasks and their functionality. Finally, we describe the map-making process

We investigate single-file particle transport within a box featuring particle-specific attractive walls, focusing on the dynamics of individual particles as they approach the wall. Our analysis examines the duration of initial exits near the wall, defined as the time from a particle's release to its first departure, alongside the time to its final exit. We investigate how these metrics influence distance fluctuations and the single-particle entropy profile. Simulation results indicate that duration statistics can be characterized by two distinct regimes: a Gaussian regime occurring at large distances and a non-Gaussian regime at small distances. Furthermore, we establish a qualitative link between the non-Gaussian behavior of duration statistics and the entropy-driven single-file diffusion process. Finally, we demonstrate that the relative significance of these two effects is governed by the strength of the attractive wall potential. These findings offer a framework for understanding single-file diffusion systems and suggest that specific experimental observables could be employed to investigate the entropic origins of these effects. This paper introduces the tiny limit of the universal relation governing "infinite" QCD plasmas and examines its implications for tiny systems. This work is a 2020 master's thesis by Dongfang Li, offering several novel findings. The thesis is organized into two parts. The first establishes a homological theory within the category of free left $\mathcal{A}$-modules, where $\mathcal{A}$ denotes the Steenrod algebra over a field of prime characteristic $p$. This framework introduces the concepts of homological length and the homological Poincaré series for such modules. The theory finds applications in analyzing the homological structure of specific $\mathcal{A}$-modules, leading to the definition of homological thickness—a property that can be satisfied by modules with infinite homological length. Furthermore, the notion of homological depth is introduced; while generally lacking additivity, it exhibits this property when the depth is at least one. The second part investigates the non-ignorable elements in the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra, denoted as $H^*(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{F})$. The study demonstrates that these elements are concentrated in a narrow degree range, with their distribution heavily influenced by the topological degree of the corresponding cohomology operations. This insight yields a method for calculating the dimensions of $H^*(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{F})$ for certain special $\mathcal{A}$-modules $\mathcal{F}$. Additionally, the paper establishes a criterion for identifying trivial cohomology operations and investigates their ideal generation. Finally, the thesis calculates $H^*(\mathcal{A};\mathcal{F})$ for specific cases involving 1-dimensional representations. Keywords: Steenrod algebra, homological length, homological thickness, homological depth, topological degree of cohomology operations.

The Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) filter is designed to allow photometric measurements of Ly$\alpha$ emission from hydrogen II regions within the interstellar medium (ISM) of high-redshift galaxies. Originally developed for use in a vacuum, this filter enables astronomers to conduct photometry in the Lyman break range, which extends from Ly$\alpha$ to the continuum. This paper introduces a model for the Ly$\alpha$ filter that incorporates the effects of galactic extinction and cosmological redshift. We examine the model's behavior under various scenarios, specifically considering different levels of neutral hydrogen column density ($N_{HI}$) and extinction. Additionally, we illustrate the filter's response curves and demonstrate how to calculate the Ly$\alpha$ emission line flux at specific redshifts. Our findings indicate that the Ly$\alpha$ filter is most effective at redshifts between 1.5 and 3.5, where the Ly$\alpha$ line falls within the filter's passband. We conclude that the proposed model is highly valuable for predicting the flux of Ly$\alpha$ emission lines from galaxies at high redshifts. Furthermore, we provide a web interface that allows users to input redshift and $N_{HI}$ values to quickly determine the flux density of the Ly$\alpha$ emission line. This online tool is accessible at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~akrugh/LyalphaFilterModel/ (Krugh et al. 2019). We anticipate that our model will assist astronomers in planning observations using the Ly$\alpha$ filter. The flux density values for Ly$\alpha$ emission lines, derived from our model and the online tool, can be utilized to establish exposure times for capturing images of high-redshift galaxies. Additionally, we have made the source code for the Ly$\alpha$ Filter Model available on GitHub at https://github.com/akrugh/LyalphaFilterModel, enabling users to modify the model as needed. We encourage astronomers to utilize our model and provide feedback to facilitate future improvements. This letter introduces a keyless verification framework for communication systems operating over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. In this approach, the transmitter and receiver jointly generate a verification key through channel interaction, which is then used to check the integrity of transmitted messages. The study examines single-user and multi-user scenarios under both cooperative and non-cooperative transmitter-receiver assumptions. For single-user AWGN channels, an infinite-length random coding argument demonstrates that reliable keyless message verification is achievable when the mutual information between the input and output is strictly less than the output entropy. In the multi-user context, we prove that reliable keyless verification of individual user messages is possible if the mutual information for each user's input relative to the channel output is less than that output's entropy. Furthermore, we establish that if the sum of mutual informations across all users is less than the channel output entropy, it is feasible to reliably verify a subset of user messages using randomly assigned codes. These findings are supported by simulations. Notably, the proposed scheme outperforms traditional three-party authentication methods in terms of achievable keyless message rates within a given mutual information constraint. Additionally, the analysis reveals a trade-off between keyless message length and the keylength required for authentication. Finally, the study indicates that for a fixed keylength, increasing the keyless message length causes the failure probability of verification to initially decrease before eventually rising. These insights are validated through simulation results. The results suggest that the failure probability can be minimized by selecting an optimal keylength and a non-negligible, yet optimized, keyless message length. This optimal keylength is found to be shorter than the random coding analysis prediction, while the optimal keyless message length remains shorter than the maximum rate derived from random coding. Furthermore, the failure probability decreases as the codeword length increases. The paper concludes by outlining several avenues for future research. To access the simulation code, please visit https://github.com/raja-krishnan/Keyless-Verification. Keywords: Keyless verification, authentication, additive white Gaussian noise channel.

We demonstrate that the Washboard Energy (WE) and the phase (PH) currents exhibit a linear relationship across a wide range of bias voltages, a phenomenon we term "uniform transport" (UT). This finding is based on the analysis of a Dimer (Di) model, which is the minimal configuration for sustaining UT. The model parameters are derived from the "resonant tunneling" (RT) theory, a framework we introduce to explain why both PH and Barkhausen currents display linear bias voltage dependence. The name "resonant tunneling" is chosen because the RT theory relies on the principle of "current matching," a condition that facilitates the tunneling of information between Josephson elements. Furthermore, the model predicts that current matching is the sole mechanism enabling UT, a hypothesis supported by the successful explanation of experimental data. Consequently, the RT theory offers a comprehensive understanding of Josephson tunneling, with the Dimer model serving as the foundation for developing a unified theory of "weak link" circuits. This work also clarifies the relationship between current matching and the "coherent" nature of UT. Finally, the RT theory provides a means to determine the optimal parameter values for achieving UT, thereby guiding the design of circuits capable of supporting it. (Note: The concepts of WE, PH, Di, and RT were previously introduced in the authors' 2019 paper, "Theoretical Analysis of Uniform Transport in Washboard Energy Systems," published in the International Journal of Theoretical Physics, Vol. 58, No. 11, pp. 3400-3413.) The angular Casimir momentum of a charge moving within a uniform magnetic field in a void is derived using the Green's function approach within the Landau gauge. The resulting expression is a finite sum of algebraic terms and damped trigonometric functions, with each term corresponding to a specific Landau level. We demonstrate that this angular momentum momentum is non-zero and exhibits periodicity with respect to the observer's position relative to the accelerating charge. Furthermore, we establish the reciprocity between the force exerted on a mirror by the electromagnetic field and the angular Casimir momentum of the point charge. This reciprocity is maintained through the reciprocity of the angular acceleration of the charge and the kinetic momentum transferred to the mirror by the field. Finally, we compare our findings for angular Casimir momentum with the kinetic angular momentum of a point particle in a void, as previously established in reference [1]. Additionally, we note the existence of a non-zero dual force and emphasize the significance of these results for the quantum Hall effect. Our study reveals a novel aspect of the quantum void: the angular momentum of a Landau charge, which is absent in the angular momentum of a point particle. This phenomenon arises from the non-locality of the charge current. We anticipate that these results will facilitate the development of new technologies, such as quantum engines, by providing a deeper understanding of the quantum vacuum. Specifically, the discovery of non-zero angular momentum in the void may enable the design of more efficient quantum devices. For instance, the reciprocity between the angular momentum of a Landau charge and the force acting on a mirror suggests that the angle at which light strikes a mirror could influence the mirror's motion. This insight could lead to the creation of highly sensitive light sensors and more precise measurement instruments. Additionally, the non-zero angular momentum of a Landau charge may offer new avenues for controlling the orientation of light beams, potentially revolutionizing optical communication systems. The periodicity of this angular momentum with respect to the observer's position could also have practical applications, such as in the development of new types of optical modulators or in enhancing the stability of laser beams over long distances. Overall, these findings highlight the intricate relationship between angular momentum and the motion of mirrors, opening up new possibilities for advancing quantum technology. The dual force associated with angular momentum could also play a crucial role in manipulating the polarization of light, leading to the creation of new tools for optical manipulation and manipulation of quantum states. Fining-grained Entity Typing (FGNET-RH) is a challenging subtask of Named Entity Recognition (NER), which involves classifying identified entities into their respective subtypes. Unlike coarse-grained entity classification, which typically operates in Euclidean space, FGNET-RH leverages the intrinsic properties of Hyperbolic space to model the fine-grained relationships among subtypes. Specifically, we introduce a loss function that encourages the modeling of subtle distinctions between similar subtypes. Furthermore, we propose a refined hyperbolic embedding space designed to capture the nuanced relationships between adjacent or near-adjacent subtypes. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art method by 1.15% in accuracy. Additionally, we validate the effectiveness of our refinement strategy through visualization analysis. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/FGNET}.

The growing adoption of Virtualization as a Service (VAS) has driven significant interest in prepartitioning Virtual Machine (VM) resources. This approach enables cloud service providers to accept pre-booked VM reservation requests from customers. However, the order in which these requests are processed can drastically impact load distribution across a data center's resources. This paper introduces a load distribution strategy designed to minimize the total number of resources consumed by a batch of pre-booked VM requests. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed strategy reduces the average count of used resources in a test environment compared to a random ordering approach. Furthermore, load testing reveals that the strategy scales linearly with the input size, ensuring that response times remain within acceptable limits. Finally, the prepartitioning method is applied to a real-world cloud environment, and performance tests confirm its efficiency regarding execution time and CPU usage. These findings indicate that prepartitioning is a viable solution for managing VM reservation requests in virtualized data centers. Additionally, the source code for this load distribution strategy is made available as open-source. This paper introduces the Anticipation through Fixed Point Network (AFFNET), a novel approach designed to anticipate the outcomes of extensive-form games. We demonstrate that the anticipated equilibrium of any extensive-form game can be represented as a fixed point within a specific continuous function, which is the core principle behind AFFNET. The framework comprises two components: the Game Representation Network (GRNet) and the Fixed Point Network (FPNet). The GRNet converts an extensive-form game into a continuous function, while the FPNet computes the fixed point (equilibrium) associated with that function. Extensive experimental results indicate that AFFNET surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in accurately predicting equilibria across both real-world and synthetic extensive-form games. Furthermore, we apply this prediction capability to the field of treatment recommendation, where accurately forecasting patient responses to treatments is critical. To this end, we have constructed a new treatment prediction dataset and evaluated AFFNET, establishing it as the current state-of-the-art method for this application. Our analysis suggests that AFFNET's superior performance stems from its ability to effectively model patient responses to treatments. Additionally, we explore how AFFNET can be utilized to calculate treatment effects, offering a fresh perspective on treatment recommendation. Finally, we examine the AFFNET model through the lens of explainable AI, providing insights into its internal mechanisms and decision-making processes. This study derives novel limits for causal inference across diverse settings, utilizing advanced information-theoretic techniques. The findings demonstrate that probability mass can be relocated from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ ($m \neq n$) without loss only if the source distribution possesses sufficiently low differential entropy. Additionally, we establish a limit on the distance between distributions under optimal transport metrics when one differential entropy is constrained. These results yield fundamental bounds for causal inference in various frameworks, including linear, $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ black box, and bottleneck models. Furthermore, they reveal the inherent limitations of representation learning in cause-effect pairs, specifically regarding latent variables that cause transformations only when sufficiently "concentrated." Finally, the paper explores extensions of these limits to the mutual information between a random variable and its deterministic transformation. These insights offer a capacity to quantify the distinguishability of a cause from its effect (or transformed effect) and suggest avenues for constructing novel metrics to assess the quality of learned representations. The technical proofs are presented in the appendices. The findings were initially presented in [1]. The code is available at https://github.com/ashwinb20/OT-DTLimit.

This paper introduces a new framework for unscented Kalman filtering (UKF) that incorporates a predictive surveillance layer to detect stealthy attacks on linear time-invariant (LTI) systems. The primary advantage of this layer is its ability to significantly lower false alarm rates caused by process noise. The layer operates by generating multiple Monte Carlo samples from the UKF's predicted state distribution; if all samples fall outside a predefined attack set, the system is flagged as potentially under attack. This design ensures that process noise can only trigger a false alarm after exceeding several standard deviations, a capability demonstrated through an example system. Additionally, the layer's predicted covariance is proven to be less conservative than the UKF's, and its overall detection performance is shown to surpass that of the UKF without surveillance. The study concludes by outlining directions for future research. Finally, the paper provides a concise review of the stealthy attack model, briefly covers the background on UKF, and offers a detailed summary of the proposed predictive surveillance layer. Keywords: cyber-physical systems, linear time-invariant systems, linear matrix inequalities, linear matrix inequality attacks, linear matrix inequality constraints, linear matrix inequality region of interest, linear matrix inequality test, linear matrix inequality, linear quadratic regulator, linear quadratic regulator attacks, line of sight attacks, Monte Carlo methods, predictive surveillance, region of interest, stealthy attacks, unscented Kalman filter, wiretap attacks.

Korchm\'aros, as well as J. P. Beckman and K. Zhevlakova. Additionally, we establish a corresponding description for these S-rings via their relative rank. Finally, we demonstrate that an S-ring is of Noether type if and only if every subgroup within its group of units possesses finite codimension. Furthermore, we examine the properties of S-ring modules of finite codimension and the concept of an S-ring of finite coheight. We prove that an S-ring of finite coheight admits an S-ring of Noether type as a factor, and we explore the implications of this finding for modules and units of finite coimension. Additionally, we introduce the notion of an S-module of finite coheight and investigate the relationship between this concept and that of finite codimension. We also detail the properties of completely reducible modules and their composition factors, providing a criterion for the complete reducibility of an S-module based on the coheight of its submodules. Finally, we derive a criterion for the complete reducibility of an S-module where the S-ring is of Noether type, utilizing the coheight of its submodules. In the context of units, we establish a criterion for the complete reducibility of an S-module via the coimension of its ideals, and we provide a criterion for the complete reducibility of an S-module using the coimension of its submodules, assuming the S-ring of scalars is of Noether type. Furthermore, we present a criterion for the complete reducibility of an S-module over a Noetherian S-ring using the coheight of its submodules, and we develop a criterion for the complete reducibility of an S-module based on the coheight of its ideals, given that the S-ring of scalars possesses finite global coheight. Finally, we characterize those Noetherian S-rings that contain a completely reducible faithful module with a single composition factor, and we characterize Noetherian S-rings whose units constitute a nilpotent group of finite coimension. We also characterize Noetherian S-rings that possess a faithful module with a single composition factor, as well as those that possess a unique maximal faithful module with a finite coheight. Additionally, we characterize Noetherian S-rings with a finite composition length and with a finite core height

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, serving as a critical technology for connecting physical devices to the web and facilitating data exchange. However, this widespread adoption has introduced significant security and privacy challenges, including vulnerabilities to hacking, spoofing, and data breaches. This paper proposes a new intelligent home monitoring system designed to securely track IoT devices and regulate access to smart appliances. The proposed blockchain model leverages the benefits of distributed computing to enhance security and privacy within the framework. Furthermore, the study addresses challenges related to data integrity, security, and privacy, proposing advanced solutions to foster trust among users and stakeholders. Consequently, this blockchain-assisted localization is well-suited for deployment in real-world intelligent home gadget monitoring applications.
