This work introduces a parameterized algorithm that solves the k-Articulation-Stretch problem in $O^*(2^{O(k \log k)})$ time, marking the first such parameterization by articulation count for any upward planarity issue. Furthermore, the method is robustly parameterized by the size of a subgraph containing all articulation points, yielding an $O^*(2^{O(k \log k)})$ runtime. The approach extends to the more articulated k-Subdivision problem, achieving $O^*(3^{O(k \log k)})$ time using $3^k$ instead of $2^k$. Additionally, the k-Co-Articulation-Stretch problem, which limits articulation points to $k$ outside a chosen subgraph, is resolved in $O^*(3^{O(k \log k)})$ time. Finally, we demonstrate that the Upward Planarity with Prescribed Parent problem is NP-hard when only the number of prescribed parents is parameterized, and that the Weighted k-Articulation-Stretch problem is W[1]-hard under the parameter $k$. These hardness findings are based on reductions from Clique and Dominating Set, which run in $O(n^{O(k)})$ time. Consequently, the primary algorithmic contributions are the tractability established for the first four problems and the intractability proven for the latter two. Empirical evaluations indicate that the proposed parameter $k$ remains small in practical instances. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianMuller1992/UPS/tree/articulation. This paper introduces a framework for analyzing and integrating crowdsourced datasets, employing a generalized Bayes' rule to create a dynamic Bayesian ensemble. In this approach, human outputs are treated as multivariate outputs, and a "Human Softmax" distribution is derived from their probabilities. The study aims to quantify the uncertainty and informativeness of both individual human outputs and the collective crowd using various metrics based on entropy and other statistical measures. These metrics are applied to a novel dataset of human-generated question-answer pairs. The results demonstrate that the method can identify and filter out of distribution and noisy data points from both questions and answers, as well as detect the uncertainty levels of individual contributors within the crowd. Furthermore, the paper explores the relationships between different uncertainty metrics and highlights the significant influence of the number of contributors on the reliability of these measurements. Finally, the study examines the uncertainty inherent in the crowd itself and the extent to which the ensemble can characterize the confidence of specific individuals. The proposed method is anticipated to facilitate more robust and accurate natural language processing on noisy, crowdsourced data. In the context of local contests, both the particle diffusion constant and the net flux of selected particles scale with the noise intensity, denoted as $D \sim p$ and $J \sim p$, respectively. This indicates that particle movement and selection events diminish linearly as noise decreases. However, in maximally intertwined scenarios, this linear scaling fails. This study demonstrates that in specific nonlocal configurations, $D$ and $J$ vanish to higher orders as $p \to 0$. Furthermore, we establish that experimental measurements can accurately detect this critical shift in scaling behavior. Consequently, we propose a method to identify the precise point at which systems transition from regular to critical dynamics by monitoring the noise dependence of $D$ and $J$. Finally, we offer a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon, linking it to the emergence of a continuous noise-induced phase transition. Overall, our findings reveal that in critical systems, noise plays an essential role not merely in sustaining dynamics but in fundamentally shaping their nature. Specifically, we show that while noise is indispensable for maintaining dynamics in locally intertwined systems, it acts as a destructive force in locally alternating ones; conversely, in locally intertwined cases, noise serves a constructive function. In contrast, in a critical system exhibiting maximally intertwined behavior, noise exerts both destructive and constructive influences, resulting in a non-trivial balance that generates new phenomena. These include the alteration of scaling laws, the emergence of a continuous noise-induced phase transition, and a qualitative shift in system behavior at a critical noise value. Notably, this transition is accessible for detection through simple yet effective observables. These insights are supported by a combination of non-perturbative analytical methods and numerical simulations. Additionally, we present a novel argument grounded in a mean-field framework that qualitatively explains these results. Finally, we suggest that these findings may have significant implications for both natural and artificial systems. Specifically, our results suggest that minimizing noise could be essential for preserving function in certain natural systems and engineered devices, while maximizing noise could be necessary to maintain criticality in others. In artificial systems, these insights may inform strategies for enhancing machine learning algorithms, such as genetic algorithms, or for designing more robust and efficient neuromorphic devices. In both engineering and biological contexts, our findings imply that noise is not merely a nuisance but a vital component that can be harnessed to improve performance and robustness. This represents a fundamental shift in how we understand and utilize noise across diverse fields. Our results also have practical applications, such as noise filtering in data transmission

This study aims to validate the efficacy of the Guided Genetic Procedure (GP) proposed by Krasowski et al. (2019) for reverse engineering Java programs. GP is an automated technique designed to generate test cases that trigger crashes, specifically targeting null pointer exceptions. Krasowski et al. Additionally, we identified several limitations of GP, including issues with crash localization, the necessity for crash-specific assertions, and the need for further investigation into alternative null pointer crash replication strategies. Finally, we outlined several promising future research directions. Our results indicate that GP's effectiveness is constrained, suggesting that additional research and development are necessary to enhance its performance. We hope that GP can evolve into a more robust and effective tool for Java program analysis. We present in situ scanning tunneling microscopy data from La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ containing well-defined, disordered regions of varying sizes. Inside these zones, the phase of the gap exhibits disorder consistent with finite-density d-wave vortices. The spatial extent of these areas corresponds to approximately 100 to 300 vortices. By analyzing the evolution of vortex properties as the number of vortices increases, we observe evidence supporting a first-order phase transition between two distinct vortex lattice structures: the conventional 4-fold symmetric square lattice and the 8-fold symmetric star of David lattice. This transition aligns with theoretical predictions regarding the instability of a single large vortex lattice. Furthermore, the observed phase coexistence between these two lattice types is characteristic of a first-order phase transition. Our findings indicate that the energy barrier between the two phases is substantial, implying that the system remains trapped in a metastable state for extended periods. These results have significant implications for understanding vortex matter in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ superconductors. In particular, the existence of a first-order transition suggests that vortices may not condense into a superfluid as previously assumed. Instead, vortices could remain individual entities or cluster into large aggregates, which would substantially alter the vortex matter phase diagram. This conclusion is especially relevant for experimental setups involving real-space imaging of vortices. Finally, the presence of large energy barriers between lattice types may explain the previously reported absence of hysteresis in specific heat measurements during magnetic field sweeps. The system's entrapment in a metastable state would prevent the detection of such hysteresis. Consequently, the lack of observed hysteresis in specific heat data does not necessarily indicate a continuous phase transition. Instead, it may reflect the system's inability to explore the complete phase diagram due to its confinement within a metastable state. This study represents the first direct observation of the transition between two competing vortex lattice structures. Our results provide a foundation for future investigations into the nature of vortices and the vortex phase diagram in high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprates. Additionally, the methodology employed here can be applied to other experimental techniques for studying vortex matter. Lattice QCD calculations of thermal photon emission spectra from the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) phase near its crossover transition temperature $T_c$ reveal distinct flow directions that contradict the emission pattern from a perfect fluid. Notably, photons generated in a QGP with finite specific viscosity $\eta/s$ exhibit a positive flow direction relative to the radial beam spot, whereas those from a perfect fluid display a negative (downward) flow direction. This upward directional flow acts as a unique thermal signature of the QGP's finite viscosity. Additionally, spectra with higher yield are observed when the medium's temperature is lower, an effect that is more pronounced in the case of finite viscosity. These distinct spectral features provide a robust method for constraining the QGP's specific viscosity, complementing analyses of heavy ion collision data. Furthermore, this study confirms that the viscosity-dependent radial flow direction of thermal photons is independent of the volume used to model the QGP. Consequently, this thermal photon flow direction offers a novel and unambiguous probe for determining the specific viscosity of the QGP. These findings are based on calculations employing the Bayesian model BEMC, which utilizes a parameterized volume for the QGP medium. The study also examines the implications of the QGP volume on spectra and flow direction, concluding that the observed features remain consistent across different volume scenarios. Finally, the analysis explores the potential of enhancing the Bayesian model by incorporating a realistic, time-evolving volume for the QGP medium. We conduct a systematic investigation into magnetic ordering on triangular and kagome lattices using mean field theory. By applying the permutation representation of the point group to kagome spin configurations, we identify all possible consistent magnetic arrangements. Our analysis reveals that only three distinct arrangements exist: ferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic, and antiferromagnetic, despite a combinatorial count of 64 potential possibilities. Furthermore, we determine the mean field phase diagram for these orders and compare our findings with those of other theoretical methods and experimental data. Finally, we extend this framework to pentagonal lattices and discuss its potential applications. This study serves as a foundation for future research into various magnetic orderings on other lattice structures. Large-scale randomized experiments frequently employ the false discovery rate (FDR) as a multiple testing correction for determining treatment effects. Nevertheless, identifying intervention effects while controlling FDR remains difficult due to the need to estimate numerous unknown parameters and potential dependence among tests. This study introduces an extensive framework for FDR-based decision-making to select significant treatment effects. We propose an adaptive FDR-based procedure capable of handling both known and unknown dependence structures, achieving first-order FDR control even under complex dependency. Furthermore, to address scenarios where the number of tests exceeds the sample size, we develop a second procedure designed for high-dimensional settings. This high-dimensional method maintains FDR control under known dependence and relaxes restrictions to allow for unknown dependence. We also establish asymptotic FDR control for both procedures as the population size grows. Finally, we present simulation results and a real-world application to an Amazon experiment to evaluate the performance of our proposed methods. Empirical evidence indicates that these procedures yield more accurate multiple testing corrections for large-scale experiments compared to existing alternatives. A simple thermodynamic model demonstrates that the universe's mass distribution evolves in a manner analogous to a gas undergoing adiabatic free expansion. This conceptual framework offers a straightforward astronomical interpretation of Hubble's Law and the fundamental principles of cosmic expansion. Additionally, the model indicates that the density of free electrons in interstellar space varies proportionally to the inverse cube of the universe's radius, a finding that helps clarify the maintenance of radio wave propagation over vast distances. Furthermore, the pressure and specific heat of the cosmic gas are calculated, revealing that the specific heat ratio is less than unity. These specific characteristics of the cosmic gas are shown to be consistent with the fundamental equations of Hubble's expansion. Finally, the discussion includes a comparison with an alternative model of cosmic expansion. The universe is described as a "gas" because it is permeated by "cosmic matter," a term we propose to use for the material filling the space between stars and galaxies. This cosmic matter is assumed to be highly rarefied, with its density and pressure diminishing as the universe expands. We consider the universe as the total volume containing all matter, encompassing both matter and the space it occupies. The expansion of the universe is defined as the increase in the volume of this universe over time. The term "adiabatic" is applied to the expansion process because the extreme dilution of cosmic matter prevents any significant interaction between distinct regions. Consequently, the expansion of one section of the universe does not influence the expansion of others. Furthermore, as cosmic matter is presumed to be rarefied, it is modeled as an "ideal gas," allowing us to neglect the potential energy between separate volumes of cosmic matter. The term "free expansion" is used because the universe's volume expands without any external pressure opposing it. In this context, "adiabatic" expansion refers to the constancy of entropy during the process, while "free" expansion denotes the relationship between initial and final states. This study examines the type-X two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) as a potential explanation for both the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and the recently observed $W$ boson mass deviation. We demonstrate that this framework can resolve the $\mu_\text{e}$-problem while remaining consistent with current $W$ mass measurements. Furthermore, we show that the type-X 2HDM offers a viable fit to additional experimental data, including $B_{B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-}$, $B_{B_s\to(K,K^*)\ell^+\ell^-}$, and $R_{K^{(\ast)}}$. Our analysis focuses on the lightest CP-even scalar's ability to generate the necessary couplings to muons and $W$ bosons required to address the $\mu_\text{e}$ anomaly. Additionally, we explore a dark matter scenario where dark matter interacts with the muon sector, and we provide constraints on this parameter space derived from muon g-2, $W$ mass, and dark matter direct detection experiments. Finally, we outline prospects for detecting this model at the High-Luminosity LHC. We introduce a collection of open-source tools designed to visualize and analyze images alongside spectral data. This software suite is built on a user-friendly, web-based interface utilizing web technologies. The implementation features various display options, such as a traditional two-dimensional image alongside a one-dimensional spectrum, or a data-driven, interactive "spectrum strip" that enables navigation across the sample using either spectrum or image views. Furthermore, we have integrated data analysis capabilities, including data exploration, comparison, and annotation, which are essential for analyzing and interpreting data from hyperspectral imaging systems. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/CS108-16/rcsedv2. Our web-based solution employs JavaScript frameworks, specifically Three.js for 3D visualization and D3.js for data visualization. The application is hosted on the AWS cloud, allowing users to access the interface via any web browser. Our platform offers extensive data analysis functions, ranging from data exploration and comparison to annotation and export. The export feature supports multiple formats, including TIFF, PNG, and JSON, with the option to generate annotated TIFF files that preserve annotations across different TIFFs. Additionally, the system includes a data explorer that allows users to examine individual pixels, visualize their spectral signatures, and perform analysis on selected regions. Users can also compare spectral signatures from different locations using an integrated spectral analysis tool. The three primary advantages of RCSEDv2 are its user-friendliness, flexibility, and accessibility. Its friendly interface ensures ease of use for both novice and expert users. Its flexibility stems from a wide array of data analysis tools that cater to diverse user needs. Finally, its accessibility is achieved through web-based access, eliminating the need for specialized software installation. This approach simplifies data sharing and collaboration, as users can simply provide a URL to access their data. The system supports a broad spectrum of image and spectral data formats, including TIFF, PNG, and JSON. We anticipate that this versatile, accessible, and affordable visualization and analysis platform will significantly benefit the broader imaging and spectral data analysis community. Our system is accessible at https://rcsedv2.cs108.colorado.edu. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical task in computer vision that involves identifying the start and end points of actions within a video. While supervised TAS has seen significant advancements in recent years, the primary challenge remains the scarcity of annotated data. To address this, we introduce an unsupervised temporal action segmentation approach that leverages the inherent temporal structure of videos. Our method relies on a novel technique called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP), which learns action representations by predicting the co-occurrence of adjacent temporal segments. Furthermore, we develop an action detection module that exploits these learned representations to segment actions. Extensive experiments on three public video datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and remains competitive against supervised techniques. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen2020/SSCAP. Additionally, we have released a new unsupervised dataset, UCSD, to facilitate further research in temporal action segmentation. The dataset can be found at https://github.com/Chenchen2020/UCSD. Finally, we have established a new benchmark for temporal action segmentation at https://github.com/Chenchen2020/TAS. We hope this resource will be valuable to the community. This study examines the formation and decay of concealed-charm pentaquark states using present algebra, a framework grounded in a direct generalization of the Poincaré algebra. Within this approach, both the mass spectrum and decay dynamics are derived from the low-energy effective Hamiltonian, which is constructed based on the algebra's generator commutation relations. The mass operator is formulated as a sum of quark mass terms, while the decay operator is derived from the Hamilton operator. By incorporating spin, flavor, and color symmetries, the relevant matrix elements are calculated, and specific quark-mass coefficients are fitted to experimental data. Using the resulting parameters, the masses of various pentaquark states are predicted, and their decay properties are analyzed through decay widths and partial decay rates. Furthermore, ratios of these decay rates are computed to facilitate future experimental verification. Finally, the research explores the influence of the effective-mass parameters on the physical observables. These findings offer a theoretical basis for understanding the internal structure of pentaquarks and their associated physical properties. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to investigate other multiquark hadrons, such as tetraquarks. All results are presented in natural units. The computational code used for this analysis is available upon request. Software testing education is a critical component of computer science curricula, yet it is often difficult to implement effectively. A primary obstacle is the lack of accessible, cost-efficient tools capable of reliably assessing students' understanding within automated testing contexts. This paper introduces and validates the Testing and Quality Assurance Conceptual Response Tool (TQART), a low-cost, user-friendly application designed to facilitate the efficient and reliable assessment of software testing concepts. Built using the Inquiry-Based Conceptual Response technique, TQART offers a pedagogically sound alternative to traditional detailed evaluation methods. To validate this approach, an empirical study was conducted comparing its performance against that of a traditional mechanism. The findings indicate that TQART is more efficient than traditional methods when evaluating software testing concepts. Furthermore, the study confirms that TQART is a sound, effective, and reliable tool for teaching and learning these concepts. The research concludes that TQART represents a viable alternative to conventional assessment strategies in software testing education. Additionally, the tool's source code and user interface are publicly available for educational purposes. This work demonstrates that TQART enables instructors to design, implement, and assess testing concepts efficiently and cost-effectively while maintaining high quality. Ultimately, TQART facilitates the focused instruction of specific topics and promotes student self-awareness regarding their own performance. The tool is freely accessible for use in software testing education. By integrating TQART into the learning process, students can evaluate their conceptual understanding, identify knowledge gaps, and develop strategies to address them. Ultimately, this approach enhances the overall effectiveness of the learning experience. The study confirms that TQART is a viable alternative for assessing software testing concepts, and its adoption is expected to improve the quality of the learning process. A demonstration video of the tool is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=114222222222. This paper introduces a novel gas core reactor, termed the liquid-droplet gas core reactor (LDGC), designed for space propulsion in missions requiring long durations and high thrust. Unlike the conventional gas core reactor (GCR), which circulates a gaseous fuel, the LDGC circulates small liquid fuel droplets, allowing the engine to operate at significantly lower temperatures. The study presents the fundamental design of the LDGC, analyzes its thermodynamic cycle, and offers the governing equations and performance metrics for LDGC-based propulsion systems. These results establish a robust foundation for designing and simulating such systems. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the LDGC's viability as a remote space propulsion solution by addressing critical GCR issues, including high operating temperatures, high radiation levels, and fuel oxidation. Finally, the remote propulsion application of the LDGC is illustrated through a specific mission profile. The results indicate that the LDGC achieves specific impulse and thrust-to-power ratios comparable to standard GCRs while operating at substantially lower temperatures. Additionally, the LDGC exhibits significantly reduced radiotoxicity and radiation, making it better suited for remote space environments. These findings suggest that the LDGC is a highly promising candidate for future space propulsion applications. This work is intended to inspire further research into space reactor design and engineering. The proposed LDGC technology is expected to play a crucial role in advancing space exploration and development. The full paper is available at arXiv:2101.01004. Keywords: gas core reactor, space propulsion, nuclear thermal propulsion, nuclear electric propulsion, nuclear powered mission.

This work investigates the relationship between the deductive and axiomatic groundings of ASP-based semantics, exploring the possibility of deducing a theory's deductive grounding from its axiomatic counterpart. We demonstrate that while such deduction is impossible in general, it holds true for a significant subset of ASP encodings. Specifically, we establish that if a $P$-theory $T$ lacks $P$-choice operators and nominals, the deductive grounding of $T$ is included within the axiomatic grounding of $T$. Furthermore, we examine the algorithmic implications of this finding. We introduce a novel algorithm that determines the deductive grounding of any $P$-theory by directly computing its axiomatic grounding. This approach is shown to be more efficient than the standard method of deductive grounding, which involves iteratively applying $T$'s rules. Additionally, we present experimental results that validate our findings. Our algorithm successfully computes the deductive groundings for various ASP encodings, achieving performance improvements of up to two orders of magnitude compared to existing methods. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our algorithm through a practical application: identifying all valid groundings of a specific encoding that counts the shortest paths in a graph. This task is accomplished by computing the axiomatic groundings of a $P$-theory, a process that is provably more efficient than traditional deductive grounding. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of utilizing ASP groundings for algorithmic purposes. In conclusion, we argue that the ability to compute groundings directly is a highly valuable feature for ASP. We anticipate that our algorithm will facilitate this capability for a broad range of encodings, thereby enhancing the efficiency of ASP-based algorithms. In the future, we aim to extend our approach to handle groundings that include choice operators and nominals. Additionally, we plan to investigate methods for computing $P$-theory models based on their groundings, with a specific focus on $P$-theory satisfiability. Finally, we intend to extend our algorithm to compute $P$-theory extensions, which are essential for reasoning about nonmonotonic logic. These proposed extensions will enable the application of ASP groundings to practical problems, such as generating plans and diagnosing faults. Ultimately, we believe that computing groundings directly is a critical advancement for ASP. By directly computing groundings, ASP can be made more accessible to domain experts, thereby broadening its adoption. We hope that our findings will inspire further research into the application of ASP groundings

Initial laws characterize how universal quantum resources fundamentally evolve during early-stage dynamics. This study establishes an initial law for quantum states possessing at most two distinct eigenvalues, known as universal quantum ergodic states. We demonstrate that all quantum operations within an information-theoretic framework obey this initial law, which indicates that every operation either adheres to it or increases it, with strict inequalities applying unless the law remains invariant. Furthermore, we show that all quantum channels and bipartite operations are governed by this law. Specifically, we prove that all quantum and bipartite processes are monotone with respect to the law, and we derive initial expressions for the quantum divergence between two ergodic states based on this framework. Additionally, we examine applications of these findings to thermodynamics, showing that the law aligns with thermodynamic principles and can be interpreted as a modification to the first law. Finally, we construct a Hamiltonian for an ergodic system using the law and investigate the law's relationship with thermodynamic length. These findings suggest that the law serves as a quantum analogue to the conservation of energy. Finally, we outline a path toward extending these results to a broader class of quantum states. We introduce a technique for reconstructing angular correlations from the power spectrum and principal component variances of galaxy number density fields. This approach enables the analysis of how large-scale structure influences galaxy selection and identification. By applying a multi-scale quasi-linear model to simulate large-scale density fluctuations and their impact on local densities, we calculate the resulting power spectrum and principal component variances for various scales. This reconstruction accurately captures the primary effects of large-scale structure on local clustering, though it fails to reproduce the tails of the conditional probability distribution function. We demonstrate the application of this reconstruction using the KiDS-1000 catalogue, revealing that the quasi-linear model effectively describes the dependence of the two-point correlation function on the large-scale matter density field, despite some residual evidence of non-Gaussianity. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between the principal component variances in the KiDS-1000 catalogue and the reconstructed values. These findings suggest that this model can effectively account for the influence of large-scale structure on galaxy observations. Finally, we discuss the potential for utilizing this framework to infer the properties of the underlying mass distribution from catalog-derived information. The code used for these reconstructions is publicly accessible at https://github.com/brunocorbelli/asessing_data_from_moments. Future research will focus on refining the model to better capture the distribution of individual galaxies within large-scale environments. Ultimately, this method offers a means to evaluate the information content of the mass distribution encoded in galaxy catalogs and the constraints achievable through multi-probe analyses. This represents a significant advancement in understanding the data contained in galaxy catalogs. Future studies will explore the information content of the mass distribution and the constraints derived from multi-probe analyses, leveraging this method to assess catalog information and inform multi-probe strategies. This work marks a substantial step toward understanding the data within galaxy catalogs. (Abridged)

This work addresses inference for stable and sub-sublinear non-linear time series, deriving asymptotic behavior for sample covariance matrices and associated linear combinations of observations. The study proposes a robust estimator for the spectral measure in stable linear time sequences and constructs an asymptotically valid estimator for sub-sublinear non-linear trends within the spectral measure. Additionally, a local limit theorem is applied to non-linear stable processes to facilitate inference regarding linear combinations of the observations. Finally, numerical simulations are employed to compare various estimators and test procedures. As a practical application, the methodology is utilized to analyze daily returns from the S&P500 index. Supplementary materials, including a package for R and an Rmarkdown document containing the analysis code, are provided. The analysis includes estimating model parameters, forecasting, and risk management techniques such as Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. Furthermore, the research explores the impact of model selection on forecast accuracy and risk estimation, demonstrating that simpler models can outperform more complex ones. This finding underscores the necessity of selecting appropriate models when dealing with heavy-tailed data. Efficient decoding for quantum LDPC codes is a critical area of research with significant implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing. In this context, \emph{sparsity} refers to a code having constant rate and distance alongside linear check and trace degrees, whereas a \emph{fast decoder} is one that operates in linear time relative to the number of qubits. We introduce a new class of random quantum LDPC codes, termed \emph{balanced}, which are both efficient and capable of reliable transmission over the depolarizing channel. This class encompasses a broad spectrum of existing codes, such as surface codes, which are known to achieve optimal scaling of distance with respect to circuit size. We demonstrate that for any binary symmetric channel with a rate below a specific constant, the probability that a balanced code fails to decode correctly diminishes exponentially with the code's distance. Furthermore, we establish that the probability of a balanced code failing to detect an undetectable error also decreases exponentially with the distance. These findings confirm that balanced codes possess both fast decoders and strong distance properties. Additionally, we provide a method to construct a family of efficient, differentially private, and locally decodable codes. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of a class of quantum LDPC codes that simultaneously satisfies all these desirable attributes. The construction relies on a novel application of the \emph{Lov\'asz theta function}, a graph parameter that has recently attracted significant attention in theoretical computer science. We prove that the existence of an efficient approximation algorithm for the Lov\'asz theta function would imply an upper bound on the constant in our main theorem that is at least as tight as the Gilbert-Varshamov lower bound on the achievable rate-distance trade-off for quantum LDPC codes. This suggests that balanced codes may represent the limit of what is achievable for quantum LDPC codes. Finally, we discuss how our results extend to potentially more practical erasure channels, which are particularly relevant for superconducting quantum computers. Our approach utilizes the \emph{high-dimensional expansion} of bipartite Tanner graphs associated with these codes, a concept that has recently garnered substantial interest in theoretical computer science. We demonstrate that the existence of an expansion gap in these bipartite graphs is equivalent to the existence of a constant strictly greater than the channel's rate, which is necessary for any code to enable reliable communication. This study investigates the distributed decision complexity of Distance-$r$ Dominating Sets (DrDS) on sparse graphs with high girth. We demonstrate that for any fixed $r$ and girth $g$, there exists a probabilistic algorithm operating in polylogarithmic time and polylogarithmic communication rounds. Concurrently, we establish that for fixed $r$ and $g$, random DrDS instances are unlikely to admit solutions smaller than $\frac{1}{\alpha} n$, where $\alpha$ approaches 1 as $r$ and $g$ increase. Leveraging these findings, we prove that no distributed decision algorithm can solve the problem in sublinear time with probability exceeding $1 - n^{-\omega(1)}$ unless the algorithm's runtime or communication rounds scale exponentially with $r$ and $g$. Furthermore, we show that the existence of such an algorithm would imply a collapse in the hierarchy of distributed complexity classes. Finally, we examine the application of these results to graph streaming and propose a conjecture regarding the relationship between streaming algorithms for DrDS and the parameter $r$. Additionally, we present a construction that yields a lower bound on the size of Distributed Distance-$r$ Dominating Sets. Collectively, these contributions indicate that distributed decision algorithms for DrDS on sparse high-girth graphs are inherently limited in performance. Specifically, the most efficient algorithms are those that sample a random DrDS and verify membership, which operate in polylogarithmic time and communication rounds. The paper concludes by outlining several open questions for future research. Notably, the decision version of DrDS is solvable in polylogarithmic time and communication rounds in the randomized decision model, yet the combination of polylogarithmic time, constant communication rounds, and randomized computation rules remains an unresolved challenge. Addressing this would require either resolving open problems in random graph theory or proving that the decision version of DrDS is at least as hard as the optimization problem. Additionally, the question of whether a linear-time distributed algorithm exists for DrDS on general graphs remains open. Finally, the possibility of a randomized algorithm for Bounded Degree Dominating Sets in polylogarithmic time and sublinear communication rounds warrants further exploration. These limitations are particularly pronounced in the context of graph streaming, where even a constant-approximation algorithm for the problem remains an active area of research. A mass-boundary correspondence extends the well-established bulk-boundary principle to higher-order topological systems, where additional bulk topological invariants signal the presence of internal boundary states. This study investigates how this correspondence holds in higher-order topological insulators featuring disorder localized at their bulk-boundary interfaces. We demonstrate that while bulk and boundary states remain sensitive to disorders within these states, the bulk-boundary correspondence is preserved as long as the bulk stays in a topologically nontrivial phase. The research focuses on the two-dimensional higher-order topological insulator model, known as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain, with point-like disorder applied to its bulk and boundary topological superconducting variants. Our findings indicate that while disorders enable transitions between topological phases, the bulk-boundary correspondence is only violated when disorders fall within a specific range. We also explore the relevance of this work to experimental settings. Finally, we highlight the potential for extending these results to higher-dimensional higher-order topological models. This paper introduces a study of 13 TeV proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, which has an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Utilizing a multivariate analysis technique, the study targets the squark and gluino production region within the two-generation supersymmetry scenario. The analysis relies on the same signature previously examined in the gluino to two-body bottom quark decays study, which explored supersymmetry parameter space up to 2.5 TeV using 5 fb$^{-1}$ of 8 TeV data. By incorporating 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV data, this work investigates the same space down to squark and gluino masses of approximately 1.2 TeV. For the scenario involving gluino decays to two-body bottom quarks, this study examines gluino masses as light as 650 GeV, with corresponding charginos, chargino, and squark masses of 450, 350, and 650 GeV, respectively. This analysis complements the chargino and gluino decay into $\gamma \ell \nu$ and $\gamma \gamma$ channels, which probe the same parameter space using 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV data. Combining all three channels, squark and gluino masses as low as 700 and 650 GeV, respectively, are excluded. Additionally, the study examines the sensitivity of the 13 TeV analysis on the mass of the lightest neutralino, the lightest Higgs boson, and the mixing angle $\theta_{23}$, finding that the 95% CL lower limits on these parameters are 25, 125, and 0.75, respectively. These findings are consistent with the limits derived from the 5 fb$^{-1}$ 8 TeV data analysis. The 95% CL lower mass limits for the heaviest gluinos and charginos are 650 and 450 GeV, respectively, which are lower than the limits obtained from the same-sign dijet plus photon signal. The 95% CL upper limits on the $\theta_{23}$ mixing angle are 0.75, consistent with the 0.71 limit obtained from the same-sign dijet plus photon

We introduce a neural volume rendering technique designed for point sets that correspond to bright-field X-ray radiographs. In this approach, each point is depicted as a pixelized, transparent, bright-field X-ray-like radiograph. The method employs a novel ray-marching algorithm utilizing ray-casting to project these 2D projections onto a screen. We developed a new shading model capable of producing realistic visual results and successfully applied the technique to a set of 2.5 million points extracted from a 3D mesh. Our implementation is accessible on both desktop and mobile platforms. Additionally, we demonstrate its utility as an interactive tool for visual analysis and as an asset for 3D animated point cloud projections. Finally, we explore applications within virtual and augmented reality domains. The application can be found here: https://github.com/3dvisionlab/BrightFieldNeuralVis. This study presents speckle interferometric data for 100 binary systems observed at the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope (SOAR) during 2021. The dataset includes 27 new systems, 72 systems measured for the first time, and 15 previously published systems. For each pair, we determined the relative separation, position angle, and orbital elements where feasible. Additionally, we provide photometry for the companion stars, which is often more precise than the primary star's photometry. All findings are available in the ESO Science Archive. Notable new discoveries include a potential eclipsing binary system (HD 183263) and a system with a separation of just 0.1 mas (HD 190222). We also report the discovery of a third companion for the star HD 183263, bringing the total number of third companions found at SOAR to 12. Furthermore, we identified 11 new binary systems with separations below 0.2 mas. Among the 27 new detections, 14 are classified as giant stars, while the remaining 13 are main-sequence stars. Among the 72 first-time measurements, 32 are giants and 40 are main-sequence stars. Among the 15 replications, 6 are giants and 9 are main-sequence stars. The average photometric uncertainty for the 27 new detections is 0.003, compared to 0.008 for the 72 first-time measurements and 0.004 for the 15 replications. The median uncertainty for the 27 new detections is 0.002, versus 0.004 for the first-time measurements and 0.001 for the replications. We discuss the implications of these results and conclude that SOAR's speckle interferometry remains a highly effective tool for measuring the relative positions of close binary stars. The average image quality achieved in 2021 was 0.2 mas, with the best images reaching 0.08 mas. These results suggest that SOAR speckle interferometry can reliably detect companions with a 50% probability down to a separation of 0.2 mas. Color-kinematics duality has recently been extended to integrable systems, where it manifests as a differential equation with a unique solution defined by local expressions. In this study, we apply the duality to the self-dual Yang-Mills theory, whose integrability is represented by the SDW equation. We construct the corresponding local dual variables and solve the color-kinematics duality equation. The solution reveals that the local three-particle interaction vertices can be decomposed into a basis of independent vertices, each possessing a specific kinematic structure. We then build the heavenly chiral algebra utilizing these vertices and demonstrate that it coincides with the three-dimensional Yang-Feldman algebra, which encapsulates all scattering amplitudes of the self-dual Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, we elucidate the connection between the non-local Yang-Feldman commutators and the local dual basis through a unique matrix. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings within the framework of the amplitude/Ward identity correspondence. As a concluding remark, we note that our methodology can be extended to both linear and nonlinear Yangians. We anticipate that this work will advance our comprehension of color-kinematics duality in integrable systems and its relationship to the holomorphic amplitudes of chiral theories. Additionally, our approach may hold significance for investigating the color-charge separation problem in integrable systems. Solar jets are believed to originate from magnetic reconnection occurring in the low corona, yet their precise formation mechanisms remain unclear. This study presents LOFAR observations of a jet-driven piston surge detected during a multi-frequency radio survey of the low corona. The surge appears as a dark feature, likely caused by the jet's plasma flow compressing and displacing coronal material. By analyzing the surge's morphology and motion, we determined the jet's speed to be approximately 100 km/s. These findings align with jets identified by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) in the mid-corona and low chromosphere, as well as with jets observed by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) in the low corona. Our results suggest that jets form through a relatively slow process, potentially involving the gradual opening of a magnetic field line or the slow ejection of plasma from a magnetic reconnection site. Furthermore, the surge's dark appearance at 150 MHz indicates that the jet is optically thick at this frequency, implying a speed of roughly 1000 km/s. This supports the hypothesis that jets are fast, compact plasma ejections originating from the low corona. Additionally, the persistent appearance of the surge across multiple frequencies implies a large physical size, estimated at approximately 100,000 km. These results are consistent with the surge being a coronal mass ejection (CME), suggesting that CMEs may also result from a relatively slow process. Finally, the observed speed is comparable to the speed of Alfvén waves in the low corona, indicating that the jet could be a form of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wave. Overall, this study demonstrates that LOFAR can detect jets and surge-like features in the low corona, providing a valuable tool for investigating their formation and characteristics. Future research should aim to identify a common source for both the jets and surges to better understand their origins. This will require combining LOFAR's low-frequency observations with high-resolution imaging from other instruments, such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the millimeter band and the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) in the extreme ultraviolet. Additionally, spectral analysis of the jets will help determine their plasma properties, such as density and temperature. Ultimately, this research will enhance our understanding of solar jets and their role in solar and heliospheric processes. The LOFAR data used in this study can be accessed via the LOFAR Science Archive

This study introduces a functional probabilistic differential equation (fobe) designed to model random whirlpool dynamics, building upon the framework established by Mao and Marboe in \cite{mao2019functional}. The primary objective is to demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the fobe. This proof relies on a novel transformation that converts the fobe into an standard probabilistic differential equation. By applying this change of variables, we utilize established techniques to show that the resulting equation admits a unique solution. Subsequently, we define a stochastic differential equation to represent the trajectory of a particle within a random whirlpool. We establish that if the unique solution to the transformed fobe exists, then a unique solution for the particle's trajectory also exists. Finally, a numerical simulation is presented to illustrate the behavior of such particles in two-dimensional random whirlpools. Through this simulation, we examine the impact of various drift and diffusion functions on particle behavior and demonstrate that, under specific drift conditions, particles may exhibit infinite repulsion. Overall, this research provides a new method for analyzing the dynamics of particles in random whirlpools. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to capture complex flow behaviors—such as spiraling, oscillating, or radial motion—more effectively than traditional flow field models. These findings hold significant potential for applications across diverse fields, including fluid dynamics, plasma physics, and meteorology. Furthermore, the methodology offers a foundation for investigating biological phenomena, such as animal movement patterns and the spread of infectious diseases. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to be difficult for classical computers to replicate. This study demonstrates that the full state vector required for this process possesses entanglement across every possible partition of the system's modes. Furthermore, we establish that the mode-partition entanglement entropy within the boson sampling state vector adheres to a universal law, growing linearly with the number of modes. Consequently, this state vector exhibits the maximum possible entanglement for any bipartite system of the same size. These findings hold true for inputs consisting of Fock states with arbitrary photon numbers. Additionally, we show that the eigenvalues of the bipartite reduced density matrix can be calculated analytically using random matrix theory, and the entanglement spectrum can be derived from the universal eigenvalue distribution of the Ginibre ensemble. Finally, the methodology employed in this work can be extended to analyze entanglement in the full state vectors of other quantum computational models. This insight enables the investigation of entanglement properties in various quantum states, even when the states are defined implicitly. As an application, we investigate the entanglement structure of the complete state vector for a specific instance of quantum supremacy: Gaussian boson sampling. In this case, the universal eigenvalue distribution of the bipartite reduced density matrix is determined by the GUE random matrix ensemble. The analysis reveals that the Gaussian boson sampling state vector exhibits less entanglement compared to the photon number (Fock) state case. This difference is attributed to the reduced rank of the reduced density matrix in the Gaussian boson sampling scenario. The results of this study may aid in understanding the entanglement properties of quantum states, particularly those generated through Gaussian unitary transformations. Furthermore, the proposed analytical framework can facilitate the investigation of the entanglement structure in diverse quantum states. Finally, our findings indicate that the quantum state underlying Gaussian boson sampling does not achieve maximum entanglement. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the entanglement spectrum of this quantum state is non-uniform. The non-uniformity of the entanglement spectrum is caused by the non-universality of the eigenvalue distribution, which stems from the restricted rank of the reduced density matrix. These findings suggest that the quantum state in Gaussian boson sampling does not maximize entanglement. We introduce Temporal Guided Learning (TGL), a novel sequence learning architecture designed to handle brief, high-dimensional temporal sequences found in life science datasets. TGL integrates two components: the Sequence Guided Learning module (SGL), which adapts the Guided Learning module from Saeed et al. (2020) to learn from brief sequences, and the Annotation Guided module (AG), which enables the model to leverage expert-derived guidance. We demonstrate that TGL surpasses leading models in predicting growth rates from time-lapse microscopy images of bacteria. Furthermore, we show that the AG component facilitates the learning of brief, high-dimensional sequences from limited examples without requiring back-propagation through the neural network. Finally, we outline the training and testing protocols that allow TGL to generalize effectively to unseen datasets. Our findings indicate that TGL achieves a 1.5-fold improvement in test performance compared to the best existing model. The TGL code is accessible at https://github.com/abdo-saeed/TGL. Reinforcement learning (RL) addresses agents operating within a partially observable environment, a scenario that introduces significant challenges. To address this, an agent must maintain a belief state—a condensed synthesis of all past observations and actions—which RL algorithms then treat as the input state. This study investigates the capacity of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to function as belief states within a RL framework using the 'Rainbow' agent architecture. We demonstrate that RNNs can effectively solve a simplified version of a previously proposed '2-room' challenge. Furthermore, we show that RNNs with a single hidden layer can partially succeed on the more intricate 2-room challenge, which features a more complex observation space. Finally, we explore the application of attention mechanisms to manage a multi-layer RNN, yielding promising results. These findings suggest that RNNs serve as a viable alternative to traditional belief states derived from RL algorithms, particularly in contexts requiring partial observability. Additionally, the 2-room challenge is anticipated to gain renewed interest as a rigorous test of the ability to learn from partial observations. Our Rainbow agent, which incorporates attention mechanisms and multi-layer RNNs, achieves an average score of 1100, surpassing the current state-of-the-art score of 800. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/aleksandar-milojkovic/2-room-rainbow-agent. Source code for this agent is also available on GitHub. Furthermore, we have released a new algorithm for the car-racing environment, which incorporates attention mechanisms and multi-layer RNNs, achieving an average score of 1000, compared to the current state-of-the-art score of 700. In human action detection, context is vital for identifying actions within complex settings. However, most existing methods rely on spatial or temporal cues, often neglecting the environmental context that significantly influences action recognition. This paper introduces a weakly guided, graph-based multi-view framework to capture semantic context. The proposed weakly guided approach utilizes an action context graph to highlight relevant context and a graph-based multi-view network to integrate various context types. Furthermore, the semantic context graph is dynamically adjusted during training to better reflect the scene. Experimental results on the JHU-UDC dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/ICCV19-WGAGC. This short paper introduces and examines the second edition of the Image Similarity Challenge, which was hosted as part of the 21st International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR 2021) in Roanoke, Virginia, USA. The challenge aims to identify image similarity relationships across a diverse collection of image classes. The outcome reveals that achieving a strong correlation between predicted and ground-truth labels is difficult, even for models specifically trained for this task. Furthermore, an analysis of the discovery-phase dataset suggests that current deep learning techniques are effective at detecting similarity within semantically related categories but struggle in visually similar, semantically distinct cases. This finding underscores the necessity for a discovery-oriented evaluation metric for image similarity, a goal that will be addressed in future challenges. Overall, the results highlight the need for new image representation learning approaches that prioritize visually and semantically meaningful features rather than relying solely on category identity. Additionally, we demonstrate that leveraging transfer learning from vision-and-language models can enhance performance on this task. Finally, we argue that the Image Similarity Challenge is well-suited for developing models that generate image similarity graphs, thereby supporting various downstream applications. The challenge dataset and benchmark can be accessed at https://www.kaggle.com/c/icsc2021. Supplementary materials are available at https://www.kaggle.com/sv272/discovery-phase-datasets/data. The source code for our proposed models is located at https://github.com/DeepMind/icsc2021.

This monograph examines the diffusion process $u_t=D(x,u)u_{xx}-f(u)_x$ defined on a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^1$ subject to boundary conditions. The function $D(x,u)$ represents a diffusion coefficient that may degenerate to zero, whereas $f$ denotes a reaction term; the study does not impose growth restrictions on $f$. The primary objective is to analyze metastability and long-term dynamics, with specific attention to boundary conditions. The analysis covers various boundary value problems, including Dirichlet, Neumann, and insulated types, alongside more complex scenarios such as mixed, Robin, and dynamic boundary conditions. Furthermore, the text addresses boundary homogenization and provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in the field. The material is structured to serve as both a reference and a textbook. Key issues explored include the existence and uniqueness of solutions, the construction of weak solutions, regularity properties, the behavior of disturbed systems, asymptotic dynamics, metastability, and boundary layer phenomena. The final chapter explores boundary layer formation, the approach to metastable states, and the validity of Dirichlet-Neumann reductions. The work concludes with an appendix on measure theory and integration. The intended audience comprises graduate students and researchers in mathematics, physics, and engineering. This study investigates the properties of symmetric nuclear matter at supra-nuclear densities under intense magnetic fields using the LOCV framework. The results indicate that these properties remain largely insensitive to the magnetic field, even at extreme intensities. Specifically, the saturation density and energy exhibit only minor variations with changing field strength. Notably, protons and neutrons experience different splitting energies due to the field, leading to significant isospin asymmetry effects. Furthermore, the neutron fraction rises monotonically with magnetic field strength, reaching a maximum of 0.62 at $B = 10^{18}$ G. Finally, the magnetic field induces a significant reduction in both the scalar and vector mean fields. These findings are compared with previous studies to assess the validity of the conclusions drawn. Additionally, the computed symmetry energy and its density dependence are compared with Lattimer and Sawyer's results to evaluate the accuracy of the current study. Finally, the skin thickness is observed to increase as the magnetic field strength increases. These results are also compared with other studies to determine the validity of the findings presented here. Finally, the text examines the implications of these findings for neutron stars and magnetars. Specifically, the study explores the possibility of inverse magnetic catalysis, where nuclear matter becomes more stable in the presence of a magnetic field. This could have significant implications for the structure and evolution of neutron stars, particularly in the extreme conditions found in magnetars. The paper concludes by discussing the potential for further research in this area, including the development of more sophisticated models to better understand the effects of magnetic fields on nuclear matter. Additionally, the study suggests that the findings could have implications for the search for new types of compact objects, such as quark stars, and the study of gravitational waves emitted by merging neutron stars. Finally, the paper notes that the LOCV method has been successfully applied to nuclear matter for over 50 years, and the current findings are consistent with previous studies using the same method. This study introduces a novel framework called DP-REC, designed to enhance privacy and privacy-utility trade-offs in federated learning (FL) by minimizing communication costs. REC (Recursive Encryption) is a new communication protocol that enables the transmission of encrypted model updates without revealing sensitive information to the server. We present a theoretical analysis of REC and establish a method for calculating the privacy leakage of DP-REC, which involves adding noise to REC-encrypted gradients. Our experiments demonstrate that DP-REC surpasses current privacy-preserving FL protocols in both privacy protection and model utility. Furthermore, we validate the REC protocol's security within the FL context, confirming that DP-REC effectively safeguards participant privacy. Finally, we explore the application of DP-REC to private federated inference. Our results indicate that transmitting an SqueezeNet model via REC-encrypted weights results in negligible accuracy loss on the CIFAR10 dataset. Additionally, we confirm the security of REC during the inference phase, ensuring the confidentiality of the model's internal states. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) imaging surveys of the Taurus, Perseus, and Auriga regions using the FUV-2 and FUV-3 filters on the {\it International Ultraviolet Explorer} (IUE). These observations were specifically targeted to detect the Lyman-$\alpha$ emission line from the accretion process in young stellar objects (YSOs). The study successfully identified Lyman-$\alpha$ emission in 10 out of 11 observed Taurus-class YSOs, with 8 of these detections being reported for the first time. Additionally, we observed FUV emission from 10 YSOs in Perseus and Auriga, including Lyman-$\alpha$ from 5 of them, which are also noted as new detections. For the 19 Taurus YSOs exhibiting Lyman-$\alpha$ emission, we analyzed the relationships between this emission and other spectral lines, as well as correlations with stellar mass and luminosity. The FUV flux from these Lyman-$\alpha$ emissions shows a strong correlation with H$\alpha$ flux, a trend that is also evident in the 5 FUV-detected YSOs from the Perseus and Auriga regions. Furthermore, the ratio of FUV flux to H$\alpha$ flux appears to be independent of stellar mass and luminosity. Finally, we observed that the FUV flux from Lyman-$\alpha$ emission in Taurus YSOs is positively correlated with their accretion luminosity. Overall, the data indicate that the FUV flux from Lyman-$\alpha$ emission is primarily driven by accretion luminosity rather than stellar luminosity. These findings align with previous studies, confirming that accretion luminosity is the dominant source of far-UV radiation in young stellar objects. The IUE's ability to observe the Lyman-$\alpha$ line in a significant number of YSOs demonstrates the FUV filter's effectiveness in studying accretion processes. However, the limited IUE observation time allocated to YSOs necessitates a future FUV survey of the Taurus region using a more sensitive filter and a more efficient instrument. Extracting tabular data from documents, particularly those generated by Microsoft Word, poses significant challenges due to the varied and often complex rendering of tables across different media, including digital formats like PDFs. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to determine the structural layout of such tables within PDF files. The method involves training a GNN to predict the binary adjacency matrix representing a table's structure, thereby offering a general representation for table extraction. To facilitate this, the study proposes a new method for converting raster images in PDFs into vectorized graph representations, which are subsequently processed by the GNN. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves promising performance in both table localization and structure recognition tasks. The code and data required to replicate the method are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1997/GraphNeuralNetworksForTableStructure. Furthermore, the authors have developed a Python package, PyPDFTable, which implements the method and includes a Python interface for users. This package is available on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/pypdftable/. The package's source code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1997/PyPDFTable. Additionally, the paper includes a tutorial on utilizing PyPDFTable, which can be found at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1997/PyPDFTable/blob/master/PYPDFTable_Tutorial.ipynb. Finally, the study presents a new dataset, PDFTable, comprising 1,000 pages annotated with binary masks for table locations and a binary adjacency matrix for table structure, available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1997/PDFTable. This dataset is also accessible via the Table Structure Database website at https://tabledatabase.org/ and can be downloaded from the corresponding author's website, https://www.cs.uaf.edu/~ahmedhassan1997/. The dataset includes examples of diverse table structures, such as hierarchical tables, tables with empty cells, and tables containing merged cells. The authors hope this dataset will facilitate further research in the field. Interested parties are invited to contact the corresponding author at ahmedhassan1997@cs.uaf.edu for more information. The paper also features a section on limitations, acknowledging that the current method has certain constraints, including the potential for misclassification of table elements and the possibility of incorrect predictions for table structures. Cognitive layers provide a framework for addressing sequential games under information insufficiency. By utilizing a Bayesian network to model a player's information state, this approach enables the simultaneous solution of a game with multiple state types. However, this method assumes that players accurately estimate the conditional probabilities within the Bayesian network. The study demonstrates that when players miscalculate these conditional probabilities, the resulting equilibrium strategies and payoffs can diverge significantly from those predicted by standard cognitive layers. Consequently, an alternative approach is introduced to solve such games that does not rely on conditional probability estimates from the players. This new method is validated through a comparison with an extensive form representation of a two-player strategic interaction, which explicitly details the players' sufficient statistics. The findings indicate that for two-player games, the strategies and payoffs in equilibrium are invariant regardless of whether the game is expressed via explicit sufficient statistics or the alternative cognitive layer-based strategy space. Furthermore, the paper successfully applies this framework to a three-layer supply chain, effectively capturing the uncertainty surrounding the new product launch. In this application, the alternative strategy space proves more effective than the traditional cognitive layer approach for games where players do not possess conditional probability estimates. Finally, the study examines how the uncertainty of a new product launch influences the behavior of a strategic supply chain. Results show that when launch success is uncertain, players adopt more cautious attitudes toward the new product, leading to reduced order quantities and higher wholesale prices. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the uncertainty surrounding a new product launch can be more detrimental than the absence of any information. Finally, the paper explores how information sharing impacts the strategic decisions within a new product launch context. It demonstrates that when information is shared, the launch firm can achieve higher profits, whereas the supply chain's overall performance may decline. Furthermore, the study finds that the impact of information sharing is contingent upon the specific structure of the Bayesian network. Specifically, the benefits of sharing increase when the conditional probability estimates are more accurate. In contrast, when conditional probabilities are inaccurate, the strategic decision-making process may be adversely affected by information sharing. These insights are particularly relevant for new product development and marketing initiatives. Finally, the paper outlines several promising avenues for future research. For instance, extending the proposed framework to scenarios involving a finite number of players would be a valuable contribution to the existing literature. Additionally, the framework can be adapted to model a new product launch as a multi-player game, thereby generating significant practical value. Population estimates serve as a foundation for numerous critical sectors, including resource allocation, urban planning, and public health. In many nations, these counts are conducted through physical surveys known as census operations. Although censuses offer robust demographic data, they are resource-intensive and necessitate repeat efforts at regular intervals. To address this burden, countries are increasingly adopting model-based approaches that utilize machine learning to forecast census metrics like population and fertility rates. This study evaluates the efficacy of such methods in sub-Saharan Africa by examining a model trained on extensive demographic data from across the region. The research highlights key challenges in developing sustainable population estimation systems and proposes a framework for implementing autonomous population estimation within government agencies. Specifically, we outline ongoing collaborative efforts between the University of Edinburgh and the government of Mozambique to build an autonomous system capable of generating population estimates for this country. This initiative involves integrating domain expertise with cutting-edge machine learning techniques to enhance the accuracy of predictions. Ultimately, we argue that achieving true autonomy in population estimation requires sustained collaboration between academia and government bodies. This partnership ensures long-term support for model maintenance, monitoring, and evaluation, thereby fostering sustainable autonomous systems. The entire workflow, from data collection to model deployment and feature engineering, is designed to be executed remotely, allowing for periodic retraining and updates without direct access to the target country's infrastructure. By facilitating accurate and timely estimates, this approach enables governments to make informed decisions regarding development and resource distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that remote access to computational resources can yield state-of-the-art results in population estimation. This work establishes a framework for advancing sustainable, autonomous population estimation in sub-Saharan Africa. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/evgeny123/Mozambique-Population-Estimation. Our findings are detailed in the paper titled "Towards Sustainable Survey Autonomous Population Estimation in Mozambique," published in the Proceedings of the 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT 2023). The authors include Evgeny Osipov, Katerina Danovska, and Stephen Roberts from the University of Edinburgh, along with Nelson Tete and Carlos Mucumbuta from the Government of Mozambique. This paper introduces a novel class of membership query algorithms designed for streaming data, where the server must dynamically estimate the size of a stream that may or may not include a given query element. The proposed algorithms are classified as either sharp or non-sharp. Sharp members are further subdivided into estimated membership query filters with no false positives (EMQ-FNF) and those allowing false positives (EMQ-FP). On the other hand, non-sharp algorithms are known as cardinality estimation filters and are also treated as either producing no false positives or permitting them. The study presents the first family of FNF EMQ algorithms, demonstrating that they achieve significantly lower space complexity compared to existing cardinality estimation techniques. Additionally, the paper outlines the advantages and limitations of these methods. A key finding is that the first FNF EMQ algorithm surpasses the first FNF cardinality estimation filter in both space efficiency and the breadth of applicable techniques. Finally, the results of experiments conducted to verify the claimed properties of these algorithms are presented. This study theoretically examines spinor recombination events involving three alkali atoms. These processes encompass both two-body and three-body mechanisms, with the latter facilitating atom-molecule transitions within spinor states of a Bose-Einstein condensate. The investigation highlights the potential of three-body recombination to generate highly excited molecules with significant spin. Furthermore, the work outlines the necessary experimental conditions for observing these spinor recombination phenomena in cold-atom experiments. Finally, the study establishes a quantitative link between the binding energy of the resulting molecule and the anisotropy of its spin distribution. These findings could advance the understanding of spinor dynamics and enable the creation of spinor-based quantum simulators. Additionally, the results may prove valuable for enhancing the efficiency of laser-induced three-body recombination methods for molecule production. This paper introduces a new framework designed to investigate the complex dynamics of fluid-structure interactions (FSI) and two-phase flows (TPF) within porous media. The study examines scenarios involving a flexible structure situated in a porous environment subjected to fluid currents, as well as cases where two fluids of differing densities interact with a permeable boundary. To achieve this, the study employs a hybrid approach combining Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) for fluid simulation with the Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method for structure simulation. A key advancement is the development of a novel interface detection strategy that identifies fluid-structure and two-fluid contacts in a fully automatic, contact-free manner. This method relies on the interaction between fluid particles and a background grid to establish a binary mesh, which subsequently facilitates the integration of fluid forces at the interface. The framework's efficacy is validated through a series of numerical experiments, including the simulation of fluid currents acting on a flexible structure and two-phase flows interacting with a permeable boundary. These results demonstrate that the proposed method is highly effective in representing the specified physical phenomena. Furthermore, the study confirms that the DG method remains robust in the presence of fluid forces, maintaining stability and accuracy. The paper concludes by discussing potential future applications, such as simulating two-phase flows within porous media. Finally, the authors emphasize the critical role of the background grid in this approach, noting that it serves as the foundation for the proposed interface detection technique and offers a viable solution for addressing the traditional paradoxes associated with FSI and TPF simulations. Additionally, the framework is well-suited for parallel computing environments, with both SPH and DG methods supporting adaptive mesh refinement. This capability allows for the dynamic adjustment of mesh resolution in regions of interest, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the simulations. The study ends by outlining potential future research directions, including the extension of this framework to simulate electrokinetic phenomena in porous media. This prospective application would involve modeling two fluids of distinct densities and viscosities within a porous medium subjected to an electric field, where the fluid viscosities correspond to their respective electrical charges. In such a scenario, the background grid would be essential for implementing the proposed interface detection method, and fluid forces at the interface would need to account for electrokinetic effects. Consequently, the fluid structure would be modeled using the coupled Navier-Stokes and Nernst-Planck equations. This represents a promising avenue for future research, as it would enable the simulation of electrokinetic phenomena in porous media using a hybrid SPH-DG

Machine learning is a rapidly expanding field that has recently integrated quantum mechanics to create data processing methods with superior scalability and lower energy consumption compared to classical alternatives. Although numerous quantum-enhanced techniques have been proposed, they often depend on error correction, are susceptible to noise, or lack experimental validation. This study evaluates various quantum unmonitored and instructed learning approaches across different noise environments, ranging from local to global decoherence. Our findings indicate that multi-qubit systems can outperform multi-qubit logical counterparts even without requiring error correction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that logical qubits achieve data processing accuracy comparable to physical qubits but fail to match the performance of standard multi-qubit systems. These conclusions are supported by experiments conducted on superconducting quantum processors. Additionally, we illustrate how quantum unmonitored and instructed learning can be utilized for anomaly detection within time series data. The code for our methods is publicly accessible at https://github.com/QuantumMachineLearning. These results establish a foundation for developing quantum data processing methods that are superior in both performance and cost-efficiency relative to existing state-of-the-art solutions. By leveraging the exponential reduction in space complexity inherent to quantum computing, these methods are well-suited for deployment on near-term quantum hardware. Ultimately, this research is expected to catalyze further advancements in the field of quantum machine learning. Supplementary materials are available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-021-01477-2.
