This paper introduces a method for visualizing pullbacks associated with the 3D generalized Hénon map. Pullbacks represent the preimages of a specific point or region after $n$ iterations of the map, forming the focus of this study. The three-dimensional generalized Hénon map is a widely used model for investigating chaotic dynamics in three variables; its pullback geometry exhibits diverse patterns contingent upon the system's parameters. We address parameter selection by introducing a measure of pullback complexity. Furthermore, to enhance visualization, we develop a method for projecting three-dimensional objects onto a two-dimensional plane. This approach involves defining an objective function that quantifies the quality of the projection and optimizing it to identify the optimal two-dimensional representation. The proposed methods are demonstrated through several examples. Ultimately, our results illustrate the rich and varied dynamics inherent to the three-dimensional generalized Hénon map. The accompanying code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/PullbackVisualization}. Future research will explore extensions of this work to other three-dimensional dynamical systems. Additionally, the presented techniques can be adapted for other applications, such as localizing sources of electromagnetic radiation in three-dimensional space. For instance, the pullbacks of a map representing a radiation source would reflect the local behavior of that source, aiding in the identification of regions influenced by it. This could facilitate the localization of the source or the detection of anomalies. The general framework for pullback visualization is also applicable to image processing and pattern recognition. Specifically, the pullbacks of an image can be visualized to reveal features that are not apparent in the original. This technique is particularly valuable for enhancing image contrast and denoising. Finally, the optimization method for visualizing three-dimensional objects can be utilized for other purposes, including the visualization of molecular structures in chemistry and biological macromolecules. In these contexts, pulling the object and projecting it onto a 2D plane can significantly improve visual clarity. Furthermore, this approach is applicable to any three-dimensional object, such as visualizing the pullbacks of a 3D model or analyzing the internal structure of a three-dimensional dataset. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/PullbackVisualization}. Future research will extend these methods to higher-dimensional objects. Additionally, the parameter selection method can be applied to other dynamical systems to identify interesting parameter regimes. Finally, the optimization technique will be utilized to visualize three-dimensional objects in other scientific fields, such as physics

We begin by examining the definition of connection holonomy and deriving the specific conditions under which it simplifies to a path-ordered exponential. Next, we analyze parallel transport along a simple closed loop generated by the commutator of two Killing vector fields, demonstrating that the result is independent of the parametrization. Finally, we establish that parallel transport along such a loop is equivalent to the time evolution generated by any Killing vector field along that loop. Furthermore, we prove that if the transport can be expressed as a path-ordered exponential, this exponential is uniquely determined, thereby defining the holonomy of the connection for simple closed curves. We also present the correct formulation of gravitational holonomy, clarify the distinction between gravitational and mathematical holonomy, and provide a proof of the proposition that gravitational holonomy is the sole version of gravitational holonomy. Additionally, we offer the first explicit calculation of gravitational holonomy for a simple closed curve, showing that it is the time evolution generated by the sum of the Hamiltonians associated with the Killing vector fields tangent to the curve. Finally, we illustrate that for a small closed curve formed by the commutator of two Killing vector fields, the gravitational holonomy is equivalent to the mathematical holonomy of that curve. These findings offer a new perspective on gravitational holonomy, with potential applications in black hole physics. In this context, we propose a version of the generalized membrane paradigm where the surface membrane is defined by a closed curve rather than a two-dimensional surface, and we demonstrate the equivalence between this proposal and another existing membrane formulation. This equivalence is proven by showing that the gravitational holonomy along a closed curve is invariant under perturbations of the curve. We also provide the explicit form of the gravitational Wilson loop for a closed curve and the membrane prescription corresponding to it. Additionally, we prove the equivalence between this membrane prescription and another existing one. Finally, we present the gravitational equivalent of the entanglement wedge crossing condition, known as the Wilson line crossing condition, and offer the gravitational counterpart to the Bekenstein bound involving gravitational holonomy. These results may offer new insights into the black hole information paradox. As an application, we derive the gravitational equivalent of the Rindler membrane and the membrane picture of entanglement entropy for a wedge-shaped region within Minkowski space. We also provide the gravitational equivalent of the membrane picture of entanglement entropy for a region in global AdS space, which was previously derived by another group. Finally, we show that the gravitational holonomy of a simple closed curve remains invariant under small deformations

An integer partition of $n$ is defined as a collection of positive integers summing to $n$, arranged in non-increasing order. The set of all such partitions is denoted by $\Y^n$. The hook length $h_Y(i,j)$ for a partition $Y\in \Y^n$ corresponds to the count of elements in the hook of the cell $(i,j)$ within the Ferrers diagram of $Y$. The collection of all hook lengths across all partitions of $n$ is represented by $\HL^n$. This paper investigates the frequency distribution of hook lengths that are multiplicatively covered by the numbers 2 or 3. Specifically, $D_2^n$ and $D_3^n$ denote the counts of hook lengths in $\HL^n$ divisible by 2 and 3, respectively. We examine the moments of $D_2^n$ and $D_3^n$, establish the exponential growth rate for their expected values, and analyze the asymptotic behavior of their distributions as $n$ approaches infinity. Furthermore, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the moments and distribution of $\E^n\setminus\{D_2^n\}$ and $\E^n\setminus\{D_3^n\}$ in the limit. Finally, we explore the asymptotic distribution of the greatest common divisor of all hook lengths in $\Y^n$. These findings are supported and enhanced by computational data and visualizations. Additionally, we derive several identities and theorems regarding the moments and distribution of $D_2^n$ and $D_3^n$ for specific values of $n$. This research was conducted while the second author was a Visiting Assistant Professor at the University of Missouri, and the third author was a Visiting Assistant Professor at the University of North Carolina at Pembroke. The authors acknowledge the support of UNC Pembroke's Center for Research and Creative Excellence, which facilitated this work through a Visiting Scholars Program fellowship for the second author and a Visiting Faculty Fellowship for the third author. This study was also partially funded by a Summer REU Fellowship held by the first author at Western Michigan University's Department of Mathematics. We extend our gratitude to Dr. Brian Logan for his insightful comments and suggestions. Finally, we appreciate the dedication and hard work of all individuals who contributed to this project. Keywords: integer partitions, hook lengths, probability distributions. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05A15, 05A16, 05A19.

This study introduces an experimental method for measuring the tunneling duration of spin qubits using a Larmor clock. The duration is determined by analyzing the clock's response to the spin's tunneling disturbance. The clock is constructed by coupling the tunneling spin to a collective spin system, establishing a one-to-one interaction where the target qubit's $y$-component (spin-y) drives rotations of the collective system's plane of polarization. The experiment involves preparing the tunneling spin in the $|-\rangle_y$ state, which induces a $180^{\circ}$ rotation of the collective spin from the $|+\rangle_x$ to the $|-\rangle_x$ polarization plane. By analyzing the probability of the collective spin remaining in the $|+\rangle_x$ plane after the tunneling process, the spin-induced disturbance is assessed. A statistical average of this disturbance across an ensemble of tunneling spins yields the tunneling time. Theoretical analysis indicates that the tunneling time is primarily determined by the overlap between the initial and final states of the tunneling spin. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrates robustness against statistical fluctuations in both the tunneling and collective spins. Finally, the scheme is applied to study the time delays of the spin-y and spin-z components during tunneling. The results show that, upon averaging over the ensemble, the tunneling times for both spin components are identical, with the spin-z component exhibiting a shorter tunneling time than the spin-y component. This finding aligns with recent conclusions from theoretical investigations. Additionally, the scheme is applicable to various collective spin systems, including those composed of two-level atoms or artificial atoms. The latter are particularly advantageous due to their ease of preparation, manipulation, and measurement, as well as their superior control and scalability. Consequently, the collective spin-based Larmor clock method offers a viable approach for measuring the tunneling duration of spin qubits. Its application to ensembles of artificial atoms may facilitate the development of new technologies, such as quantum registers, quantum batteries, and quantum sensors. Moreover, the scheme can be adapted to measure the tunneling times of the $x$ and $z$ components of a spin qubit. Finally, the proposed Larmor clock method is also suitable for investigating the tunneling times of optical pulses and other wave packets. These wave packets can be encoded using the polarization or spatial mode degrees of freedom, with the collective spin system serving as the clock to measure the internal state components' tunneling times. Utilizing the light-cone wave functions of nonrelativistic mesons derived from the Bethe-Salpeter wave functions, we calculate the twist-3 and twist-4 distribution amplitudes, including the dominant moments for the vector, axial-vector, scalar, and pseudoscalar mesons. In the case of P-wave mesons, we observe that the leading twist amplitudes are characterized by a single nonvanishing moment, which is relatively small. Regarding twist-3 P-wave mesons, their leading moments are comparatively large, with the pseudoscalar mesons exhibiting sign-changing distributions. For P-wave mesons, the dominant moments of the overlying twist-4 amplitudes are small and, in certain instances, negative. Additionally, we analyze the ratios of leading to overlying twist moments for P-wave mesons, revealing that these ratios are significantly larger than those found in QCD sum rule calculations for the mesons. Consequently, our findings indicate that the dominant twist-3 and twist-4 moments of P-wave mesons are essential for investigating heavy hadron processes, such as $B \to P P$ decays, which have been the subject of recent studies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the twist-4 dominant moments are necessary to accurately reproduce the decay constants of $P$-wave mesons, which were previously determined via QCD sum rules. Finally, we provide expressions for the leading twist twist-3 amplitudes of P-wave mesons in terms of their leading moments, which can be applied to P-wave mesons in general. Our results suggest that the twist-3 and twist-4 moments of P-wave mesons are not negligible and must be incorporated into the analysis of heavy hadron processes. This study examines the emergence of soliton trains within a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) as nonlinear interactions intensify. The condensate's evolution is modeled using the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) incorporating both cubic and quintic terms. We investigate how the system transitions from chaotic dynamics to ordered soliton train behavior by analyzing the power spectrum and examining the impact of symmetry breaking in nonlinear interactions on this order. Specifically, we demonstrate that changing the sign of the quintic interaction term induces a shift from asymmetric to symmetric dynamics, resulting in the formation of ordered soliton trains. Furthermore, we show that within the symmetric regime, increasing the strength of the quintic interaction gradually reduces the number of solitons in the train from three to one. Finally, we provide insights into the microscopic mechanisms driving this order-induced phase transition. These findings may hold significant implications for understanding phase transitions in other nonlinear systems. Additionally, we illustrate the potential utility of BEB-based quantum switches in nanophotonic devices. Keywords: Bose-Einstein condensate; Bose-Hubbard model; quantum switch; nonlinear interaction; symmetry breaking.

We introduce a framework for any quantum field theory where soft theorests exhibit factorization across multiple orders, contingent upon the existence of a modified symmetry generated by a modified soft charge. This approach elucidates the connection between soft theorems and S-matrix elements at distinct energies and offers a method to construct asymptotic symmetries and their charges. We demonstrate that this methodology is satisfied by "double soft" theories, which possess a straightforward formulation and interpretative clarity. Specifically, we derive the modified symmetry and its charge for a single and double photon soft theorem; the resulting charge comprises not only the standard soft charge but also a descendant term arising from the commutator with the Poincaré group. Furthermore, we establish a mapping from modified symmetry parameters to BMS charges, revealing that large supertranslations correspond to modified symmetry parameters and thereby linking modified symmetry transformations with large supertranslations. Finally, we present a detailed analysis of the double graviton case. These findings suggest a pathway to understanding the physical significance of modified symmetry charges, such as those associated with multiple soft theorems, and their link to conserved charges of the BMS group. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for black hole physics, including the information paradox. This work is a collaborative effort with Andrew Hamilton, who has generously shared his insights into these issues. A companion paper will address the consequences of the BMS algebra for the Page curve. Our collaborative research can be found at https://aschh12.github.io/. The source code for the double soft sector of the graviton S-matrix is available at https://github.com/AndrewCHamilton/DoubleSoftGravitonSM. Our GitHub repository, https://github.com/AndrewCHamilton/ModifiedSymmetry, contains source code for the double soft sector of the photon S-matrix, the modified symmetry and soft charge for a single soft photon, the mapping to BMS charges, the entanglement entropy of gravitational radiation, and the entanglement entropy of gravitational radiation within a shell. The latter is derived from the extended phase space formalism of gravitational path integrals, as detailed in arXiv:1905.08928. The source code for the entanglement entropy of gravitational radiation in a black hole is available at https://github.com/AndrewCHamilton/GravitationalPathIntegral. The concept of gravitational path integrals in extended phase space was introduced in arXiv:1905.08928.

Over the last few years, significant advancements have been made in the fields of computer vision and neural networks, yielding remarkable outcomes in areas like object detection, image classification, and facial recognition. Nevertheless, most deep learning models are trained on static datasets and cannot accommodate new data once deployment begins. This limitation restricts their utility in scenarios where new data continuously arrives after release. To address this, we introduce a novel architecture designed for ensemble models to incorporate new data while preserving previously learned information. This approach enables the automatic construction of an efficient ensemble without necessitating retraining of individual submodels. Furthermore, the system supports online learning, allowing it to adapt to new data while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed structure effectively learns and integrates new data while retaining prior knowledge. Additionally, the model can handle data with varying dimensions and is applicable to a broad spectrum of tasks. We validate the structure's performance through a series of experiments on classification and regression tasks. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/OnlineEnsemble. Finally, we have established a new structure called \textbf{Neural Structure for Online Ensemble} (OnEn), which offers a more efficient and effective approach for ensemble learning. OnEn is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/OnlineEnsemble. Given that OnEn enables online learning, it offers a more flexible and robust solution for ensemble model construction. We invite researchers to explore OnEn for their own applications. If you find OnEn beneficial for your ensemble learning tasks, please cite our work. Thank you. Intestinal worm categorization serves as a critical diagnostic tool for medical professionals, enabling patients to receive appropriate treatment. Traditionally, physicians visually examine stool samples to identify and classify worm types. However, this method is labor-intensive, demands specialized expertise, and is prone to human error. This study addresses the challenge by applying machine learning to automatically classify the three most prevalent worm types: Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Ankylostoma duodenale (hookworm), and Taenia solium (pork tapeworm). We constructed a dataset of 1,000 images scraped from the internet and partitioned it into training, testing, and validation sets. After evaluating several architectures, we selected a deep belief network (DBN) enhanced with dropout regularization. This approach achieved a 98% classification accuracy on the test set, outperforming models without regularization. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/raufi/Intestinal-Worms-Categorization. This study examines a specific non-zero-sum game involving two entities: an investor and a reinsurance company. We analyze their optimal strategies within a regime-switching Markov chain context, where the jump-Diffusion processes for both entities are driven by the same common Poisson process. The objective is to determine the optimal investment and reinsurance policies that minimize the expected discounted time the investor's capital falls below zero and the reinsurance company's capital exceeds the market's average, respectively. We derive the explicit forms of these optimal strategies and subsequently construct the value function as the solution to a system of ordinary differential equations. Furthermore, we validate the model using real-world data from the Standard & Poor's 500 Index. This study introduces a novel flight controller for quadrotors, designed to manage the motor speeds of all four rotors. The controller utilizes a bio-inspired Genetic Filter to estimate the states of the quadrotor, alongside a model predictive control strategy that leverages the full dynamics of the system. This model predictive approach incorporates a penalty term to smooth the trajectory of the flight path. To ensure the dual problems associated with the predictive controller remain feasible, the dual stochastic dual simplex algorithm is employed to solve the dual of the optimization problem. The resulting dual stochastic dual simplex algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to established alternatives like the primal dual interior point method and the standard dual simplex method. Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed controller enables a quadrotor to execute a smooth and steady flight along a sinusoidal path, effectively competing with existing state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, the efficient solution of the dual problem allows the controller to handle a significantly larger number of control inputs than previous methods. This model-based predictive control approach facilitates a sinusoidal flight path with minimal control effort, thereby conserving the quadrotor's battery power. Additionally, the ability to solve the dual problem efficiently permits a greater number of future control inputs to be considered during prediction, resulting in a more refined control solution. The paper provides a detailed description of the proposed controller, including its advantages and limitations, and includes numerical simulations for comparative analysis. Finally, the study addresses the computational complexity of the proposed dual stochastic dual simplex algorithm. Given that the dual problem involves a large number of variables, the solution requires substantial computational time. Consequently, the dual genetic algorithm is employed to generate an initial feasible solution for the dual problem, demonstrating that this hybrid approach yields a superior control solution in reduced time. This advancement is particularly beneficial for quadrotors, which typically operate under tight time constraints. The authors conclude that the dual genetic algorithm effectively reduces computational time for solving the dual problem. The study also examines the computational complexity of the dual genetic algorithm and its suitability for large-scale TSP instances. The Phase-I Pixel Pilot Edge (PXPE) reconstruction software serves as a proof-of-concept prototype designed to validate the migration of the CMS pixel reconstruction framework to the Cloud-based Computing Environment (CCE). This environment is intended to host the Phase-2 Upgrade's L1 Trigger and Pixel Readout Systems, facilitating a seamless data flow from the detectors to the CMS offline reconstruction. As an initial proof-of-concept, the PXPE software was evaluated to assess its performance and effectiveness. This evaluation involved analyzing PXPE outputs using both simulated data and real data from the CMS Phase-0 Run. The results demonstrated that the PXPE software achieves excellent hit reconstruction performance with simulated data, while also maintaining a low rate of fake hits and demonstrating robustness when processing real data. This document serves to document the PXPE software and the outcomes of this assessment. The findings presented in this report will guide the development of the Phase-2 Upgrade pixel reconstruction software to be deployed on the CCE. Furthermore, the lessons learned during the PXPE evaluation phase will inform the design of the Phase-2 Upgrade pixel software for the CCE. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the PXPE software; Section 3 details the performance analysis of pixel hits reconstructed by PXPE on simulated data; Section 4 examines PXPE performance on real data; and Section 5 presents the conclusions. This study employs machine learning to analyze shapes in optical imaging, specifically targeting active galactic nuclei (AGN) at redshifts $0.1 < z < 0.5$ identified within the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey (HSC-Wide) time-series data. We utilized the HSC Wide Area Deep Imaging (WADI) catalog, which offers multi-band $i$-band imaging for over 10 million galaxies, to investigate AGN host galaxy morphologies. By combining HSC-Wide spectroscopic redshifts with SDSS $u$-band photometry, we constructed a training dataset of 1,000 AGN hosts with confirmed elliptical or spiral classifications. We trained a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to classify these hosts, achieving a test accuracy of 90%. Applying this CNN to 1,000 HSC-Wide AGN sources yielded 500 elliptical and 500 spiral host galaxies. Cross-matching these results with the MPA-JHU catalog revealed that 80% of our classified AGN hosts are also categorized as elliptical or spiral by that catalog. Furthermore, we found that HSC-Wide imaging is more effective than SDSS imaging for distinguishing between these two host types. Finally, our analysis indicates that spiral galaxies are more prevalent as AGN hosts than elliptical galaxies. This research demonstrates the utility of CNNs for AGN host classification and establishes a foundation for morphological studies of AGN hosts using future wide-field time-series imaging. Future work will expand the training sample and refine the CNN architecture to enhance classification accuracy. The HSC-Wide survey is anticipated to provide even larger datasets for training, thereby improving the reliability of such classifications. We introduce a method for creating phase-space distributions that reveal the momentum and spatial coordinates of atoms within short-range correlations. This technique leverages the fact that the distribution is directly linked to the characteristic function of the momentum-space density operator, allowing for the extraction of momentum distributions without altering the system. We demonstrate this approach using strongly interacting Bose gases, analyzing the positions and momenta of atoms in atom pairs, three-body clusters, and six-body clusters. We calculate the corresponding distributions and validate them through numerical finite-size exact diagonalization. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between these distributions and the characteristic functions of their Fourier transforms. Finally, we illustrate how these phase-space distributions can characterize the phase and amplitude of the short-range component in the one-body density matrix. This methodology holds significant potential for the quantitative investigation of few-body correlations in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium quantum many-body systems. Complex numbers are frequently encountered in science and engineering, yet they are rarely utilized in machine learning. This paper addresses this omission by introducing a method to extend real-valued machine learning to the complex domain, enabling the processing of complex inputs and the application of complex-coefficient transformations. Specifically, we develop an extension of coordinate equality to match complex-coefficient affine transformations and project complex inputs into a complex-coefficient equality space. This framework allows for the construction of complex-coefficient linear basis functions and ensures that complex-coefficient least squares remain equivalent to their real-coainted counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of this equality-space approach in deep learning by designing complex-coactivated neurons and extending the complex-valued unit disk attention mechanism. Experimental results confirm that our proposed model effectively captures complex characteristics in both input data and co-domain transformations, significantly outperforming existing methods. Additionally, we observe that our model exhibits greater robustness to complex noise compared to previous approaches. These findings underscore the critical role of leveraging complex-coadecimal co-domains for scientific machine learning applications. Finally, we have released an open-source Python library implementing this framework, which includes implementations of complex-valued deep learning architectures such as the complex-valued unit disk network and graph. The saturation of the gluon distribution within the nucleon marks the beginning of Geometrical Scaling (GS) in the nucleon's gluon distribution and in $np\to \jet X$ reactions. Furthermore, gluon saturation in the heavy nucleus responsible for creating the large-x jet is expected to induce GS not merely in the differential cross section but also within the transverse momentum ($p_T$) and azimuthal angle ($\phi$) distributions of the produced jet relative to the incoming nucleus. This behavior is particularly evident in heavy ion collisions at RHIC and the future FS-EC. Additionally, GS may influence the $p_T$ distributions of heavy quarks and quarkonia, as well as those of light hadrons in $AA$ collisions. The data from PHENIX at RHIC and LHC will be utilized to demonstrate these saturation effects. The saturation of the gluon distribution in the nucleon and heavy nuclei, along with Geometrical Scaling in various observables, is anticipated to become a crucial tool for characterizing gluon saturation in both nucleons and heavy nuclei. Ultimately, GS serves as a valuable observable for probing the gluon saturation regime in both nucleons and heavy nuclei. This work is conducted in collaboration with Prof. X. N. Wang. This paper introduces a comprehensive toolkit designed for assessing and comparing the sensitivity of machine learning predictions to variations in model inputs. We develop analytical and simulation-based methodologies to generate "first-order" and local sensitivity metrics, as well as Bayesian methods to produce "global" sensitivity measures that integrate uncertainty across input parameters. These toolkit methods are validated through applications within a Bayesian framework and demonstrated using financial literacy data. Our findings indicate that the uncertainty in the sensitivity of machine learning forecasts regarding financial literacy is reduced when forecast inputs are derived from a structural economic model. Furthermore, we observe that the forecasts themselves are highly sensitive to the specific structural model employed to represent the distribution of forecast inputs. These conclusions are robust to the selection of the specific forecast or the particular dataset utilized. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the policy application of machine learning forecasts. Overall, the proposed toolkit offers a versatile design for evaluating the sensitivity of ML forecasts, with the analysis in this study being the initial application to a single forecast case. Future research will expand this approach to compare multiple forecasts, a direction suggested by our sensitivity analysis. Additionally, the work discusses the potential for detecting low-energy cosmic neutrinos, including those from supernovae and the cosmic neutrino background. The paper concludes by outlining current challenges and necessary advancements to fully realize the potential of this novel detection method. Finally, it presents the PALEOCCENE project as a promising initiative for developing low-threshold recoil detectors, with a specific focus on their utility for CEvNS detection. To conclude, the work examines the challenges associated with detecting CEvNS and the cosmic neutrino background, while also exploring strategies to mitigate background interference. We investigate the dynamics of a colloidal particle suspended in an ultrasmall fluid volume, where the activity of the surrounding molecules creates a gradient of chemical density across the particle. This scenario is relevant to experiments involving colloids in active baths, such as those composed of self-propelled bacteria or colloids driven by surface proteins. Because the particle is significantly larger than the driving fluid molecules, it experiences an effective force and noise that deviate from standard forms, necessitating a stochastic model for a particle driven by an ergodic non-equilibrium noise source. We begin by deriving the effective force and noise, revealing a non-Gaussian distribution for the noise. Subsequently, we formulate an equation of motion for a colloidal particle in three dimensions and analyze its steady-state behavior. We demonstrate that the colloidal particle can reverse its swimming direction relative to activity gradients, contingent on the activity strength, gradient orientation, and the ratio of the particle's hydrodynamic radius to the bacteria's correlation length. Furthermore, we show that the diffusion constant is not constant but depends on the activity gradient's orientation. Finally, we compare our theoretical findings with recent experimental data obtained from a 2-micron silica bead within a bacterial bath. Our results indicate that the effective force is approximately three orders of magnitude larger than the gradient of the chemical density, and we discuss the potential for controlling the position of such a colloidal particle. These findings suggest that colloidal particles can be manipulated by engineering gradients of activity or chemical density. Additionally, we explore the possibility of controlling the particle's orientation, which is governed by the hydrodynamic drag tensor. Controlling both position and orientation could enable the study of colloidal diffusion in non-equilibrium environments, the design of colloidal sensors, and the development of new nanomachines. Finally, we examine the potential for using optically trapped particles to measure bacterial mobility and to test whether these microorganisms operate within a non-equilibrium environment. These measurements could facilitate the design of new materials and devices that exploit the energy of active colloidal particles. Finally, we discuss the stability of such an ultrasmall system. Specifically, we show that the particle can escape the system if the confinement is too tight, and we provide an estimate for the minimum confinement size. This analysis is crucial for future experiments, as it ensures that the system remains stable and that the colloidal particle stays confined. In summary, our findings suggest that the manipulation of colloidal particles in non-equilibrium environments is feasible, opening up new avenues for research and technological applications. This paper introduces a geometric approach to the problem of detecting, identifying, and isolating epidemiological outbreaks on networks. The proposed method begins with a complete network where a subset of nodes is initially infected, triggering the spread of the virus to the rest. The objective is to partition the remaining nodes into two groups: one free of the virus and another that, if isolated, halts further transmission. We analyze this clustering challenge using geometric graph theory concepts, specifically examining node degree and eccentricity. The study presents a heuristic algorithm designed to cluster and isolate both small and large outbreaks. Furthermore, numerical simulations on various network models demonstrate the method's effectiveness in clustering outbreaks of different sizes. Finally, the advantages of this approach are highlighted. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions, such as adapting the method for outbreaks with varying transmission rates, geometric networks, and outbreaks occurring on networks with pre-existing cluster structures. Additionally, future work could address the related issue of recombining two isolated networks that have reached epidemic states. Finally, the method's applicability to other fields, including the removal of malicious nodes in computer networks, is suggested. This study presents a straightforward method for bypassing spurious features generated by pixel origin points when applying a maximum likelihood algorithm to create CMB maps from polarized Q and U Stokes parameters. We present a global shadow estimation framework designed to characterize quantum channels, extending the recently developed quantum circuit model for many-body pure state tomography. Applied to a many-channel scenario, our method demonstrates that the statistical error in estimating a many-channel map scales linearly with its sparsity. This computational efficiency surpasses existing approaches for quantum channel tomography, which typically require more measurements to achieve comparable accuracy. Additionally, we illustrate the application of this method to the simulation of noisy quantum computations. Finally, we examine several key issues regarding the characterization of quantum channels, such as the significance of symmetry in reducing shadow counts and the link between classical simulability and the complexity of shadow estimation. These insights pave the way for future applications of shadow algorithms in quantum information science. Graphene's charge carriers engage in strong Coulomb interactions, which can be analyzed using the renormalization group approach. This method examines a system of two coupled, slightly anisotropic bilayers, focusing on both charge and spin degrees of freedom. The study investigates the flow of interaction vertices and the emergence of new instabilities beyond the Fermi surface. Specifically, it identifies multiple instabilities, including charge density wave, nematic, and incompressible spin liquid phases. Additionally, a phase diagram is constructed for a system where only charge-charge interactions are present. In this scenario, a metal-insulator transition occurs, accompanied by the formation of a novel incommensurate charge density wave phase. The resulting phase diagram reveals a competition between incommensurate and commensurate charge density wave phases, as well as between charge and spin instabilities. Furthermore, the influence of anisotropy on these instabilities is explored. Finally, the paper details the instability of fermionic excitations at the Fermi surface, which gives rise to a non-Fermi liquid state. This state is characterized by a modified density of states, a distinct low-temperature specific heat coefficient, and a temperature-dependent scattering cross-section. Finally, the impact of this non-Fermi liquid behavior on the phase diagram is examined. The stability of molecular conformation is a critical factor in the design and application of molecular machines. This study reports an in situ, in situ temperature-dependent scanning tunneling microscopy investigation of the structural stability of the molecular motor Sc2TbN@C80 when adsorbed on an h-BN monolayer supported by a Ni(111) substrate. In situ measurements reveal that temperature fluctuations induce a reversible conformational change in the molecular motor. Furthermore, the reversible nature of this transition suggests that the change is driven by thermal energy. Ex situ analysis indicates that the alteration in the molecular motor's conformation is driven by the desorption of water molecules from the system. These findings offer valuable insights into the stability of molecular motors and their potential applications. Additionally, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of h-BN/Ni(111) as a model substrate for investigating the structural stability of complex supramolecular machines. Finally, the study underscores the significance of in situ techniques for accurately interpreting the behavior of molecular machines. The results are consistent with density functional theory calculations. The Internet of Things (IoT) encompasses a vast network of interconnected devices capable of communication, data exchange, and control. These devices are categorized based on their computational capabilities into Low Energy IoT (LE-IoT), Mid-sized IoT, and High-performance IoT. While High-performance IoT devices are equipped with advanced processors and can execute complex cryptographic algorithms, LE-IoT devices are characterized by limited processing power, minimal memory, and high energy efficiency. Consequently, they require lightweight cryptographic solutions that are computationally efficient and easy to implement. This survey examines the current state of lightweight cryptography, analyzing existing algorithms and their performance metrics such as execution time, memory usage, and energy consumption. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive comparison of the most popular lightweight encryption and authentication algorithms designed for IoT environments. Finally, we address the challenges associated with implementing lightweight cryptography in LE-IoT devices and explore future research directions. This survey aims to provide valuable insights for researchers developing security and privacy mechanisms for these devices. Specifically, understanding the traits of lightweight cryptography and the landscape of existing solutions will facilitate the creation of more efficient and secure protocols for IoT applications. Additionally, the survey offers an in-depth analysis of future research opportunities, which will be valuable for researchers pursuing security and privacy innovations within the IoT domain. This work is supported by the project "Secure and Privacy-Preserving Solutions for the Internet of Things" (Grant No. 17-05-00998A), funded by the Russian Science Foundation. This survey is also available on arXiv at arXiv:1909.00010. Keywords: Internet of Things, Lightweight Cryptography, Low Energy IoT Devices.

Adaptive measurement techniques enable sequence design that minimizes uncertainty, enhances efficiency, and optimizes resource allocation. Among these, Ramsey sequences are widely utilized to detect small parameter variations. We introduce a Bayesian trial formulation that facilitates adaptive trial planning for Ramsey sequences, enabling continuous angle adjustment during measurement. This approach is highly effective for detecting minute shifts in parameters. By integrating this trial formulation with a sequential decision rule, we derive an optimal adaptive protocol that surpasses traditional trial methods and demonstrates superior performance compared to both adaptive and static measurement strategies. Furthermore, we propose a Bayesian framework for adaptive decision-making applicable to general measurement scenarios. Numerical simulations validate these findings using phase shift detection as a case study. Additionally, we illustrate the framework's utility in analyzing adiabatic phase detection within microwave-driven Bose-Hubbard models. Our results indicate that adaptive measurements can enhance detection capabilities in quantum many-body systems, offering a pathway to mitigate decoherence effects. This advancement holds significant promise for advancing quantum information processing. The associated Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1995/Adaptive_Ramsey. Supplementary materials are available at https://doi.org/10.1103/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.18.014029.1. Finally, we provide a tutorial on Bayesian adaptive measurements for quantum systems, published as a white paper in *Frontiers in Physics*, 10, 612203 (2022). This tutorial utilizes the same example and Python code, offering a pedagogical resource for researchers entering the field of adaptive quantum measurements. Additional details regarding these resources can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00021. We introduce a technique for identifying network hubs by analyzing the relationships between triples of nodes. By examining the lengths of all such triples, we can assess network centrality through the lens of the triangle inequality. The Gromov Centralities metric is defined as the average triangle inequality surplus across all triples involving a specific node. This metric offers both a theoretical and computational framework for interpreting centrality in terms of geometric relationships among nodes. Furthermore, Gromov Centrality serves as a multi-scale measure, capable of distinguishing between central nodes at various network scales by adjusting a user-defined threshold. Empirical results demonstrate that these Gromov Centrality scores align with traditional centrality metrics, confirming their effectiveness as a complementary, multi-scale tool for evaluating network node centrality. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of Gromov Centrality in identifying central nodes within a newly developed biological network. This paper introduces the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity (ASToG), which posits that gravitational effects stem from the flow of space-time matter along closed timelike curves. In ASToG, gravity is conceptualized as a velocity field, distinguishing it from the density field used in Azimuthally Symmetrical Fluid Dynamics (ASFD). ASToG relies on four field equations and four boundary conditions. The first two equations address the evolution of gravity and space-time matter velocity, while the third links the velocity potential to the flat space-time metric. The azimuthal symmetry of ASToG is reflected in its boundary conditions. This theoretical framework is applied to derive the metric for the Schwarzschild spacetime, and the resulting metric is compared against observations. The comparison demonstrates that ASToG accurately reproduces the velocity field within the solar system, including perihelion precession and light deflection. Furthermore, the velocity field predicted by ASToG aligns with the Schwarzschild velocity field. Additionally, the theory yields the correct gravitational potential for Schwarzschild spacetime, thereby satisfying the Schwarzschild Equivalence Principle. Finally, the gravitational effect of a point mass is calculated, and the resulting potential matches the Coulomb potential. The third part of this series will explore the application of ASToG to rotating spacetimes. Keywords: Gravity, Schwarzschild spacetime, Metric, Velocity field, Equivalence principle. We develop a generalization of the established T-duality relationship between family Tors and Poincaré biextensions on site-twisted tori within Poisson manifolds. These generalized duality relations maintain the functorial nature of the original construction and align with the extended T-duality framework of Schomerus and Siebert. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the C*-actions inherent to these Poincaré biextensions correspond to the shift operations on groupoids defined by Schomerus and Siebert. Consequently, the C*-action on the Poincaré biextension serves as a novel artifact of extended T-duality, specifically arising from shift T-duality. This concept offers a fresh perspective on the shift T-duality previously identified by Schomerus and Siebert. Additionally, our findings suggest a new approach to understanding the contribution of odd T-duality to vector bundles on a torus. Finally, we provide an explicit characterization of Poincaré biextensions through the cohomology of a specific sheaf. This sheaf is constructed using the homotopy quotient of a family of twisted tori by a discrete lattice, thereby encoding the monodromy of the discrete fibration formed by the classifying space of the family of twisted tori. The cohomology of this sheaf is isomorphic to the cohomology of the classifying space of the homotopy quotient of the family of twisted tori by a contractible space; this latter cohomology represents the extension of the original T-duality to its fully dualizable form. The original T-duality can be viewed as a truncation of this fully dualizable structure. The sheaf's cohomology also describes the original T-duality via the cohomology of the classifying space of a specific 4-groupoid. Building on prior research into generally monotonic systems, our analysis demonstrates that all $\omega$-limit sets consist exclusively of hyperbolic fixed points or hyperbolic periodic orbits. Consequently, every trajectory either converges to a fixed point, approaches a hyperbolic periodic orbit, or exhibits chaotic non-convergent dynamics. Given that strongly monotonic systems under certain conditions are topologically conjugate to differentiable strongly monotonic systems in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k \ge 2$, our findings offer the most comprehensive description to date of the global behavior of smooth strongly monotonic dynamical systems. Furthermore, we extend these results to cover the long-term dynamics of general strongly monotonic systems and present several applications. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a hybrid algorithm designed to determine the ground state energies of quantum systems by combining classical and quantum resources. This study introduces a qubit-excitation-driven adaptive VQE (AQVNE) framework that builds upon the original VQE algorithm. The process begins with a standard VQE execution using a qubit-adaptive Hamiltonian ansatz; the resulting expectation values and variational parameters then identify significant qubit excitations within the many-body quantum system. These selected excitation terms are incorporated into a new circuit, which is then processed by VQE. This iterative procedure continues until the algorithm converges to a solution with sufficient accuracy. The effectiveness of AQVNE is demonstrated through ground state calculations for various quantum systems, including the hydrogen molecule, benzene, and a one-dimensional spin chain. Additionally, an analytical formula for computing Qubit Excitation Energy (QEE) is derived, and a method to estimate QEE without directly measuring the Hamiltonian is also presented. Furthermore, a quantum chemistry application is explored, which utilizes pre-measured expectation values to calculate QEE. All of these contributions are implemented within a comprehensive framework that supports both classical and quantum computing environments. Finally, the paper examines the scalability of AQVNE and its potential for application to larger molecular systems. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-ASU/AQVNE. The term AQVNE is an acronym for Qubit-Adaptive Quantum-Driven Variational Eigensolver. Although training neural networks typically relies on minimizing expected loss, Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation can also be utilized, particularly for representation learning. This paper investigates the impact of employing MAP estimates during the training of generative models. We introduce a unified framework that encompasses various techniques for enforcing structured posterior distributions in deep generative models, demonstrating that this approach is equivalent to training under a specific loss function. Furthermore, we examine an alternative method for implementing MAP estimation during the training of probabilistic encoder-decoder architectures. Our experiments indicate that utilizing MAP estimates can substantially enhance the performance of both encoder and decoder networks. Additionally, we explore a unified perspective on stochastic optimization techniques, such as KL divergence clipping and truncation, showing that they function as approximations to MAP estimation. Finally, we present a novel optimization algorithm designed to achieve exact MAP estimation, which is applicable to a broad class of probabilistic models. Our results demonstrate that this algorithm can significantly improve the training of both generative and discriminative models. Overall, our findings suggest that leveraging MAP estimates can lead to substantial gains in model performance. The code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/probabilistic_optimisation. Recent gravitational-wave (GW) experiments, including PPTA, EPTA, and Jodrell Bank (collectively NANOGrav), as well as the EHT, have identified a common-spectrum process (CSP) in their data. This study explores the accuracy cosmology of a theoretical model that explains the NANOGrav 15yr CSP as a distant, amplified GW background, while the EHT CSP is attributed to supermassive black hole binaries. The model posits that primordial GWs from inflation are amplified by dark matter domain walls and detected by Earth-orbiting GW antennas in the future. We demonstrate that this model can resolve the Hubble tension and account for the excess CMB power observed by Planck. Furthermore, we outline the future capabilities of space-based detectors like LISA and NGAS to test this hypothesis. Specifically, the frequency and amplitude of the amplified GW background can be constrained by the number and signal-to-noise ratio of detected binary systems, with LISA targeting supermassive black hole binaries and NGAS targeting masses appropriate for the NANOGrav CSP. We calculate the 95% confidence lower limits on the binary population using a Bayesian framework, finding that the NGAS signal can be lower-limited at frequencies below 0.01 Hz. Finally, we discuss the implications of these limits for CMB physics, inflation, and dark matter. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in real-world applications, yet their inherent complexity and the lack of exact solution methods have led researchers to rely on approximate techniques. This paper introduces a hybrid approach combining NSGA-II with a Branch and Bound (BnB) algorithm to address these challenges. The process initiates with NSGA-II to generate a diverse set of feasible solutions, which are then refined using the Branch and Bound technique. The study addresses two primary limitations of standard Branch and Bound: the necessity of exact solvability and the high computational cost. To resolve the first issue, feasibility rules are applied to the non-linear constraints. The second problem is mitigated by accelerating the Branch and Bound algorithm through the use of linearized constraints and dynamic constraint updating. To further enhance performance, the algorithm was parallelized, resulting in a 40% reduction in execution time. Finally, the efficacy of the proposed BnB+NSGA-II framework was validated using the MaMO-MINLP benchmark. Results demonstrate that this combination produces a set of non-dominated solutions superior to the raw NSGA-II output. The findings confirm that integrating Branch and Bound with NSGA-II yields high-quality solutions in a reasonable timeframe, effectively balancing solution quality with computational efficiency. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1999/BnB_NSGAII. Two groupoids $\mathcal{G}_1$ and $\mathcal{G}_2$ are linked when a continuous groupoid map exists between them. In the context of synthetic differential geometry, we demonstrate that if two linked Lie groupoids possess a Lie monoid structure, they are automatically connected. Furthermore, we show that if a Lie groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ is linked to a Lie monoid groupoid $\mathcal{H}$ via a map that is $s$-proper, then $\mathcal{G}$ is integral complete. These findings extend earlier work by L. Battenfeld and J. M. Royer, who established that all Lie groupoids with a connected base manifold are connected. Our results generalize this by proving that the connected components of the space of units in a Lie groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ correspond bijectively to the fibers of the source map $s: \mathcal{G} \to \mathcal{G}^{(0)}$. Additionally, we provide an example of a non-connected Lie groupoid where the fibers of the source map are connected. We also present an example of a non-integral complete Lie groupoid where the fibers of the source map are connected, thereby confirming that the hypothesis of $s$-properness cannot be omitted. Finally, we construct an example of a non-integral complete Lie groupoid where the fibers of the source map are connected; however, this example fails to be a Lie monoid groupoid, illustrating that the result does not extend to the broader category of Lie groupoids. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Andrew L. Lasenby. To facilitate broader application, we have included an appendix with formal proofs within an axiomatic setting. These results hold significant implications for the construction of category theory within the framework of toposes, which serves as the foundation for synthetic differential geometry. Specifically, the concept of a connected groupoid is essential for defining the internal hom object in this category. We have also verified the correctness of our proofs using the Lean theorem prover. The source code for these proofs is available in our GitHub repository. We hope this work will inspire further research into the internal category theory of synthetic differential geometry. A prevalent challenge in this field involves sampling mediators rather than measuring them for every subject, a practice called case-control sampling. This approach is cost-effective because it requires measuring the mediator only for cases and a subset of controls. However, it introduces complexities, particularly when the mediator is binary, as the probability of a subject being a case often dictates the probability of their mediator value. This study formalizes these issues and establishes identification and computational results for scenarios involving a single binary mediator. We demonstrate that the direct effect of an exposure on an outcome can be identified despite case-control sampling, provided the mediator is identified. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has provided unprecedented insights into the Sun's influence on the heliosphere by sampling the interplanetary environment at record-close distances. This study introduces the PSP's in-situ observations of solar breeze flows within the inner heliosphere, detailing findings from the first four solar rotations (days 1000 to 1400) during which the spacecraft recorded at least one interval of solar breeze conditions. By integrating data from multiple instruments, we examined plasma and magnetic field characteristics, including large-scale magnetic field line geometry, to identify the defining traits of solar breeze flow conditions. We further analyzed how these conditions vary with distance from the Sun and across different solar longitudes. Our results indicate that solar breeze conditions are defined by plasma beta values between 0.1 and 1, with plasma densities ranging from 0.5 to 2 cm$^{-3}$ and magnetic field strengths of 10 to 20 nT. Additionally, the Parker Solar Probe has detected numerous transient structures within solar breeze conditions, such as magnetic switchbacks, turbulence, and magnetic clouds. These findings establish a baseline for future studies of solar breeze conditions and the transient structures they contain. This analysis is critical for understanding the nature of solar breeze plasma and its evolution as it travels from the Sun to the inner heliosphere. These findings will also facilitate future studies of heliospheric conditions and processes, as well as the modeling of heliospheric plasma used for space weather forecasting. Finally, this research will aid in interpreting the Parker Solar Probe's observations of the heliosphere and the Parker Solar Probe-Helios mission's future observations of solar wind conditions. In the previously introduced Dual-Rotors Model (DRM) [1], the $0^{-}$ state is represented as a rigid rotor possessing a negative moment of inertia, which becomes singular at zero energy. This singularity stems from the rotors' translational degrees of freedom, which are governed by the adverse potential $V(x) = +\omega^2x^2/2$. Consequently, within the model, the rotors exhibit translationally zero-range bound states that approach the continuum as the frequency $\omega$ approaches zero from above. In this limit, the moment of inertia, defined as $I=\int dx\,x^2\rho(x)$ where $\rho(x)$ is the ground-state probability density, diverges. This behavior is mirrored in the model's lowest $0^{-}$ state, producing a locally adverse moment of inertia that displays a pronounced peak at zero angular momentum. Furthermore, the moment of inertia varies with excitation; for $0^{-}$ states, it declines as angular momentum increases, whereas for $0^{+}$ states, it rises. This paper investigates the implications of these adverse moment-of-inertia properties for the spectral characteristics of the DRM. Specifically, the adverse moment of inertia for the lowest $0^{-}$ state results in local Lorentz invariance, causing the energy of the first excited state to vary quadratically with angular momentum at low spin and linearly at high spin. Additionally, the adverse moment of inertia in the $\gamma$ vibrational mode leads to a localized moment-of-inertia profile, a feature observed in the spectra of certain nuclei. This observation is consistent with the nuclear shell model, where the moment of inertia is proportional to the number of excited nucleons. Finally, the DRM is demonstrated to generate an effective moment of inertia that is independent of angular momentum. These findings are illustrated through numerical calculations. This study introduces a cell-mean-based neural network approach designed to address various hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. By utilizing finite difference or integral formulations, the proposed method constructs a cell-mean operator that approximates spatial derivatives. These operators are integrated into a neural network architecture, where each cell-mean operator corresponds to a specific sub-network. This design enables the neural network to represent the approximate solution to the PDEs. Leveraging automatic differentiation, the method efficiently computes temporal and lower-order spatial derivatives within the solution. Consequently, for conservation law-type problems, an entropic neural network is developed by incorporating a Godunov-type numerical flux function into the cell-mean-based neural network sub-networks. For parabolic problems, a regularized version is presented, which minimizes a specific cost function via a gradient descent algorithm. Numerical experiments are conducted to assess the performance of the entropic neural network, demonstrating its effectiveness and high-order accuracy. Additionally, the results indicate that the regularized neural network provides a stable and accurate solution for parabolic problems, with convergence rates of $O(h^2)$ and $O(k)$ observed for both the cell-mean-based neural network solution and its temporal derivative. Future research will explore the application of the cell-mean-based neural network to other hyperbolic partial differential equations. The ALICE experiment's primary mandate is to investigate the conditions of the early universe and quark-gluon plasma through heavy-ion collisions, while also examining hadronization mechanisms and particle production in proton-proton interactions. To advance these research goals and maximize scientific output, a proposal has been submitted to extend the ALICE detector's data-taking capabilities and operational duration beyond LHC Run 3 and the subsequent HiLHC gap. This extension is feasible by utilizing upgraded trigger and data acquisition systems, alongside innovative data analysis techniques that leverage machine learning and the integration of ALICE with other experiments. This paper outlines the anticipated scientific results and the innovative approaches required to achieve them. Additionally, it serves as an introduction to a series of papers submitted as ALICE-92-001 through ALICE-92-009 to the CERN HI-LHC Committee. These documents detail a comprehensive upgrade plan covering the detector, data acquisition, software, and analysis frameworks, which are designed to deliver high-quality data for the experiments described in ALICE-93 to ALICE-98. The proposed enhancements are anticipated to result in significant discoveries across all ALICE research areas. Specifically, the detector upgrades outlined in ALICE-92 to ALICE-98 will enable precision studies of heavy flavor hadrons, quarkonia, and their associated jets, as well as vector mesons, providing a comprehensive analysis of heavy flavor production. Furthermore, the upgrades described in ALICE-99 and ALICE-100 will facilitate high-statistics analyses of dilepton production, including heavy bosons, and the study of charmed and bottom hadrons in proton-proton collisions. The data acquisition and analysis improvements outlined in ALICE-101 and ALICE-102 will enhance the analysis of light hadron production and jet properties. Finally, the upgrades described in ALICE-103 will significantly improve the analysis of particle spectra in small systems. Collectively, these improvements are expected to substantially advance the understanding of data analysis methods and significantly expand the ALICE scientific dataset. The analysis updates described in ALICE-92 to ALICE-99 will be implemented during the HiLHC gap, while the data quality improvements outlined in ALICE-101 and ALICE-102 are expected to be realized after LHC Run 3, thereby achieving the goal of enhancing ALICE data-taking capabilities and operations beyond LHC Run 3. The Unruh effect predicts that uniformly accelerated observers perceive the vacuum as a thermal bath, a phenomenon rooted in the entanglement between the field modes within an observer's past and future light cones. This study demonstrates that an observer accelerating through these entangled cones acquires Berry phase information contained within the field. Consequently, the presence of this information can be verified through interferometric experiments involving future and previous light cones, offering a method to detect the Unruh effect. Specifically, the proposed Unruh interferometer consists of two beam splitters and future/past mirrors; the previous mirror is immersed in the accelerated observer's Unruh thermal bath, while the future mirror is linked to the observer's past light cone. By adjusting the beam splitter angles, the Unruh interferometer successfully verifies the entanglement between the observer's past and future cones, thereby confirming the existence of the Unruh effect. Furthermore, the Unruh phase—the phase accumulated by the accelerated observer within the thermal bath—can be observed through interferometric interference. This research establishes a novel method for Unruh detection, potentially rendering the effect observable in near-future experiments. Finally, the study discusses the broader implications of this time-reversed interferometric approach for understanding quantum gravity. Event extraction remains a critical yet difficult area within natural language processing, primarily due to the open-world challenge where the model may encounter event types and arguments not present during training. To address this, we introduce a novel dataset designed to facilitate the discovery of previously unseen event types. This resource comprises multilingual data spanning 11 languages, including English, Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Hindi-English code-mixed, Gujarati, Hindi, Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Sinhala. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the dataset and release full statistics for all entities and event types. Furthermore, we evaluate several baseline models to assess their performance on this new resource. Our goal is that this dataset will assist researchers in enhancing models for Open Information Extraction tasks. The data can be accessed at https://github.com/Deepanshu-1998/MEE. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Deepanshu-1998/MEE. The interaction between a stellar wind from a massive companion star and an accretion disk around a compact object represents a critical component of the mass and angular momentum dynamics governing binary systems. In high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs), this phenomenon, known as the "stellar breeze," is particularly significant when the accreting compact object is a neutron star. This study investigates the impact of wind-disk interaction in Cyg X-1 during its hard-state phase by analyzing the effects of varying wind mass-loss rates on X-ray spectral and timing characteristics. We developed a model that incorporates both the accretion disk and the stellar wind to simulate the system. Results indicate that increasing the wind mass-loss rate ($\dot{M}_w$) from $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-5} \, M_\odot \, \text{yr}^{-1}$ causes a substantial rise in accretion rate ($\dot{M}_{acc}$), rising from $1.1 \times 10^{-9}$ to $1.1 \times 10^{-7} \, M_\odot \, \text{yr}^{-1}$. This increase in $\dot{M}_{acc}$ leads to a marked increase in the hard X-ray photon flux, which is consistent with observations. Furthermore, the interaction between the wind and the accretion disk generates an accretion shock, producing thermal emission in the soft X-ray band. Our findings suggest that a wind mass-loss rate of $\dot{M}_w = 10^{-5} \, M_\odot \, \text{yr}^{-1}$ can account for the observed soft X-ray flux. Additionally, the wind's angular momentum creates a torque on the disk, driving mass inflow and outward angular momentum transport, which influences the frequency of X-ray quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). The model predicts that a higher $\dot{M}_w$ results in a lower QPO frequency, aligning with observed data. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the interaction between the stellar wind and the accretion disk can substantially alter the mass and angular momentum of the accretion disk, significantly affecting the X-ray spectral and timing properties of Cyg X-1 in the hard state. We investigate the impact of an ether-like term within a non-abelian gauge theory framework. This term, which relies on a vector field, functions as a higher-derivative term concerning spatial derivatives of gauge fields and contributes to energy. Our analysis reveals that the presence of this term alters the phase structure of a non-abelian gauge theory, specifically affecting the Debye mass and the nature of gauge field fluctuations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the vector field associated with this ether-like term remains stable at finite temperatures. These theoretical findings are potentially applicable to quark-gluon plasma and quantum critical points. Additionally, our results suggest that a similar higher-derivative ether-like term could be significant in the context of black holes. Finally, we outline the methodology for calculating higher-order corrections to the free energy at finite temperatures. These corrections, derived from perturbative expansions, are essential for accurately describing the quantum chromodynamics of the quark-gluon plasma. This approach is particularly valuable for analyzing holographic models of the quark-gluon plasma, where such corrections are necessary to match results obtained from gauge/gravity duality. To facilitate these calculations, we also provide a Mathematica package. As an example of its utility, we apply the package to a specific gravity dual model and successfully reproduce the higher-order corrections found in reference [1]. Our findings indicate that the inclusion of the ether-like term in holographic black hole models leads to a more stable black hole configuration. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the corresponding gauge theory, which includes the ether-like term, describes a more stable quark-gluon plasma. This result is consistent with the higher-order corrections of the quark-gluon plasma derived via the gauge/gravity duality method. Ultimately, we suggest that the inclusion of the ether-like term in holographic black hole models may be essential for accurately describing the quantum chromodynamics of the quark-gluon plasma. This conclusion is particularly compelling given the known challenges in holographic models when the ether-like term is absent. This paper introduces a collaborative framework for universal syntactic and semantic analysis. Its primary objective is to develop a shared, shared-analyzer capable of processing all world languages through joint training on diverse multilingual corpora. The study evaluates several multilingual analyzer architectures and training strategies, with a specific emphasis on resolving the challenge of scarce resources for low-resource languages. Additionally, we assess fundamental analytical capabilities across all languages and investigate methods to enhance the generalization performance of joint analyzers. Finally, we present universal performance metrics designed to facilitate comparisons among multilingual corpora, analyzers, and training schemes. To support these efforts, we have established the Universal Analyzer Benchmark (UAB) initiative, which provides standardized benchmarks, datasets, and evaluation protocols for multilingual analysis. The associated code and datasets are available at https://github.com/edg211/UAB. We examine post-merger dynamics in binary neutron star systems utilizing neutrino-cooled accretion disks with a magnetized environment, focusing on how magnetic fields influence the frequency and characteristics of observed gravitational wave (GW) ejecta. Our results indicate that the presence of magnetic fields amplifies the mass of rapidly moving ($v\gtrsim0.1c$) ejecta by a factor of 10 to 100 compared to non-magnetized scenarios. This enhancement is primarily driven by the earlier onset of magnetorotational instability (MRI) in the accretion disk, which generates a fast jet. Furthermore, this jet significantly increases the angular momentum of the system, causing the merger to reach the maximum spin limit ($\chi\sim0.7$) more quickly. Additionally, we find that the frequency of ejecta production is directly proportional to the initial magnetic field strength. These findings suggest that magnetized accretion disks are crucial for understanding the origins of GW ejecta and their impact on the chemical enrichment of the universe. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that the ejecta mass and velocity are independent of the magnetic field inclination angle. However, while the mass of slow ejecta ($v\lesssim0.05c$) remains unaffected, the velocity of such ejecta is reduced in strongly magnetized systems. This reduction is attributed to the formation of a magnetosphere in the late post-merger phase, which suppresses ejecta expansion. These outcomes underscore the necessity of conducting three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations to comprehensively characterize post-merger ejecta. Furthermore, our findings align with recent research indicating that magnetized accretion disks can substantially affect ejecta properties and chemical enrichment. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the origins of GW ejecta and their role in cosmic chemical enrichment. In conclusion, we emphasize that future investigations into ejecta from post-merger accretion disks must account for the effects of magnetic fields. Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are enigmatic sources of intense, millisecond-duration radio bursts that originate from highly ionized regions at cosmological distances. While numerous models have been proposed to explain their origins, none currently account for all observed properties. This study examines the optical emission associated with FRBs, establishing constraints on both deferred and concurrent sources. We demonstrate that sources capable of producing concurrent optical radiation at the peak flux levels typical of FRBs must possess extremely large physical sizes. Furthermore, we establish a lower limit for the optical luminosity of an FRB source, showing that it must exceed the Eddington luminosity. Finally, our analysis indicates that a plasma with an electron density of approximately $10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$ is required to explain the dispersion measures of FRBs. These findings suggest that FRB sources are likely large, low-density, and highly ionized environments. Additionally, we explore the potential for observing optical counterparts to FRBs and discuss the implications of these results for various source models. We have created free open-source software designed to address the design, optimization, and modification of high-power laser systems. This tool is particularly useful for analyzing ultrashort pulse lasers, Q-switched lasers, and their feedback and control mechanisms. It is currently distributed under the GNU General Public License (GPL) version 3 and can be downloaded from our website at www.laserguide.org. Text generation models frequently overlook visual contexts, such as room layouts or product designs, because integrating visual and textual modalities in deep learning is complex. This paper introduces observing visual controls during text-based creation, such as adjusting brightness or contrast on a graphic. We posit that large language models like GPT-3 already infer similar commands from subtle cues in prompts and output, such as darker or lighter text. To validate this, we collected a dataset of 1.2 million instruction-following examples from the Text2Transformers benchmark and the FLAN natural language processing task. Our results indicate that even the smallest model in the suite can follow these instructions 60% of the time, while GPT-3 achieves a 90% success rate. We also demonstrate that observing visual controls in creation tasks enhances the performance of smaller language models. Finally, we show that textual representations of visual elements, such as image embeddings, enable language models to directly manipulate visual content, for instance, by darkening or lightening a displayed image. Our code is available at https://github.com/robertkurland/visual-observing. Given that text creation is a common human activity, we propose that enabling computationally efficient manipulation of visual content through language models could significantly advance computer science and human-computer interaction. We anticipate that the community will explore new applications of observing visual controls and investigate the underlying mechanisms of how language models handle these tasks. We also look forward to advancements in computer vision and human-computer interaction driven by these capabilities. Finally, we expect that observing visual controls will be applied to new areas of text and visual creation. We anticipate that the community will discover the benefits of computationally efficient and direct manipulation of visual content using language models. The community may also examine the mechanisms by which language models observe visual controls.
