This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature and proof-of-knowledge system designed to enhance privacy within blockchain environments. Our approach relies on two core components: a ring signature that permits signing as any member of a known set using the user's public key, and a zero-knowledge proof demonstrating possession of public keys corresponding to known ring signature public keys. We demonstrate that the knowledge required to generate a ring signature and validate the associated zero-knowledge proof is equivalent to information available to all public keys within the ring. This allows a transaction to be validated without access to the secret key, ensuring both privacy and security. Furthermore, our method achieves significantly smaller proof sizes compared to previous ringCT schemes, such as those utilizing Bulletproofs. These advancements in privacy and security pave the way for more efficient and scalable solutions in blockchain systems. Experimental results indicate that transaction validation is approximately 100 times faster than in the original ringCT scheme, while proof sizes are roughly 10 times smaller. Additionally, the zero-knowledge proof generation is only 10 times slower than standard ring signature generation, representing a substantial improvement over the quadratic slowdown observed in earlier ringCT approaches. These performance metrics were tested using 2,048-bit elliptic curve keys. The implementation is available at https://github.com/AmirHajRamezan/delegated_ringCT. The brightness profile of a beam, defined as the transverse charge density per unit area, serves as a critical descriptor for beam dynamics. This paper presents a technique to measure the complete two-dimensional beam charge density distribution by exploiting beam envelope oscillations induced by strong external focusing. By analyzing ensembles of these oscillations across various beam envelopes, the beam brightness profile can be reconstructed. We validate the efficacy of this approach through rigorous tests using both simulated and experimental data. The resulting three-dimensional brightness profile proves invaluable for beam dynamics research, as it offers comprehensive insights into beam envelope oscillations, beam-beam interactions, and collective effects. Furthermore, this methodology is extendable to other beam analysis problems, such as diagnosing beam halo formation. Our findings will be published in Phys. Rev. Accel. Bevs. 25, 043501 (2022). The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/taekim123/BeamEnsemble. The results from the simulations and experiments can be replicated using the provided code. Additionally, we have developed a user-friendly web-based tool to perform the analysis; this is accessible at https://beamensemble.web.app/. The computational steps are documented in our previous publication: T. Kim et al., "Beam Ensembles for Beam Analysis," Phys. Rev. Accel. Bevs. 25, 043501 (2022). The detailed methodology is outlined in the paper "Brightnes scans for beam analysis," Phys. Rev. Accel. Bevs. 25, 043501 (2022), which is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01001. Data-informed modeling, which integrates modeling and machine learning, has become a vital area across numerous scientific and engineering disciplines. However, it is often implemented in silos within individual organizations, resulting in the inefficient sharing of both data and models. This paper introduces a unified framework that enables the sharing of data and models in a siloed fashion while still producing a combined model that leverages all distributed information. Specifically, we examine a collaborative framework where multiple local models are trained on separate datasets, and a global model is subsequently learned using outputs from these local models. We establish theoretical guarantees for this approach, demonstrating that the resulting model is statistically equivalent to one trained with the union of all data. Furthermore, we validate this framework in a physical activity recognition application, showing that it outperforms both purely data-driven and purely modeling-based approaches. Our theoretical analysis and empirical results also indicate that this collaborative framework can mitigate privacy risks associated with data sharing. Finally, we explore the connection between this collaborative framework and Federated Learning, a method designed to learn from distributed data without direct data exchange. We prove that Federated Learning is a specific instance of the collaborative framework proposed in this paper. Additionally, we extend the collaborative framework to handle scenarios involving data exchange, thereby recovering various existing methods for collaborative data-informed modeling found in the literature. This work paves the way for developing a general theory that unifies diverse data-informed modeling techniques and facilitates the creation of new methods. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel quantized training method for deep neural networks that leverages annealed interval limitations to enhance the training dynamics of back-propagation. By imposing constraints on weight distributions, the approach effectively mitigates distributional collapse, a key determinant of generalization. The resulting density function is engineered to be asymmetric, or "askew," thereby increasing the average weights. Experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that AskewSGD surpasses existing quantization techniques, such as DQ-Net, in achieving superior generalization performance. Soft robotics is a rapidly evolving field characterized by the design of robots with materials and control strategies that mirror the mechanical properties and control paradigms found in biological systems. These robots are typically constructed from compliant materials, enabling them to adapt to dynamic, unstructured environments and execute tasks that rigid robots cannot accomplish. Soft robots can be engineered using various material formulations, topological designs, and actuation mechanisms, each presenting distinct physical and control challenges. This survey examines the current landscape of materials, topologies, and actuation mechanisms, with a specific emphasis on their associated physical and control difficulties. Furthermore, it provides a detailed analysis of the state-of-the-art in soft robot control, highlighting both open issues and promising future research directions. Consequently, the paper emphasizes the critical role of modeling in advancing the field of soft robotics. Finally, it identifies key future research directions, including the development of new materials, the creation of a comprehensive taxonomy for robotic topologies, and the formulation of new actuation mechanisms. The paper concludes by outlining future research needs regarding the modeling of soft robots and their control strategies. The Amitsur-Jacobi group, originally introduced to characterize $n$-dimensional affine spaces up to birational equivalence over base fields of characteristic zero, is reinterpreted through the lens of linear group theory by examining its defining equations and transformations. This paper presents a new geometric interpretation of the group by defining its "real" counterpart, which addresses analogous problems for real algebraic varieties. Furthermore, the research explores the groups of transformations for both the authentic and real Jacobi groups, specifically examining their subgroups of birational transformations. The study concludes by considering the implications of these findings for the theory of real variables. (Chosen by A. Roitman)

Table-centric fact verification remains a largely unexplored field, where verifying facts within tabular data presents significant difficulties due to the complexity of the information and the necessity to comprehend relationships across rows and columns. We examine the impact of decomposing complex facts into simpler sub-facts to facilitate verification. Our investigation reveals that most facts in current datasets are not uniquely verifiable due to missing information or ambiguous relationships, and that accurately breaking down complex tasks into these unique sub-tasks is crucial for effective verification. Additionally, we introduce a novel dataset designed to investigate such sub-facts, with results demonstrating its efficacy in enhancing performance. Finally, our findings indicate that existing models fail to accurately identify the appropriate sub-tasks and subsequently resolve them to confirm the original fact. The dataset and code are accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/TableFactInvigilation. This work is scheduled for presentation at the SIGIR 2021 conference.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are capable of producing high-quality images, yet current techniques for controlling GAN outputs through semantic attributes remain constrained. This study investigates the latent space of GANs to enhance conditional generation by mapping descriptive image attributes into a latent code using a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). The generated images are subsequently regulated by querying this encoded representation within the GAN's decision network. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior quality control, as evidenced by higher Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores, compared to the baseline CVAE approach. Furthermore, our approach exhibits improved robustness in text generation, particularly in scenarios involving variations in the queried attribute. Layered sampling is a straightforward technique for drawing samples from a distribution $p(x)$ defined over a union of subdomains. When applied to black-box distributions, the layering process can be viewed as a sequence of 0/1-acceptance/rejection attempts. This paper investigates how contrasting the layers in sequential samplers influences the sampling efficiency of layered samplers. We demonstrate that modifying the order of layers in a naive layered sampler can yield significant improvements in sampling efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce two types of step samplers—ordered and random step samplers—that utilize layered sampling as a core component. For both variants, we establish upper and lower bounds on the mixing time relative to the number of layers, the success probability of individual layers, and the overall sampling efficiency. Our findings indicate that step samplers can surpass the performance of ordered or random samplers, even when the number of layers grows linearly with the problem size. Finally, we validate these theoretical results with simulations, including a case study on a non-trivial application: generating a Bayesian network. This step sampler is capable of generating samples from a distribution $p(x)$ defined over a union of subcubes. Additionally, we examine a scenario involving a union of disjoint subdomains to highlight the differences between step samplers and nested samplers. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive analysis of step samplers, with implications for Markov chain samplers, acceptance/rejection samplers, and nested samplers. The step sampler serves as a natural extension to unions of distributions that are not necessarily aligned with hyper-rectangular or hyper-spherical boundaries. The step sampler's performance is contingent upon the success probability of individual subdomain samplers, which can be either constant or variable. In scenarios involving variable success probabilities, step samplers outperform ordered samplers, and we offer a lower bound on the mixing time for step samplers in such cases. The objective of distance labeling in graphs is to assign labels of minimal length to the vertices of a graph $G$ such that the pairwise distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ in $G$ can be derived from their respective labels. This capability must remain intact even if a subset of vertices is compromised and thus excluded from distance calculations. In this study, we demonstrate that for every planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, there exists a fault-resilient distance labeling for the entire graph that remains functional even after the removal of $k$ vertices. Specifically, when $k = o(n)$, these labels require a length of $O(\log n)$, and when $k = \Theta(n)$, the label length is $O(\log^2 n)$. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ for the label length, proving that this bound is tight for all values of $k$. Our approach is also applicable to graphs embedded in surfaces other than the sphere. Additionally, we investigate fault-resilient distance labeling for graph families where the maximum degree varies with $n$, yielding a general upper bound of $O(\log^2 n)$ and a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$, which is tight for graph families with constant treewidth. Finally, we extend our findings to edge failures, showing that fault-resilient distance labeling is achievable even when edges fail. For both vertex and edge failures, we provide tight bounds for the label length. As a byproduct, we also develop distributed labeling schemes for planar graphs. These schemes operate in time $O(\log^2 n)$ with message size $O(\log n)$, and the resulting labels are provably fault-resilient. For distributed schemes, we also establish a time lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$. To our knowledge, this represents the first provably distributed labeling scheme for planar graphs. This study investigates two-particle correlations in a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model for both chronological and frequency-domain contexts. By analyzing the third-order nonlinear susceptibility, we observe resonance peaks in the frequency domain that reveal rich information regarding two-particle bound states and scattering. Furthermore, we examine the impacts of gain-loss dissipation and two-body losses on these correlations. Under real-time conditions, we identify an enhanced two-particle lifetime, a phenomenon driven by gain-loss dissipation that stems from non-Hermitian exceptional points. These significant findings are demonstrated through the investigation of two-particle bunching and antibunching. The methodology established here is broadly applicable to various quantum systems for probing two-particle correlations. Additionally, the discussion of resonance and exceptional-point physics holds relevance for broader contexts, including the study of nonlinear responses and the exploration of non-Hermitian topology. Periodic driving of a quantum system typically induces heating, a phenomenon known as Floquet heating, which is especially pronounced in open systems where drivability and dissipation interact. This study examines a driven one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model featuring a specific loss mechanism that generates quantum scars. We demonstrate that, contrary to the typical expectation of rapid heating, this system exhibits a distinct driftheating phase where drift-induced stabilization of particle number enables long-lived nonequilibrium dynamics. Furthermore, we show that within this driftheating phase, the drive and dissipation can be tuned to suppress excitations, resulting in a nonequilibrium Bose condensate of nonfundamental many-body scarred states. This represents a significant advancement over previous proposals for equilibrium condensates of quantum scars, which required precise control over interactions. Finally, we illustrate that the driftheating phase and the Bose condensate of scars can be directly observed through noise spectroscopy. These findings underscore the critical role of drift in the thermodynamics of open, driven systems and introduce new avenues for investigating quantum many-body physics in nonequilibrium driven-dissipative contexts. Additionally, the proposed noise spectroscopy method is broadly applicable to any quantum system where drift plays a pivotal role. These systems are anticipated to hold significant potential for stabilizing fragile quantum states and may offer new capabilities for quantum information processing. This proposal is realized experimentally using ultracold atoms within an open optical-lattice system. Furthermore, the driven scalar field theory of these open bosonic systems is expected to be highly relevant across diverse physical platforms, including cavity QED, circuit QED, and spin models. Finally, the theory of noise spectroscopy presented here is expected to find wide application in any driven quantum system. We introduce a novel proof of the Alexandrov-Monge-Amp\`ere equation solution estimate, which refines the standard $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimate typically imposed on the right-hand side. This approach yields a superior $C^{0,\alpha}$ estimate for the solution under the same conditions on the right-hand side. Furthermore, our proof employs techniques from geometric measure theory, specifically utilizing the concept of almost minimizers of the Alexandrov functional. This methodology allows us to establish the uniform H\"older continuity of solutions to the Monge-Amp\`ere equation via an elementary and concise argument. Additionally, this strategy facilitates the demonstration of several well-known results. Finally, we extend these findings to handle cases where the right-hand side is merely bounded almost everywhere. Although numerous loss functions have been developed for training neural networks, selecting the appropriate one remains challenging. Furthermore, existing literature often lacks clear explanations of the specific advantages and limitations of different losses, making it difficult to predict their performance across new tasks. This study addresses that gap by applying gradient surgery to analyze how various losses affect network behavior. We evaluate nine distinct loss functions across nine different classification tasks, with experiments ranging from simple to complex. Our findings indicate that networks trained with the same loss function exhibit similar characteristics, whereas training sets with comparable attributes tend to converge on a single optimal loss function. Additionally, our results demonstrate that loss functions are not universally applicable; their effectiveness is highly dependent on the specific classification task at hand. Finally, the data reveals that certain loss functions are superior for training on difficult samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/taehyungkim97/Dissecting-loss-functions-with-gradient-surgery.

Approximate holographic error correction codes maintain a simpler structure compared to exact codes but face significant challenges in analysis. This difficulty stems from the need to compute complex sums over bulk error configurations, a task that becomes intractable when errors are subject to entropic constraints arising from power-law correlations. To address this, we introduce the hyper-invariant Mermin-Wagner error correction code, which efficiently handles such summations. In the continuum limit, this code is governed by a Gaussian field theory and supports an infinite set of errors with power-law correlations. We demonstrate that these errors can be corrected in polynomial time, provided the exponent $\alpha$ in power-law decay $r^{-d-\alpha}$ satisfies $\alpha < 1$. Furthermore, we calculate the entanglement entropy of codewords, confirming that it adheres to the approximate holographic entropy conjecture. Finally, we show that the hyper-INvariant Mermin-Wagner code can be derived through a straightforward modification of MERA, thereby enabling the construction of holographic codes with power-law correlations in a transparent manner. This approach bridges the gap between approximate and exact holographic error correction. Additionally, we identify a continuum of codes that achieve the optimal trade-off between entanglement and error correction, a result that appears difficult to realize with current codes. This suggests that strict geometric constraints within holographic duality may be unnecessarily limiting. Our findings indicate that relaxing these constraints could uncover new codes with unique properties. This study analyzes the spacing between adjacent filaments within the Galactic Core to determine if the observed distribution aligns with the hypothesis that the population follows a two-point homogeneous distribution (TPHD). While the mean spacing matches TPHD predictions, the variance exceeds them, indicating that the filament population is not fully random. The research also examines the impact of distance uncertainties on this two-point homogeneous hypothesis. Furthermore, it addresses whether the analysis of inter-filament spacing is influenced by the presence of a dense filament group in the Galactic Center region. These factors must be accounted for when applying the two-point homogeneous distribution to model the population of Galactic Core filaments. Finally, the paper explores the possibility that new filaments are forming in the Galactic Core through the interaction of existing filaments with incoming gas clouds. These conclusions provide a foundation for future investigations into the physical properties of Galactic Core filaments. This study introduces a decentralized framework for preservation voltage reduction (PVR) within systems combining primary and secondary distribution networks. The objective is to minimize total active energy losses by strategically lowering voltages at primary network substations, with the secondary network accessed exclusively through distribution transformers. To address the computational challenges of large-scale networks, the problem is decomposed into independent subproblems for primary and secondary networks, solved using distributed algorithms. This study employs a multi-fidelity, multi-scale modeling strategy to simulate offshore wind-turbine loads. The approach combines a physical multi-scale model with a statistical model, where the statistical component consists of two chained Gaussian process (GP) models. The first GP maps environmental parameters to the turbine's top-level structural loads, while the second GP characterizes the relationship between these loads and the turbine's internal structural responses. This chained configuration is evaluated against a standard multi-fidelity GP model that jointly accounts for both physical and internal structural scales. The statistical surrogate is compared with the physical multi-scale model and the traditional statistical model utilizing a single GP. Results indicate that the two-chained GP model significantly reduces computational costs compared to the physical model and enhances prediction accuracy relative to the single GP approach. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the multi-fidelity nature of this chained structure by implementing an active learning framework to optimize the sampling of both physical and statistical models. Finally, a comprehensive uncertainty quantification is conducted to assess the reliability of the proposed surrogate models. The methodology is applied to a 5 MW offshore wind turbine situated in deep water. The study confirms that the two-chained GP surrogate offers substantial computational efficiency and superior prediction accuracy, while its multi-fidelity characteristics enable the construction of an efficient active learning sampling scheme. Additionally, the uncertainty quantification reveals that a multi-fidelity GP model with 100 physical samples and 1000 environmental parameters achieves a mean squared error of 0.001, with uncertainty propagation from environmental parameters to internal structural responses remaining within acceptable limits. These findings suggest that GP-based statistical surrogate models are viable for supporting design optimization and reliability analysis of offshore wind turbines. The paper concludes with a discussion on the methodology's limitations and potential future research directions. This statistical surrogate framework is applicable to various offshore wind-turbine configurations and can be extended to other engineering systems. The study's methodology and findings are expected to advance the fields of offshore wind-turbine modeling, analysis, and design. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews relevant literature; Section 3 details the methodology; Section 4 presents the case study; and Section 5 provides the discussion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $S_{ab}$ term in [2] corresponds to the entropy of the interface in the boundary CFT. We also explore the relationship between reflected entropy and the entropy of the bulk deformed by the double-trace operator, particularly within the context of AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ duality. Additionally, we investigate the Euclidean entropy of the annulus sector, deriving an analytical expression for a specific limit. Finally, we compute the entanglement entropy for both AB and A$\bar$B sectors and confirm the entanglement inequality $E_{AB}\geq E_{A\bar{B}}$. In the low temperature regime, we prove that the difference between entanglement entropies remains constant. However, in the high temperature limit, the two entanglement entropies converge. This behavior aligns with the reflected entropy results, thereby validating the following inequality: $E_{AB}\geq E_{A\bar{B}}\geq S_{ab}$. We anticipate these results to be applicable to other relevant CFTs. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the holographic entanglement entropy conjecture. COVID-19 digital applications utilize Inferred Proximity Discovery (IPD) to manage user data for the public good by identifying individuals who may have been exposed to the virus. However, the risk of data leakage remains a significant challenge. This study evaluates the confidentiality of the Coronav\'irus-SUS application under the Coronav\'irus Data Protection Act (PLDCD-19) in Brazil through an adversarial machine learning attack. We demonstrate that, despite the model's high predictive accuracy, it fails to ensure the privacy of sensitive user attributes, including gender, age, and height. The attack successfully infers gender with 96.1% precision and 94.1% recall, age with 85.4% precision and 82.1% recall, and height with 89.1% precision and 84.4% recall. These findings indicate that the application does not meet PLDCD-19 standards, highlighting the urgent need for further research into the privacy-preserving capabilities of such applications. This paper introduces a C code creator grounded in a shallow embedding of C within ACL2. The syntax for this shallow embedding is largely identical to C, with the primary distinction being the use of logical types instead of machine types. The code creator translates valid C programs featuring this syntax into ACL2 theorems that formally describe the C program's semantics using a specific semantic model. Additionally, the theorems generated by our system can be utilized with an existing proof generator to automatically derive corresponding C proof terms. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through examples drawn from real-world C programs. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of a shallow embedding for C for the purpose of generating proofs. Furthermore, the advantages of a shallow embedding over a deep one are particularly evident in the context of code creation. We validate the correctness of our semantic description using ACL2 and illustrate the utility of the resulting theorems by applying them to actual C programs. Finally, we compare our method against alternative approaches, including semantic equivalence checking and abstract interpretation. A recent surge of interest has emerged in applying machine learning to solve central problems within algebraic topology, a field focused on classifying mathematical structures based on their shape and holes. This discipline is crucial for physics, as algebraic topology underpins key concepts in quantum field theory and condensed matter, where topological invariants determine properties like anyon behavior and topological order. This survey examines recent advances in utilizing machine learning for algebraic topology, with a specific emphasis on machine learning applications within physical systems. The review begins with a concise overview of essential algebraic topology concepts, including homology, homotopy, and the nerve lemma. It subsequently details various algorithmic approaches, such as computing homology and homotopy in complex datasets, identifying and detecting topological features, and generating synthetic data with specified topological characteristics. Finally, the discussion highlights specific applications in physics, including the analysis of topological order in Bose-Hubbard models and the study of anyon braiding in topological superconductors. The survey concludes by addressing open challenges and proposing future research directions. This work is intended to assist both mathematicians and physicists in exploring the intersection of algebraic topology and machine learning. Furthermore, it serves as a prerequisite for the accompanying tutorial, which will cover the mathematical foundations and introduce a framework for applying machine learning to algebraic topology. The tutorial's Python code is publicly available at https://github.com/akshaykumar2002/MLforMAT. Additional resources can be found at https://algotop.github.io/. Although the 6-digit personal identification number (PIN) in the Signal messaging application is intended to bolster privacy by ensuring message confidentiality, a significant portion of users have been found to forgo creating them. To gain deeper insight into this behavior, this study examines users' perspectives on PINs through 20 semi-structured interviews. The findings reveal that Signal users are often unaware of how PINs function, with many interpreting them incorrectly as message-reading notifications rather than security barriers. These conceptual misunderstandings are exacerbated by the casual and user-friendly design of the Signal interface, which inadvertently promotes a perception of the platform as secure, even among enthusiastic users. Consequently, the research proposes that the application's design should be revised to more clearly communicate the benefits of using PINs. This includes implementing a more prominent opt-in mechanism for creating them and providing an onboarding tutorial to educate new users on their purpose. Furthermore, the study recommends that Signal developers conduct user research to gain a deeper understanding of end-user needs and preferences. This approach would enable the company to align its product design and marketing strategies more effectively with user expectations, thereby strengthening Signal's market position. The study's outcomes are grounded in a user-centric design framework, offering valuable insights for the broader messaging industry. The paper concludes by discussing potential limitations of the study and suggesting directions for future research. This study introduces an algorithm designed to precisely and rapidly evaluate integrals of the form $\int_0^T f(t)w(t)dt$, where the weight function $w(t)$ adheres to a solar day cycle. The proposed method, termed solar quadrature, is a variant of Gaussian quadrature that incorporates these periodic weights. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the positive definiteness of the corresponding moment matrix and the positivity of its eigenvalues, which guarantees the existence of Gaussian nodes and coefficients. To ensure high precision across all functions integrable under solar weights, we develop a hybrid quadrature rule that supplements Gaussian quadrature with a trapezoidal correction term. This approach, called solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature, achieves $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2})$ precision for smooth integrands using only $N+1$ non-uniform nodes within each quadrature step. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method is sufficiently precise to accurately compute the solar forcing required for climate models. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule is both precise and efficient. The implementation is provided as an open-source Python package. Supplementary materials include detailed proofs, additional examples, and further discussions on the rule's properties. This work is inspired by the fourth author's experience as a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellow. However, calculating curvature for complex functions is computationally prohibitive, and existing curvature estimation techniques often fail to provide accurate approximations. This paper introduces ViViT, a novel approach designed to efficiently estimate the generalized Jacobian of the diminishing factor within a generalized Gauss-Newton framework. ViViT is constructed from multiple layers, where each layer comprises a curvature estimation unit (CEU) and a curvature projection (CP) unit. The CP unit filters irrelevant information, while the CEU calculates the diminished curvature of the diminishing factor. By utilizing the back-propagation algorithm, ViViT can efficiently determine the diminished generalized curvature of the diminishing factor. Furthermore, the chain rule for the diminished generalized curvature of the diminishing factor's composition is derived. ViViT is capable of estimating the diminished generalized curvature of the diminishing factor's composition, with its accuracy and efficiency validated through various numerical examples. The results demonstrate that ViViT achieves significantly higher accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. Additionally, the relevance of ViViT is illustrated by showing that it can be integrated into the Adam optimizer to enhance the training performance of deep neural networks. Finally, the code for ViViT is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/ViViT. An element $g \in G$ is deemed charmable relative to $\Gamma$ if it facilitates an expansion of $\Gamma$ when added to the generated group $\langle \Gamma, g \rangle$. The property of charmability for $\Gamma$ is established if a charmable element exists inside a Borel subgroup of $G$. Similarly, $\Gamma$ is considered rigid if it satisfies a comparable condition, but with the element $g$ residing in a compact Cartan subgroup. We demonstrate that both charmability and rigidity are asymptotic properties, implying that they hold true for a subset of $\Gamma$ of finite index. Furthermore, we establish that these concepts are interconnected and closely related to the question of whether $\Gamma$ is uniform. The paper concludes by examining specific instances and offering several open problems. Notably, for every non-compact type (NCT) arithmetic lattice $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{SO}(3,2)$, we prove that $\Gamma$ is charmable but not rigid. Additionally, we show that for any $\mathrm{SO}(3,2)$ lattice $\Gamma$, there exists a finite index subgroup $\Gamma^{\prime} \leq \Gamma$ such that $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is charmable and uniform, yet $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is not rigid. This result underscores the existence of a hierarchy among these groups, situated between uniformity and charmability. Finally, we present a uniform lattice $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{SO}(3,2)$ that is rigid, thereby confirming that rigidity can occur within this class of groups. The Irish LOFAR station, operating at the edge of the LOFAR array, is uniquely positioned to identify both local and distant radio transients. To enhance the station's scientific utility, a real-time transient detection and alert system is being developed and deployed. This system will identify radio transients within the field of view and generate alerts for follow-up observations. The backend described here is the initial implementation of this system, designed to detect transients in the LOFAR Extended Array (LEA) and generate alerts. Utilizing the CHORD real-time transient detection algorithm, the system identifies transients by analyzing the real-time data stream. It determines the data time, integrates the time with the LOFAR station's UTC, calculates the transient's position, and issues a time-stamped alert. Alerts are formatted in both XML and JSON, with the latter distributed via an MQTT broker. This service is being tested and refined to improve detection efficiency and accuracy. The paper details the methods employed to evaluate the detection system and presents the resulting performance metrics. Additionally, the system's transient detections are compared against other real-time and post-processing transient identification methods. Finally, the alert generation and formatting processes are outlined, along with a description of the backend's architecture. The study concludes by outlining future enhancements to the system. The REALTA backend is now fully operational, having identified hundreds of transients daily and generated thousands of alerts. These alerts are being utilized to investigate various solar and astrophysical phenomena, including solar flares, solar radio bursts, Jupiter's decametric emissions, Jupiter's decametric bursts, Io decametric bursts, and geostationary satellites. Furthermore, the system has facilitated the creation of a new real-time LOFAR station data visualization tool. This tool displays the station's data stream in real-time, allowing users to examine data from any time within the last 24 hours. Users can select data points to view time series plots, light curves, and spectra, as well as access the corresponding time-tagged alert. The paper provides an overview of this visualization tool. In recent years, metaphotonics has emerged as a promising field that leverages the wave-like characteristics of light-carrier waves to manipulate information-bearing optical waves. This methodology enables the enhancement of light manipulation, control, and information processing through mechanisms rooted in optoelectronics and radio-frequency technology. This review examines current advancements in metaphotonics, with a specific focus on customizing and controlling optical wavefronts, designing information-carrying optical waveforms, and developing hybrid photonic platforms. Finally, it outlines future prospects for metaphotonics. Given its foundational role in information and communication technologies, metaphotonics is poised to significantly impact various sectors, including optical communications, computing, and sensing. Furthermore, the synergy between machine learning and metaphotonics holds immense potential to drive future technological progress. Consequently, metaphotonics is expected to be pivotal in shaping tomorrow's world. Cyber-physical networks are increasingly recognized as the foundational infrastructure for society, underpinning domains such as transportation, energy, and healthcare. These systems are inherently complex and interconnected, forming a society-wide network of networks. The primary objective is to utilize the capabilities of advanced cyber-physical systems to improve the functioning of these systems of systems. This paper outlines the scientific challenges associated with the cyber-physicalization of complex systems of systems and proposes addressing them through scientific discovery, innovation, and invention. Specifically, we examine application areas including smart power grids, intelligent transportation systems, and smart healthcare networks. Furthermore, cyber-physical systems offer the potential to fundamentally transform how complex systems of systems are managed, controlled, and protected. The study concludes by emphasizing the significance of emerging concepts like network science, security, and privacy. Additionally, it advocates for a holistic, cross-disciplinary, and multi-scale approach to comprehending cyber-physical networks of networks. Finally, the cyber-physical nature of these systems necessitates a multi-dimensional perspective that integrates spatial, temporal, and behavioral factors. To achieve this, we propose a cross-disciplinary methodology combining cyber-physical-network science, data-driven modeling, and machine learning. This approach aims to identify, model, and predict the complex dynamics of complex systems of systems. The paper demonstrates its effectiveness through case studies in power grids, transportation, and healthcare. Ultimately, the cyber-physicalization of complex systems of systems represents a significant scientific challenge that demands innovative and interdisciplinary solutions. Addressing this issue will yield substantial societal benefits, including enhanced quality of life, improved healthcare, and more efficient and sustainable transportation and power systems. Cyber-physical systems offer the means to achieve these outcomes. Additionally, cyber-physical networks provide a framework for understanding complex systems of systems, with their associated science serving as a fertile ground for future research. This includes the study of complex dynamical systems, their control mechanisms, and their security and protection strategies. The cyber-physicalization of complex systems of systems is poised to generate numerous future research opportunities. This study introduces MAPPIES, an extension of the Monte-Carlo code previously developed by Lott and Blumenthal (2001). The original work demonstrated that accounting for polarization in electron scattering off a polarized photon field yields a significantly enhanced high-energy tail in the scattered spectrum. This high-energy component is particularly significant in the UV and soft X-ray bands for blazars, where it may explain the observed soft X-ray excess. We apply MAPPIES to investigate the origins of this excess by simulating emission from a co-linear, homogeneous, and isotropic electron distribution within a moving shock region, utilizing mean free path corrections. Our results indicate that a highly anisotropic electron distribution is required to generate scattering with sufficient intensity in these bands. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this necessary anisotropy can be naturally produced by the same mechanisms responsible for the characteristic double-exponential electron distributions found in astrophysical shocks. Finally, we show that a broad range of blazar spectra can be accurately reproduced using this model. These findings suggest that scattering off inverse Compton photons polarized by synchrotron emission is a viable mechanism for producing the soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra. Additionally, we explore the potential for constraining shock parameters through spectral analysis. This represents a significant advancement over previous studies, which relied on non-polarized Monte-Carlo simulations and assumed isotropic electron distributions. Our findings underscore the critical role of polarization in scattering processes and the necessity of anisotropic electron distributions. Consequently, the MAPPIES code is made available to the community to facilitate further research into scattering polarized photon fields. A comprehensive comparison of the MAPPIES code will be presented in an upcoming publication. The source code can be downloaded from http://www.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/~blumenthal/mappies/. We present a straightforward method for digitally assessing quantum entanglement and fidelity specifically for symmetric states within a qudit system of dimension $d$. This approach relies on applying generalized Pauli operators in sequence to the target state, recording the resulting outcome distributions, and calculating entanglement metrics directly from these distributions. Notably, the methods for digital fidelity and entanglement assessment are closely linked. A key benefit of this technique is that it circumvents the need to prepare individual quantum states for evaluation. Instead, it utilizes established procedures to generate and measure a collection of states derived from the original. Consequently, this framework is applicable to a broad spectrum of quantum tasks, including variational algorithms, quantum sensing, and simulation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's utility by evaluating the entanglement of pulse-area-law Gaussian pulse shapes relevant to quantum radar technology. This analysis reveals a strong correlation between entanglement and robustness against noise, indicating that highly entangled shapes are more susceptible to decoherence. Our findings suggest that for radar applications, an optimal pulse shape likely exists that balances entanglement and robustness, thereby maximizing entanglement while maintaining resilience against noise. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work, such as adapting the method for bosonic systems and exploring its application to non-symmetric states. These contributions establish a foundation for digital quantum verification and evaluation, particularly in the context of quantum radar and sensing. Additionally, our research highlights the significance of robust entanglement—a concept previously explored in quantum radar—as a property that is not necessarily maximized by the most highly entangled states. This insight holds critical implications for optimizing quantum resources in radar and sensing systems. Our work also underscores the advantages of the digital approach, which facilitates the development of automated verification and evaluation tools for quantum tasks. These tools can enhance the efficiency of quantum simulations and accelerate research and development efforts. Baryon generation through quantized fragmentation of a helical QCD filament is investigated. The filament's chirality determines whether the baryon density in the resulting hadron gas is positive or negative. In a universe filled with quantum filaments, baryon and antibaryon densities could be nearly identical, aligning with the observed low baryon asymmetry. Furthermore, baryon number can be transferred to other degrees of freedom, potentially explaining the significant difference between the energy densities of matter and antimatter in the early universe. Additionally, this mechanism offers a potential explanation for the small baryon asymmetry observed in the present universe. These findings may also contribute to explaining the unexpectedly low entropy density of the cosmic microwave background radiation. Finally, this framework may help address the baryon crisis in certain dwarf galaxies. These conclusions are derived from a model that does not rely on any form of anthropic principle. This study examines the impact of active region movements on global helioseismic travel-time measurements, specifically addressing the potential skewing of solar north-south asymmetry results. We analyze the contribution of active regions and their surroundings to these travel times, revealing that the spatial distribution of active regions throughout the solar cycle significantly influences the symmetry of global helioseismic measurements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the cycle-dependent asymmetry in travel times can be mitigated by weighting the data based on the active region spatial distribution. Finally, we confirm that this weighting method eliminates the cycle-dependent asymmetry in travel times, thereby ensuring unbiased measurements for solar north-south asymmetry. These findings are validated using data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), which has observed the Sun continuously since 2012. By applying a similar weighting strategy, researchers can achieve unbiased global helioseismic travel-time measurements, facilitating a more accurate investigation of solar north-south asymmetry. This approach is particularly valuable for studying the solar cycle's long-term evolution, such as the recent Gleissberg cycle modulation. Additionally, the weighting method can be extended to other 3D imaging techniques, including tomographic imaging and the deconvolution of the solar surface brightness distribution. We conclude that the weighting strategy is essential for achieving unbiased global helioseismic travel-time measurements. We investigate the detection of gravitational wave signals generated by primordial electromagnetic fields using Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs). Our study focuses on the strain deformation of the metric caused by superimposed electromagnetic modes that conform to the PTA's angular frequency range ($10^{-9}$ to $10^{-7}$ Hz). We calculated the strain produced by these primordial fields at the time of the last scattering surface and estimated the resulting metric distortion. To assess detectability, we computed the gravitational wave (GW) strain and the associated Hellings-Downs correlation function. Our findings indicate that while the metric deformation is significant, the GW strain is too weak to be observed by the PTA. Furthermore, we determined that a primordial field with an amplitude of approximately $10^{-17}$ is necessary to generate a detectable Hellings-Downs correlation, though such a field is unlikely to exist. Consequently, we conclude that PTAs are not viable for detecting GWs formed by primordial electromagnetic fields. However, this approach may become feasible in the future if PTA sensitivity improves or if the frequency range expands. This paper introduces a practical light field (LF) image compression framework that leverages disparity knowledge to enhance prediction precision. The system is composed of a prediction module, a residual module, and an entropy coding module. To boost prediction accuracy, the residual module employs disparity knowledge to refine disparity compensation. Specifically, the original image is decomposed into multiple sub-images based on pixel disparities; for each sub-image, prediction residuals are calculated using a block-based prediction method. This approach eliminates the need for complex models or algorithms, thereby reducing computational complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms state-of-the-art LF compression methods in terms of rate-distortion performance. Additionally, an objective model is developed to predict compression performance, which exhibits a strong correlation with actual results. Finally, the module's practicality is validated by applying it to two real-world LF datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/KP-LF-ICIP.

Cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) has recently gained significant attention, driven by the emergence of vector-based approaches. These methods leverage interactive and non-native language representations to map text into a shared semantic space, facilitating efficient CLIR. However, the current state-of-the-art in this domain relies exclusively on non-interleaved token embeddings, neglecting the benefits of interleaved embeddings. This study investigates the interaction between interactive and non-interactive frameworks to determine their relative performance. Our findings indicate that interactive embeddings outperform non-interactive ones in CLIR tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that integrating an interactive embedding model with a non-interleaved architecture yields superior results compared to existing methods. Finally, we release the newly developed cross-lingual dataset, WMT17 CLIR, to support future research in the community. This study presents design-based and model-based approaches to small-area estimation (SAE) utilizing data from a two-stage stratified sampling design implemented in Nigeria, a low-income nation in Africa. The primary motivation for conducting SAE is to derive estimates from survey designs that are cost-effective at the national level but lack sufficient sample sizes to guarantee adequate precision at the LGA (local government area) level. The Nigerian SAE data comprises a 2013/14 survey featuring a large sample with a sampling fraction of 10.2% at the LGA level, with the goal of generating estimates for 2016. We evaluate four methods: two design-based techniques (ratio estimation and calibration), two model-based strategies (small-area linearization and mixed models), and one hybrid approach (generalized linear mixed models with calibration). These methods are compared using two metrics: (1) the relationship between sampling variance and sample size, and (2) the accuracy of estimates for key indicators, including the poverty headcount ratio at the LGA level. Results indicate that model-based and hybrid methods outperform design-based approaches in delivering more precise estimates. Furthermore, larger sample sizes enhance the precision of both hybrid and model-based methods, though the magnitude of this effect varies by indicator. Finally, we offer practical recommendations for implementing SAE in low- and middle-income countries. These recommendations address a critical gap in existing literature, which predominantly relies on simulations and examples from high-income nations. By applying methods to a real-world dataset with a substantial sampling fraction, this work offers a robust basis for comparing SAE performance in resource-constrained settings. Ultimately, our findings aim to inform practitioners and researchers when selecting appropriate estimation techniques for low- and middle-income countries. In the traditional "Kelly Wager" problem, a gambler determines an optimal betting strategy to maximize long-term growth based on a known reward distribution. This study reexamines that problem by considering scenarios where the gambler does not have access to the full distribution but instead learns it continuously through observations. We demonstrate that continuous access to the underlying distribution offers a distinct advantage when the data is provided as a quantum state rather than as classical observations derived from it. Specifically, we analyze cases where the reward is modeled as a continuous variable, such as position or momentum. Our findings indicate that if the gambler can interact with the reward state via an arbitrary number of weak measurements, the optimal betting strategy can be determined with straightforward calculations. Conversely, if only classical data is available, the betting problem becomes significantly more complex. Furthermore, the paper explores how to set an appropriate bet size when the exact reward distribution remains unknown. We show that the gambler can achieve an optimal growth rate by employing a straightforward adaptive algorithm that iteratively refines its estimate of the distribution. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of broader implications and potential applications of these results. Keywords: gambling, weak measurement, continuous variable, quantum state. Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest for their unique electronic and optical characteristics, including charge carrier mobility, quantum confinement, band gaps, and excitonic effects. However, the broader class of materials formulated as MA$_2$Z$_4$ (where M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge; and Z = N, P, As) has received limited investigation. This study investigates the electronic and optical properties of this class using a combined density functional theory (DFT) and GW-BSE framework. Specifically, we examine the impact of varying the transition metal atom and the group-14 and group-15 elements, with a focus on stacking configurations. Our findings indicate that while the transition metal atom has a negligible effect, the selection of the anionic elements significantly alters the quasiparticle band arrangement. Furthermore, we identify a specific MA$_2$Z$_4$ compound that maintains a direct band gap across all stacking variants and exhibits a stacking-independent excitonic resonance. These results offer valuable insights for tailoring the optical characteristics of these materials for practical applications. Additionally, our analysis highlights that the GW-BSE method is essential for accurately describing the quasiparticle band structure and excitonic phenomena in this category of materials. Finally, we demonstrate that the DFT+U approach yields results comparable to those obtained from GW-BSE. These conclusions are supported by extensive calculations and data analysis. We present a novel one-dimensional model designed to simulate the formation of protoplanetary disks through the collapse of pre-stellar cores. This simplified framework incorporates key physical mechanisms, including the adiabatic expansion of the collapsing gas, magnetic braking, and the influence of opacity. Our findings indicate that the magnetic field is rapidly expelled from the inner regions during collapse, thereby facilitating the formation of a protoplanetary disk. By applying this model to various initial conditions, we successfully replicate the temperature, surface density, and radial extent of disks observed around young stars. Furthermore, the model accounts for the correlation between stellar mass and disk size, as well as the anti-correlation between stellar and disk temperatures. These results suggest that the collapse of pre-stellar cores can explain several critical characteristics of young stellar systems. Additionally, we have utilized this one-dimensional framework to generate radial profiles for temperature and surface density, which serve as initial conditions for our upcoming two-dimensional simulations of disk formation. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how protoplanetary disks emerge. A detailed description of the model will be published in an upcoming paper. Atmospheric models serve as essential instruments for analyzing and interpreting astronomical data. This study introduces a novel atmospheric model designed to simulate the atmo-photosphere boundary of solar-like stars, grounded in the atmo-photosphere structure of the Sun. By incorporating a non-linear transition between the atmo-photosphere and convection zone, the model enables the accurate reproduction of solar-like surface oscillations. The paper further examines the parameters governing this transition, including the depth of the atmo-photosphere, the atmo-convection zone density gradient, and the atmo-photosphere density scale height. Additionally, we investigate the impact of these atmo-photosphere characteristics on surface oscillations and their utility in characterizing solar-like stars. Finally, we outline the model's application in studying solar-like stars and propose its implementation in future space missions. We propose interpreting Pontryagin duality through the lens of classical logic, a perspective that aligns with our own work on the logical foundations of quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we intend to apply this interpretation to the study of C*-algebras and their duals. In this formulation, group elements correspond to propositions within steadfast (classical) logic, while characters represent other propositions defined over the same logic. The duality pairing is interpreted as the application of one proposition to another. We will present examples illustrating how this duality aligns with standard mathematical results. Additionally, we will offer a preliminary analysis of how steadfast logic can be utilized to investigate quantum systems, specifically focusing on their algebras of observables. This approach allows for the definition of a dual set of elements, which we will examine in the context of Heisenberg groups. Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that the uncertainty relations derived from this dual set are equivalent to the Heisenberg commutation relations. Finally, we will briefly discuss the implications of these findings for the foundations of quantum mechanics. Our ultimate goal is to elucidate the relationship between the logical structure of a system and its measurement theory. In this context, we will show that the measurement operators arising from our dual formulation are equivalent to the POVMs derived from Generalized Born Rules. This equivalence establishes a foundation for developing a dual formulation of quantum mechanics grounded in classical logic. Through this dual lens, we can derive the Schrödinger equation and the time evolution of quantum states, as well as the Heisenberg equations of motion for quantum observables, starting from a classical logical system and a C*-algebra of quantum observables. Furthermore, we will argue that the dual formulation offers a more intuitive understanding of the quantum world by providing a direct link between quantum mechanics and classical logic. Specifically, we will illustrate that the dual set of elements allows for the definition of quantum events, which can be directly associated with the projection operators used in quantum theory. This association enables a formulation of quantum mechanics that avoids the conceptual issues typically associated with the projection postulate. In the conclusion, we will outline the foundational principles of a quantum theory based on classical logic and present the foundational axioms for a dual formulation of quantum mechanics. We believe that the dual formulation offers a more natural description of the quantum world, as it resolves the inherent conflict between the classical logic of quantum events and the non-commutativity of quantum observables. We anticipate that the dual formulation will serve as a valuable tool in the ongoing development of quantum theory.

Federated learning (FL) represents a distributed approach designed to train machine learning models using data hosted on multiple client servers. Recently, FL has gained significant traction for training models on mobile devices. However, privacy concerns remain a primary obstacle to its widespread adoption. Consequently, this study investigates privacy attacks targeting FL, with a specific focus on differentially private FL (DPFL). Our findings indicate that DPFL effectively mitigates privacy risks but substantially compromises model accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce and evaluate an ensemble method for FL that integrates both stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and differential privacy (DP). This proposed ensemble method achieves a favorable balance between privacy and accuracy, surpassing the performance of DPFL in terms of accuracy while maintaining equivalent privacy guarantees. Experimental results demonstrate that our ensemble method improves accuracy by 10% on the MNIST dataset and by 15% on the CIFAR-10 dataset compared to DPFL. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of privacy budget allocation strategies on the ensemble's performance. Finally, we examine how variations in the privacy parameter $\epsilon$ and the number of ensemble models influence performance, revealing that a $\epsilon$ value of 0.5 and an ensemble size of 5 yield optimal results. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/PrivacyFL}. Given the growing popularity of FL, we hope our work inspires further research in this field. FL is anticipated to become a critical component of the Internet of Things (IoT), and we believe our proposed methods will contribute to the advancement of this domain. Specifically, our work will be valuable to researchers in the following areas: (i) IoT applications relying on FL, (ii) federated edge computing utilizing FL, and (iii) mobile devices employing FL. Additionally, our approach will be beneficial to researchers investigating the trade-off between model accuracy and privacy in FL, as well as those studying privacy attacks on FL systems. Finally, our work will be relevant to researchers exploring the integration of differential privacy into FL frameworks. By addressing privacy and accuracy challenges in FL, our proposed methods will help overcome current limitations and foster the development of FL-based solutions. Specifically, these methods will be relevant to researchers investigating the trade-offs between model accuracy and privacy in FL, as well as those specifically interested in FL privacy attacks. This paper introduces a new wireless integrated reconfigurable intelligent surface (WIRIS) framework designed to enhance the throughput of wireless energy transfer (WET) within wireless charging networks (WCN). The proposed system integrates WET with WIRIS to boost the throughput of the primary user (PU) within the WCN. To achieve this, we first formulate a throughput optimization problem for the PU, subject to constraints regarding the PU's data rate, the PU's harvested energy, and the WET user's rate. Subsequently, we develop a profound unsupervised learning (PUL) algorithm to resolve the formulated problem. The core concept of this approach is to model the WET process as a black-box function, thereby eliminating the need for explicit modeling of the channel between the WET source and the PU. Furthermore, the PUL algorithm is capable of handling PU locations that vary over time. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the benchmark method. Specifically, it achieves a substantial improvement in PU throughput, ranging from 10% to 40%, compared to the benchmark approach. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the number of PUL iterations and the PU's achieved throughput. Our findings indicate that 100 iterations are sufficient for the PU to reach its maximum throughput. Finally, we analyze the convergence of the PUL algorithm, proving that it converges to the optimal solution of the formulated problem. The proposed approach is applicable to various WET scenarios, including those involving multiple receivers. In such cases, the PUL can be adapted to optimize throughput for each individual receiver. This work is particularly relevant for future applications in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). In these contexts, the PUL can be utilized to maximize the data rate of the UAV or UGV while ensuring the ground vehicle receives a minimum level of energy. Our results show that the proposed PUL algorithm can increase the UAV's data rate by up to 40% compared to the benchmark method. Additionally, the PUL ensures that the UAV maintains sufficient energy to sustain its flight. Keywords: Wireless charging network, wireless energy transfer, unsupervised learning, throughput optimization, integrated reconfigurable intelligent surface. (Corresponding Author: Dr. M. S. Obaidat)

The beta decay of $^{186}$Hg was investigated using a Geant4-based simulation. This process was modeled as a sequence of discrete reactions, with the primary decay pathways for the resulting daughter states identified through a least-squares fit. The study determined the maximum beta-decay strength function, which peaks at $logft = 5.85 \pm 0.15$, and established the half-life of $^{186}$Hg as $3.23 \pm 0.04$ min. Additionally, beta-delayed neutron emission was observed, with a probability of $P_{\beta n} = 0.04 \pm 0.01$ and an average emission energy of $E_{\beta n} = 1.0 \pm 0.1$ MeV. The energy spectrum of the emitted beta-delayed neutrons was analyzed, and the energy of the first daughter state was determined to be $E_d = 2.5 \pm 0.1$ MeV. These findings provide valuable insights into the beta decay characteristics of mercury isotopes. We investigate a scenario where dark energy arises from the remaining soft leptons after the seesaw and baryogenesis processes are completed. Initially, these leptons exist in thermal equilibrium with the Standard Model sector; subsequently, as the temperature drops, leptons seesaw away, generating the leptonic asymmetry necessary for baryogenesis. Following this departure, the dark energy density begins to dominate. Our analysis examines the consistency of this picture, specifically determining the required initial leptonic asymmetry and establishing constraints on the dark energy sector. Additionally, we explore a model extending this framework that includes a scalar field responsible for leptogenesis, where the dark energy density is subsequently absorbed by this same field. In both scenarios, the model parameters align with observational data. However, the first scenario presents a significant challenge: it requires fine-tuning the dark energy density to the precise level needed to match current observations. The second scenario offers a more natural resolution to this fine-tuning problem. Furthermore, we note that the standard $\Lambda$CDM model fails to account for the baryon asymmetry of the universe, whereas our proposed models successfully incorporate leptogenesis and dark energy within a unified framework. This approach may also provide a potential explanation for the observed Hubble tension. Finally, we outline the observational tests required to constrain the model parameters. Our findings suggest that the next generation of cosmic microwave background experiments could impose stringent limits on the model, while future large-scale structure surveys may be able to detect the model's presence. We also examine the potential for this framework to explain the Hubble tension. In conclusion, our proposed models are viable and should be considered in the ongoing efforts to resolve the Hubble tension. Specifically, the model's ability to address this issue is independent of the dark energy amplitude, whereas the $\Lambda$CDM model would require fine-tuning to address the Hubble tension. Consequently, the Hubble tension could serve as a critical test to validate or rule out our proposed framework. Finally, we highlight that the model is consistent with the recent Planck 2018 results. Given that the Planck collaboration has observed a slight preference for the baryon asymmetry to be generated during the radiation-dominated era, our models align with this observation, whereas $\Lambda$CDM does not. Thus, our framework is supported by both Planck data and the recent radiation-dominated asymmetry finding. In summary, our models are favored by both the Planck data and the inference that baryon asymmetry was produced in the radiation-dominated era.

The success of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in robotics depends on the ability to learn policies from minimal data. However, this learning process is hindered by the "exploration-exploitation trade-off," where the agent must balance discovering new actions with maximizing rewards. This paper introduces a data-driven control framework that leverages limited data and side information to achieve this balance. We propose a data-driven control method that utilizes the average dynamics of a system to guide the exploration-exploitation trade-off. The resulting algorithm is formulated as a deep reinforcement learning problem, where the agent learns an optimal policy by weighing the immediate reward against the average dynamic deviation. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness by training a single neural network to manage four distinct subsystems of a humanoid robot, enabling it to attain, walk, swim, and fly. Furthermore, we show that training on a single subsystem generalizes effectively to the others. These findings indicate that the proposed algorithm can master multiple locomotion modes using data from just one subsystem. Additionally, the method is validated on a real-world robotic dog, demonstrating that a single controller can successfully perform various tasks. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's capability to generalize to unseen tasks, such as walking on uneven terrain. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYan2000/DDC. Our results suggest that data-driven control is a promising approach for robotics, particularly when dealing with scarce data and the need for multi-task performance. This framework is expected to be valuable for developing versatile robotic systems, including humanoids, quadrupeds, and drones. Our findings also highlight the potential of data-driven control to facilitate collaborative learning across diverse robotic platforms. We anticipate that this approach will inspire future research into advanced collaborative learning strategies for heterogeneous robots. The proposed framework is also applicable to learning control policies for new systems by leveraging existing data from similar systems. We believe this will enable the transfer of knowledge between related systems, thereby accelerating the learning process for new platforms. This work is expected to inspire further research into the transferability of data-driven control policies across different systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYan2000/DDC. Our findings suggest that data-driven control is a valuable approach for robotics, especially when facing data scarcity and the requirement for multi-task capabilities. This study derives Ward identities for the two-dimensional Toda $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ conformal field model, which corresponds to a system of three interacting scalar fields. Utilizing the model's established correlation function formula, we prove that these identities are equivalent to the classical Liouville equation governing the classical Toda equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the validity of a specific instance of the Ward identity associated with the ghost field, thereby facilitating the construction of correlation functions involving highest weight fields. This achievement marks the first application of Ward identities to the study of correlation functions in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model. The study also extends its findings to the mathematical framework of the KZ equation and the Gelfand-Zetorin system. Additionally, we examine the analytic properties of the Ward identity linked to the ghost field and explore its connection to the monodromy of the KZ equation. Finally, we detail a correspondence between the correlation functions of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model and the Gelfand-Zeitlin system. Relation networks have recently been introduced to address the challenges of long-range dependencies and overfitting in deep learning, particularly within the context of generative adversarial networks (GANs). This paper introduces a new relation GAN architecture that employs a relation discriminator to evaluate triplets of points from the same image sample. During training, the relation discriminator aims to distinguish between triplets containing points from the same sample and those from different samples, while both the generator and the relation discriminator engage in adversarial training. Our results demonstrate that this proposed architecture surpasses both standard GANs and prior relation network-based GANs. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abdolrasoulh/RelationGAN. In dual-field quantum key distribution (QKD), an optical parametric oscillator (OPO) operating at a fixed pump frequency generates a narrow-field signal, while an external laser provides a broad-field signal, enabling polarization and phase-matching encoding respectively. However, previous implementations relied on phase stabilization to maintain the OPO's field phase relative to the external laser. This requirement restricts transmission distances due to high costs and low efficiency. In this study, we demonstrate that phase stabilization is unnecessary when employing polarization encoding. This finding is grounded in the analysis of OPO properties, the characteristics of phase errors, and the principles of QKD encoding. Consequently, our results pave the way for practical dual-field QKD systems. Furthermore, experimental outcomes confirm the feasibility of eliminating phase stabilization in OPOs when using polarization encoding. These advances enhance the practicality and scalability of dual-field QKD, establishing a foundation for further research and development in the field. Additionally, the proposed scheme is applicable to other quantum communication technologies that depend on OPOs. Finally, our work offers a theoretical framework for investigating phase errors and decoding methods in other OPO-based quantum systems. **Keywords:** Quantum key distribution; Optical parametric oscillator; Phase error. **Corresponding authors:** *Y. While recent approaches have explored using large-scale image-text pairs to link words to visual entities, they often neglect the critical challenge of aligning text with specific locations within an image. To address this, we introduce a method that generates pseudo-supervision for image-text pairs by automatically extracting bounding boxes directly from training images. Our strategy involves training a detector on images annotated with these pseudo-bounding boxes to create an initial model, which in turn produces predictions that generate further pseudo-annotations. These accumulated text-image pairs are then utilized to train an retrieval system, establishing the mapping between words and visual content. Finally, this retrieval component is applied during the detection phase to identify words linked to regions in the image. This end-to-end framework achieves competitive performance using only a minimal set of initial predefined object classes. The code is accessible at https://github.com/PrincetonUniversity/PLEOD. We present new observations of ionized gas, atomic hydrogen, and photodissociation regions surrounding the Rho Oph S1 cluster using the IRAM 30m, NRO 45m, and NRO 45m/21cm telescopes. Analysis of these data reveals gas structures that align with the cluster's geometry and the radiation from its most massive stars. Specifically, the ionized gas exhibits a bipolar morphology centered on S1C, while atomic hydrogen displays a complex, clumpy distribution. Photodissociation regions are visible as dark silhouettes against the ionized emission, appearing as two distinct arcs on the eastern side of the bipolar structure and a fainter, fragmented region on the western side. The shapes and orientations of these PDRs correspond to the positions of the cluster's massive stars. We propose that the clumpy structure of the atomic hydrogen arises from the interaction between the HII regions and the PDRs. These findings offer a detailed view of how the S1 cluster influences its surrounding molecular material. Furthermore, the observed bipolar shape of the ionized gas and the fragmented PDRs suggest that the outflow from the S1C source may be obscured by the dust and gas cloud. Finally, the dispersion of ionized and neutral gas around the S1 cluster demonstrates that the S1C source is a candidate for a jet or wind origin. The IRAM 30m telescope was utilized in this study.
