This paper introduces a new multi-factor mortality model featuring time-varying factor loadings to enhance mortality prediction. Loadings are estimated using Gaussian processes, which rely on time as their sole covariate, ensuring the projections remain computationally efficient. The study details the theoretical properties of these loadings and provides an empirical analysis of US mortality data from 1969 to 2015 to evaluate the model's performance. The results indicate that time-varying loadings significantly improve long-term mortality forecasts, particularly for older ages, compared to conventional single-exponential-Cayley models and standard multi-factor models with time-constant loadings. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that a simple projection method can effectively estimate time-varying future mortality rates for long-term prediction. Finally, the paper extends the model to handle spatially correlated data for multiple regions. In this spatial context, common and spatially-specific mortality rates are modeled using factor models with time-varying loadings, and spatial correlation is captured via a Gaussian Markov random field. The corresponding spatial correlation parameters are estimated using integrated nested Laplace approximation. Spatially-specific mortality rate projections are subsequently derived using a Karhunen-Loève expansion. This spatial extension is applied to predict mortality for the 50 US states over the period 1983–2014. The resulting spatially multi-factor model outperforms a spatially single-factor model and a model assuming constant spatial factors in predicting spatially-specific mortality rates. Additionally, the multi-factor spatial model with time-varying factors yields more accurate spatially-correlated mortality projections than one using time-constant factors. The code required to implement this methodology is available at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1991/Spatial-Factor-Model. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated that well-structured performance benchmarks can identify superior models that significantly outperform their human-designed counterparts. However, when architects design search objectives based solely on a limited selection of standard benchmarks, the resulting models often fail to generalize to new, unseen datasets. This study investigates such generalization failure within the context of NAS. We attribute this issue to "overfitting to search space," a phenomenon where a specific subset of performance objectives causes architectures to optimize their own latent features to excel at those particular tasks, rather than learning generalizable representations. Drawing from the concept of interference in classical machine learning, we demonstrate that this overfitting manifests as interference among neural architectures. To address this, we propose a regularization technique grounded in the theory of interference, which has been validated on several benchmarks. This method successfully mitigates interference, yielding models that perform more consistently across a diverse range of benchmarks. Additionally, we offer a theoretical analysis of the proposed approach and present empirical results through ablation studies. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhi-agarwal-1995/interference_in_NAS.

This article introduces the theft package, which enables users to decompose, examine, and visualize time series data based on attributes such as day, month, or hour. The procedure begins by calculating at-feature summaries (for instance, mean, median, or min) through the `at()` function, followed by by-feature aggregation via the `aggregate()` function. The package also facilitates data visualization with `ggplot2` by allowing the `geom_line()` function to accept formulas of the form `at ~ var` or `at1 + at2 ~ var`. Furthermore, theft allows for the application of various time series models to decompose and visualize aggregated, non-overlapping groups within a single plot using `autoplot()`. The `at()` function supports multiple aggregation levels, such as hourly, daily, and weekly, which can be visualized simultaneously on one graph via `autoplot()`. This capability is particularly valuable for identifying anomalies and explaining sudden fluctuations in original time series data. The article utilizes several real-world datasets to demonstrate these features. Ultimately, theft serves as a specialized tool for visualizing time series data with an attribute-based focus, complementing existing time series packages in the tidyverse and forecast families. It is designed to be easily extensible for custom visualizations and to integrate with other time series models. The package is released under the MIT license and is freely available on GitHub. Within organizations, human translators are often categorized into reliable and unreliable groups based on machine translation (MT) system performance, using systems that align closely with professional standards as the benchmark. This study introduces a method to advance these evaluation efforts by introducing a Bayesian framework that determines dependability thresholds and classifies translators accordingly. The approach is evaluated using dependability data derived from an organization's historical records. The proposed Bayesian strategy is shown to significantly enhance the proportion of translators correctly identified as reliable. Furthermore, an experiment demonstrates that the method achieves these accurate classifications even with limited numbers of reliable gold-standard translations. The paper concludes by outlining potential future applications of this methodology. Additionally, a Python library implementing the proposed approach is made available for organizational use. The library's functionality is illustrated through a case study of the evaluation process at Philips. This paper serves as a tutorial on applying a Bayesian method for translator evaluation, utilizing an open-source library. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/philips-research/bayesian-translator-evaluation. Keywords: Bayesian evaluation, Bayesian threshold, dependability, machine translation, translator evaluation.

We establish sum rules for energy absorption in open, nonreciprocal scattering systems subjected to a DC bias, with applications extending to electronic and spintronic devices. These sum rules are derived from the scattering matrix of the unbiased system and, unlike previous sum rules for energy absorption, require no knowledge of the quasienergy scattering matrix under biased conditions. For the specific case of electronic transport, our findings align with sum rules previously established by different research groups. Furthermore, in the limit of vanishing bias, our results recover existing sum rules for energy absorption in reciprocal systems. We also demonstrate that, in general, energy absorption eigenchannels do not adhere to sum rules based solely on charge and spin current eigenchannels. However, for time-reversal symmetric systems, we derive explicit sum rules for energy absorption eigenchannels that depend exclusively on quasicharge and quasispin eigenchannels. These quasi and quasispin concepts are defined in terms of the scattering matrix of the unbiased system. Additionally, we present numerical results for a nonreciprocal two-channel model, illustrating the violation of sum rules for both charge and spin. Finally, we extend our sum rules to multi-terminal systems. Our findings are applicable to any open quantum system, including electronic circuits, spintronic devices, and quantum Hall edge transport. We anticipate that our results will facilitate the development of energy-efficient devices, such as low-power diodes and spin diodes. Recent studies have established that sparse, subnetworks known as "winning tickets" exist within deep neural networks and can be recovered using various techniques. These tickets often achieve performance comparable to the dense models they are extracted from, yet they require significantly fewer parameters and display distinctive traits that the larger networks lack. This paper investigates the characteristics of these special winning tickets by employing an efficient trimming method that identifies them while filtering out non-essential features. The results demonstrate that sparse winning tickets exhibit significant distinctions compared to dense networks, particularly regarding the distribution of gradients and the relative significance of final-layer parameters. Furthermore, we find that certain gradient-based winning ticket techniques can recover networks that utilize the same convolutions as ResNet. These findings offer crucial insights into the nature of these remarkable sparse subnetworks. Finally, we introduce a new initialization strategy for training winning tickets that surpasses the density of state-of-the-art methods. By applying pruning to these optimized tickets, we achieve a speedup of approximately 10 times. This rapid inference capability makes winning tickets highly promising for edge computing applications. We introduce a novel approach to decision-making within the lottery framework. We demonstrate that maximizing anticipated value necessitates optimizing the worth of a winning ticket combination by strategically selecting the composition of the remaining draws. We derive closed-form solutions for optimal purchase strategies and determine the conditions under which participation is justified. Our findings indicate that to maximize worth, one should only consider joining the lottery when the necessary majority of remaining draws can be personally supported. Furthermore, for feasible purchase options, there exists a minimum threshold for the number of draws required to make support worthwhile. Finally, our strategy entails purchasing the maximum number of draws possible, provided this count does not exceed the minimum required to achieve a positive worth. We validate these findings using empirical data from the Italian SuperEnalotto, a lottery where the author is an active participant. The SuperEnalotto is a high-profile game played by millions, and our proposed strategy could significantly enhance the worth of winning tickets. We illustrate this with a specific scenario: when the optimal strategy involves supporting 10 or more draws, the minimum prize increases from 2 euros to approximately 10 euros. This represents an 80% increase in worth for the same number of selected draws. Additionally, we validate the efficacy of our algorithmic strategy through a simulation study. The results confirm that our approach significantly increases the worth of winning tickets. Specifically, for tickets with 3 or more matches, the increase in worth ranges from 10% to 100%. For tickets with 2 matches, the increase is substantial, between 100% and 200%. These findings suggest that our strategy could significantly improve the financial stability of lottery players. The proposed algorithmic approach is implemented in a web-based tool, which we have made publicly available. This allows users to explore the anticipated worth of their selected draws and optimize it by choosing an appropriate number of supported draws. We have computed the anomalous dimension for the $\phi^Q$ operator in the $O(N)$ symmetric model up to order $O(\epsilon^3)$ within the dimensional regularization framework, achieving this through calculations of six-loop order. The computed unusual global dependence on $O(N)$ is presented as:
$$ \gamma_{\phi^Q} = -\frac{15}{2}\epsilon^2 + O(\epsilon^3). $$
This result aligns with the exact value for the $\phi^4$ model, where $Q=N-1$, and is consistent with the findings of V. V. Sokolov and A. N. Velizhanin, who determined the order $O(\epsilon^2)$ using the bootstrap method. Our findings indicate that the unusual $O(N)$ dependence of the anomalous dimension $\gamma_{\phi^Q}$ vanishes at two orders higher than that of $\gamma_{\phi^3}$. Additionally, we have calculated the mass renormalization constant and the critical exponent $\beta$ for the $\phi^Q$ operator up to the order $O(\epsilon^4)$. Finally, our results are compared against those derived from Monte Carlo simulations. Keywords: Field theory models, Renormalization group, Critical phenomena, Scaling and size effects.

The valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials is a non-linear, second-harmonic response to an external electric field. This phenomenon is governed by a Berry curvature-like term arising from inter-valley band mixing and a geometric contribution from the same type of interaction. While the first component relies on time-independent mechanisms like strain or circular magnetic fields, the second is driven by time-dependent factors, specifically phonons. The magnitude of the phonon-driven inter-valley band mixing is contingent upon the specific mechanisms of electron-phonon coupling. The study compares various phonon sources, including circularly polarized phonons, to identify the optimal condition for valley physics. Furthermore, the analysis explores the potential to enhance valley Hall physics through the simultaneous application of multiple external stimuli. Finally, the non-linear second-harmonic response is compared against the linear Berry curvature-induced contribution. The findings suggest that these results are broadly applicable to two-dimensional materials, with the specific outcomes dependent on the unique electronic band structures and electron-phonon interaction mechanisms of each individual system. Additionally, the study examines the influence of spin-orbit coupling on valley Hall physics. The ultimate goal is to establish a foundation for the design and engineering of efficient valleytronics devices. The methodologies employed, such as the use of circularly polarized phonons, are also expected to be valuable in the design of other two-dimensional materials. The code utilized in this research is publicly accessible. This paper introduces the winning strategy for the 11th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge. The competition's objective is to develop novel techniques for visual domain adaptation without access to semantic labels in the target domain, a constraint that makes semantic-based methods inapplicable. Our winning system employs a simple yet effective unsupervised domain adaptation approach for image classification, leveraging a self-supervised pretraining technique to achieve state-of-the-art results. The method utilizes a dual self-supervised contrastive learning strategy to extract both semantic and non-semantic features, combined with a semantic alignment mechanism to transfer knowledge from the source to the domain-adapted target domain. We secured first place in both the unsupervised and semi-supervised tracks, achieving accuracy scores of 71.73% and 80.00%, respectively, on the benchmark. Given the simplicity of our proposed methods, this work can serve as a valuable reference for future research in unsupervised image classification domain adaptation. Multidimensional scaling (MDS) is a widely used technique for visualizing high-dimensional data in a comprehensible manner. Recently, t-SNE has become a popular method for this purpose, excelling particularly with non-Euclidean datasets like images. However, t-SNE is restricted to Euclidean space, rendering it unsuitable for data that naturally resides on a sphere, such as directional sensor readings, spherical coordinates, or orientations. To address this limitation, we introduce VMF-SNE, an adaptation of t-SNE designed specifically for spherical data. Our approach demonstrates superior convergence and outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We validate the effectiveness of VMF-SNE using simulated and simulated-based real-world data, including orientation and spherical coordinate datasets. Additionally, we evaluate its utility in dimensionality reduction and clustering tasks. Finally, we explore potential applications within spherical recommendation systems. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi1993/VMF-SNE. Source files can also be requested from the corresponding author. Keywords: Visualization, Spherical Data, Spherical Distributions, Spherical Clustering.

This study examines the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model using fermionic Diagrammatic Monte Carlo (DMC) techniques. We present novel findings for the polaron mass and energy in both weak and strong coupling regimes, achieving relative errors of 1% or less by employing an optimized series of self-energy diagrams. Our results for the polaron energy align closely with recent exact diagonalization data. Furthermore, we investigate the transition from the polaron to the molecule as the interaction with the second species intensifies, observing the molecular fraction across various background impurity densities. Finally, we analyze the effects of repulsive versus attractive interactions between the light and heavy species on the polaron properties. Specifically, the polaron energy exhibits a minimum at a specific mass ratio between the light and heavy species, a phenomenon that is significantly more pronounced in the case of attractive interactions. These outcomes are compared with corresponding exact molecular fraction calculations. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the Kondo effect and the KZK model. Veege links, also known as link diagrams with Veech crossings, have been recently defined and investigated by J. Németh and A. Szabó. They demonstrated that the space of vector fields on link diagrams containing Veech crossings is generated by the Reidemeister moves and specific additional moves. Furthermore, they established that the invariant associated with a compact Riemann surface in Hitchin links remains invariant under Reidemeister moves and a category of "small closure moves" that include the ones from Németh–Szabó's work. In this work, we generalize the concept of a Veech crossing to the case of an arc on a Riemann surface within a Hitchin link. We show that the invariant for links with such "Veech arcs" remains unchanged under Reidemeister moves and a class of "virtual arc moves" that encompass small, large, and open/closed moves. Additionally, we prove that the arc space of links with Veech arcs is spanned by the Reidemeister moves and a class of "arc moves" that include crossing changes, along with their virtual counterparts. Finally, we provide an explicit formula for the invariant under arc moves with crossing changes and a formula for its behavior under the remaining arc moves. These findings collectively imply that the invariant is also preserved under crossing changes. Consequently, the invariant serves as a complete invariant for isotopy classes of planar immersions of surfaces with boundary that admit trivial normal bundles. This conclusion aligns with a result by J. Przytycki and P. Traczyk, who showed that the Kauffman bracket can distinguish all such isotopy classes. We also present several illustrative examples. In the concluding section, we outline several interesting open problems. In the appendix, we address a question posed by Przytycki and Traczyk by explicitly calculating the bracket for the untwisted double of a ribbon knot. Using this, we illustrate that the bracket does not necessarily distinguish between the twisted and reversed twists of ribbon knots. We further show that the bracket can differentiate between the twisted and reverse-twisted versions of fibered ribbon knots. Finally, we demonstrate that the bracket can distinguish between the twisted and reverse-twisted knots among the four hyperbolic knots with ten crossings. These findings also answer a question posed by J. Németh and A. Szabó. Over the past few years, telecommuting has gained significant traction in software engineering, yet it remains unclear how effectively distributed Scrum teams function. Results indicate that distributed teams experience delays in delivering both features and non-features, though these projects achieve higher completion rates. Chromatic alpha structures serve as a chromatic extension of standard alpha structures, designed to capture the alternating current (AC) dynamics within time series. By enabling a chromatic interpretation of the distance matrix, they facilitate the homological detection of linear and nonlinear temporal patterns. This paper introduces a steady fast homology method tailored for chromatic alpha structures. The algorithm allows for a local focus on the temporal sequence of AC and DC movements, while the homological analysis renders the results robust against noise. Furthermore, this homology serves as a crucial instrument for diagnosing various types of data. In this study, we applied chromatic homology to analyze the temporal evolution of the COVID-19 pandemic across different countries. The resulting coefficients, $H_{p,q}$, provide valuable insights for understanding the pandemic's progression. Additionally, we demonstrate that these coefficients can identify the onset of the second wave in both Italy and the United States. Finally, we emphasize the significance of chromatic homology in analyzing the temporal dynamics of alternating current phenomena. All findings are supported by reproducible, open-source code. This study examines the maximum Extremal GDoF advantage of optimally regulating transmit power to achieve a $\sqrt{K}$-order reduction in total power consumption within $K$ user interference networks, compared to using constant power levels. We establish that the greatest Extremal GDoF gain from optimally managing control parameters relative to a fixed-power baseline is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ across any topology and any combination of $\mathrm{SNR}$ and $\mathrm{INR}$. This optimal benefit is realized when network nodes are arranged in a line or grid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that networks structured as lines or grids achieve the highest Extremal GDoF benefit from optimal transmit power usage in both $\mathrm{SNR}$-limited and $\mathrm{INR}$-limited environments. Additionally, we prove that the maximum Extremal GDoF gain achievable by optimal control parameters is independent of the specific type of control mechanism employed. Finally, we establish that the Extremal GDoF benefit of optimal control is bounded by $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ for line-based topologies and $\Theta(K^{2/3})$ for grid-based topologies. These findings are derived through a novel approach utilizing the concept of "optimal network cuts." Our results indicate that the maximum GDoF gain is attained when control parameters are set to their extreme values, thereby yielding the term "Extremal GDoF." We also note that this work was partially presented at the IEEE Information Theory Workshop (ITW) 2021. This study introduces a concept lattice clustering algorithm designed for auditing applications. Within the constructed concept lattice, auditing processes are represented as auditing elements, defined as the intersections of an infinite set of auditing concepts. Each concept corresponds to a auditing rule, with the rule's antecedent serving as the context and its consequent as the object within that context. By applying Dempster-Shafer theory, the algorithm calculates belief and plausibility functions for the labeling class of each auditing element, ultimately assigning a classification based on belief. The paper demonstrates the algorithm with a specific example and further explores its potential for handling noisy data and uncertain attribute values. Additionally, the algorithm's computational efficiency is analyzed, and modifications are proposed to address large-scale auditing datasets. Finally, the study highlights the algorithm's applicability to fraud detection and risk assessment. Keywords: Formal Concept Analysis, Classification, Dempster-Shafer Theory, Clustering, Risk Assessment, Fraud Detection.

The Strauss process is a point process characterized by an intensity function that depends on the count of neighboring points within a specific interaction range, $\beta$, of any arbitrary location. While existing methods for Strauss models rely on approximations that fail to guarantee exact sampling, this study introduces an exact algorithm. The proposed method extends the stitching algorithm, originally developed for the hard-core model where $\beta=1$, to handle general values of $\beta$. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations comparing it against other existing techniques. For $\gamma=\frac{1}{2}$, the new method achieves a speed improvement of over 100 times compared to the best existing alternative. Furthermore, we show that sampling from the Strauss model can be utilized to approximate the independent set of the Potts model. By combining our method with the algorithm in [1], we construct an exact sampler for the Potts model. In this application, our approach yields an approximately 10 times speedup compared to the existing best exact algorithm. Finally, we provide experimental results indicating that our exact algorithm for the Potts model is nearly 1000 times faster than an exact algorithm for a non-Strauss model that also relies on stitching. This significant performance gap underscores the critical role of stitching properties in point process algorithms. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/akshaykumar2000/stitching.

To ensure safe and effective locomotion, monopod robots require a model that accounts for terrain compliance. This paper introduces a discrete-time state-space linear time-varying (LTV) model for robot-terrain interaction, derived from the Pontryau Popov (PP) framework, which incorporates both robot and terrain mechanical properties. This framework facilitates the co-design of robot control and parameter identification, enabling performance tuning based on specific hopping missions. Furthermore, the model supports the synthesis of reference signals that account for actual interaction dynamics rather than idealized rigid assumptions. Simulation studies validate this approach across varying parameters and initial conditions, demonstrating robust state convergence and successful trajectory tracking. Additionally, physical experiments on standard and non-standard surfaces confirm that the proposed state feedback controller and reference generator achieve the desired trajectory despite unmodeled friction and disturbances. Finally, the analysis reveals that the robot's performance is highly dependent on its specific physical parameters. To address this, the PP framework is utilized to determine optimal parameters for any given mission, yielding a 20% increase in horizontal displacement. This closed-loop adaptation mechanism, which links performance directly to physical parameters, offers a design methodology applicable to other locomotion systems. Consequently, this work provides a comprehensive solution for the modeling, simulation, and control of monopod robots interacting with compliant environments. Future research will extend this approach to multi-robot hopping systems. The PP framework is considered a foundational tool for the design and control of legged robots traversing soft terrain. Firmware updates are essential for maintaining the security and functionality of Internet of Things (IoT) devices. However, the widespread adoption of Over-the-Air (OTA) firmware updates in large-scale IoT networks introduces significant reliability and stability challenges. This paper details our findings from testing OTA updates on a real-world, large-scale mesh network. We identify the primary obstacles to dependable OTA updates and outline future research directions needed to ensure their successful implementation. Additionally, we discuss the key considerations for designing and executing such evaluations. Given the critical nature of this research, we contend that every stakeholder involved in IoT deployments should invest time and resources to understand the complexities of delivering reliable OTA updates. We conclude by proposing several research avenues to address these challenges. Specifically, we suggest that future studies should explore the application of Machine Learning (ML) to enhance the reliability of large-scale IoT networks during OTA deployments. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and provide a proof-of-concept example. Finally, we outline the necessary research steps to make ML-assisted updates a viable solution. Our discussion of these opportunities is supported by a dependability model that quantifies the reliability improvements offered by ML-assisted updates. This work is grounded in our extensive experience implementing dependable IoT services, including dependability-aware ML, on a real-world large-scale mesh network. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the practical dependability of large-scale IoT networks when performing OTA firmware updates. The source code for our ML-assisted OTA deployment and the models presented in this paper are available at \url{https://github.com/dependability4iot/ML-OTA-Deployments}. Furthermore, our experimental setup for the dependability evaluation can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/dependability4iot/Experimental-Setup-ML-OTA-Deployments}. Finally, our results are published in our paper on ML-assisted OTA Deployments \cite{10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3055000}. We believe this work will inspire further research into the practical dependability of large-scale IoT networks regarding OTA firmware updates. Our paper demonstrates that the practical dependability of large-scale IoT networks can be significantly improved through ML-assisted updates. We also show that ML-assisted updates can achieve a dependability level of 99.99999999999999999999999999999999999999

We demonstrate that the scaling behavior of the Fock-space propagator, which depends on density and interaction strength, exhibits distinct regimes for both the many-body localization (MBL) transition and an associated critical point known as shift. Notably, the shift displays a universal scaling form with a critical exponent of $\nu=2.5$, closely resembling the scaling of the spectral stiffness. In contrast, the shift displays a non-monotonic dependence on interaction strength, peaking near the shift point, whereas the spectral stiffness reaches a maximum at significantly lower interaction levels. Furthermore, we establish that the shift displays universal scaling across a broad spectrum of disorder strengths, spanning from close to the MBL transition to very high disorder values. Finally, we show that multifractality is not essential for the emergence of either the shift or the MBL transition. Additionally, by comparing our scaling results with the area law of entanglement entropy, we provide evidence that the shift point does not coincide with the MBL transition point. These findings underscore the critical role of interactions in the physics governing the shift. Our study is based on a two-component lattice model with random interactions, where we numerically calculate the full many-body wave function in the Fock space. We also discuss the potential extension of our methodology to other interacting spin models, such as the Heisenberg model. Our results are supported by 10,000 CPU hours. This study addresses a search scenario where a user seeks to locate $k$ target items within a vast database of $n$ items, limited to a strict budget of $b$ adaptive queries ($b \ll n$). The user engages interactively with the search process, issuing adaptive queries, while each item is characterized by a confidence value representing the probability of being the target. The proposed algorithm requires no assumptions regarding the underlying distribution of these values. It achieves a worst-case success rate of $1 - e^{-k/b}$ and maintains a failure rate no higher than that of the optimal method capable of success with probability 1 given an unrestricted query budget. This result is robust, as the failure probability approaches zero when the budget is sufficient ($b \geq k$). Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness against noisy confidence values and performs efficiently. Experimental results indicate that the algorithm surpasses the best existing approaches in literature, even those designed for a non-exhaustive search of a single target. To the authors' knowledge, this work presents the first algorithm offering a non-trivial success probability for finding multiple targets under a tight budget constraint. Additionally, the paper includes a lower bound proof, establishing that the achieved success rate is optimal up to a constant factor. Finally, the methodology is extended to handle cases where target items possess associated costs. The resulting algorithm retains the same success rate and offers optimal cost performance relative to any algorithm possessing a non-zero success probability. This approach also exhibits robustness to noisy costs and ensures efficient execution. The study concludes with a detailed analysis of parameter selection. The paper is structured into two main components: theoretical results and experimental findings. Keywords include interactive search, clustering, clustering validation, and robustness. Quantum classifiers are increasingly utilized in machine learning, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks remains a significant concern. This paper proposes generating global adversarial instances and disturbances specifically tailored to quantum classifiers. By leveraging class labels and the unitary transformations within a quantum classifier, we construct global adversarial instances. Subsequently, we produce global adversarial disturbances based on these instances. Experimental results demonstrate that qubits perturbed with our global adversarial disturbances misclassify more often than those perturbed by existing methods. Furthermore, our approach remains effective against quantum classifiers modified via hardware noise. Consequently, this study establishes a foundation for advancing the reliability of quantum machine learning. Keywords: Quantum machine learning, Quantum classifiers, Global adversarial instances, Global adversarial disturbances.

This study examines Steklov eigenvalues associated with a Dirichlet Neumann condition on the boundary of a domain. Focusing on two-dimensional almost spherical regions, we investigate how these eigenvalues vary based on the domain's geometry. Our findings are conducted within a mean-field framework, where we establish that the variations of the Steklov eigenvalues are bounded by the Dirichlet energy of the corresponding eigenmode defined on the sphere, multiplied by the measure of the deformation from the sphere, measured in the $H^1$-norm. Additionally, we provide examples of two-dimensional domains that validate our results and demonstrate the sharpness of the constants involved. Finally, the paper outlines several potential directions for future research regarding this topic. Key concepts include Steklov eigenvalues, Dirichlet energy, and mean-field theory. Verifying compliance with business process regulations is a critical challenge, especially when rules are expressed as temporal constraints on trace segments. While existing literature has addressed rule compliance using pre- and post-fix alignments of complete traces, this paper introduces a novel approach based on infix alignments of process trace segments. Although combining pre- and post-fix alignments can yield inconsistent results, we demonstrate that two infix alignments are always consistent. The proposed method constructs compliance checkers for trace segments based on these consistent infix alignments. Furthermore, we illustrate how to reduce the number of generated checkers by identifying redundant inferences and how to integrate rule compliance verification into process discovery. Experimental results confirm the practicality of these methods. To support compliance verification for process trace segments, we have also released a new benchmark dataset. In addition to the existing EFQM dataset of real-world processes, we have incorporated the TRACEXL dataset, which contains annotated process trace segments. Power expansion planning is a critical challenge in the energy sector, aiming to determine the most efficient combination of power generation assets and transmission networks to meet future demand. Mathematical models are commonly employed to address this issue, with linear models being the standard approach. Nevertheless, computational efficiency often necessitates the use of simplified assumptions, such as the "nodal" or "radial" network topologies. This study examines the linear programming objective function under both topological constraints to evaluate the practicality of these simplifications. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the deviations between the objectives are negligible for small-scale networks but become significant in larger, more complex systems. Consequently, this finding underscores the critical role of network topology in power expansion planning. Furthermore, we introduce and validate the concept of model responsiveness, which quantifies the sensitivity of linear programming objectives to topological changes. This metric is particularly valuable for assessing the trade-off between solution accuracy and computational time. Finally, we illustrate the utility of model responsiveness in two specific applications: tuning the radial model to achieve a desired level of topological approximation and selecting the most appropriate model for a given network based on available computational resources. The proposed methods are implemented in an open-source Python package available at https://github.com/fernando-ramos/responsiveness. This study establishes global-in-time well-posedness for Vlasov-type equations featuring confined boundary conditions, encompassing the Vlasov-Poisson system within bounded containers and the kinetic boundary value problem linked to the Fokker-Planck equation. The initial data are assumed to be admissible, ensuring non-negative solutions that remain confined. By employing the confining method, we derive uniform estimates that guarantee the persistence of these admissible properties. Leveraging the weakly discontinuous Galerkin method, we subsequently prove the existence of a unique weakly continuous Galerkin solution to the system. Notably, the proof relies exclusively on elementary tools, avoiding advanced concepts from modern analysis. Furthermore, a variant of the argument yields an alternative proof of the local existence theorem originally established by P.-L. Lions and E. Papanicolaou. The research also addresses various related kinetic models. For the Vlasov-Poisson system in a container, we demonstrate that the data are admissible provided the initial energy remains below a specific threshold. Additionally, we show that if data are admissible and possess sufficient regularity, a unique regular solution exists locally in time. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of an open problem. These findings represent a significant advancement in the mathematical theory of Vlasov equations. The work is dedicated to the memory of P.-L. Lions. Ultrasonic vibrations can substantially alter the rheological and flow behaviors of colloidal gels. This study examines the rheo-acoustic characteristics of a model colloid, consisting of 1.5 wt% polystyrene spheres in an aqueous 10 mM NaCl solution, subjected to continuous-wave ultrasound at 30 kHz and 100 mW. We demonstrate that the yield stress of this colloid can be reduced by up to three orders of magnitude through ultrasound exposure. Furthermore, we investigate the rheological and flow properties of the ultrasound-softened gel, revealing that it exhibits shear-thinning, viscoelastic, and Bingham fluid characteristics. Additionally, the gel displays a critical shear stress that scales with the square root of the shear rate, indicative of a yield-stress fluid. We attribute these findings to the real-time, continuous disruption of the gel network by ultrasonic waves. Finally, we explore the potential applications of rheo-acoustic gels, which offer tunable mechanical and flow properties. These materials may find utility in various fields, including drug delivery, tissue engineering, and the development of new sensors and actuators. To facilitate these applications, we propose a theoretical framework for characterizing the rheo-acoustic properties of such gels. This work paves the way for further investigations into the fundamental mechanisms governing gel response to acoustic fields and their resulting applications. Additionally, we outline the necessary equipment and procedures for conducting rheo-acoustic experiments. Our research holds significant implications for the design and manipulation of colloidal gels in diverse settings, such as microfluidics, controlled drug release, and drug delivery systems. We anticipate that these findings will inspire additional research into the acoustic properties of colloidal gels and their applications. We have also provided open-source code to assist other researchers in replicating these experiments. Classifying scientific documents is essential for large-scale document retrieval. However, simply relying on textual content often yields inaccurate results because research papers contain substantial non-textual mathematical figures. This study examines the internal structures of documents within a scientific domain to more accurately represent their identity. We hypothesize that mathematical entities serve as strong indicators for categorizing documents in scientific fields. Consequently, we introduce a method that leverages the distribution of these mathematical entities to facilitate document categorization. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms a baseline that considers only textual content. Finally, we apply this classification model to extract the implicit association between mathematical entities and document categories, thereby contributing to the understanding of authoring activities in scientific documents. The dataset used in this research is accessible at https://github.com/taekyungkim/math-paper-classification. The source code can be found at https://github.com/taekyungkim/math-paper-classification. We introduce a new framework for the stable marriage problem that models the gradual evolution of relationships through three phases: an initial engagement phase where one party initiates contact, a subsequent pairing phase where a marriage is formed, and a final separation phase where unmatched individuals leave the system. To analyze this, we define a new stable marriage variant called "Stable Engagement," which determines the likelihood of transitions from engagement to pairing. In this game, an agent's utility is defined as the probability of remaining paired until the end of the process, minus the cost of the match if engaged. We demonstrate that this game always possesses at least one stable engagement outcome and that all such outcomes can be generated by adding negative edges to the original preference lists. Furthermore, we examine the algorithmic complexity of identifying an engagement phase where only a specific subset of possible proposals are made. We show that if the resulting pairing phase is constrained to a fixed set of preferences, this problem is generally NP-hard. However, for the standard stable marriage scenario, we prove that a linear-time algorithm exists to find an engagement phase limiting each suitor to exactly one proposal. Finally, we explore the case where preference lists are unknown, showing that an agent can determine an optimal time to make a proposal to maximize their final utility. These findings are supported by experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm significantly reduces engagement and marriage costs while increasing the proportion of agents who remain paired at the conclusion of the process. This suggests that encouraging only a single proposal per individual is a more effective strategy for long-term stability than restricting the number of allowed engagements. These insights are particularly relevant to modern dating applications, where users typically engage with only a single potential partner at any given moment. We believe that cost-aware matching could substantially enhance the user experience on such platforms. To facilitate this, we have developed a tool for analyzing cost-aware matching in stable marriage problems, available at https://github.com/ashwinb22/engagematch. This tool includes pre-processed datasets from both synthetic sources and real-world applications. We selected a sample of 10,000 users from this dataset to demonstrate the analysis. The code is publicly accessible, and we encourage researchers to utilize it to analyze other real-world datasets. LiDAR, featuring high precision and robustness in adverse weather, effectively complements the rich semantic details provided by cameras. This paper presents BEVFusion, a novel and straightforward framework for LiDAR-camera fusion that operates within the common bird's-eye view (BEV) representation. The method begins by projecting camera 2D features into BEV space using a 3D anchor-based technique to fuse features with LiDAR-based BEV features. To enhance the robustness of camera features, we introduce a frequency filter that removes high-frequency noise and an uncertainty-aware alignment mechanism that mitigates errors from misalignment. Additionally, we propose a depth-aware camera fusion training strategy, which leverages camera depth estimation to improve the model's generalization in unseen scenarios. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that BEVFusion significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art framework CenterPoint3D by 2.1 AP in 2D detection and matches CenterPoint3D's mean average precision (MAP) score of 61.0. Furthermore, BEVFusion surpasses CenterPoint3D's BEVDepth variant, which also utilizes camera depth features, by 0.6 AP in 2D detection and 1.8 AP in 3D detection. In this study, we investigate the dissipation-quantifying property of turbulence in incompressible fluids, which is captured by the divergence of Davenport's vorticity flux. We demonstrate that the 4/5 law of Kolmogorov turbulence is expressed through the mean value of the spectral energy flux, whereas the energy flux and the divergence of the vorticity flux represent fluctuating and integral components of the 4/5 law, respectively. Furthermore, we establish that the velocity divergence of the vorticity flux is proportional to the Laplacian of the Laplacian of the kinetic energy. This proportionality factor, denoted as $\alpha$, is found to be approximately 0.1, with its fluctuating component exhibiting a significantly greater influence on turbulence than the integral component. Additionally, we examine the analogy between Davenport's vorticity flux and the heat flux in heat conduction. Finally, our analysis indicates that the thermal disturbance component of Davenport's vorticity flux exerts a more significant effect on turbulence than the integral component. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of the dissipation-quantifying property of turbulence. By integrating the fluctuating and integral components of the energy flux and vorticity flux, we derive a new definition of turbulence disturbance. This new definition expresses the dissipation-quantifying property of turbulence as the sum of the kinetic energy dissipation rate and the thermal energy dissipation rate. Consequently, we propose that the disturbance field of a fluid is defined as a vector field comprising the thermal disturbance and the Davenport vorticity flux. We conclude that the disturbance range of turbulence extends beyond the dissipation range, thereby expanding the definition of the turbulence boundary. Finally, we demonstrate that the disturbance range of turbulence is not contingent upon the Reynolds number. The implications of these findings are particularly significant for the study of the transition from laminar to turbulent flow. Specifically, our results suggest that the disturbance range of turbulence may exist within the flow field even under low Reynolds number conditions. This could explain the occurrence of laminar separation bubbles and the mechanisms behind the transition from laminar to turbulent flow. Moreover, the existence of the disturbance range of turbulence offers a potential explanation for the phenomenon of flow re-laminarization. The proposed definition of the turbulence boundary also provides a framework for understanding the existence of the wake region behind a body and the development of the mixing layer. This study presents a numerical analysis of laser-induced thermal profiles within liquids, designed to explain the origin of complex diffraction patterns. It is observed that liquid molecules, driven by rapid thermalization, function effectively as a continuous medium. By resolving the heat diffusion equation, we demonstrate that the thermal profile evolves dynamically in response to laser-induced heating and molecular thermal relaxation. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm that the resulting thermal profile can be approximated using a closed-form analytical expression, offering a more efficient alternative to solving the heat diffusion equation. Finally, numerical calculations validate the multislit diffraction model proposed by Liu et al. (Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 173601, 2018) for describing the complex diffraction patterns of liquid molecules. The findings of this work are anticipated to aid experimentalists in interpreting their data and facilitate physicists in gaining a deeper understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms. Additionally, the study introduces a novel, straightforward, and intuitive method for numerically solving the heat diffusion equation, which is expected to be widely applicable. The findings are expected to be of interest to physicists and mathematicians. The manuscript includes detailed numerical data, computational methods, and code. Designers frequently utilize digital tools to exchange messages and images, generating complex streams of multimodal design dialogues. Due to the intricate nature of these dialogues, automated mining for redesign suggestions remains a significant challenge. This study investigates the robustness of natural language mining techniques against variations in language style and content within a specific multimodal design dialogue context. The analysis identifies four primary techniques: machine learning-based approaches, few-shot learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and prompt engineering applied to large language models. Results indicate that prompt engineering and retrieval-augmented generation are the most robust methods, while few-shot learning yields the poorest performance. The paper concludes by offering a novel perspective on the role of prompts in this domain and suggests potential future research directions. Designers can leverage these design dialogues to automatically extract redesign suggestions, potentially improving efficiency in design processes. However, the identified robustness issues must be resolved to ensure the reliability of automated mining across diverse dialogue styles and contents. For over a decade, research has focused on processing and analyzing high-speed data streams, yet most systems fail to effectively handle data histories. These histories offer crucial analytics capabilities that streams alone cannot provide, including context for individual events, support for ad-hoc analysis, and access to historical data through features like time travel. This paper introduces H-STREAM, a new architecture designed to bridge the gap between streaming processing and data history management. The proposed solution integrates three key components: (1) a new stream processing model based on data versioning, (2) a streamlined implementation of a streaming execution engine, and (3) specialized analytics pipelines for querying and analyzing data streams. We evaluated this model and its implementations using various methods to ensure compatibility with existing streaming frameworks. Our results demonstrate that H-STREAM enables the construction of novel, efficient solutions for data stream analytics and analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate how this model facilitates new query approaches and implements data versioning through data deduplication. Ultimately, our model and system design provide a foundation for delivering innovative data stream analytics and analysis services. We present a calculation of the cross section for light Higgs boson production via the primary loop-level process $pp\to h+ b\bar b\bar{\ell}\ell$ in $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV proton-proton collisions. This mechanism involves a five-parton final state where two bottom quarks, two charged leptons, and one neutrino pair are generated simultaneously through a diagram containing a full top quark loop. We utilize the one-loop diagrammatic expansion tool `diagrammatic expansion` to compute the primary diagram and one-subleading top quark loop diagrams within the mass-insertion approximation. Furthermore, we incorporate QCD corrections via the two-loop mass-insertion approximation. Our approach allows for arbitrary transverse momenta of the bottom quarks and charged leptons, as well as arbitrary transverse momenta of the top quark loop momentum. To enhance computational efficiency, we introduce the `nonresonant graph` class, which represents the top quark loop as a single vertex. This framework enables the direct application of Monte Carlo techniques to calculate the cross section. We provide a detailed description of our methodology and compare our results with other methods in the literature. Finally, we discuss the utility of our approach for studying the top quark's role as a bridge between Yukawa and gauge couplings. Our findings indicate that this class of diagrams is significant in the low transverse momentum region of the top quark loop momentum. Additionally, we observe that the mass-insertion approximation accurately describes the primary diagram, with corrections of approximately 10% at 13 TeV. Knowledge Base Machine Translation (KBMT) involves converting a knowledge base from one ontology to another using a mapping knowledge base, ensuring that instances and triples in the target ontology align with a specified language. Recent neural approaches have demonstrated that neural machine translation (NMT) models can achieve this by directly translating individual sentence-like knowledge base entries. However, existing state-of-the-art methods often suffer from redundant duplicate mechanisms that fail to filter out duplicate information from the target knowledge base. This paper introduces a novel duplicate filtering mechanism designed to eliminate such redundancy. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art performance, successfully reducing knowledge base size by a factor of 2.33 while maintaining high query answering performance (92.35%). Furthermore, we demonstrate the approach's effectiveness on real-world data through a case study. Given that neural duplicate mechanisms are a significant source of NMT inference costs, our work holds substantial potential for improving the efficiency of future SPARQL-based KBMT systems. We introduce a straightforward approach to assess scholarly contributions without relying on traditional citation metrics. This method utilizes the venue at which a paper is published and can be expanded to incorporate venue-specific publication trends. By leveraging vast datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this methodology. Our analysis reveals that venue-based evaluation is a more reliable predictor of future impact than citations alone. Furthermore, an optimal prediction model combines paper quality (inferred from historical citations) with venue selectivity. Additionally, we find that this approach is less susceptible to well-known citation biases, such as the field effect and the time lag effect. Finally, we highlight the utility of venue-based assessment for detecting misconduct, including citation manipulation and potential bias against women in STEM fields. These findings suggest that adopting venue-based metrics could significantly mitigate various forms of citation bias. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexandervarg/venueinsights. Given the accessibility of venue data, we anticipate that this analysis will be replicable across different disciplines. We believe that venue-based metrics will serve as a valuable alternative to citation-based ones, fostering a more sustainable scholarly ecosystem. This study examines the validation of neural networks employed in control systems. We first outline the two primary approaches: absolute validation, which establishes a guaranteed performance bound independent of the specific neural network implementation, and relative validation, which determines a performance bound based on the characteristics of the implementation. Subsequently, we detail the resources necessary for each approach and analyze the properties of neural network validation for both. Finally, we connect these control-focused validation methods to their counterparts in machine learning. Regarding absolute validation, we concentrate on the lattice structure of the neural network parameter space; this allows us to define the essential information required for validation and to bound the approximation errors of the neural network functions. The required parameter for this analysis is a measure of the variation within the function class, which can be computed via volume-based and function-based metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to extend absolute validation from static to dynamic scenarios. In the case of relative validation, we focus on standard deep learning techniques, including cross-validation and generalization error estimation. We conclude by highlighting the challenges and open questions associated with validating neural networks in control applications. Specifically, we address the need for a unified framework that harmonizes absolute and relative validation methods and examines the trade-off between computational cost and accuracy in validation procedures. Overall, this survey aims to offer a comprehensive reference for researchers entering the field of neural network validation for control. By bridging machine learning and control theory, we identify significant opportunities for future advancements in both domains. Additionally, the insights gained may assist practitioners in making more informed decisions when implementing neural networks for control purposes. Given that this field is in its nascent stage, we anticipate it will evolve into a substantial and vibrant research area in the coming years. Object detection and segmentation are critical yet challenging tasks in computer vision, where identifying all instances of a target class within an image constitutes the goal. Current leading methods rely on a greedy approach: individual predictions are made for image regions, and a metric like Intersection over Union (IoU) determines if regions overlap; if they do, they are grouped together. However, this process is non-deterministic and lacks a clear categorical hierarchy. To address these limitations, we propose a hierarchical grouping framework that simultaneously recovers a categorical hierarchy and optimizes grouping based on predicted scores and IoU. We also present a novel loss function that encourages the simultaneous optimization of detection performance and hierarchical recovery. Experimental results demonstrate that this end-to-end framework effectively reconstructs a categorical hierarchy, outperforms existing methods, and achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks. Furthermore, we validate the framework's efficacy on tasks beyond standard detection and segmentation, specifically addressing hierarchical classification and zero-shot learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb22/FunHGr. Our results indicate that the hierarchical grouping framework is versatile and can recover categorical hierarchies across various domains. Additionally, we explore applications in hierarchical object detection and image classification, showing that our approach can recover unknown hierarchies and outperform current state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in few-shot learning, where it outperforms existing few-shot hierarchical classifiers. Overall, our work shows that the proposed hierarchical grouping framework is versatile and capable of recovering categorical hierarchies in diverse scenarios. By viewing these problems through a unified lens, we show that our framework can recover categorical hierarchies and outperform current state-of-the-art solutions. Streaming tensor ring networks (STRN) are established deep learning models designed for image restoration, utilizing a U-Net-like architecture to process streaming pixel-based tensors. However, traditional STRN models are restricted to static images and cannot handle streaming video restoration effectively. This paper introduces a patch monitoring-based streaming tensor ring model to address this limitation. By incorporating a saliency-guided patch-based saliency monitoring network, the proposed method selects high-quality patches while discarding low-quality ones. This mechanism optimizes the global STRN model by reducing computational costs and enhancing restoration performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. Furthermore, comparisons with various patch-based deep learning networks confirm that the proposed approach achieves superior performance at lower computational costs. This paper establishes that, for every finite traditional complex reflection group, the Nichols algebras of certain rank 2 types are finite-dimensional, with the exception of 14 specific cases. These exceptions correspond precisely to the list of 14 non-real finite traditional complex reflection groups. Additionally, the finite-dimensional Nichols algebras associated with the remaining rank 2 types are explicitly described. Notably, the algebra linked to a finite traditional group of rank 2 is finite-dimensional if and only if the group itself is real. This result provides an alternative proof of a theorem by Shepler and Zhang. Furthermore, the finite dimensionality of Nichols algebras for all rank 2 diagonal types was previously demonstrated by He, Zhang, and Li. Direct numerical simulations of three-dimensional inviscid turbulence under a Coriolis force, subjected to random forcing and large-scale damping, reveal a $-5/3$ energy spectrum in the inertial-wave range. This range extends up to a critical wavenumber $k_c$, beyond which gravity waves emerge. The magnitude of $k_c$ is governed by the ratio of the forcing wavenumber to the damping wavenumber; when this ratio is sufficiently high, the $-5/3$ spectrum persists across the gravity-wave regime. Furthermore, within the gravity-wave region, an energy cascade proceeds via a Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum characterized by a $-7/3$ spectral slope. These findings align with the weak turbulence theory proposed by Nazarenko (2003, *Phys. Rep.* 400, 95-188) for weakly nonlinear inertial waves, thereby offering experimental confirmation of the theory. Additionally, these results validate the efficacy of the wave-turbulence framework in describing energy transfer mechanisms in rotating systems. Finally, the study confirms the existence of an inverse energy cascade, consistent with the inverse energy transfer predicted by Nazarenko (2003) and Bobylev and Nazarenko (2007, *J. Math. Phys.* 48, 063503). This inverse cascade is observed as an energy flux directed toward lower wavenumbers within the inertial-wave regime. We show that the collection of isomorphism types of graphs $H$ that standardize $G$ maximally is non-empty and finite. We also relate this to the concept of a maximum weight autonomous set, which is a subset of vertices of a graph that induces a maximum-weight subgraph under any vertex labeling. This study reports the first low-frequency observations of the binary system CR Draconis, a young, active star exhibiting frequent radio bursts. We utilized the LOFAR Low Frequency Array and the Green Bank Telescope (GBT) to monitor the system over a 10-year period. Our results indicate that the radio bursts in CR Draconis are non-thermal, polarized, and likely generated by an electron-cyclotron maser mechanism. The observed radio flux correlates with the optical brightness of the star, and the bursts occur with a periodicity of approximately 1.7 days, matching the system's known orbital period. These findings suggest that the bursts originate from interactions between the two stars. Furthermore, we demonstrate that low-frequency monitoring of young stellar objects can detect radio activity at much lower flux levels than previously thought possible. This capability allows for the identification of a population of quiescent systems that remain undetected at higher frequencies. Consequently, such monitoring offers a means to study the long-term activity of young stars and the evolution of their magnetic fields. Our data imply that a significant number of young stellar objects may engage in a low-frequency surveillance campaign. Additionally, we show that LOFAR can detect electron-cyclotron maser radiation from CR Draconis at flux densities roughly 100 times below the sensitivity limit of previous radio studies. This underscores the critical need for future low-frequency observations of young stellar objects. To achieve this, we propose establishing a dedicated low-frequency surveillance facility for active stars, such as the proposed Low-Frequency Survey of Active Young Stars (LOSA-Y). This initiative would facilitate a comprehensive investigation of the low-frequency radio emission from young stellar objects. A key objective of LOSA-Y is to explore the low-frequency emission characteristics of quiescent systems, thereby elucidating the nature of their magnetic fields. The Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR) network addresses a critical yet underexplored challenge in neural radiance field rendering: virtual avatar rendering with a novel camera using an articulated model trained from a single-image multi-viewpose sequence. Unlike standard neural rendering, this process requires a trained model to be retrained for every new camera position, a step that is computationally expensive and often unnecessary since the original geometry is already visible. ANR efficiently resolves this by integrating model articulation into neural rendering, enabling the use of a single-image model across multiple camera views. The method consists of two core components: (1) a neural radiance field conditioned by skeleton joints to generate novel camera views for a specific pose, and (2) an image warping strategy that aggregates warped images from various poses to produce a single-view synthesis for a new camera position under articulation. Additionally, the approach incorporates a novel single-shot skeleton tracking technique to enhance rendering performance. As a neural radiance field method, ANR avoids the need for dense 3D surface sampling, thereby reducing memory requirements and accelerating rendering. Furthermore, the framework is flexible enough to be adapted for other neural rendering tasks involving articulated objects. Experimental results demonstrate that ANR accelerates rendering by approximately 100 times compared to traditional neural rendering methods while maintaining comparable image quality. Deep learning models are increasingly being employed to automatically alter images with high fidelity, yet their internal decision-making processes remain opaque. This study investigates how varying levels of opacity in image alterations affect both human and machine perception and acceptance. In a controlled experiment, we manipulated the visibility of deep learning-generated object insertions and deletions by adjusting contrast and local motion blur. Our findings indicate that while machines prioritize semantic correctness, humans are more swayed by visual realism. Specifically, human acceptance of altered images is highly dependent on the visibility of the modification, with human performance reaching 80% accuracy at the opacity settings where machines perform at chance level. These results underscore the necessity for developing automated opacity controls to enhance the usability of deep learning image editors for human users. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective method for adapting language models to zero-shot learning tasks. We treat dataset collection as a meta-learning process, utilizing it to implicitly adjust the pre-trained model. Furthermore, we explore the use of cue collections to directly meta-tune the pre-trained model. Evaluations across standard image classification datasets show that our approach significantly enhances the performance of GPT-2 and BERT-base. Specifically, our dataset collection and cue collection techniques enable GPT-2 to achieve zero-shot accuracy on Caltech-101 and Stanford400 that matches or exceeds that of ViT and other vision-based methods. Additionally, our GPT-2 results surpass current zero-shot state-of-the-art methods on Sticker300 and ImageNet100, while our BERT results beat state-of-the-art on CIFAR100. Finally, we demonstrate that our cues and fine-tuning procedures are domain-invariant, allowing them to be directly applied to other domains. The code is available at https://github.com/1614Zeyi/LLM4ZS.

This study examines a scenario where the $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Standard Model (NMSSM) undergoes a metastable phase transition into a new phase characterized by non-zero vacuum expectation values for two Higgs doublets and one singlet. The analysis evaluates the consistency of this scenario with current Lattice QCD constraints on the phase transition, specifically the ratio of the critical temperature to the present-day cosmic background temperature. Furthermore, it investigates the NMSSM implications for LHC searches regarding both the Higgs boson and dark matter candidates, while also exploring the potential for detecting gravitational waves generated by this transition. Finally, the work examines the probability of observing these gravitational waves through both space-based and ground-based detectors. Finally, it is noted that within this specific scenario, the NMSSM Higgs sector is capable of inducing a strong phase transition. Consequently, this research represents a significant contribution to the broader effort of incorporating a strong first-order phase transition into cosmological models, a feature considered essential for explaining the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe. This is achieved through the generation of baryon number violation, CP violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium during the transition, which can be rigorously calculated within the NMSSM framework. The resulting Higgs and dark matter phenomenology is examined in a manner analogous to our previous studies. In this context, the NMSSM dark matter candidate is a real, odd-parity state that remains stable due to a discrete $Z_2$ symmetry arising from the combined effects of space-time and internal symmetries. The study concludes with a discussion of the NMSSM Higgs and dark matter phenomenology, which is expected to differ significantly from that of the standard $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM. We introduce a novel diagnostic method designed to validate the reliability of very high-redshift (z > 10) galaxy candidates from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). This approach is essential for the upcoming submillimeter and infrared era, as it will enable the discovery of increasingly distant galaxies. We demonstrate the technique's efficacy by analyzing a z = 10.6 candidate recently identified in the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's "Cosmic Evolution" program and detected by JWST in the "Deep Field" survey. JWST observations reveal that the source's emission is primarily driven by star formation, with negligible dust contribution. Leveraging these findings, we developed a new statistical tool to verify the source's robustness against the cosmic microwave background (CMB) dipole. This method involves dividing the sky into equal-area cells and applying a "Sudoku" test to identify statistically significant fluctuations in the number of galaxies per cell. Our results indicate that the source's redshift is robust, with a less than 1% probability of a spatial shift caused by the dipole. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this diagnostic method is broadly applicable to any high-redshift candidate, regardless of the specific data used. This finding is particularly significant for JWST, which is currently unable to measure redshifts for galaxies at z > 10 due to the faintness of Lyman-$\alpha$ emission. Consequently, we conclude that the source is robust, possessing a redshift of z = 10.60$^{+0.05}_{-0.10}$ and a luminosity of $L_{\rm IR}$ = 1.1$^{+0.2}_{-0.1}$\times 10$^{12}$ L$_{\odot}$. This object represents the most luminous star-forming galaxy known at z > 10. Finally, we discuss the implications of this discovery for the (sub)millimeter and infrared era, emphasizing the critical role of a diagnostic like Sudoku in validating high-redshift candidates. This tool will be vital for the upcoming era of (sub)millimeter and JWST surveys, which will facilitate the discovery of galaxies at even greater distances. The data and analysis code required to apply the Sudoku test are publicly available at https://github.com/astro-berkeley/SudokuTest. The source is accessible at https://doi.org

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice to explore the dynamics of symmetry-disrupted and liquid phases. Utilizing the coordinate transformation technique, we reduce the computational complexity of large spin clusters within finite-temperature Monte Carlo simulations. Our results indicate that finite-size scaling analysis yields thermodynamic exponents consistent with those of the $K$osterlitz-Thouless transition. Furthermore, we examine the specific heat and magnetic susceptibility to investigate potential signatures of liquid phases at zero magnetic field and zero external anisotropy. We find that heat capacity data can be interpreted as evidence for a liquid phase, characterized by a maximum heat capacity that varies with cluster size. Additionally, we demonstrate that the magnetic susceptibility displays signatures of a spin-liquid phase under weak external magnetic fields. Finally, we discuss the relevance of our findings to experimental data regarding the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet $\mathrm{Cu}_3(\mathrm{V}^{5+})_2\mathrm{P}_2\mathrm{O}_{10}$. These outcomes suggest that symmetry-breaking and spin-liquid phases are thermodynamically stable in this material. We conclude that finite-size scaling analysis is a viable method for detecting phase transitions in both heat capacity and magnetic susceptibility. The proposed approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of frustrated magnetic systems. The accompanying computer code is available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkumar1984/coord-transf}. This study introduces a kinetic model utilizing a hard sphere-like potential energy field and a speed-dependent collision frequency to capture quantum mechanical effects in rarefied gas flows. The collision frequency is derived from the Born approximation, which provides an analytical solution for the intermolecular potential. This formulation offers a straightforward method to approximate interaction dynamics between gas molecules and solid walls, as well as the frequency of molecular collisions. The model's validity is confirmed by comparing its predictions against exact solutions from the Boltzmann equation across various dimensionless Knudsen numbers. Furthermore, numerical simulations demonstrate that the model can represent interaction phenomena in supersonic rarefied gas flows. These results indicate that the proposed kinetic model is effective for capturing interactions within both low and high Knudsen number regimes. Finally, the model's applicability to other areas of physical chemistry is also explored. This study presents an approach to training semantic analyzers that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by leveraging minimal data through a novel paradigm. We introduce the Familiarized Semantic Analyzer (FSA), which is trained exclusively on a single sample of ground truth labels. By employing unsupervised pre-training on extensive corpora, we simulate the capabilities of multi-label semantic analysis using only one labeled instance. This technique is particularly valuable for applications where annotating data is costly or difficult, such as in medical domains. Our findings demonstrate that the FSA achieves performance comparable to supervised models in tasks like disease mention normalization and semantic role labeling. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/FSA.

The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is designed to investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei, as well as the interactions between them. The detector slated for the EIC will feature an inner tracking system utilizing silicon sensors with a pixel size of 50x50 $\mu$m$^2$, positioned at a radius of 3.5 cm. This study examines the EIC's radiation environment and the methodology for designing silicon sensors capable of withstanding those conditions. We present a sensor configuration comprising a 3.5 cm thick bulk sensor paired with a 700 nm thin sensor, which has been successfully tested up to a total ionizing dose of 100 krad and an average surface fluence of 1x10$^{15}$ n$_{eq}$/cm$^2$. Additionally, we explore the potential of implementing a two-sided readout architecture for the EIC inner tracker. Finally, the efficacy of various sensor materials and geometries will be assessed through a multi-physics simulation framework. This approach integrates charge transport, mechanical stress, and heat transfer analyses to evaluate silicon sensor performance under extreme operational stresses. Results will be displayed.
