We introduce Highdicom, a Python framework designed for the creation and exchange of image-based remarks and machine learning (ML) inferences using the DICOM SR Document standard. This tool facilitates the development of robust diagnostic assistance systems for histopathology and radiology, which depend on pixel-level evaluations. Our framework offers a high-level, user-friendly, and extensible API for rapid prototyping and deployment, enabling the generation of both standalone DICOM documents and web-based viewers. Additionally, we provide a pre-built pipeline for training neural networks and annotating datasets that generates pixel-level Highdicom instances compatible with our framework. These documents can be utilized as hard constraints during the annotation process and integrated into existing ML pipelines. Furthermore, we have developed a web viewer for inspecting and interacting with DICOM SR documents, which is pre-integrated into the framework and accessible via a public URL. This viewer supports querying and visualization via the DICOMweb standard and includes features for displaying pixel-level annotations alongside image slices. By utilizing Highdicom, researchers and clinicians can streamline the development and deployment of diagnostic assistance tools, while ensuring that diagnostic information remains accessible and interpretable for clinical review. This service is accessible via a REST API and can be queried using standard REST calls or the provided Python library. This paper investigates the Noether surface term arising from the Einstein-Hilbert action, specifically within an asymptotic framework. By employing the Dirac method and adhering to the Brown-Zakharov formalism, we calculate the surface and bulk components of the Noether current using an arbitrary symmetry. We demonstrate that the surface term is exclusively determined by the symmetry and the spacetime metric, whereas the bulk term depends on the matter fields. Furthermore, we derive the most general form of the surface term, which comprises three distinct contributions: a superpotential linked to the spin connection, a term involving the Riemann tensor, and a term associated with the trace of the extrinsic curvature. In the context of two-dimensional gravity, we apply this generic formula to stationary black holes, thereby recovering the corresponding charge. Additionally, we analyze the surface term's dependence on gravity and time reparametrization disorders. When both disorders are present, the surface term diverges, whereas it remains finite if only the time reparametrization disorder is considered. Finally, we compute the Virasoro algebra for asymptotically flat two-dimensional black holes. For asymptotically AdS$_2$ black holes, the algebra is governed by the bulk term, while the surface term vanishes. The surface term in AdS$_2$ can be derived from the holographic stress tensor, which is linked to the trace anomaly. Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective method for DNA pattern analysis, yet the selection of suitable architectures remains a critical challenge. This study addresses that gap by introducing a novel, unified representation learning framework that integrates various DNA patterns. Within this approach, the embedding layer is eliminated, allowing the model to automatically learn and represent DNA patterns without manual feature engineering. We demonstrate that this unified framework unifies existing methods and establish that the proposed learning mechanism is highly effective across diverse applications. Furthermore, the results indicate that this learning strategy is robust for representing DNA patterns in scenarios lacking sufficient training data. The validity of this methodology is confirmed through an extensive evaluation across a wide spectrum of DNA pattern analysis applications. This method is particularly advantageous when high-quality labeled data is scarce, as it mitigates the need for manual feature engineering. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/taehyuklee/Unattended-DNA-Repr-Learning. Additionally, the application code required to replicate our results is available at https://github.com/taehyuklee/Unsupervised-DNA-App. Finally, we have released a new dataset for DNA pattern analysis, accessible at https://github.com/taehyuklee/DNA-Pattern-Analysis-Data. This comprehensive resource includes diverse DNA patterns alongside corresponding labels and performance metrics. We anticipate that this unified framework will facilitate the development of novel and innovative DNA pattern analysis techniques. Furthermore, the dataset will enable researchers to easily compare their results against our methods and contribute to the advancement of DNA pattern analysis in the field. The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in V$_2$O$_3$ has been extensively researched, yet the specific roles of surface and termination remain unclear. This study examines the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$ films grown on Al$_2$O$_3$(0001) substrates using first-principles calculations. Results indicate that while bulk V$_2$O$_3$ exhibits a first-order MIT, the surface layer undergoes a second-order transition driven by the filling of a surface state. In contrast, the bulk-like interior lacks a surface state and experiences a first-order MIT. The surface termination critically influences this MIT: a bulk-like termination results in a metallic ground state, whereas a vanadium-terminated layer acts as an insulator. Furthermore, surface states are highly sensitive to the relative rotation between the V$_2$O$_3$ film and the Al$_2$O$_3$ substrate. These findings offer new perspectives on the MIT in surface films and suggest that the complex surface and bulk behaviors observed in V$_2$O$_3$ may be applicable to other transition metal oxides. Additionally, the presence of surface states could provide a pathway for controlling the MIT in surface layers through electrostatic gating. Finally, the study explores the potential for achieving a room-temperature ground state in monolayer V$_2$O$_3$ through appropriate lattice matching with the substrate. These insights could be valuable for the development of vanadium-based spintronic and electronic devices. We demonstrate that, for a specific subset of these representations, the authorization of a designated function set is equivalent to the existence of corresponding dualized 1-forms. The study also explores various applications, including dualization procedures, the identification of invariant surfaces, and the analysis of damping and driving mechanisms. Notably, for certain representation spaces, the classification of all authorized variable sets is completed, and for others, a comprehensive classification framework is introduced. These results are particularly significant for systems where all known Clebsch representations have already been authorized. We introduce a catalog containing 108 new planets and 10 non-detections, identified through an automated systematic search of KMTNet light curves. This analysis focuses on 2018 sub-prime field planets exhibiting planetary irregularity signals. The catalog includes 19 new planets with period ratios less than 1.1, which are likely to be captured by the upcoming SKMTNet. Additionally, we report 10 non-detections with similar period ratios; their upper limits are comparable to those of the corresponding planet candidates, suggesting they may have been missed by the SKMTNet survey. We also present 42 new planets with period ratios between 1.1 and 1.2, and 26 non-detections with comparable period ratios. Furthermore, we identified 25 new planets with period ratios greater than 1.2, along with 14 non-detections. The 2018 sub-prime field shows a notable gap in the period ratio distribution between 1.1 and 1.2, which we attribute to the fact that most planets with period ratios greater than 1.2 possess periods exceeding 100 days. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for planet formation and dynamical evolution theories. This study represents the first systematic effort to search for and confirm irregular planets using the KMTNet survey. The cataloged planets and non-detections are available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1000. The code used for the systematic search will be released on GitHub. This paper is the sixth in a series; the others can be found at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1001, https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1002, https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1003, https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1004, and https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1005. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the data and methods, Section 3 describes the results, Section 4 presents the discussion, and Section 5 provides our conclusions. The references are listed in Section 6. This work is based on observations from the Southern Southern Sky

Building upon the previously defined conservation laws for mass, momentum, energy, and entropy, this paper introduces conservation principles regarding contact surfaces and shocks within comoving frames, as well as adiabatic and isentropic evolution in comoving and lab frames during the evolution of matter characterized by perfect conductivity. These principles serve to simplify the compressible Navier-Stokes equations by eliminating viscous and heat flux terms in the comoving frame for such matter. Subsequently, applying conservation principles to shocks yields additional simplified forms of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The study concludes by providing examples of matter satisfying perfect conductivity conditions, specifically ferromagnetic and paramagnetic materials, along with their respective simplified Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, the conservation conditions for comoving and lab frames across comoving and shock surfaces are applied to both the general and simplified compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Finally, the paper examines the compressible Navier-Stokes equations for perfect conductivity matter in the context of two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics. Various conservation conditions for comoving and shock surfaces are derived for the simplified magneto-hydrodynamic equations, and examples of this simplification are presented. Furthermore, the paper explores the conservation of magnetic flux in comoving frames and the conservation of magnetic flux surfaces in both comoving and lab frames, providing several examples of these phenomena. Finally, simplified conservation conditions for shocks are applied to the simplified magneto-hydrodynamic equations. The authors extend their gratitude to the editors for their valuable suggestions and encouragement. Additionally, the authors acknowledge the significant contributions of their families, colleagues, and students, who have been instrumental in advancing the simplification of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. This work is dedicated to them. Finally, the authors express hope that the simplified compressible Navier-Stokes equations will facilitate a deeper understanding of fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics. Keywords: Conservation conditions, conservation surfaces, comoving frame, shock, comoving and shock surfaces, magnetic flux, magnetic flux surfaces, ferromagnetic, paramagnetic, magneto-hydrodynamics.

This study evaluates the performance of various machine learning algorithms in predicting whether a bank loan will default. We processed a bank's numerical personal loan dataset by selecting appropriate features and eliminating irrelevant ones. After dividing the data into training and testing sets, we applied seven machine learning models to the training set and assessed their accuracy using the hold-out test set. Feature importance was assessed using the tree-based model results. The Random Forest algorithm emerged as the most effective model, achieving an 82.5% accuracy rate with Gini impurity as the selection criterion. Furthermore, the 'age' feature demonstrated the highest significance, showing the greatest impact on both the target variable and the overall dataset. These findings can assist the bank in identifying the most influential factors for default risk. Additionally, the success of the Random Forest model underscores its potential for future default risk assessments. This research is expected to aid banks in mitigating losses from failed loans and support borrowers in understanding the key determinants of loan approval. The analysis was conducted using R version 4.1.1.

Dyck paths form a significant and well-studied class of combinatorial objects with numerous equivalents across various fields, such as lattice paths, Young tableaux, and plane partitions. The study of Dyck paths is driven by their intrinsic interest and their extensive applications in diverse areas, including representation theory, algebraic geometry, and graph theory. This paper investigates the chromatic symmetric polynomials of Dyck path posets. Leveraging the strong combinatorial and algebraic frameworks surrounding Dyck paths, we establish new findings and deepen existing understanding. Specifically, we demonstrate that the chromatic symmetric polynomial for a Dyck path poset can be expressed as a product of polynomials related to "affine Coxeter groups," which generalize the symmetric group. Furthermore, we prove that this polynomial is always "positively integer-valued" on certain subsets of an associated lattice, a property that implies log-concavity. Our proof techniques integrate combinatorial and algebraic methods, utilizing concepts from q-rook theory. Additionally, we provide chromatic symmetric polynomials for specific Dyck path posets in terms of their generating functions. Finally, we extend our results to a broader class of posets known as "generalized Dyck path posets." Our methodology involves calculating the chromatic symmetric polynomial for a single instance of such a poset and subsequently deriving a formula based on its generating function. This work was presented at the 2022 Joint Mathematics Meetings in San Diego. For more information, visit: https://galoisgrouptheory.com/Research/CDP/CDP.html. Keywords: posets, chromatic symmetric polynomials, Dyck paths, q-rook theory.

This paper introduces a novel convolutional network architecture designed to handle orientation. We posit that incorporating an orientation convolutional layer enables a single filter to detect multiple orientations, thereby reducing the parameter count compared to maintaining separate filters for each orientation. This approach is realized by defining the orientation convolution operation as the composition of the standard convolution and a Fourier Fourier Inverse (FFI) operation. The proposed method is evaluated on the CIFAR-100 dataset using varying numbers of filters and regularizations. Results indicate that a Fourier operation alone can merge two orientations, while a carefully designed Fourier FFI operation allows for combining three orientations. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that integrating Fourier FFI operations with the convolution operation yields superior performance. Finally, we illustrate that applying Fourier FFI operations in conjunction with strided convolutions can serve as an effective form of spatial downsampling. Our network achieves state-of-the-art performance when utilizing 15 filters to combine two orientations, 10 filters to combine three orientations, or 7 filters to combine four orientations. Additionally, we observe that combining two orientations with spatial downsampling via stride 2 is more efficient than the standard strided convolution approach. Linear intervals and spherical functions serve as the foundation for Poisson summation within the theory of Euclidean lattice packings. This paper extends these concepts to curved linear intervals, deriving series expansions for their Fourier transforms. Leveraging this extension, we construct a relative trace formula within the Euclidean framework and apply Poisson summation. The resulting expression features a spectral side composed of spectral data from $L^2(L)\rtimes L$ that encodes information about the spectrum of the Laplacian on a Drinfeld curve. We demonstrate that this information is sufficient to distinguish adjacent linear intervals from non-linear time curves. The formula offers a new perspective on the geometry of linear intervals and their application in the study of lattice constructions. Furthermore, it provides a fresh approach to the challenge of achieving a complete characterization of curved linear intervals, addressing a key issue in lattice network design. The study of this geometry is grounded in harmonic analysis on locally compact abelian groups. The theory of Fourier transforms on curved linear intervals represents an application of the general theory developed by the second author. The development of the relative trace formula is the primary focus of this work. The relative trace formula is derived from the Laplacian on the Drinfeld universe, which is defined as a quotient of the Drinfeld half-plane by the modular group. This relative trace formula is designed to characterize the geometry of curved linear intervals. The geometry of linear intervals is well understood, whereas the geometry of curved linear intervals remains an open question. This work offers a solution to this problem, as evidenced by the generation of new data regarding linear intervals. Specifically, we examine the case where the linear interval is generated by the set $\{1,2\}$. We show that its boundary consists of a component defined by the spectral function of a Drinfeld universe, whose spectrum can be identified using the relative trace formula. We also present data for the case where the interval is generated by $\{1,3\}$. Finally, we provide numerical evidence supporting the conjecture that the boundary of the $\{1,2\}$ interval is defined by a linear interval generated by $\{1,3\}$. This evidence includes numerical verification of the relative trace formula, the spectral side of which comprises the spectrum of the Drinfeld universe, while the algebraic side involves the geometry of curved linear intervals. Let $G$ be a connected graph where each node $v$ has a specified degree $d_G(v)$. A sequence of nodes $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_t$ is defined as valid if, for every $i$ from 1 to $t$, there exists a neighbor $v_j$ of $v_i$ (with $j \leq i$) such that the degree of $v_j$ is at least $i$. The edge-dyeing problem involves identifying the maximum $t$ for which a valid sequence of $t$ nodes exists, under the constraint that no two edges $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ and $(v_k, v_{k+1})$ share the same color. This constraint implies that for any $i < k < j$, the edge $(v_i, v_j)$ must be colored differently from the edge $(v_k, v_{k+1})$. In this study, we derive a formula for the maximum $t$ when the graph $G$ is nearly regular, meaning every node $v$ satisfies $d_G(v) \in \{d, d+1\}$ for some degree $d$. Furthermore, we present a conjecture applicable to arbitrary graphs. Additionally, we propose an algorithm to determine the colors of edges within a valid sequence that maximizes $t$. Finally, we provide computer-generated examples for nearly regular graphs with degrees $d=2$ and $d=3$. Low-dose Computed Tomography (CT) scans are frequently employed in clinical settings for diagnosing COVID-19, offering a cost-effective alternative to standard-dose scans while significantly reducing radiation exposure. However, analyzing low-dose CT images presents challenges due to artifacts and a reduced signal-to-noise ratio, which can hinder the detection of subtle early-stage lesions. To address these issues, we introduce a two-stage time-distributed capsule network (TD-CN) designed to extract and aggregate high-level features, demonstrating superior performance in classifying both COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 cases. The initial stage utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to process input images, generating feature maps that are subsequently processed by time-distributed capsule networks (TD-CNs). The subsequent stage employs a TD-CNs-based routing mechanism to iteratively refine and consolidate feature representations across multiple iterations, enhancing the model's discriminative capabilities. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art methods in accuracy, achieving 98.1% precision, 98.2% recall, and 98.1% F1-score on a validation dataset. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the TD-CN architecture plays a critical role in boosting classification performance. This paper introduces a mathematical framework for spatial efficiency within low-Earth orbit, designed to facilitate the quantitative evaluation of future orbital traffic management strategies. The model treats orbital slots as a public good, thereby creating potential for negative externalities. We propose a mechanism that leverages the willingness to pay of both current and prospective operators to allocate these slots. This approach addresses the challenge of time-varying demand, which is critical for assessing the efficacy of such allocation methods. Our strategy is demonstrated to be both mechanism-efficient and truthful. Furthermore, we develop a discrete-time economic model to analyze the evolution of demand over time. This model incorporates the concept of orbital slot agnosticism, where the value of a specific slot is independent of the mission's specific requirements. We demonstrate the existence of a unique Nash equilibrium under these conditions and examine the impact of a potential learning curve on demand dynamics. Finally, we present numerical simulations to validate our analytical findings. The results indicate that, in the absence of a traffic management strategy, the number of active missions in low-Earth orbit could rise exponentially, leading to a significant increase in collisions. Conversely, the proposed traffic management strategy effectively mitigates this risk. Additionally, our analysis shows that the learning curve substantially diminishes the likelihood of a growing market for Low-Earth Orbit missions. These insights are anticipated to be valuable for policymakers and stakeholders engaged in LEO satellite constellation development. Finally, we outline potential future research directions, including the extension of the model to accommodate varying levels of mission-specific agnosticism. By integrating the value of an orbital slot with mission-specific needs, our generalized framework could offer a more comprehensive and realistic approach to space traffic management. This could involve developing a mechanism that allows such missions to request and acquire a Low-Earth Orbit slot, thereby optimizing space resource allocation. This paper introduces a novel framework for generating coarse quad meshes with regular topology, including holes and boundaries, directly on CAD models. The process begins by constructing an initial coarse quad field on a quadradized CAD model, followed by the construction of a dual graph where vertices represent mesh faces and edges correspond to mesh faces on dual vertices. The user then defines a set of constraints in the form of linear equations, which are solved using Integer Linear Programming to determine an optimal assignment of dual vertices. This selection of dual vertices enables the construction of a regular topology quad field featuring holes and boundaries directly on the CAD geometry, satisfying the user-defined constraints. The resulting coarse quad fields serve as a foundation for the automatic generation of a full regular topology coarse quad grid. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and robustness, and the final section outlines potential applications. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to produce regular topology coarse quads on CAD models that were previously considered unmeshable, while also offering the flexibility to address various topological requirements through user-specified constraints. This text examines the application of the $S$-matrix approach to gravitation, gravity waves, and scattering events within general relativity and quantum gravity frameworks. It begins by deriving the properties of massless spin-2 particles from fundamental axioms, demonstrating that their unique self-interactions necessitate the field equations of general relativity. The discussion then transitions to the quantum regime by exploring how black hole formation and evaporation impose constraints on low-energy quantum gravity $S$-matrices. Furthermore, it explores the implications of unitarity, analyticity, and causality for gravitational wave scattering, with a specific focus on the recent findings of Arkani-Havd et al. Finally, the text outlines the principles of the modern $S$-matrix program, emphasizing its aim to derive spacetime concepts from abstract quantum principles and its potential to uncover the structure of a future theory beyond the Standard Model and general relativity. The text concludes by outlining several upcoming experiments and observational initiatives designed to test the $S$-matrix program's hypotheses. Throughout, no reliance on quantum field theory in curved spacetime is made. Key terms include $S$-matrix, axiomatic quantum field theory, asymptotic symmetry, asymptotic Hilbert space, massless spin-2 particle, black hole, quantum gravity, $S$-matrix program, string theory, experiment, and observation. The intended audience comprises graduate students and researchers in theoretical physics. This work is based on a series of mini-courses delivered in 2019 and 2020. The recommendation system industry faces significant challenges in fostering user trust. While the field of Explainable AI (XAI) has traditionally concentrated on increasing system transparency, this paper shifts the focus to enhancing the fairness and stability of explanations. Specifically, we investigate the stability of XAI within the LIME-RS framework, a recent approach designed to explain recommendation system outputs. Our key contribution involves reformulating the original LIME-RS objective function to optimize for stability rather than explanation accuracy. We evaluate this new formulation using established metrics for instance-based fairness and explanation stability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method generates more stable attributions, thereby improving the stability of explanations. Furthermore, we develop and assess a novel stability-based stability metric, which proves to be more effective than existing alternatives. Finally, we extend the method to explicitly address instance-based fairness concerns, showing that it successfully identifies and mitigates unfairness in the resulting explanations. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/fernandoPereiraXAI/LIME-RS-Stability.

The effectiveness of band alignment engineering in achieving Fermi-level control within quantum-well-based two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) systems is critically dependent on the near-surface band gap engineering of the barrier material. This study investigates Fermi-level anchoring in near-surface quantum wells made of III-V semiconductors by examining their band gaps as a function of composition. Utilizing the next-nearest-neighbor tight-binding model, we analyze how the band gap evolves with quantum confinement in these structures. We identify specific compositions where the Fermi-level control problem is resolved, demonstrating that this optimal composition shifts as quantum confinement increases. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the rate of Fermi-level anchoring and the quantum-confined barrier band gap. Finally, we explore the potential for solving Fermi-level anchoring issues by selecting an appropriate quantum-well material. These findings are anticipated to guide future developments in quantum wells designed to produce high-mobility, low-density 2DEGs. Additionally, the methodology employed to study Fermi-level anchoring can be applied to other quantum-well systems, including those involving quantum dots. The code used for the calculations is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/abhishekdeshmukh123/nntb2DEG}. The discovery of exoplanets has driven significant interest in characterizing their atmospheres and compositions. High-energy radiation from their host stars plays a critical role in this context, influencing atmospheric chemistry and thermal structures. This study examines the correlation between ultraviolet (UV) flux and stellar activity as a function of X-ray activity levels, utilizing data from the AU Microscopii (AU Mic) system. The research analyzes extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and far-ultraviolet (FUV) light curves from the *International Ultraviolet Explorer* (IUE) and *Hubble Space Telescope* (HST), alongside far-ultraviolet (FUV) and X-ray data from the *Swift* mission. By examining the relationship between UV flux and stellar activity across varying X-ray states, the study aims to identify trends that can inform models of stellar flare frequency distributions. The results indicate that, during both eruptions and periods of stellar dormancy, EUV flux shows a strong correlation with FUV flux, which in turn correlates with far-red (FR) flux. Furthermore, the UV flux scales with the fractional X-ray luminosity ($L_X/L_{bol}$) in a manner consistent with observations from other young stars. These findings suggest that FUV flux can serve as a reliable proxy for both EUV and FR fluxes. Additionally, the data reveals that AU Mic exhibits a higher rate of FUV eruptions compared to other young stars, a characteristic that may have significant implications for the atmospheric evolution of its planets. Finally, the study addresses the impact of these UV fluxes on AU Mic b and c, noting that while the FR flux received by AU Mic b is sufficient to sustain a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere, it is likely stripped of its hydrogen envelope by EUV fluxes. In contrast, AU Mic c, located in the habitable zone, may retain a hydrogen envelope, though its atmosphere could be rendered uninhabitable by high UV fluxes. The research concludes by discussing the potential for using FUV observations to assess the habitability of planets orbiting active stars. Overall, this work underscores the necessity of considering stellar activity when interpreting exoplanet atmospheric data. Future observations of AU Mic are recommended to further investigate the effects of stellar activity on its planets and their atmospheres. The data presented in this study is accessible via the Astrophysics Source Code Library (ASCL 1801.001). The associated code can be found at https://doi.org/10.5445/ASCL

Furthermore, we explore the potential for designing such materials and highlight their significant implications for the evolution of particle motion within the interstellar medium. This paper introduces a statistical approach to C-N Neighbor Classification on biased data. C-N classification is a foundational data mining technique that operates on the principle that similar objects share the same class label. However, existing studies indicate that C-N neighbors are most effective for classification when data is balanced, meaning each class has an equal number of objects. In contrast, real-world data is often biased, resulting in unequal class distributions. To address classification on such biased data, this study proposes a statistical method. The core concept involves dividing biased data into multiple balanced sub-datasets, where the class of a new object is determined by a weighted vote from its class labels. We evaluate this method using both synthetic datasets and real-world benchmarks. Results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in classifying objects from minority classes within biased data. Furthermore, we provide an R package to facilitate the application of this statistical approach. The source code and package are accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1985/closest-neighbor. Additionally, synthetic data can be generated via: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1983/synthetic_data_generator. Finally, we offer a step-by-step tutorial for conducting C-N classification on biased data using the provided package, available at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1985/cn_classification. This resource includes various examples and exercises covering different scenarios. Our hope is that this method will assist researchers in addressing the challenge of C-N classification on biased data. We welcome your feedback and suggestions for improvement. Thank you. This study presents findings from the second phase of the Ultra-bright High-redshift Quasars from SkyMapper (UHQS) survey, which leverages the SkyMapper Southern Survey Sky Atlas (S-SkysA) to identify and confirm ultrabright quasars. The primary objective is to detect the luminous end of the bright quasar luminosity function at high redshifts. In this work, we report the confirmation of 11 new UHQS quasars, bringing the total sample to 22. The average redshift for these 22 UHQS quasars is $z=2.2$, with a mean absolute $M_{1450}$ of $-27.2$ mag. We demonstrate that UHQS quasars extend the bright quasar luminosity function to magnitudes as bright as $M_{1450}=-30.5$ mag at $z\sim2$. Furthermore, we show that the UHQS sample follows the same bright quasar quiescent mode luminosity relation as lower luminosity quasars, and that UHQS quasars with $M_{1450}<-27.5$ mag at $z\sim2$ are predominantly hosted in galaxies with stellar masses exceeding $10^{10} M_{\odot}$. Finally, we provide evidence suggesting that the most luminous quasars in the Hubble Deep Field (HDF) and COSMOS fields are also members of the UHQS sample. These results imply that the brightest quasars are detectable via S-SkysA down to an apparent magnitude of $m_{r}\sim12.5$ at $z\sim2$. Consequently, the UHQS sample offers a unique opportunity to investigate the behavior of the luminosity function at the extreme luminous end. We also discuss the potential for detecting the most luminous quasars through deep optical imaging. Ultimately, this sample will facilitate a more precise measurement of the luminosity function's slope at the extreme luminous end and provide a deeper understanding of the physical properties of the most extreme quasars. The UHQS quasars identified here will be valuable for studying the evolution of the bright quasar luminosity function and the physical characteristics of quasars at the extreme luminous end. We investigate charge tunneling mechanisms between a quantum dot and a superconducting reservoir by analyzing the impact of gate capacitances on the gate charging energy. By examining the temperature dependence of tunneling rates and the quantum dot charge distribution, we identify the transition from a coherent to an incoherent regime. Furthermore, the observed charge fluctuations indicate the emergence of Andreev processes within the weak coupling regime. Finally, our findings suggest that maintaining the quantum dot charge in a delocalized state is more effective than the configuration proposed by Li et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 106801 (2019)]. This conclusion is supported by an analytical model that accounts for gate capacitances and the quantum dot's coupling to charge reservoirs. Additionally, we demonstrate that the delocalized state can be achieved at lower temperatures using a shorter superconducting tunnel barrier. These results are expected to facilitate the realization of Andreev bound states in double quantum dot systems. Finally, we outline potential applications of this system for developing charge-to-qubit converters and designing novel charge-to-Andreev conversion devices. This research investigates the conservation law $u_t + v(u)_x = 0$ for a scalar density $u$ within the framework of hyperbolic balance laws. The study examines entropic discontinuities, which are introduced by replacing the flux $v(u)$ with a source term $f(u) = -\bar{v}(u) + \bar{v}(u_-)$, where $\bar{v}(u)$ denotes a convex relaxation of the original (potentially multivalued) flux $v(u)$, and $\bar{v}(u) - \bar{v}(u_-) \geq 0$ holds. These specific entropic discontinuities are characterized by a drop in the convex relaxation across the jump, satisfying the condition $v(u_-) - u_- f'(u_-) \geq v(u_+) - u_+ f'(u_+)$. The primary contribution of this work is a set of three contraction properties for the hyperbolic balance law under consideration. The first property asserts that the convex relaxation of $v(u)$ serves as an upper bound for the entropic hyperbolic balance law. The second property demonstrates that the framework of hyperbolic balance laws is contracted with respect to the $L^1$-Wasserstein distance. The third property establishes that the framework is also contracted under the $L^1$-Wasserstein distance when the convex relaxation is not strictly convex. Collectively, these findings enable the derivation of an error estimate between the solution of the convex relaxation and the solution incorporating the source term. Furthermore, the paper presents an explicit example of a framework of conservation laws that is not contracted in the $L^1$ norm. Finally, all theoretical results are supported by illustrative examples. Notably, the examples for error estimates include cases with non-strictly convex relaxations, whereas the counterexample for the $L^1$ contraction involves a strictly convex relaxation. The methodology for the error estimate relies on the $L^1$ contraction property, while the counterexample utilizes the strict convexity of the relaxation. Additionally, the proofs for the contraction properties of convex relaxations depend on the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions of the original $v(u)$ flux. Finally, the code required to reproduce the examples is available on GitHub. This code also implements the original hyperbolic balance law, which is known to be contracted in the $L^1$ norm. Experimental results demonstrate that DiffDreamer not only matches current state-of-the-art quality but also delivers significant improvements in inference speed. **Objective:** To assess the reliability of ultrasound-based scoliosis measurement when performed by a robot compared to manual scanning conducted by humans.

**Study Design:** A randomized controlled trial.

**Setting:** University Hospital.

**Participants:** The study enrolled 20 healthy volunteers (10 male, 10 female; mean age 26.9 ± 4.6 years) who demonstrated no prior spinal curvature.

**Methods:** Scoliosis curvature was quantified using the Ultrasound Scoliosis Measurement (USM) technique. Each volunteer underwent robotic ultrasound scanning three times, while two sonographers independently performed manual scanning three times on the same participants. The USM method calculates the Cobb angle by analyzing the convexity of the dorsal vertebral profile.

**Results:** The mean Cobb angle derived from robotic scans showed no statistically significant difference from that obtained by the first sonographer (p = 0.12). However, manual scanning by the second sonographer yielded a statistically significant difference compared to the robotic scans (p = 0.001). Bland-Altman analysis revealed a mean bias of 0.1° (95% limits of agreement: -1.5° to 1.7°) between robotic and first sonographer measurements, versus a bias of 1.5° (95% limits of agreement: -4.2° to 7.2°) for the second sonographer.

**Conclusions:** The findings indicate that automated scoliosis curvature measurement via ultrasound is feasible. The study confirms the technical viability of robot-assisted ultrasound scanning for measuring scoliosis curvature. Furthermore, the high agreement between robotic and sonographer measurements suggests that the technique is reproducible. These results support the potential clinical application of ultrasound-assisted robotic systems in scoliosis assessment.

**Keywords:** Scoliosis; Ultrasound; Robotic; Reliability; Reproducibility.

This study introduces a smoothness-based control (SBC) approach for the electric drive of an industrial robot joint, utilizing auxiliary encoders to measure speed. The primary goal is to enhance joint smoothness, thereby improving the robot's end-effector quality and consistency. By integrating a feedforward-based model following controller with SBC, the design ensures high performance while reducing computation time. Model following handles the majority of control demands, allowing the model-based SBC to focus solely on smoothness. This separation enables the SBC to be robust against modeling errors. The feedforward-based SBC is developed, experimentally validated, and demonstrated on a joint equipped with auxiliary encoders. Results from a joint smoothness benchmark show a 20% improvement in smoothness, measured by the minimum jitter acceleration. Furthermore, the proposed SBC is shown to be effective in smoothing the end-effector's motion profile, achieving a 25% reduction in both peak and root mean square (RMS) acceleration. The entire design is implemented in less than 100 CPU cycles, making it suitable for integration into the torque controller without increasing the computational load on the main controller. The complete implementation is provided as open-source. The findings indicate that auxiliary encoders are cost-effective for achieving superior smoothness, and the proposed SBC is a viable solution for next-generation industrial robots. Additionally, the method is robust to parameter variations and does not compromise performance. This study introduces a multiple state examination approach designed for multiple time-to-occurrence data. The method represents time-to-occurrence events as transitions between states within an irreducible, discrete-time Markov chain. It constructs life paths by defining them as state sequences over a lifetime and investigates the joint probability distribution of these sequences. The analysis focuses on the distribution of runs—consecutive occurrences of the same event type—and examines how various event types influence one another. The methodology is applied to a dataset comprising multiple time-to-occurrence event records for patients who experienced myocardial infarction. Results indicate that the approach offers a straightforward and effective framework for investigating the interdependencies of time-to-occurrence events, while demonstrating that time-to-event data can be readily converted into a multiple state examination format. Furthermore, the study explores the potential for constructing interpretable models of disease progression using this technique. Additionally, it presents a novel method for estimating the distribution of state trajectories, which are conceptualized as time-indexed sequences of states. This enables the assessment of how specific risk factors impact an individual's life path. The multiple state examination represents a new method for analyzing time-to-event data, with applications extending beyond myocardial infarction to various other recurrent disease contexts. Moreover, the approach is applicable to a broader range of data than just time-to-event data. The authors propose that the proposed methodology can facilitate a more nuanced understanding of disease progression. Finally, the study suggests that incorporating time-to-event data into life path analysis will enhance our comprehension of how risk factors influence health over time. Key words: multiple time-to-occurrence data, multiple state examination, multiple state runs, multiple state examination, life paths, time-to-event data. We introduce a quadrature approach to evaluate the molecular continuum of multi-electron atoms and ions across the entire spectrum, spanning both bound and highly Rydberg states up to the molecular continuum. This technique integrates multi-site quadrature routines, specifically NAG's D01AFC, originally designed for bound states, into the molecular continuum region. The method is validated using LiH as a proof-of-concept, where we compute photoionization cross sections for the 1s2s$^3$U state, comparing our results against prior literature. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's applicability to more complex scenarios, including ion-atom collisions, by extending the NAG D01AFC call into the molecular continuum while incorporating state-switching conditions. Finally, we illustrate the method's robustness in handling complex geometries through an example involving a three-atom chain. Finally, our findings indicate that the computational cost of the NAG D01AFC call remains negligible, even when the integration grid is significantly subdivided at state-switching locations. This ensures that the overall performance of the photoionization cross section calculation is unaffected. Consequently, the proposed method is ideal for multi-center quantum chemistry computations, such as those required for ion-atom collision calculations. Additionally, it is highly suitable for scenarios demanding accurate continuum calculations within complex geometries, including the photoionization of large molecules. This paper investigates the metric dimension of graphs as a parameter function of various structural parameters, including feedback vertex set size, modular number, and parameterizations rooted in graph width concepts. Our primary findings are three theorems establishing $fpt$-algorithm ($f$ denotes an arbitrary function) constructions for metric dimension parameterized by feedback vertex set, module number, and clique number. Additionally, we demonstrate that metric dimension admits a $fpt$-algorithm when parameterized by treewidth, alongside an $fpt$-kernel with a size of $9(\omega+1)^2$, where $\omega$ represents the graph's clique number. Finally, we prove that metric dimension is fixed-parameter tractable parameterized by vertex cover number, and it possesses a kernel of size $9(n - \omega)^2$, parameterized by graph order and clique number. Notably, metric dimension is known to be W[td]-hard when parameterized by treedepth. The notation $fpt$-algorithm signifies fixed-parameter tractable, $fpt$-kernel denotes a polynomial-size kernel, and $W[t]$-hard indicates W[t]-hardness. Furthermore, $n$ and $\omega$ represent graph order and clique number, respectively, while $fpt$ stands for fixed-parameter tractable. Finally, W[t]-hardness refers to the W[t] complexity class.

Utilizing a three-dimensional general circulation model, we investigated the impact of atmospheric carbon dioxide fluctuations on simulated climate dynamics. Our results indicate that episodic floods occur within greenhouse climates, driven by a feedback mechanism where elevated surface temperatures trigger a sharp rise in water vapor, thereby increasing the hydrological cycle. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent during periods of high atmospheric CO2, as these gases also warm the surface, accelerating evaporation. We conclude that such flooding events could have played a significant role in populating Earth's surface with liquid water during the early stages of its evolution. Furthermore, our findings suggest that similar flooding episodes could occur on exoplanets orbiting M-type stars. However, we also demonstrate that the presence of a dust haze, which is common in such atmospheres, can substantially mitigate this flooding effect. Finally, we note that a runaway greenhouse effect can also trigger episodic flooding, though this typically occurs only after most surface water has already been lost. These insights could aid in interpreting observations from upcoming space missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, and enhance our understanding of the habitability of early Earth and other exoplanets. We introduce the concept of a twistor creature, which acts analogously to a particle within self-dual Yang-Mills (SDYM) theory. This framework allows for the generalization of SDYM (and, subsequently, self-dual gravity) to accommodate the scattering of higher-spin fields. The resulting self-dual higher-spin (SDHS) theory maintains a strong resemblance to SDYM, notably allowing for a natural extension of the SDYM Lax pair. Medical imaging datasets often contain label noise, which can severely hinder model performance. While traditional noise mitigation strategies either ignore noisy data or discard labels, they frequently fail to identify corrupted samples or determine the original correct class. This paper introduces the Statistics Directed Label Renovation Mechanism (SLRM), a novel approach that renovates noisy labels based on image statistics. SLRM is a lightweight, data-driven, and unsupervised framework capable of simultaneously detecting noisy samples and correcting their classes. We further integrate SLRM with a Bayesian statistics model, creating the Bayesian Statistics Directed Label Renovation Mechanism (BS-SLRM). This mechanism leverages Bayesian principles to refine training data and improve the uncertainty calibration of deep neural networks. Extensive experiments on three public medical image categorization datasets demonstrate that BS-SLRM surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving an 11.1% increase in accuracy and a 14.4% improvement in the coefficient of variation for category predictions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/BS-SLRM. This study underscores the efficacy of Bayesian methods and label renovation techniques for mitigating label noise in medical image categorization. Additionally, it highlights the critical importance of uncertainty quantification in this domain, offering a promising pathway for enhancing the reliability of deep learning models in clinical settings. Future research will explore extending this framework to semantic segmentation tasks. The work was conducted during Chen Chen's internship at the University of Surrey. This paper introduces the transition probability matrix for a related random walk on a graph. We define its distinctive polynomial as the determinant of the transition probability matrix minus a scalar $\lambda$ and provide two alternative formulations for this polynomial. For any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, we demonstrate that the constant term of this polynomial corresponds to a divisor of $n!$. Furthermore, we establish that the distinctive polynomial is independent of the edge weights. We also investigate the properties of this polynomial for specific graph classes, including empty graphs, complete graphs, and complete bipartite graphs, and provide a computational method to determine it. Finally, we derive the distinctive polynomial for both the complete graph $K_n$ and the complete bipartite graph $K_{p,q}$. In the case of a complete graph, the transition probability matrix becomes the adjoint of the incidence matrix, and the distinctive polynomial of the incidence matrix is identified as the chromatic polynomial. Additionally, we prove that the transition probability matrix for a complete bipartite graph is non-singular. The paper concludes with several open problems. As an application, we confirm that the incidence matrix of a complete graph possesses a chromatic polynomial, thereby resolving a conjecture proposed by Liu and Liu [10]. Finally, we demonstrate that the transition probability matrix of a related random walk on a complete graph functions as a fractional permutation matrix. This work extends the findings of Liu and Liu [10], Liu and Liu [11], and Liu and Liu [12].

Keywords: Related random walk, transition probability matrix, distinctive polynomial, fractional permutation matrix, Hadamard matrix, Hadamard determinant, incidence matrix, chromatic polynomial.

The proposed definition is formulated within HOL and represents a time-dependent function based on a sequence of events. We present an efficient decision procedure for this definition, demonstrating its application in various time-related computations. This study introduces a data-informed enhancement to coherent structure-based models for instantaneous, non-stationary wall turbulence. In the atmospheric surface layer, this methodology utilizes the complex interplay between the coherent structure framework and large-scale advection by the free-stream flow. Specifically, it incorporates free-stream velocity fluctuations and the inclination angle to refine predictions of friction velocity, which are derived from standard meteorological measurements. The data-informed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional models, thereby increasing the accuracy of weather forecasting and the reliability of climate change projections. Furthermore, the methodology is easily adaptable to other environments and can be readily integrated into existing coherent structure-based models. This model holds significant potential for applications in urban weather forecasting, urban heat island analysis, and climate change assessments. Additionally, it is applicable to non-hydrostatic, non-hydrostatic rotating, and rotating wall turbulence scenarios. The model is implemented within the widely used WRF-SDL (Weather Research Facility - Shear Driven Layer) atmospheric surface layer model. The resulting data-informed coherent structure-based model is accessible at https://github.com/ChenY1993/Coherent-structure-based-model-for-atmospheric-surface-layer. We investigate a Hofstadler-Weyl semimetal under a magnetic field that breaks translational symmetry, specifically through potential modulation. By introducing term-by-term analysis, we demonstrate that Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals can exist across multiple regions of the Brillouin zone, with the count of Weyl points determined by the geometry of the Hofstadler butterfly. Furthermore, we show that the Chern numbers of these bands can be calculated directly from the Hofstadler-Weyl semimetal's wave functions. Finally, we highlight the possibility of hosting Weyl points with non-trivial time-reversal-violating Chern numbers within these Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals. This research expands the landscape of topological semimetals and may facilitate the discovery of novel quantum states in artificially engineered condensed matter systems. Additionally, our findings offer a theoretical basis for the recent observation of Hofstadler-Weyl semimetals in term-modulated bismuth films. We present a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna design that enables the creation of efficient and robust single-photon sources (SPSs) at the dielectric-plasmonic interface. This system comprises a dielectric nanoparticle positioned on a metal film, with a quantum dot embedded within the dielectric. By adjusting the quantum dot's vertical position relative to the substrate, we can control the nature of the light quantum emission. When the dot is embedded in the device, the structure functions as a standard plasmonic nanoantenna, supporting both electric and magnetic dipole modes. Conversely, if the quantum dot is placed exactly at the dielectric-substrate boundary, only magnetic dipole plasmonic modes are excited, resulting in pure magnetic dipole-plasmonic nanoantennas. This hybrid approach leverages the complementary characteristics of dielectrics and metals to overcome individual limitations, offering a straightforward method to achieve either electric or magnetic dipole-plasmonic nanoantennas. This tunability allows for the design of quantum dots that emit either luminous or plasmonic single-photon states. Our findings indicate that the proposed system can achieve a single-mode emission probability exceeding 99% and a Purcell factor greater than 100. Furthermore, the system supports unidirectional photon sources with a directionality ratio surpassing 99.99%, a capability not previously realized in plasmonic nanoantennas. These results suggest that the hybrid nanoantenna design holds significant promise for applications in quantum information processing and quantum communication. Additionally, we outline viable pathways to experimentally validate the single-mode emission, luminous or plasmonic photon states, and the high degree of directionality. Finally, we demonstrate that the system's performance remains stable under realistic conditions involving material imperfections. These outcomes highlight the effectiveness of the hybrid nanoantenna approach in addressing the inherent limitations of conventional plasmonic nanoantennas. Consequently, this design offers a viable solution for developing practical plasmonic single-photon sources suitable for quantum information processing and quantum communication. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into the design and fabrication of nanoantennas utilizing this innovative hybrid configuration. Anomalous screening, a phenomenon where smaller particles preferentially fall through gaps rather than around larger ones, has been observed in both gravity-driven and sheared environments. This study examines the mechanism behind anomalous screening within a two-dimensional, dry, geometrically non-cohesive granular system under shear. The process is elucidated by a balance between a normal force generated by shear-induced particle collisions and the gravitational load. Our findings indicate that this shear-induced normal force fluctuates significantly during the gap development phase of screening events. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these experimental results align with the normal force calculations derived from the Discrete Element Method. Consequently, the proposed theory, which incorporates shear-induced normal forces, accurately replicates the anomalous screening process. This confirms that the theory effectively accounts for the influence of shear on this behavior. Finally, the paper discusses the connection between anomalous screening and shear-induced segregation. Segregation is predicted to occur when the shear-induced normal force varies with particle size in a manner opposite to that of the particle masses. Given that the force is inversely proportional to the mass, the mass-dependent and anomalous screening processes are shown to be fundamentally linked. Ultimately, the theory is validated by comparing it with a one-dimensional segregation model that accounts for anomalous screening. The results confirm that the theory can successfully predict segregation occurring in both the solid-rich and solid-poor regimes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the proposed theory offers a robust framework for predicting anomalous screening and segregation in two-dimensional granular systems. Additionally, the study underscores the critical role of accounting for shear-induced normal forces in such predictions. Finally, the theory is applied to a segregation scenario involving a two-size mixture with a size ratio of 2.5, a system that was not directly investigated in this work. The predicted segregation patterns are consistent with previously reported observations, further validating the theory. This suggests that the proposed approach can facilitate the design of granular processes, such as mixing and separation, in two-dimensional settings. Furthermore, the theory can be extended to three-dimensional systems, provided that shear-induced normal forces are computed using an appropriate methodology. Finally, the potential for integrating the theory into computational fluid dynamics models for particle-laden flows is explored. This could enable the prediction of anomalous screening and segregation in particulate flows, including sediment transport and dust dynamics. The paper concludes by discussing the limitations of the theory and identifying future research directions. This study investigates the structural and electronic properties of silicene supported by hexagonal borane nitride (hBN) using density functional theory. Our findings indicate that while pristine silicene exhibits bond angles of 100.2° relative to the hBN substrate, the presence of Mn adatoms induces a shift to bond angles of 110.4°. The electronic band structure reveals that both pristine and Mn-decorated silicene samples display semiconducting behavior. Furthermore, Mn adatoms introduce a metallic state at the Dirac points, thereby altering the semiconductor-semimetal transition of the system. Additionally, the magnetic moment of the Mn adatoms is observed to be 4.96 Bohr magnetons. These results demonstrate that Mn adatom decoration effectively tunes the electronic and magnetic characteristics of silicene, offering a promising avenue for developing novel spintronic devices. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that an explosion within G1.93+0.3 can disperse the cluster, offering a potential explanation for the recent non-detection of RCW 36's young stellar population. Although text classification is typically framed as a multi-category problem, most research and software tools concentrate exclusively on binary or multi-binary scenarios. This article investigates the impact of treating multi-category text classification as a collection of binary problems and evaluates various strategies to mitigate the resulting sample imbalance. We introduce a comprehensive overview of advanced techniques for generating training data in such imbalanced settings. Our findings indicate that for sufficiently large training corpora, reducing imbalanced multi-category tasks to multi-binary problems incurs negligible accuracy loss. Furthermore, when dealing with the inherent imbalance, our experiments demonstrate that solving the reduced problem using a support vector machine with a custom class-weighting function—rather than relying on basic oversampling methods—yields superior results. This study examines the relationships between regional news coverage, COVID-19 metrics (cases, deaths, media consumption), and regional audience demographics. Utilizing data from the News Data Consortium, the study analyzes coverage volume and trends across various demographics, including race, education, and political affiliation. Results indicate that while news reports on COVID-19 were sparse in the early stages of the pandemic, coverage has since become widespread and is linked to rising case numbers. Additionally, the research demonstrates that news consumption and coverage volume correlate with regional audience characteristics, such as age, race, and education levels. These findings offer valuable insights for regional news organizations aiming to better inform their specific audiences. The accompanying data can be utilized to examine additional audience-related factors, such as income and health status. Given that media plays a critical role in disseminating information, understanding these connections is essential for informing public health decisions. Furthermore, this analysis helps identify disparities in information access across different demographics, highlighting areas where news organizations may need to adjust their coverage to ensure more equitable distribution. The code used for this analysis is available at: https://github.com/andrewkirk/rdn-covid.

The preservation of angular momentum serves as a critical validation metric for electromagnetic scattering algorithms. In recent years, the Rapid Multipole Method (RMM) has gained significant traction due to its exceptional computational efficiency. However, despite these advantages, there has been a notable absence of studies evaluating the accuracy of far-field radiation patterns generated by RMM. This paper presents a detailed analysis of angular momentum preservation within the RMM framework. Furthermore, we offer an updated implementation of the RMM that ensures accurate angular scattering distributions. To achieve this, we examine the construction of incident fields in RMM and propose a corresponding correction. Finally, our results are validated through comparisons with the Multipole Expansion Method (MEM) and the Method of Moments (MoM). We provide a comprehensive collection of scripts covering polarization, poynting vector, and power calculations, which are included in PyVista and are easily accessible via the library. We conducted a one-dimensional study of the polarization shift from the initial to the final proton in the elastic $ep$ scattering process, defined as $Q_{TS} = \frac{D}{A}$. Utilizing a high-precision potential model, we evaluated $Q_{TS}$ for both unpolarized and polarized electrons. Our findings indicate that $Q_{TS}$ is highly sensitive to the pseudoscalar meson mass, particularly when the momentum transfer $Q^2$ is low. Furthermore, we determined that $Q_{TS}$ is negative at low $Q^2$ for the neutron, whereas it remains positive for the proton. Additionally, we compared our results with those derived from the chiral effective Lagrangian model. Finally, we suggest that future experimental investigations into the proton polarization shift should employ high-energy electron beams. These measurements would enhance the precision of the neutron electric form factor, $G_E^n$, and provide valuable insights into the internal structure of both the proton and neutron. This research was conducted within the framework of the International Initiative on the Structure of the Nucleon (iSNEP). The corresponding author is Dr. A. V. Afanasev. This paper introduces a new method for unsupervised data augmentation designed to create labeled examples from an unsupervised dataset, utilizing a parametric generator. Our approach leverages the distributional statistics of a parametric model that encodes an supervised distribution over the unsupervised dataset, specifically targeting the label conditional marginals. We demonstrate this method within two frameworks: first, for image generation using an unsupervised image set, and second, within a semi-supervised classification setting where an unsupervised image set is available for a specific classification task alongside a training set containing only examples from one of the classes. We evaluate our approach on the CSUCI-2000 and CIFAR-10 datasets, demonstrating that it yields state-of-the-art performance in semi-supervised classification and high-quality image generation on CIFAR-10. The source code can be found at https://github.com/abhishekkakkar/Label-Conditional-Marginals. This study investigates the non-resonant double production of Higgs bosons in conjunction with either a W or Z weak boson, or a top-antitop pair. The analysis utilizes proton-proton collision data from the ATLAS detector at the LHC, collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The primary focus examines the Higgs duo decaying into four leptons (two electrons and two muons) or decaying into two photons, while the remaining Higgs boson decays into a charged lepton and neutrino. The observed data align with the Standard Model predictions, and the analysis establishes a 95% confidence level upper limit of 2.0 times the Standard Model cross-section on the Higgs duo production rate associated with a vector boson or top-antitop pair. Furthermore, this search represents the first instance of combining multiple final states to set such a limit. Additionally, a separate analysis targets Higgs duo production with a top-antitop pair, where the duo decays into two photons and the top quarks decay into lepton+jets and jets+bosons+lepton final states. This search also observes no significant deviation from the Standard Model, yielding an upper limit of 3.4 times the Standard Model cross-section at 95% confidence level. Notably, this is the inaugural search for Higgs pair production in association with a top-antitop pair. The two analyses are integrated to produce an overall upper limit of 1.6 times the Standard Model cross-section at 95% confidence level. Finally, the study demonstrates that the cross-section upper limit can be enhanced by refining the signal region selection criteria. Utilizing a BDT classifier trained on simulated signal and background events, an optimal region is identified, resulting in an upper limit of 1.2 times the Standard Model cross-section at 95% confidence level. This outcome underscores the efficacy of the combined analysis approach and the potential for future enhancements through the application of machine learning techniques. We introduce a new class of quantum optical and electronic sources known as "spin lasers," which rely on the collective alignment of spins within a laser-active medium. By supplying sufficient pump energy, the polarization of the spins in the active material can be controlled. Leveraging the interaction between spin-polarized particles and photons, these spin lasers offer a unique platform to investigate and harness non-equilibrium spin dynamics in solid-state systems. Furthermore, they hold significant potential for diverse applications, including quantum information processing, photon-spin polarisation transfer, and the development of quantum and hybrid devices. In this study, we utilize an electronic system composed of alkali vapours doped with alkali metals possessing different nuclear spins to demonstrate a broadband "rubidium spin laser." The laser-active medium consists of $^{87}$Rb vapour doped with $^{85}$Rb. The required non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarization of the $^{87}$Rb is achieved through a nuclear spin-exchange optical pumping (SEOP) technique that couples the electronic system to the nuclear spin-polarized $^{85}$Rb. We show that the characteristics of the Rb spin laser are governed by the ratio of the hyperfine splitting to the optical pumping rate. Additionally, we examine the impact of magnetic field fluctuations on the laser's performance and explore potential applications in quantum information processing. Our findings provide a versatile platform for quantum and photonic technologies, as well as for the fundamental study of non-equilibrium spin polarization in vapour-based electronic systems. We investigate a dark matter candidate known as the "decomposing neutralino," which decays into a pair of long-lived, nearly massless Majorana neutrinos. This specific decay pathway is forbidden for a pure neutralino due to conservation laws, though it can occur within a minimal extension of the minimal supersymmetric standard model. In this framework, the neutralino remains the primary constituent of dark matter, while the secondary decay products form a significant portion of the dark matter density. Furthermore, the degrading neutralino predicts the cosmic gamma-ray background observed by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The gamma-ray spectrum is characterized by the dark matter mass and the lifetime of the deconfined neutralino, with the latter being constrained by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis limits. Additionally, the deconfined neutralino may decay into a photon and a neutrino, with the neutrino absorbing most of the energy, resulting in a mono-energetic gamma-ray signal. We also examine the potential for detecting these gamma rays through neutrino oscillations and their impact on diffuse gamma-ray emission. Finally, we outline the necessary experimental parameters to constrain the parameter space of this model. This scenario offers a viable, well-motivated framework for dark matter that could be tested by upcoming gamma-ray observatories. This paper introduces a probabilistic algorithm with provable performance guarantees for estimating the genus of dense graphs. The proposed method achieves a $3/4$-approximation of the exact genus, thereby addressing an open question posed by Alon et al. in 1997. Furthermore, the algorithm's running time is independent of the genus value, offering a significant advantage over existing methods. The study also explores various extensions and enhancements of this approach. Notably, the technique can be adapted to estimate other graph invariants, such as the Hadwiger number, even though the current paper focuses exclusively on genus estimation. Additionally, the authors examine a question raised by Thomassen in 1997 regarding the genus of graphs with specified degrees, providing a partial answer. Finally, the paper concludes with several open problems for future research. Overall, this work presents a comprehensive suite of techniques for generating accurate genus estimates. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/GenusEstimation. The authors thank the anonymous reviewers for their constructive comments and suggestions. This paper introduces and analyzes a randomized Newton approach designed for high-dimensional distributed convex optimization. In this framework, the objective function is expressed as a sum of $n$ local components, where each component is held by one of $p$ agents linked through a communication graph. The goal is to jointly leverage both high dimensionality and parallel computation to accelerate convergence. We propose a parallel algorithm that operates without prior knowledge of problem parameters, utilizing local data in parallel to minimize the function. We demonstrate that under mild conditions, this algorithm achieves polynomial-time convergence. Furthermore, we establish that when the problem is strongly convex with a Lipschitz continuous gradient, the expected function value converges linearly, while all other algorithmic variables—including parameter estimates, duality gaps, and primal-dual feasibility gaps—converge linearly. Additionally, we extend the analysis to scenarios involving noisy local functions and stochastic subgradients, proving convergence in both parallel and sequential execution modes. Finally, we illustrate the method's performance on real-world data using both homogeneous and heterogeneous datasets. Notably, the algorithm demonstrates superior performance on heterogeneous problems compared to existing parallel algorithms. Empirical results confirm that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChaoWang1996/RDN}. Experimental results indicate that fine-tuned models generally surpass fine-grained ones, particularly when an intermediate source language is employed. Furthermore, the order of transfer learning significantly influences performance; for instance, transferring from English to Hindi to Bengali yields superior hate speech identification compared to the reverse order. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that both sequential transfer strategies and the choice of source languages exert a substantial effect on the performance of neural network-based hate speech identification models. High-resolution gas time projection chambers (TPCs) function as dual detectors capable of measuring both the position and energy of nuclear recoil events. While traditional reionizing detectors rely on charge or heat for detection, tenuous ionization from low-energy nuclear recoils—typical of dark matter interactions—necessitates a shift in observables. Recent advancements in gas detection have enabled ultra-low threshold thresholds, allowing for the use of new observables optimized for these rare events. This work reviews the current landscape of such techniques, focusing on high-resolution gas TPCs that utilize both position and charge readout. We outline the advantages of gas TPCs for reionizing detector experiments targeting dark matter and other sub-GeV mass candidates, and we detail emerging methods for extracting maximum information from gas recoil data. Finally, we present preliminary results from the GEANT2SIM simulation framework, which models detector responses to include realistic detector effects. These tools facilitate the optimization of tenuous ionization detector designs and analysis strategies, ultimately enhancing the sensitivity of future experiments. A companion document provides a detailed technical description of the GEANT2SIM toolkit. Together, these papers establish a framework for the design and analysis of the next generation of gas-based reionizing recoil detectors. Specifically, the methods described here can be applied to the STEVE experiment, which is currently in its construction and commissioning phase. Stepping stone TPCs like STEVE will demonstrate the viability of this approach, paving the way for larger-scale experiments that will significantly improve the sensitivity of reionizing detectors. Furthermore, the novel analysis methods highlighted in this work will enable those future experiments to reach their full reionizing detector potential. By the end of this research, we aim to provide a complete description of the observables and analysis methods for gas recoil detection in TPCs, including a demonstration of the resulting sensitivity. This will be achieved by comparing the performance of a GEANT2SIM-modeled STEVE detector against a hypothetical large-scale version of the same design. The comparison will evaluate the detector's sensitivity to dark matter, neutrinos, and other sub-GeV masses, thereby demonstrating the value of the observables discussed in this thesis for future high-resolution gas TPCs. The code used in GEANT2SIM to generate the simulation data is publicly available. The STEVE code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/steve-tpc/steve-tpc, and the GEANT2SIM code is available at https://github.com/Geant2sim/Geant
