This paper introduces a novel Steganography network, the Bayesian Neural Network (BNN), designed for image concealment. Steganography aims to hide secret data within a carrier image while maintaining visual similarity to cover networks. Our proposed BNN employs Bayesian inference to estimate model parameters, thereby accounting for uncertainty in the network's predictions. By utilizing a predictive distribution, the BNN can randomly distort the least significant bits of the carrier image, effectively masking the presence of embedded information. We assessed the BNN's performance against the state-of-the-art Steganography network, SPIEIE, across two experimental setups. The first setup compared the average steganographic capacity of the BNN with SPIEIE, while the second setup compared their respective robustness. Our results demonstrate that the BNN surpasses SPIEIE in both capacity and robustness metrics. Furthermore, we provide an ablation study to pinpoint the specific components of the BNN responsible for these superior performance gains. Finally, we have made the BNN's code and pre-trained models publicly accessible via GitHub. We present ALMA observations of a massive molecular outflow in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 4943, detected across CO(3-2), HCN(4-3), and HNC(3-2) transitions. The data reveal a large-scale outflow extending up to 1.5 kpc from the galactic center, driven by a central supermassive black hole of 10^7 solar masses. The outflow's kinematics indicate a mass ranging from 10^7 to 10^8 solar masses, expanding at velocities between 200 and 400 km/s. The HNC/CO and HNC/HCN line intensity ratios suggest that HNC is primarily excited by collisions with H2 rather than by radiative processes. Furthermore, the HNC(3-2)/CO(3-2) and HNC(3-2)/HCN(4-3) line intensity ratios align with conditions found in low-density molecular clouds. These findings imply that the outflow originates from a low-density molecular cloud, consistent with a black hole wind mechanism. The HNC(3-2) line exhibits a total luminosity of 1.5×10^8 W/steradian, which is comparable to the luminosity of the entire CO(3-2) outflow. This makes the HNC(3-2) line the most luminous CO-rotationally transition line ever observed in a molecular outflow, offering a promising tool for detecting similar outflows in distant galaxies. The HNC(3-2) line is also the most luminous CO-rotationally transition line detected in any galaxy, including the Milky Way. This result underscores the significance of HNC as a molecular tracer in starburst environments. Finally, the HNC(3-2) line is approximately 100 times more luminous than the commonly observed CN J=1-0 line, suggesting that HNC is a more effective tracer for starburst galaxies than previously thought. These observations provide the first evidence of a black hole wind in a nearby starburst galaxy, and the high sensitivity of the HNC(3-2) line offers a new method for identifying and characterizing such winds in distant starbursts. These findings are crucial for understanding the role of black hole winds in cosmic chemical evolution. The data are available at https://www.almaobservatory.org/data/ALMA-2019/201

This paper introduces the first fully conservative Galerkin solver, applicable to both steady-state and time-dependent scenarios, designed for quasilinear diffusion equations governing gyrokinetic turbulence. The implementation ensures strict conservation of both gyrokinetic free energy and zonal flow momentum. Numerical tests, including convergence studies and simulations of zonal flow evolution under a analytic turbulence spectrum, confirm the solver's accuracy and conservation properties. These capabilities are essential for obtaining reliable, quantitative results when using gyrokinetic turbulence predictions as input for zonal flow and neoclassical transport models. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to other quasilinear diffusion problems, such as those involving zonal flow evolution or kinetic Rutherford equations. All associated code is publicly accessible. Keywords: Magnetohydrodynamics, turbulence, quasilinear diffusion, zonal flows, numerical methods. This study investigates the optimal portfolio selection problem under a power utility function, where both total and relative wealth are considered within the absolute value framework. By applying duality techniques, the authors transform the primal optimization problem into a dual one. In the general case, the dual problem is formulated as a Skorokhod reflection problem involving a convex set. For a complete market, an explicit solution is derived using the tangent mapping of this convex set. This mapping is subsequently characterized as the solution to a backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE). The primary difficulty lies in the complex structure of the convex set, which prevents the direct use of standard methods for BSDEs. To address this, the authors introduce a novel approach by recursively decomposing the set into a countable union of convex sets. Leveraging the monotone convergence theorem, the explicit solution is constructed as the limit of a sequence of approximating solutions. Finally, the solution to the primal problem is obtained by utilizing the duality relationship. As a practical application, the model is extended to a multi-asset market featuring correlated defaults, yielding a specific mapping for the dual problem. Through this specific mapping, explicit solutions are again derived for both the primal and dual problems. The methodology and findings are applicable to any finite number of assets. Market data indicates that default correlations among countries in the EU have increased over time, suggesting a growing need for models that account for these correlations. This research offers a viable solution for pricing and hedging credit default swaps within a multi-asset framework incorporating correlated defaults. Furthermore, the study provides a new perspective for modeling and analyzing the interaction between assets in a multi-asset environment. The paper concludes with a discussion of the broader applicability of these results. Hydrogen recombination lines from the intergalactic medium surrounding nearby dwarf galaxies offer a novel method for investigating the physical characteristics of their neutral gas. This approach enables the study of gas reservoirs that are too faint to detect with current instruments and located beyond the limits of standard observations. We present findings from a search for recombination lines around three Local Group dwarfs: the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), and the Segue 2 (Seg2) dwarf galaxy. Our analysis reveals that Seg2 possesses an ionized gas volume with an emission measure of approximately $10^{5}$ cm$^{-6}$ pc$^{3}$, situated roughly 1 kpc from the galaxy's center. The LMC shows no significant excess emission beyond the known nebula NGC 3918, whereas the SMC exhibits a marginal detection of ionized gas about 1 kpc from its core, characterized by an emission measure of roughly $10^{4}$ cm$^{-6}$ pc$^{3}$. These results establish a baseline for future investigations aimed at characterizing the ionized gas within and around dwarf galaxies. Such a characterization is crucial for understanding the star formation and chemical evolution of these galaxies, as well as the impact of their supernovae on the surrounding intergalactic medium. Furthermore, we outline the scientific potential of these searches and identify the instrumentation necessary to conduct them effectively. This study is the first installment in a series that will present the outcomes of these searches. Subsequent papers will detail the findings from our most sensitive searches, which will be conducted around galaxies with the highest star formation rates and around galaxies that are currently or were recently forming stars. We anticipate that these searches will reveal a significant population of ionized gas around dwarf galaxies, thereby enhancing our understanding of the feedback mechanisms between stars and their environments. The remaining papers in this series are designated as H20-01 through H20-04. The specific targets for each are: H20-01 (LMC and SMC), H20-02 (Seg2 and Seg3), H20-03 (M31 and M33), and H20-04 (M82 and NGC 4449). This work is designated as H20-01. This paper derives several asymptotic formulas for the orthogonal polynomials $\{P_n\}$ associated with the logarithmic weight function $w(x) = \log \varphi(x)$, where $\varphi(x) = \sqrt{1-x^2} + x^2$. Since $w(x)$ is nonnegative and vanishes at $x=1$, standard results from classical polynomial theory do not apply. While Barrios, Carmona, and Kim [Barions-Carmona-Kim-2015] previously established specific asymptotic formulas for these polynomials, this work extends those findings to generate additional asymptotic expressions. Specifically, we provide the asymptotic behavior for the ratio of consecutive polynomials, $\frac{P_{n+1}(x)}{P_n(x)}$, within the gap region $(-1, 1)$, and establish an asymptotic expansion for the recurrence coefficients. Furthermore, we analyze the asymptotic properties of the zeros of $P_n(x)$, demonstrating that they exhibit logarithmic capacity zero. Finally, we present a strong orthogonality relation for $\{P_n\}$ and examine the first few coefficients of the expansion for $\frac{P_n(yx)}{P_n(x)}$ as $n \to \infty$, where $|x|<1$ and $|y|<1$. These findings collectively contribute to the understanding of the asymptotic properties of orthogonal polynomials under logarithmic weights. Additionally, the methodologies employed here are anticipated to be useful for investigating the asymptotic properties of other polynomials orthogonal with respect to logarithmic weight functions. Human evaluation remains a critical component of natural language processing, yet it is often costly and difficult to implement. This study investigates the reliability of Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) worker pools specifically for summarization tasks. We introduce a new method for characterizing these pools by analyzing individual worker performance across a calibration task designed to mirror the challenges of summarization. Our findings reveal that, despite the common assumption that finding skilled workers is easy, identifying them on MTurk is surprisingly difficult. We demonstrate that by targeting a small fraction of high-performing workers, researchers can achieve evaluation results that are both more robust and more reliable. These results are consistent whether the task involves abstracting documents or generating summaries of news and social media content. We contend that our approach of focusing on top performers should be adopted in future studies. The code and worker data required to replicate these results are available at https://github.com/joshuagill/needle-in-a-haystack. Furthermore, we have made the calibration task available as a new sample selection option for summarization on Amazon MTurk. Finally, we argue that our findings have broader implications for other NLP tasks that depend on high-quality worker performance. The paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.00028. Text-video retrieval (TVMR) is a critical yet difficult task that demands a deep contextual grasp of both modalities. However, current state-of-the-art models often overlook the inherent hierarchical structure of data, particularly the frame-level granularity within videos and the token-level granularity in texts. To address this, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel architecture that employs a Token Shift module to capture local features and a unimodal Choice Transformer that aggregates tokens into frames or class tokens to model long-range dependencies. Furthermore, we incorporate a cross-modal Shift module to align text and video representations. Extensive experiments on the Web4Video, LISA, MSRVTT, and VWFE datasets demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that the proposed modules effectively capture both local and long-range dependencies while aligning the modality representations. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/111111111111111/TS2-Net.

We introduce a directed hybrid random network that integrates Preferential Attachment (PA) and Uniform Attachment (U) mechanisms. In this model, a node attaches to an existing node $v$ with a probability proportional to $v$'s in-degree plus a constant. This mechanism is combined with the Uniform Attachment process, where new nodes connect to each other uniformly at random. Our primary contribution is a comprehensive analysis of the resulting degree distributions. We demonstrate that this hybrid mechanism produces nodes with power-law in-degree and exponential out-degree distributions. Furthermore, we establish that the network exhibits a giant component and possesses a diameter of $O(\log n)$. Finally, we validate these theoretical findings through simulations. The Python implementation of both the theoretical model and the simulations is accessible at: https://github.com/akm1992/PADirectedHybrid. Additional code can be found at: https://github.com/akm1992/PAExponential. The associated Python package, PAExponential, is available at: https://github.com/akm1992/PAExponential. This package includes a generator for the directed network with power-law in-degree and exponential out-degree, along with a verification tool for the network's properties. These features have been utilized in various research papers. The Python package can be installed via pip using: pip install PAExponential. The package also provides tools to analyze random networks generated with other models. While current approaches rely on manual feature extraction to enhance transmission quality, these techniques are often sensitive to specific disturbance types. This paper introduces a multi-label Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture designed to detect and classify multiple wireless disturbances simultaneously. The model utilizes a shared layer structure for disturbance classification and applies a sigmoid activation function to enable independent classification of each disturbance. Evaluated on real-world wireless channel data, the proposed architecture demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the study confirms the model's utility in distinguishing between different disturbance types and offers insights into their relative frequencies. Finally, the research explores how signal-to-noise ratio and modulation schemes influence disturbance occurrence. These findings facilitate the creation of robust neural network models capable of withstanding simultaneous disturbances to improve network stability. Additionally, the results provide a quantitative analysis of how varying signal-to-noise ratios and modulation types affect system performance. Ultimately, this work offers a foundation for future studies on automatic disturbance classification and their impact on network behavior. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field that has evolved rapidly over the past few decades, becoming deeply embedded in our daily lives. As our reliance on AI grows, so does the need for greater transparency and trust in its operations. Currently, AI systems are largely automated, requiring minimal human interaction once deployed. However, as these systems become more autonomous, the necessity for increased human oversight over decision-making processes has emerged. This concept of enhancing AI through human contribution is termed Enhanced Artificial Intelligence (EAI). The following paper proposes a conceptual framework for EAI, which is anticipated to significantly influence the future trajectory of AI development. Furthermore, EAI offers novel human-computation paradigms, diverging from traditional human computation models. We expect this paper to inspire researchers to investigate various EAI-related topics, thereby advancing the field of AI further. We investigate the realization of graphs using homomorphism counts within finite abelian groups. Specifically, for any two graphs $G$ and $H$ where $H$ is not a single vertex, there exists a group $A$ such that $G$ cannot be realized over $A$, whereas $H$ can be realized over some finite abelian group. Furthermore, if $G$ is realized by a non-cyclic finite abelian group, it is also realizable by a cyclic finite abelian group, with the potential realizer being an arbitrarily large prime. Finally, we characterize the family of all degenerate graphs based on their realizations. Additionally, we provide a complete description of the degenerate graphs that can be realized by cyclic groups of any fixed order, as well as by groups that admit a homomorphism to the additive group of integers. The realization of general graphs by finite abelian groups was previously addressed in [J. Algebra 500 (2018) 1-22]. A primary obstacle in applying Gaussian process (GP) models is selecting appropriate kernels that reflect the underlying characteristics of the target function. While numerous well-established GP kernels exist, they are often difficult to interpret, and the vast volume of available options can be overwhelming. This paper introduces a framework for developing new GPs by deriving kernels from fundamental mathematical expressions. We propose four specific kernels using this approach and compare them against existing models. Our results demonstrate that the proposed kernels are interpretable and, in certain scenarios, outperform traditional options. Furthermore, we illustrate the framework's utility by making it possible to incorporate domain-specific knowledge into GP models. Our findings suggest that this methodology can facilitate better kernel selection and aid in interpreting learned kernels. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1998/gp-kernels-from-math-expressions. This work is based on a doctoral dissertation completed at the University of Amsterdam. Spartan addresses the challenge of non-differentiability inherent in zero-precision constraints by conveyscing the non-differentiable indicator function of the zero-precision set. This approach unifies the benefits of contemporary convex regularizers, such as the Lasso and generalized elastic net, with precision control previously only achievable through greedy algorithms like Orthogonal Matching Pursuit. Additionally, we establish that Spartan's solution space is more flexible than existing methods, effectively balancing sparsity and accuracy in linear and logistic regression. Beyond this primary effect, further analytical terms can be identified that account for the emergence of a non-topological threshold in the response function at the impurity wave vector. This phenomenon signifies that, within this specific regime, the fluid's behavior transitions from that of an almost free Bose gas to an almost free Fermi gas. These findings suggest that beyond the leading order, the expansion in the scattering length of a low-density Bose gas—whether dilute or concentrated—generates Pauli obstructions in a systematic and unambiguous manner. This underscores the existence of an emergent Pauli principle within this Bose fluid. Additionally, numerical calculations of the compressibility support these conclusions. Finally, we explore the potential implications of our results for understanding the Bose-Mott transition in superfluid $^4$He. Specifically, we propose that the Pauli obstructions arising in the weak-coupling expansion of a Bose-Mott insulator are responsible for its finite compressibility, in contrast to the zero compressibility observed in superfluid $^4$He. Test odors are a subjective assessment of the perceived quality of a test suite. This study examines the quality judgments of various developers with a specific focus on how serious they consider these test odors. The research employs a survey approach, recruiting participants from an online forum and a university department. The findings indicate that developers vary in their tolerance toward test odors, with the degree of seriousness often depending on the specific nature of the odor. Additionally, developers express a desire for more objective methods to detect test odors. The study concludes that understanding varying attitudes toward test odors is essential for effectively communicating their significance. Furthermore, recognizing that developers seek more objective detection methods may inspire future research into such approaches. Finally, the paper explores the potential benefits of eliminating test odors. Although the link between removing these odors and enhancing the test quality perception of non-experts remains unclear, eliminating them could still offer other advantages. The paper discusses these potential benefits and suggests that they may be realized through the automatic refactoring of test code. The authors intend to investigate the impact of refactoring test code to remove odors on both developer perception and the overall quality of the test suite. The tool accurately models both soft and hard photon emission, including initial and final state radiation as well as photon-photon collisions. Furthermore, KKMCee supports the simulation of Standard Model boson pairs, such as Higgs-Higgs and top-top, alongside their photon radiation. This enables the creation of comprehensive event samples for various collider scenarios, including those involving off-shell Higgs bosons or off-shell electroweak boson pairs. Additionally, we have incorporated the radiation of collinear photons, which is essential for applying experimental collinear cuts. The Stochastic Singular Value Transformation (SSVT) is a method designed to compute a tensor's singular value decomposition (SVD). It operates by applying a series of SSVT steps, with each step significantly enhancing singular value localization. This paper introduces a modification to the traditional multi-pass SSVT algorithm, enabling users to determine whether sufficient passes have been executed. The proposed algorithm terminates when the count of required passes is fulfilled, or if a "stop" signal is detected during execution. The necessity for multiple passes stems from the fact that while the first pass achieves high localization for a few singular values, it often fails to sufficiently localize all of them. The study investigates the impact of first-pass singular values on subsequent passes and examines the algorithm's performance on randomly generated tensors. Numerical experiments indicate that allowing a user-specified number of passes can significantly speed up tensor SSVT execution. Furthermore, the proposed method offers a straightforward approach to assessing the convergence of each pass. The paper concludes that the second pass consistently localizes all singular values, demonstrating robustness even with poorly chosen initial guesses. The ground state of $^7$H is characterized using a three-body model that treats the system as a linear excitation of the $^3$H + 2n configuration. In this framework, the $^3$H core interacts with the two neutrons via a Gaussian potential, while the two neutrons are paired in an s-wave with a realistic neutron-neutron potential. The resulting wave functions are normalized through their overlap with the $^3$H + 4n state. Calculations indicate that the $^7$H ground state corresponds to a $^3$H + 4n excitation with an overlap of 0.99, confirming it as predominantly a fully neutron-rich state. Furthermore, the model predicts a narrow resonance near the $^7$H + Q value, which could be accessible in experiments utilizing a $^7$H beam. This narrow resonance is identified as the $^3$H + 4n excitation and exhibits strong coupling to the $^7$H state. Additionally, the energy splitting between the $^7$H ground state and this narrow resonance is estimated to be less than 10 keV. These findings suggest that the narrow resonance should be observed as a distinct peak in the momentum distribution of the remaining nucleons following the breakup of a $^7$H beam. The study also calculates the binding energy of $^7$H, which is found to be 0.15 ± 0.15 MeV. These results provide a theoretical basis for the recent experimental measurements of the $^7$H momentum distribution. Finally, the findings support the conclusion that the $^7$H ground state is a multichannel resonance. The implications of these results for the existence of a $^7$H bound state are also discussed. In machine learning, the representation of data is paramount. This paper introduces an innovative framework for developing deep data representations by leveraging geodesic information. We propose a new loss function grounded in Sinkhorn geodesic distance, designed for learning these representations. This geodesic distance metric quantifies the divergence between two datasets, assuming one follows a specific distribution on a Riemannian manifold. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of this loss function and its associated gradient, demonstrating its utility in optimal representation learning. Furthermore, we validate our approach's effectiveness across a diverse range of tasks, including unsupervised and supervised learning, semi-supervised node classification, and image classification. In these applications, our method geodesically transforms training data into clusters that enhance downstream performance. Finally, we show that our method generates training data representations that are more robust to distribution shifts caused by test-time noise. These results underscore the advantages of geometric representation learning, particularly when geometric information is unavailable during training. The implementation code is available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Sinkhorn-Geodesic-Learning. This study employs a stochastic SIR model to simulate the impact of contact tracing on COVID-19 transmission within England. We specifically investigate how the reporting rate of infections and the fraction of infections traced affect transmission dynamics. Furthermore, we analyze the sensitivity of transmission reduction to tracing delays and the test sensitivity required to achieve a 50% decrease in transmission. A key contribution of this work is the examination of different collaborations between local tracing teams and national laboratories. Our findings indicate that increasing the reporting rate of positive tests from the current 20% to 50% could reduce population-level $R_t$ by 5%, whereas tracing only 30% of infections (compared to a target of 60%) would increase $R_t$ to 1.05. Additionally, we observe that a local tracing system relying on tests conducted and reported by national laboratories will struggle to lower population-level $R_t$ below 1.0. Finally, we demonstrate that a national tracing system utilizing nationally conducted tests and achieving a 60% tracing rate would need to incur up to 4 days of delay to maintain $R_t$ below 1.0. These results have significant implications for the COVID-19 response in England. Specifically, we conclude that a national tracing system must test using national resources and collaborate with local systems to gather data on up to 60% of infections to effectively inform transmission dynamics. This approach would enable timely identification of superspreading events and the subsequent implementation of targeted interventions. We establish a bound for the expected Betti numbers of random level sets of Gaussian processes, valid when conditional level sets are rare. Specifically, for a homogeneous Gaussian process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a positive definite covariance kernel, we demonstrate that for any $k \in [0,d-1]$, the expected $k$-th Betti number of a random level set is bounded by an integral geometric quantity of order $k+1$, provided the linear conditional level sets are sufficiently sparse. This result extends previous findings by P. B. Belyaev and P. L. Kuznetsov, which were limited to scalar functions. Furthermore, we prove that this bound is sharp in terms of its dependence on the noise standard deviation. Finally, we apply these findings to construct Gaussian wavelets that localize winding number estimates in the time-frequency plane. These wavelets are generated by applying a Gaussian low-pass filter to a linear combination of a mother wavelet and its adjoint, where the mother wavelet is created by modulating a sparse wavelet with a Gaussian envelope. We then employ this construction to estimate the spectral support of functions within the Sobolev space $H^1(\mathbb{R})$. The proposed estimator is shown to be sharp regarding its convergence rate and achieves the minimax optimal rate for functions in the class $H^1(\mathbb{R})$. Additionally, it is sharp for functions with a separated spectrum, where the convergence rate matches the minimax optimal rate established by D. Donoho and J. Stark in their 1987 study on signal recovery from sparse data. Finally, we illustrate the application of this spectral support estimator to analyze the power spectral density of a signal. In this context, we show that the estimator's convergence rate is sharp with respect to the sample size. However, when the signal is a sum of two sinusoids, we observe that the estimator fails to resolve the individual frequencies. This limitation is also evident in the classical MUSIC algorithm, which utilizes a similar approach to estimate the number of signals in a mixture. However, the preprocessing stage required to obtain a bounded tree decomposition remains a significant bottleneck. This study introduces a straightforward, single-pass treewidth algorithm that is y-nested, where y represents the treewidth of the input graph. The algorithm's time complexity is $O(n + m + 2^{yO(\sqrt{n})})$, with $n$ and $m$ denoting the counts of vertices and edges, respectively. By integrating this result with Bodlaender's algorithm, we demonstrate that the $yO(\sqrt{n})$ factor can be reduced to $yO(\sqrt{n}\log n)$. Furthermore, we present a novel algorithm for compact vertex diversifiers, which are versatile components applicable to various treewidth algorithms. This method operates in $O(2^{yO(\sqrt{n})})$ time, improving upon the prior best time complexity of $O(2^{yO(n)})$. Finally, we establish that the $\sqrt{n}$ dependency in our algorithm is optimal. Notably, the algorithm's runtime is nearly linear when treewidth is bounded by a constant, such as $y \leq 10$. Grouping algorithms are frequently employed to analyze networks, typically involving the assignment of group labels to nodes and the optimization of a grouping criterion. However, the application of these methods has expanded to more intricate scenarios, including the use of node attributes or weights, the integration of multiple criteria, and the analysis of multiple networks. This paper examines how the standard modularity criterion and its extensions are adapted for various weighted, directed, and inferred network contexts. It demonstrates that these adaptations do not always yield a single optimal solution but rather a set of near-optimal network partitions. Furthermore, we explore how node weights and the selection of near-optimal partitions influence clustering outcomes, highlighting that near-optimal modularity can effectively distinguish between degree distributions in weighted networks. Finally, we address specific challenges in implementing near-optimal modularity when dealing with multiple networks and how node weights interact with criteria derived from joint network modularity.

In a subsequent section, we outline how to formulate interpretations for when a node belongs to a group, how to define near-optimal community structures, and how to select a single partition from among the many possible solutions. We also discuss how incorporating node attributes can mitigate the small-world problem. The paper concludes by presenting open questions and potential future research directions.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a machine learning approach that integrates prior knowledge of physical systems into training objectives. Although this method has demonstrated significant potential for solving complex engineering challenges, it often yields solutions containing substantial unphysical artifacts. This issue arises because current PINN frameworks lack mechanisms to identify or correct these anomalies. To address this, we introduce a novel error estimation technique for PINNs, enabling the automatic detection of unphysical regions within estimated solutions. We validate this method using two case studies: first, a benchmark problem where the PINNs fail to replicate expected experimental data, and second, a high-fidelity fluid dynamics simulation where results violate the second law of thermodynamics. Our proposed technique successfully identifies these unphysical regions, allowing for the construction of a piecewise solution that aligns with physical reality. This advancement effectively establishes a new paradigm for the reliable application of machine learning in engineering contexts. By introducing a new error estimator for PINNs, our work facilitates a shift toward a more rigorous application of machine learning in science and engineering. Specifically, our method allows for the identification of scientifically valid solution regions and the development of strategies to achieve overall physical consistency. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to any existing PINN formulation, offering a universal method for achieving physical consistency in machine learning applications. Finally, we have made our code publicly available to facilitate the broader adoption of this technique. These contributions collectively pave the way for the authorized use of machine learning in science and engineering. By enabling the identification of physically consistent regions and providing methods to achieve global consistency, our work supports the responsible application of machine learning. Additionally, our technique supports verifiable machine learning by allowing for the assessment of result reliability and the correction of inaccuracies. The public availability of our code further enhances the reproducibility of these findings. Finally, our research advances the field of data-driven physics by opening new avenues for the integration of machine learning with physical laws. Specifically, our work explores new pathways for estimating PINN errors and for achieving physical consistency in data-driven physics through hybrid methods. These contributions are integral to advancing the application of machine learning in science and engineering. This study examines three case studies on atmospheric pollution modeling within epidemiological research, highlighting the synergistic roles of geostatistics and machine intelligence. Initially, we present a spatio-temporal kriging framework for estimating nitrogen dioxide across Greater London. Subsequently, a neural network is employed to forecast nitrogen dioxide levels in the same region for the years 2015 through 2019. Finally, we analyze a causal inference study investigating the health impacts of air pollution in Los Angeles, utilizing geostatistics to characterize the spatial structure of particulate matter. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of integrating geostatistical and neural network methods for atmospheric modeling in epidemiology, offering a robust basis for pollution estimation and forecasting. Furthermore, the third case study underscores the necessity of high-resolution pollutant data for advancing epidemiological research. Ultimately, the approaches discussed in this study hold significant potential for future applications in the field. Keywords: atmospheric pollution modeling, geostatistics, machine learning, neural networks, epidemiology.

While linear bandit literature predominantly assumes a uniform action set (typically a unit ball or hypercube) across all problems, many real-world applications involve varying action sets for each decision. This divergence complicates standard analysis, as established regret bounds rely heavily on uniform geometric properties. This paper examines the consequences of such varying action sets on both analysis and inference. We introduce a novel framework where regret is measured against an optimal policy's historical performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that standard regret analysis and the confidence intervals necessary for inference fail in this setting. To address this, we propose a new confidence interval that adapts to the geometry of each action set, achieving optimal statistical performance. Empirical results confirm that this proposed interval outperforms existing methods in this context. Additionally, we identify a specific condition that allows for closed-form regret bounds, which we apply to several practical use cases. Finally, we reveal that common experimental designs, such as A/B testing, are specific instances of this general framework. A/B testing is a prevalent method for determining product feature preferences; we illustrate how our approach can be applied to this domain. Notably, our analysis shows that the confidence intervals used in standard A/B testing are suboptimal for this purpose. While the valley Hall effect in graphene is typically suppressed by graphene-specific mechanisms, this study demonstrates that introducing a second sublattice allows the effect to emerge. We demonstrate this using the orbital Hall effect, which is intrinsically a graphene-specific phenomenon. By constructing a model that incorporates both sublattice degrees of freedom, we show that the orbital Hall effect can be observed as an alternative to the valley Hall effect. This model is realized through a heterostructure formed by graphene and a graphene-like material exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling. Our findings indicate that the orbital valley Hall effect in this system is substantial, reaching approximately $10^5$~cm$^2$/Vs at an orbital valley splitting of $10$ meV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the effect is highly sensitive to variations in interlayer distance and gating. These results suggest that the orbital valley Hall effect is a promising candidate for valleytronics applications. Additionally, we explore the potential for detecting this effect through magnetotransport measurements. This sensitivity could offer a novel method for identifying topological phases in graphene-based materials. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the orbital valley Hall effect and the orbital Hall effect, which is also unique to graphene. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically designed for processing data on graphs, demonstrating strong performance in fields like chemistry and biology. However, their performance can be severely compromised when nodes in the training set are missing or when graphs contain communities. This study investigates how data contamination techniques can exploit these vulnerabilities. We introduce a data poisoning framework where an adversary employs reinforcement learning to maximize the discrepancy between a GNN's predictions on a test set and a target set of $y$ values. Our approach demonstrates significant efficacy in predicting target $y$ values, even when the training dataset is missing nodes. We validate the framework's effectiveness across various real-world datasets, including both synthetic and real instances. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses existing graph contamination approaches in terms of accuracy. Furthermore, we find that the reinforcement learning process converges rapidly, requiring only a few episodes to achieve the target labels. Finally, we highlight the practical implications of our findings for graph-based data privacy. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/RL-GNN}. Catalogue matching serves as a critical yet computationally demanding task in modern astrophysics, typically requiring the identification of matches between two catalogues with known relative astrometry. This process involves a preliminary preliminary co-adding of images to generate source lists, followed by the calculation of relative positions and magnitudes for each source pair using a catalogue-coordinates matching algorithm. This relative photometry and astrometry are subsequently compared against a tolerance region defined by source uncertainty and a search radius to determine a match. However, the computational cost of this algorithm grows significantly with the number of sources in both catalogues. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that expands the search radius for pairs and filters out pairs that cannot possibly match based on their photometric properties. This method effectively shifts the focus from pure astrometry to combined astrometry and photometry, thereby reducing the computational load of catalogue matching. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to match Gaia DR2 sources with Hubble Space Telescope images from the Gaia-ESO Survey. Our results show that the average search radius can be reduced from 10 milliarcseconds to 1.5 milliarcseconds, representing a 90% decrease in search area. Furthermore, we illustrate how to integrate colour information to further refine the search area, demonstrating that both improvements can be combined to achieve colour and position offsets as small as 2.5 sigma. Ultimately, our findings indicate that combining colour and position data allows for a search radius reduction of up to 99.9%, leading to a substantial decrease in matching time. This represents a significant advancement in efficiency, which is essential for processing future large-scale surveys. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tperez1999/CatMatch. The problem of whether a minimal edge cover exists is equivalent to the existence of a choice set for a family of non-empty finite sets of cardinalities that approach one. Ontologies serve as formal, explicit specifications of concepts within a particular domain and the relationships linking them, enabling various applications such as knowledge management, data integration, and reasoning. Given their scale, ontologies necessitate effective visualization methods for browsing and comprehension. Current ontology visualization techniques often fail to accommodate the diversity of relationship types or struggle with scalability when dealing with large collections. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization approach that integrates force-directed graph layout with hierarchical tree rendering to display ontologies up to 100,000 in size. By representing concepts as nodes and relations as edges, the system effectively handles various relationship types, including those with high cardinality and directionality. Furthermore, OntoPlot supports interactive features such as node highlighting and navigation, which facilitate the identification of key concepts and enable the detection of knowledge gaps. A case study demonstrates the method's effectiveness on the DBpedia ontology, which contains approximately 1.2 million concepts. The results indicate that OntoPlot significantly enhances browsing and understanding, offering a promising solution for managing large ontology sizes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ontoplot.

This study addresses semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (SE-ASR) within codebook-driven acoustic-model-based systems. In practical applications, speech data from different recording environments often exhibits distribution shifts, making it difficult to acquire training sets from every possible recording condition. CycleGAN is frequently employed to mitigate this issue; however, we demonstrate that it can inadvertently degrade SE-ASR performance by generating speech with artifacts. To resolve this, we introduce an SE-ASR-enhancing Inter-domain penalty. When applied, this penalty lowers the cycleGAN loss, thereby improving the cycleGAN training objective and boosting SE-ASR performance. Experimental results on real-world speech datasets confirm that the Inter-domain penalty outperforms no penalty and the FID penalty, achieving speech-to-text word error rate (WER) improvements of 1.5 and 2.0 percentage points, respectively. Additionally, we show that the Inter-domain penalty is effective across various SE-ASR systems, codebook types, and speech environments. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/kenjiyoshida/SE-ASR-Inter-domain-penalty}. Furthermore, we provide a repository containing source code and datasets for reproducing our experiments, available at \url{https://github.com/kenjiyoshida/SE-ASR-Inter-domain-penalty/tree/master/reproduction}. Finally, we have published a paper detailing the Inter-domain penalty's impact on SE-ASR performance in non-realistic scenarios, which can be found at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07000}. Given these outcomes, we believe this work holds significant potential for enhancing ASR systems in challenging practical settings. The Inter-domain penalty is a valuable tool for ASR practitioners, particularly in scenarios where data collection is unfeasible. We anticipate that this work will contribute to advancing ASR systems in such difficult recording conditions. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/kenjiyoshida/SE-ASR-Inter-domain-penalty}. We look forward to this work aiding ASR practitioners in addressing data scarcity and distribution shift issues in challenging recording environments. Active inference offers a unified computational framework for integrating perception, action, and decision-making. However, current implementations typically address only single-task problems, such as object localization or image classification. This study demonstrates how active inference can be adapted for multi-agent navigation by employing independent value functions. These functions represent distinct hypotheses regarding an agent's state within a shared environment, with their independence enforced through a sparsity-inducing prior. We evaluated this approach using both simulated and real-world robotic platforms. The results indicate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in navigating complex settings and facilitates easier training. Furthermore, the framework proves capable of solving challenging multi-agent navigation challenges. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/profound_nav. Given its robust perception and decision-making capabilities, independent value function active inference holds significant promise for diverse applications, including autonomous driving and exploration. Through a combination of numerical simulations and analytical modeling, we show that the internal freedom of movement (IFOM) of soft molecules significantly influences a molecule's tendency to migrate in concentration gradients, a phenomenon crucial to the Soret effect observed in polymer electrolyte membranes (PEMs). Specifically, our analysis reveals that the IFOM of side chains in these membranes plays a pivotal role in determining how molecules respond to thermal gradients. Additionally, we explore the broader implications of these findings for understanding thermal fractionation across diverse systems. Finally, by linking IFOM to the Soret effect, our research advances the fundamental understanding of how the internal dynamics of soft molecules influence their non-equilibrium behavior. This advancement holds significant potential for guiding the design of advanced materials, such as high-performance PEMs for fuel cells and efficient heat management solutions for microelectronic devices. Furthermore, our methodology offers a pathway to investigate the impact of internal degrees of freedom on other material properties, including permeability and sorption. Ultimately, this work underscores the critical importance of internal molecular dynamics in Soret phenomena and provides a robust framework for future investigations into complex molecular systems. By elucidating the intricate relationship between internal molecular motions and material responses to thermal gradients, our findings pave the way for a deeper comprehension of non-equilibrium phenomena in complex materials, thereby facilitating the development of innovative technologies for sustainable energy and advanced manufacturing. Automated Composition Evaluation (ACE) assesses how well students have mastered a new language. This study introduces CeBERT, a resource designed to facilitate the rapid development of high-quality ACE models. CeBERT comprises a dataset of over 100,000 graded essays from U.S. high school students, along with pre-trained BERT and RoBERTa models specifically fine-tuned for ACE using these essays. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by evaluating ACE models built upon it using various scoring methods, including holistic scoring, topic-based scores, and holistic scoring adjusted for topic. Our findings indicate that models utilizing CeBERT surpass existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, we observe that these models exhibit a correlation with human holistic scores that remains consistent across different topics. Finally, we provide evidence that CeBERT demonstrates the capacity to detect topic shifts within student essays. The entire resource is released under the MIT license and can be accessed at https://github.com/edgar12345/CeBERT. Our pre-trained models are available on the Hugging Face model repository at https://huggingface.co/edgar12345/CeBERT. The paper accompanying this resource is also available on the arXiv. Domain adaptation is essential for domain shift issues in security-critical tasks like pedestrian identification, yet it often generates a large number of false positives. To address this, we introduce Box Re-Ranking, an unsupervised method designed to mitigate false positives in a further adaptive domain. This approach re-ranks candidate boxes using an unsupervised domain adaptation technique called Adversarial Feature Alignment, which targets box centers as the key feature. By adapting the model to domain centers rather than boxes, the method reduces false positives while maintaining strong performance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets and two real-world scenarios demonstrate that our approach significantly and effectively reduces false positives compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we release a new real-world dataset, ShanghaiPedID, collected in Shanghai. The source dataset comprises 1.5 million images from 10 public sources, while the target dataset includes 2.2 million images from 25 public and private sources. We also incorporate 1.2 million images from 10 private sources in the Shanghai domain as a transfer test. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/robinzhang1993/BoxRe-Ranking. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03001. This work was presented at CVPR 2022. This study examines how mistakes in throwing arise from an insufficient grasp of release dynamics. We present FauxThrow, a modified version of the optimal control framework by Todorov and Jordan, which incorporates errors in release velocity and angle. Our findings indicate that this enhanced model generates movement trajectories that align more closely with experimental data than the original equations. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the model produces greater variability in signal-to-noise (s/n) ratios and peak acceleration when simulating individuals with lower throwing skill. These results suggest that the proposed model offers a more realistic simulation of both skilled and unskilled throwing. Ultimately, this research underscores the critical role of understanding release velocity and angle in preventing throwing errors. By integrating these factors, our work advances the modeling of throwing mechanics, with potential applications in sports science, physical therapy, and human-robot interaction. Furthermore, this framework may facilitate more accurate simulations of various motor skills, thereby deepening our comprehension of human movement. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) relies on beam decoding to enhance translation quality, yet this approach lacks a mechanism to incorporate grammatical knowledge, resulting in outputs that are occasionally incoherent. To address this, we propose a sentence-level syntactic link generation process that integrates syntactic data directly into the NMT model. This links the generated parse tree to the input sentence by predicting links between non-terminal nodes and their corresponding input words. By utilizing tree-structured decoding based on these linked nodes, the model can condition the decoding process on the overall sentence structure. We applied this method to the English-to-German translation task and achieved state-of-the-art translation performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model learns to predict the overall sentence structure, yielding improved sentence-level coherence. Additionally, we show that the model can perform joint parsing and tree-dependent machine translation. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/eyalfriman/SyntacticLinks}. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the model's behavior, including an examination of its ability to detect ambiguous translations. These findings indicate that our approach effectively leverages syntactic knowledge to improve the quality of NMT outputs. Experimental results are available at: \url{https://github.com/eyalfriman/SyntacticLinks}. The Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP) offers access to binding energy data for water, methane, and carbon monoxide on grain surfaces, calculated using high-level quantum chemical methods. BEAP is a web-based database that provides the binding energy distributions derived from these calculations. The platform is designed to support astrophysicists and astrochemists by enabling the selection of binding energies appropriate for their specific grain surface models. Access is free and unrestricted. The website is available at http://beap.chem.ox.ac.uk. Future updates will expand the database to include additional molecules and surface materials. This article outlines the platform's purpose and details the procedures for obtaining binding energy data. It also discusses the computational protocols employed to ensure the reliability of the results. The current database was constructed to address the need for robust, reliable binding energy values, which are essential for accurately modeling the chemical evolution of molecular clouds. The study analyzes a class of one-dimensional multiplicative stochastic processes constrained by a lower-bound limit that varies with the history of each trajectory. This model is particularly suited for describing the dynamics of a particle confined within a potential well, where the minimum energy is defined by the product of two stochastic processes. The authors derive the generalized Fokker-Planck equation for this system and develop an approximate time-dependent solution. They propose that this framework holds significant value for describing a specific type of matter found in various physical contexts, including the formation of matter in the early universe, the interiors of stars, and the behavior of particles in high-energy accelerators. Furthermore, the paper investigates the distribution of this specific matter type, the propagation of stochastic waves, and the dynamics of charged particles under electromagnetic fields. Finally, the authors suggest that this matter may constitute a component of dark matter. The appendix provides a derivation of the Fokker-Planck equation for cases involving both additive and multiplicative stochastic processes, alongside the appropriate boundary conditions. Keywords: Stochastic process, Fokker-Planck equation, Dark matter, Matter distribution, Electromagnetic wave. PACS: 05.40.-a, 95.30.Fv, 98.80.-k, 52.35.-g, 52.35.Sw.

We introduce a probabilistic quantum algorithm designed to efficiently assess expectations of many-body operators within thermal states. The method utilizes probabilistic circuits composed of low-depth random Clifford gates to prepare a state that matches the target thermal state up to third-order terms in $1/\text{poly}(N)$. The algorithm's efficiency relies on large sampling multiplicities, which can be achieved through parallel execution. Additionally, we examine how this approach extends to expectation values involving two distinct thermal states, a setup relevant to randomized benchmarking protocols. This work establishes a foundation for future state preparation techniques, such as those using purifying systems or purification exchange protocols. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method remains effective for purifying states of thermal states, which has applications in techniques like purification exchange. Finally, we show that the algorithm can be adapted to approximate ground states by substituting the thermal states with appropriate purifying states. This yields a novel, efficient probabilistic quantum algorithm for approximating ground states of many-body Hamiltonians, which may find applications in ground state preparation. Our findings indicate that these prepared states can serve as valuable initial states for ground state searches using quantum algorithms like the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. This finding contrasts with standard nonlinear Schrödinger equations, where the asymptotic behavior relies on the $L^2$-norm of the function itself. Consequently, our results apply to a broader class of functions. This discovery directly impacts the small data theory for DSII equations, particularly the recent work by Dodson and Lenzmann [DOL16], which currently relies on the integral of the L^\infty norm of the nonlinearity. We demonstrate that the same small data argument holds if the condition is based on the $L^2$-norm of the derivative of the nonlinearity, leveraging our derived insight regarding the reflection coefficient. This approach is especially relevant for DSII equations due to the distinct large $|k|$ asymptotics of the $y$-derivative of the nonlinearity compared to the original equation. Our primary application focuses on the DSII defocusing equation with radial symmetry. The success of text categorization models largely depends on the quality of their training data. However, in many scenarios, labeling errors exist within the training data, which can severely undermine model performance. To address this, we introduce Sibylvariant Modifications (SyM), a data augmentation technique designed to enhance dataset reliability. By applying plausible transformations to existing labeled texts, SyM increases the diversity of the training set. We evaluated the method's effectiveness using the AG News dataset, demonstrating that SyM can be applied to various levels of text granularity, from characters to sentences. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies to identify the specific contributions of individual transformations. Our findings indicate that the average F1-score improved by 0.015, and sentence-level accuracy rose by 0.012. The source code is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/Sibylvariant-Modifications. Additionally, we provide a Python package, Sibylvariant, for easy access to the implementation. Our results confirm that Sibylvariant is a promising approach for text categorization data augmentation. Project link: https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/Sibylvariant. Package: Sibylvariant.

Low-resource multilingual machine translation (LRMT) is crucial for facilitating communication in languages lacking sufficient data. However, building end-to-end models directly is often impractical due to limited resources, whereas pretraining via transfer learning is a more feasible approach. This method typically involves training a base encoder-decoder on a high-resource language and then adapting it to low-resource target languages. Recent studies indicate that utilizing smaller, pretrained transformer models can further enhance performance. Nevertheless, the high computational costs of large models and the time required for pretraining make this approach resource-intensive. To address these issues, this paper explores the potential of quantizing high-capacity models to create lightweight, efficient architectures. We evaluate the stability of these quantized models against extracted submodels across various target low-resource languages, demonstrating that lightweight models generally outperform extracted ones in both accuracy and inference speed. Finally, we offer recommendations for future research in low-resource multilingual machine translation. The code and data for this work are available at: https://github.com/DeepMind/lrmt-quantization.

We introduce a hypergraph model featuring an illogical Lagrangian density, where each hyperedge represents a hyperedge variable. The density functions nonlocally on the variational hyper-solitary graph, which is defined by a set of identical edges. This density generates a solitary hypergraph through the Euler-Lagrange equation. Consequently, the density drives the formation of the solitary hypergraph. We derive and analyze the profile function of this solitary hypergraph using the phase-plane method. The model demonstrates that the Lagrangian density functions nonlocally on the Fock space of the Fock-Soliton hypergraph, which is constructed from the sets of identical hypernodes. We also provide examples of many-membrane solitons, including a double-McKean-Vegas soliton, and examine a long-time asymptotic property of a soliton double peak. Furthermore, the density is interpreted as a hyper-force field that propagates without time and drives the formation of the solitary hypergraph. Finally, we show that a phase-plane method for analyzing a soliton double peak can be generalized to the Fock space of the Fock-Soliton hypergraph. This work extends the principle of the "force field that forms a force line" from classical mechanics to the force field of the hypergraph. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a theory of a solitary hypergraph. We introduce a method that segments pneumonia lesions within chest X-rays using minimal labeled data, a challenge often termed semi-supervised segmentation. Our approach combines data augmentation with a segmentation network, where the latter is trained via a new semi-supervised scheme. This training strategy alternates between teaching the network to predict masks for unenhanced images and predicting enhancements for unlabeled, unenhanced images, subsequently training the network to segment these enhanced versions. Our results demonstrate that this scheme outperforms both fully supervised models and baseline semi-supervised approaches when trained on the same limited set of labeled images. Furthermore, we show that these methods surpass the state-of-the-art semi-superseded technique, DataAugmentationNet, when evaluated against different benchmarks. Finally, we analyze the model's performance to gain deeper insights into its behavior. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/SeparationOfLungFieldsInXrayUsingImageEnhancements. Given the computational cost of training, we have also made a training-ready checkpoint available for direct evaluation. Our findings indicate that with this checkpoint, our method exceeds the current state-of-the-art in semi-supervised segmentation for pneumonia detection. The checkpoint URL is: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/SeparationOfLungFieldsInXrayUsingImageEnhancements/tree/master/Checkpoint. We anticipate these contributions will aid future researchers in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Additionally, we plan to release a dataset of enhanced chest X-rays for potential use by other researchers in related fields. This collection includes 1,000 enhanced images and 100 corresponding labeled paired images (enhanced and original), which can be accessed here: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/SeparationOfLungFieldsInXrayUsingImageEnhancements/tree/master/data. We hope this resource will benefit the broader research community. Our contributions are as follows: 1. Controlling the image description output of large-scale multilingual models (LSMs) remains an unresolved challenge. While existing research has focused on generating complete sentences, this work addresses the requirement for regulatable IDM—producing image descriptions of a specified length in both English and Spanish. To achieve this, we introduce Prompting Regulatable Image Description (PRID), a prompting-based framework that converts the generative task into a span classification problem. We evaluate our approach on existing IDM datasets and introduce a novel regulated regulation dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that PRID successfully generates descriptions matching the specified length. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the Regulatable Prompting Module and the Regulatable Span Classification Module are the primary drivers of our method's effectiveness. Finally, we show that PRID can induce variations in description content without altering the predicted length. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-Chen/PRID. Voice translation handles multilingual speech processing by directly converting spoken words from one language into another. While most existing systems rely on an intermediate text representation, such approaches often result in error accumulation and degraded performance. To address this, we introduce a direct zero-shot voice translation framework. Specifically, our model is trained within a single-source, many-target language environment using attentive alignment and latent monotonic sequence transduction. Furthermore, we demonstrate zero-shot inference to translate into languages that the model has never encountered during training. Experiments on the Librispeech and Converseverse datasets indicate that our method significantly outperforms prior zero-shot voice translation solutions and achieves results comparable to those of source-target specific models. Additionally, we release an audio pre-trained TTS model alongside the code for both the model and inference process. Finally, we present an audio demo to highlight the effectiveness of our approach. Our code and models are publicly available on GitHub. Please refer to our project page for more details.

Accurate and timely probabilistic load forecasts are essential for managing low-voltage network loads. This study evaluates the impact of forecast horizons and forecast fusion on the performance of a probabilistic machine learning model designed for smart meter smart-grid load forecasting. Furthermore, high-load events are analyzed using both historical data and forecasted values derived from both short-term and long-term perspectives. The analysis reveals that forecasted values are more effective than historical values for predicting low-load events, while load prediction accuracy improves through the fusion of multiple forecast sources. Additionally, an analysis of high-load events is conducted using forecasted values to identify recurring daily high-load patterns. The paper also examines the characteristics of these recurrent high loads, the influence of uncertainty on their prediction, and the potential for improving accuracy through the integration of historical and forecasted data. Ultimately, the proposed methodology facilitates smarter planning for grid reinforcement and the deployment of demand response strategies. A Python-based open-source implementation is made available to support research and development in smart-grid management. The study's findings are expected to be replicated in future research. Although significant strides have been made in developing AI-based medical image analysis tools for COVID-19, current systems often exhibit biases stemming from skewed data distributions regarding disease severity. This bias can result in unfair performance when these models are applied to out-of-distribution cases, such as mild instances. To address this, we introduce a weakly guided learning approach for lesion localization and segmentation that steers models away from data distribution biases. Our methodology involves two key components: first, an anchor-guided data augmentation technique that expands training data by using well-defined anchors to expand class boundaries; second, a weak guidance loss function designed to prevent the model from learning biased representations. We evaluated the proposed framework using the provided LaSID dataset, comparing it against several state-of-the-art methods. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance in both lesion localization and segmentation. The code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/WGLab.

Accurate localization and recognition of vertebrae in CT images are fundamental prerequisites for automated spine assessment. This study introduces a novel framework that integrates a cost function with vertebra-specific and vertebra-to-vertebra constraints. The method comprises three primary components: (1) a fast spine localization strategy utilizing a spine rectification network; (2) a vertebra recognition approach grounded in anatomical knowledge; and (3) a vertebra recognition optimization algorithm designed to resolve the optimization problem. The proposed framework was evaluated on 1,000 anonymized CT scans, comparing results against a conventional deep learning-based recognition method. The findings demonstrate that the proposed framework surpasses the baseline in both recognition accuracy and robustness, achieving an average recognition accuracy of 94.1%. Furthermore, the framework's performance and efficiency are robustly validated through ablation studies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYan1992/VertebraRecognition.

This study examines resonant electron scattering and polarization dynamics when a single-mode light field couples strongly with a two-level atom outside any dressed-state or dynamical-cavity-regime context. The atom is positioned at a standing-wave node within a cavity, where the light-field amplitude approaches its maximum possible value. We demonstrate that the scattering resonance exhibits distinct features in both the differential cross section and the atom's time-dependent polarization. Notably, the atom absorbs a significant portion of the incident electron wave function even at a resonant energy offset, a phenomenon we attribute to vacuum oscillations between the atom and the electron wave function. This resonant scattering event is followed by a rapid decay of the atom's polarization over a timescale comparable to the inverse of the light-field Rabi frequency. This behavior is explained by vacuum oscillations between the atom and the cavity light field, which induce a resonant emission of a photon into the mode upon electron departure. This process is characterized by a large effective light-field Rabi frequency, resulting from the specific combination of the light-field amplitude and electron velocity. We provide numerical results for the differential scattering cross section, recovery time of the atomic polarization, and its decay time. Furthermore, we establish that this resonant light emission is not merely a perturbation effect but is instead driven by vacuum oscillations between the atom, electron, and cavity light field. Finally, we outline potential experimental realizations of this phenomenon. These effects are expected to be observable in systems where the coupling strength between a quantum emitter and a confined light field is comparable to, or exceeds, the emitter's transition frequency. This condition is crucial for achieving strong or ultrastrong coupling, which is currently being pursued in various experimental settings. We conclude that the effects described herein are likely to be observed in experiments involving the coupling of quantum emitters to microwave fields. This is because emitter-gamma-ray coupling is currently unfeasible, while optical coupling remains challenging due to the high energy required to drive the atom. In contrast, microwave coupling is feasible because the ultrastrong regime is more easily accessible at lower frequencies. To illustrate this, we present numerical results for a quantum emitter interacting with a microwave field in the ultrastrong coupling regime. These results show that the scattering cross section displays a pronounced peak at the resonant energy, and the atom's polarization undergoes ultrafast decay following the scattering event. Recent years have seen significant advancements in designing and controlling elastic actuators for legged robots, enhancing both their dynamic capabilities and energy efficiency. However, existing research predominantly addresses the control of constant-impedance actuators, where the relationship between applied torque and rotation is linear and governed by a fixed stiffness parameter. This study introduces a learning-based controller for robots equipped with elastic actuators, where the torque-angle relationship is non-linear. By employing model-free reinforcement learning, the robot can adapt to the complex, non-linear characteristics of these actuators. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through whole-body control simulations involving quadrupedal locomotion and manipulation tasks. The results demonstrate that the actuator-based reinforcement learning robot achieves superior locomotion and energy efficiency compared to a controller designed for constant-impedance actuators. Furthermore, the study confirms that model-free reinforcement learning facilitates the transfer of skills between robots with distinct elastic actuator designs. These findings suggest that model-free reinforcement learning serves as a robust framework for the design and control of legged robots utilizing elastic actuators. This study examines the dynamics of the tearing instability, which typically begins with a "small-scale" component before evolving into a "large-scale" one. This process is critical for understanding the nonmonotonic, oscillatory behavior of magnetic field energy density distribution functions observed in both laboratory and space environments. By combining analytical and numerical methods, we investigate the initial growth of the small-scale part. Our analytical approach extends the reduced Harris current slab model to encompass the full range of $k\delta$, covering both small and large scale lengths. The initial growth phase is governed by the local magnetic shear, which can be either positive or negative. Our results indicate that the small-scale mode is unstable if the local magnetic shear is positive, leading to a positive growth rate. Conversely, a negative local magnetic shear causes the magnetic field line to bend in the opposite direction, resulting in an unstable large-scale component with a positive growth rate. In contrast, small-scale tearing modes do not exist when the local magnetic shear is negative. These theoretical predictions are confirmed by two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that oscillations in magnetic field energy density distribution functions arise from the superposition of multiple unstable small-scale modes, each with distinct growth rates. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings. Specifically, small-scale tearing in the magnetosheath is primarily driven by the local magnetic shear, which is generally positive. Additionally, small-scale tearing may play a significant role in the formation of electron and ion tearing modes, as well as in the tearing instability associated with double layers. These insights are supported by numerical simulations and experimental data. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the initiation of small-scale tearing, with potential applications in various plasma environments. The study also highlights several unresolved issues and suggests directions for future research. Solving linear ill-posed problems in Banach spaces through dual gradient descent remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a dual gradient method that converges in the norm of the Banach space's dual, addressing the solution of linear ill-posed equations. For convex Banach spaces, the approach employs the Fenchel dual of the cost function combined with a dual averaging technique. Applying this to Hilbert spaces yields a method equivalent to Kaczmarz-type algorithms, which are recognized for resolving linear ill-posed problems in $\ell_1$. Furthermore, the dual method is demonstrated to be dual-equivalent to a Newton method utilizing the Bregman distance derived from the cost function. In scenarios where the cost function exhibits strict convexity, the dual gradient approach achieves local convergence to the unique solution. When applied to sparse recovery in $\ell_p$ spaces for $p \in (0,2)$, the method converges at a rate of $O(1/k)$, where $k$ represents the iteration count. Additionally, numerical experiments on compressed sensing tasks confirm the algorithm's efficiency. The study also explores connections to dual methods within variational inequalities and differential inclusions. Finally, an extension of the dual gradient technique is presented for solving a specific class of non-linear ill-posed problems. The proposed approach is shown to be equivalent to the proximal point method, a renowned iterative scheme for handling monotone operators. Numerical tests on sparse recovery problems with non-convex regularization confirm the method's dual-equivalence and efficacy. The paper concludes with a discussion on extending the approach to handle non-linear ill-posed problems in Banach spaces. Expense creators are frequently employed in light field processing to derive corresponding variables, such as depth, from multiple views. However, these methods often fail to account for occlusion, which degrades the quality of the resulting depth maps. To address this, we introduce a novel occlusion-aware expense creator designed for depth estimation. This framework utilizes a patch-based approach to generate reliable depth values for each view by analyzing local features. We further introduce a new loss function that enhances the network's sensitivity to occlusion, thereby improving the accuracy of depth estimation for occluded regions. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we have developed a new dataset, the Occlusion-aware Depth Creator Creator (ODCC), to facilitate research in this area. Non-Riemannian gravitational theories offer valuable frameworks for investigating phase transitions away from standard Riemannian geometry, particularly in contexts involving a non-vanishing string metric dilaton and/or a generalized metric. This study examines a class of non-Riemannian theories derived from components of the generalized dilaton sector within generalized Dirac brackets. By utilizing a modified generalized dilaton that incorporates corrections dependent on both the generalized dilaton and the generalized metric, we demonstrate that the resulting theories align with specific non-Riemannian theories found in the literature. Furthermore, by substituting the modified dilaton with a dilonector, we derive a non-vacuum theory featuring both torsion and double field theoretical double Wick-rotation. Finally, we analyze the equations of motion for these theories, noting that the equations for non-Riemannian models are significantly more complex than those in standard Riemannian contexts. These findings suggest that solving such equations may necessitate novel mathematical techniques, such as non-Riemannian extensions of the Lichnerowicz-Bochner formula. Ultimately, these results could aid in constructing non-perturbative solutions for various non-Riemannian gravitational theories. In Home WiFi environments, devices (Extends) from the same vendor are frequently deployed to broaden network coverage. However, when an Access Point (AP) malfunctions, Extends may fail to retrieve critical information from it, leading to suboptimal network decisions. To address this, we introduce a novel, lightweight, and vendor-agnostic protocol extension for IEEE 802.11 that enables Extends to actively assess the load on nearby APs. This approach allows the network to dynamically select the most suitable AP for each Extend based on real-time load conditions. We successfully implemented this solution in a real-world scenario and tested it across various vendor-specific WiFi networks. The results demonstrate that, in most cases, comparing signal strength with AP load significantly enhances Extend association, thereby improving overall network performance. Furthermore, this mechanism is compatible with IEEE 802.11k, facilitating the rapid development of additional 802.11k applications. Our findings indicate that Extends can achieve up to a 100% increase in throughput by actively monitoring AP load. Additionally, Extends can dynamically adjust their transmission power to match local conditions, thereby reducing interference with nearby APs. We have also provided a detailed analysis of the impact of IEEE 802.11v on network performance. Overall, the proposed mechanism is vendor-agnostic and vendor-independent, making it applicable to any IEEE 802.11 network. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/802.11k.
